rankedInterventions.intervention: A written, rehearsed in-race fuelling plan: ~75 g carbohydrate/hour from glucose+fructose products, a gel every 20-25 min starting at 40 min, water to thirst. Gut training (daily carb-during-run exposure) must start in week 1 — the adaptation takes two weeks.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 5-9 min, best guess 6 (full range 0-11). The 0 end applies if he already takes 5-6 gels; the 9-11 end if he currently races on the recreational norm of ~35 g/h (measured in real marathons, Pfeiffer 2012).
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: A-. Hansen 2014 is a controlled trial in almost exactly his population (28 non-elite male marathoners, 3:38-3:49): a prescribed protocol beat freely-chosen eating by 10:55, or 4.7% (p=.010). It has never been replicated in twelve years, was matched-pairs rather than randomised, and n=28. Backed by the only verbatim official prescription in this whole exercise — World Athletics' distance-running consensus says '75-90 g/hr in the longest races' — and by the one marathon-distance running trial with a finish-time outcome (Tsintzas 1995: 2.0% faster on just 19 g/h, n=7).
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Gut distress if he jumps to 75 g/h untrained. Four long runs of rehearsal removes almost all of that. Cost is about £40 of gels.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Pace the first half at what the 12 September half actually justifies — not at goal-time arithmetic. For a 1:46-1:48 half, that is roughly 5:25-5:35/km, and it means being passed for 25 km.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 3-9 min in expected-value terms. Working: 28% of male recreational marathoners hit the wall, and when they do it costs 31.5 min (measured, 717,940 runners). Risk peaks at 40% for men in the three years before a personal best — his exact situation. 0.28 x 31.5 = 8.8 min of expected loss available to remove, but it shares its mechanism with #1, so do not add the two at full value.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B. Enormous observational dataset in exactly his population, zero trials. Pacing has never been randomised.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: None except discipline. The failure mode is emotional, not physiological.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Cap the peak week at 65-70 km, not 100. Ramp roughly 38 / 50 / 62 / 68, then taper. His lifetime-best week is 57.1 km and his last four weeks were 27/35/0/15.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: +3 to +5 min relative to running the ratified plan, and it protects everything else on this list. Working: a single 7-13 day training gap in the final 3-7 weeks costs 4.25-5.4% of finish time (10-13 min) in a within-runner paired analysis of 292,323 runners — each runner serving as his own control, the best-designed number in the entire record. If the 100 km ramp raises the probability of such a gap by even 30 percentage points, that is ~3.5 min of expected loss, against a volume benefit that no six-week trial has ever demonstrated.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B. Feely 2023 is strong. The injury-progression evidence is weaker than usually claimed (Nielsen's >30% threshold gave HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, p=0.07 — not significant) but a directly relevant trial that neither research pass found (Damsted 2019, 261 half-marathon-preparing runners) found a 22.6% risk difference (p=.041) for a 20-60% weekly increase. His first week as ratified is a ~300% increase.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Forgoes whatever six weeks of extra volume would have bought — which every randomised and quasi-randomised test says is close to nothing on this timescale, though that evidence is itself weaker than it was presented as being.

rankedInterventions.intervention: A disciplined taper: three consecutive down weeks, final fortnight averaging 41-60% below peak, intensity and running frequency held. One hard session every taper week, at or faster than race pace. Nothing longer than ~13 km inside the last 14 days.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 2-6 min. Working: 2.38% for a male strict 3-week taper in 158,117 recreational marathoners = 5.6 min against a minimal taper; but against a merely sloppy 2-week taper the differential is 1.09% = 2.6 min. Which number applies depends on what he would otherwise have done.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: A-. Two independent designs converge: 27 controlled studies (Bosquet 2007, optimum = 2 weeks, 41-60% volume cut, intensity and frequency unchanged) and 158,117 recreational marathoners (Smyth & Lawlor 2021). Elite British marathoners independently do the same thing — 14 days, volume to 53% of normal, intervals at 114% of race pace. Caveat found on audit: the dose-response bands are less certain than presented — the between-band tests in the 2023 replication are non-significant (volume p=0.32), and a distance-running trial found an 85% cut improved 5 km by 3% (p<0.005), contradicting the 'never cut more than 60%' rule.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Taper madness. The direct evidence against it: runners habituated to 81 km/wk cut to 24 km/wk for three weeks with no loss of 5 km time, VO2max, power or citrate synthase.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Carbohydrate loading, 36-48 hours out: ~8 g/kg/day (about 680 g for him), displacing fat and fibre. No depletion run.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 2-5 min, expressed mostly as reduced pace decay after 30 km rather than a faster first half.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B. Williams 1992 found -2.7% over 30 km, but that rests on a 6-man subgroup with no significant between-group effect. Bussau 2002 established that maximal glycogen is reached in 24 h at 10 g/kg with no depletion phase. Important correction: a 30-study meta-analysis found running achieves only ~58% of the cycling supercompensation response (156.5 vs 269.7 mmol/kg dw), and the running estimate's 95% CI spans 61 to 252 — a four-fold range.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Feeling heavy and bloated. Rehearse it once before a long run. Shares currency with #1 — both defend the same glycogen, so do not add them at full value.

rankedInterventions.intervention: More running volume than his last six months, ramped survivably — roughly a doubling of his six-month average rather than a quadrupling.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-5 min inside six weeks, and honestly unquantified. The cross-sectional numbers are large (Fokkema: 20.4 min between the <40 and >65 km/wk categories; and a published dose-response equation fitted to 126 recreational male marathoners, which neither research pass found, gives 20.7 min for 24.4 to 76 km/wk) — but every one of those prices HABITUAL volume built over months, not six weeks of it. Two of his six weeks are taper, so it is really four loading weeks.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C for the six-week question. No randomised trial has ever assigned recreational marathoners to different weekly volumes with marathon finish time as the outcome. Not one. The nearest randomised evidence was presented as showing volume buys nothing, but the audit found it is actually a high- versus low-intensity trial with volume yoked to intensity — so it cannot isolate a volume effect either way. The honest position is that nobody knows.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: This is where the injury risk lives. It is the intervention most likely to end the block.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Two quality sessions a week — one threshold (5 x 1000 m at half-marathon pace, or 4 x 8 min), one longer-interval. Never more than 5-6 repetitions. Never a third hard session.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 1-3 min. Working: the trained-athlete category effect is ~2% (4.7 min on his time), halved because the longest outcome anywhere in that literature is a 40 km cycling time trial of about an hour, and his race is four times longer. Discount again: the trained subgroup showed significant small-study bias (Egger p=0.002) and heterogeneity of I-squared 89.8%.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B+. Rosenblat 2021 is the single best-fitting study in the record — 29 studies, 491 participants, mean VO2peak 52.0 against his 53.0, intervention window 2-10 weeks. Its structural findings are firm: longer work bouts beat short ones in trained athletes (+0.37%/extra minute), every rep beyond the fifth costs 0.2%, and a third weekly session is not distinguishable from nothing (1.0%, 95% CI -0.2 to +2.2, p=0.115). Its magnitude for a marathon is not firm.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Every hard session competes with the volume ramp for the same recovery. Two is the ceiling here, not the floor.

rankedInterventions.intervention: A proper pre-race breakfast: ~170 g carbohydrate (2 g/kg) about three hours before the start. Rehearse it twice.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-4 min. Zero if he already eats a real breakfast; 2-4 if he currently races on a banana and coffee.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C+. The trial behind it is cycling, small, and used a fasted comparator (312 g gave 15% over nothing; 45 g and 156 g gave nothing over placebo). The dose recommendation comes from the ACSM/Dietitians position stand (1-4 g/kg, 1-4 h prior), which is a real official document.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Nausea if untested. Two rehearsals fixes it.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Three or four long runs of 26-32 km, the last one thirteen days out, one of them finishing with 8-10 km at goal marathon pace.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-4 min. The relevant comparison in the only dataset that has ever binned long-run distance finely: a 25-30 km longest run versus 30-35 km cost +6.40 min adjusted — with a 95% CI of -0.04 to +12.82, which touches zero. Going beyond 35 km bought nothing (-4.86 min, CI -13.5 to +3.8).
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C+ for the distance, D for the composition. No randomised trial has ever manipulated long-run distance. The marathon-pace-finish idea has literally zero trials — a full-index search returned no records. Two independent older datasets found that once weekly volume and training pace are held constant, doing that volume in fewer, longer runs predicted SLOWER marathons, and a widely-used prediction equation fitted to recreational marathoners contains no long-run term at all.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Each one costs 3-5 days of quality. The 20-mile-run orthodoxy is coaching practice, not evidence.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Wear the watch overnight for five consecutive nights, then extend sleep toward 8 h if there is a deficit. Bank three good nights before the race rather than relying on the night before.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-4 min, and which end applies is currently unknown to everyone including him. Five nights of measurement gives a good estimate of habitual sleep and costs nothing.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C. The only endurance sleep-extension study is 9 cyclists doing a ~58-minute time trial. The chronic-extension evidence is uncontrolled pre-post studies in 19-year-old basketball players at 10 hours in bed nightly. The sleep-deprivation meta-analysis is solid (SMD -0.52, and longer efforts are hit harder) but converting a standardised effect to minutes requires an assumption that could be wrong by a multiple. One genuinely on-population finding: 1,041 working adults aged 21-40 established that 5 nights gives a very good estimate of weekly sleep.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: None. Do not become preoccupied with the sleep score — the official consensus explicitly warns that monitoring anxiety worsens sleep, and consumer trackers overestimate duration against polysomnography.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Caffeine, about 250 mg in capsule or tablet form, an hour before the start. Do not withdraw beforehand.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-1.5 min. The commonly quoted 2-3% is cycling-dominated. The running-specific pooled estimate is -0.71%, and the audit found that inside that same paper the recreational-runner subgroup is null (g = -0.082, p = 0.141), with the authors stating caffeine was not ergogenic in long-distance time trials.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C for him specifically, despite the field's meta-analytic depth. The population that matches him is the subgroup where the effect disappears.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Near zero if he already drinks coffee. Withdrawal headaches in race week are a real cost, so do not cut caffeine to 'resensitise'.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Drink to thirst, roughly 400-600 ml/h in October conditions. Stop treating fluid as a performance lever.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: About 0 min of upside. This is here to avoid two failure modes: carrying an unneeded litre with its gut load, and over-drinking into hyponatraemia.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: A for the null. Ad libitum drinking at half the programmed rate, producing 2.1% body-mass loss, was 0.98% BETTER, not worse. Body-mass loss up to 4% did not impair self-paced performance. The 2015 international consensus names overconsumption of hypotonic fluid as the cause of exercise-associated hyponatraemia and says drinking to thirst prevents both problems.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: None.

rankedInterventions.intervention: A plyometric warm-up (a few sets of jumps and bounds) 15 minutes before the start.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0-1 min, genuinely unknown. The reported acute economy improvement of 4.4-9.1% comes from 12 university students with a VO2max of 38 doing short steady-state stages, and there is no evidence any warm-up-induced stiffness change survives four hours.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: D.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Zero, and it is testable at the 12 September half.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Daytime naps under 30 minutes during the highest-volume weeks.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min directly. Its entire value routes through hitting the sleep-duration target, so counting it separately double-counts #10.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: D for runners. The large pooled endurance effect comes from team ball-sport athletes doing intermittent tests lasting minutes, and a broader athlete review found napping results for physical performance genuinely mixed.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Sleep inertia if longer than 30 min; skip entirely if it hurts night sleep.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Starting heavy strength or plyometric training now.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min, and plausibly negative in this block.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B for the null at this duration. The head-to-head meta-analysis breaks the effect out by duration: at 6-8 weeks, heavy resistance gives g = -0.21 with a 95% CI of -0.56 to 0.15, crossing zero; plyometrics at 4-6 weeks give g = -0.06, nothing. The effect only becomes reliably non-zero at 10-14 weeks. Four separate trials in recreational runners at his VO2max, run for 8-11 weeks, all found no change in running economy despite 35-40% strength gains — including one conducted DURING a marathon build at his exact pace. The only study in the domain reporting an actual marathon finishing time (720 first-time NYC marathoners, 12 weeks) found the strength group 3 minutes slower, p=0.35, and no injury benefit. The one evidenced periodisation of this intervention is to STOP it four weeks out.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: A resistance session raises the oxygen cost of submaximal running for up to 48 hours, and it takes about three sessions before that fades — landing in weeks 1-2, the weeks he is ramping hardest. Note that the audit dropped one of the two meta-analyses this case rested on (wrong identifier) and found the fatigue-cost study was actually a heat-stress trial in heat-acclimatised men.

rankedInterventions.intervention: HRV-guided daily training prescription — using morning readiness to decide whether to do the hard session.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B for the null, in exactly the right population and timeframe. A six-week randomised trial in 28 recreational distance runners compared heart-rate, race-pace and HRV-based prescription: no interaction effects between groups. The race-pace group got the 7 km time-trial improvement and the LOWEST inter-individual response variation. The pooled meta-analysis that was the other pillar of this case was dropped on audit (incomplete author list).
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Its mechanism is removing hard sessions when readiness is low. Nobody has tested it on someone ramping volume, and its most likely behaviour here is to strip out the sessions the block depends on. Use it as a red flag if it stays suppressed for several days — not as a daily arbiter.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Compression socks, tights or sleeves.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min. This is the one place where the null is precise enough to bound: 51 studies, 899 runners, race-time SMD -0.07 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.09, p=0.40), which brackets any true effect at roughly -1.3 to +0.5 minutes. GRADE certainty low to very low. The only reliable finding is reduced soft-tissue vibration.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: A for the null, on the exact endpoint, in the exact population.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Money. Wear them if you like how they feel.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Massage, foam rolling, ice baths, static stretching, electrical stimulation.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min, all of them.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: A/B for the nulls on performance. The largest massage analysis (29 randomised studies, 1,012 participants) found no evidence of benefit to strength, jump, sprint, ENDURANCE or fatigue — only flexibility and soreness. Foam rolling's largest effect anywhere is a 6% change in how much a muscle hurts, and no endurance endpoint has ever been measured. Static stretching for soreness is SMD +0.15 (CI 0.00-0.29), non-significant and pointing the wrong way; electrostimulation -0.28 (CI -0.59 to 0.03), non-significant. The apparent conflict with the famous recovery meta-analysis resolves cleanly: that one measured how sore and tired people FELT; these measured what they could DO.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Time and money. Legitimate reasons to keep any of them: you enjoy it, it helps you sleep, it makes you more likely to run tomorrow. Not legitimate: minutes.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Salt tablets or sodium capsules beyond what is in the gels.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B. In a 161 km race at up to 39C, total sodium intake varied fifteen-fold (2,541 to 38,338 mg) and was unrelated to hyponatraemia, cramping or nausea. Serum electrolytes and hydration status do not differ between crampers and non-crampers. If sodium supplementation does nothing there, it does nothing in a cool four-hour London marathon.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: The most reliably wasted item in a recreational marathoner's kit.

rankedInterventions.intervention: A third hard session per week, or interval sessions of 10-16 repetitions.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: About 0, with a real fatigue cost. The third-session point estimate is 1.0% but the 95% CI runs from -0.2% (half a minute SLOWER) to +2.2%. The frequently quoted pooled figure favouring three sessions is acknowledged BY THE AUTHORS to be an artefact of study allocation. Separately, every repetition beyond the fifth cost 0.2% in trained athletes — so cutting a session from 12 reps to 6 recovers about 2 minutes.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B. Genuinely unresolved rather than resolved-in-favour-of-two — but 'unresolved' plus a large simultaneous volume increase argues for two.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: Injury and overreaching risk, in the weeks he can least afford either.

rankedInterventions.intervention: Pushing in-race carbohydrate toward 120 g/h because that is what the professionals reportedly do.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: 0 min at best. The trail-marathon randomised trial always cited for this found race times of 271.7 vs 284.1 vs 278.2 min across 120/90/60 g/h — p=0.063, no difference, and race time was a baseline equivalence row rather than a designed outcome. The 2025 elite-marathoner isotope study showed better oxidation and running economy at 120 g/h but explicitly measured no performance, and found nausea, stomach fullness and cramps WORST at that dose. The best-designed test of maximal fuelling in trained runners (two weeks of high-carb diet plus gut training plus loading plus 90 g/h) produced performance identical to the low end of guidelines, with more upper-GI symptoms.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: B for the null. Two 2026 reviews conclude the efficacy of 120-200 g/h is not substantiated.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: A GI failure at 30 km costs the race. Note also that the recovery data from the trail-marathon trial were reported in this record in an order that inverts the paper's actual finding — a good example of why the underlying paper matters more than the summary.

rankedInterventions.intervention: The ratified 60/80/100/80/60 km block — specifically the 100 km peak week, which is 75% above his lifetime-best week and about seven times his last complete week.
rankedInterventions.expectedMarathonMinutes: -3 to -6 min in expectation, plus a materially raised probability of no race at all. Three converging lines: half of a trained cohort became functionally overreached after three weeks of overload, and the overreached group's peak was 2.6% below the merely-fatigued group's with a 70% infection rate versus 20%; a single 7-13 day gap in this window costs 10-13 min; and no taper study has ever tapered an athlete off a load they had never previously absorbed, because the mechanism assumes there is adaptation to retain.
rankedInterventions.evidenceGrade: C. The overreaching penalty is weaker than it looks on audit — magnitude-based inference with no p-value, measuring cycling performance in triathletes. But the disruption cost is the best-designed number in the whole record, and the direction of all three lines agrees.
rankedInterventions.costOrRisk: This is the single largest negative number in the entire exercise, and it is larger than every positive training effect on this list combined.

ranking.theHonestTotal:
Realistic range for 2026-10-24: 3:44 to 3:58, centred on 3:50-3:53. Best plausible outcome if everything goes right AND his current race execution is genuinely poor: about 3:42. Probability of being slower than his May 3:55:54: roughly 25-30% on the plan as ratified, maybe 15% on a capped plan.

The reasoning. His May marathon was 3:55:54 (235.9 min), so 1% of finishing time is 2.36 minutes. Everything below converts through that.

Start with the honest baseline, because this is where most plans lie to people. Riegel extrapolation from his 1:46:35 half at the usual exponent gives 3:42, and from his 5 km equivalent gives 3:08. Both are wrong for him, and we can prove it with his own data: solving the Riegel exponent from his actual May marathon gives k = 1.146, which is exactly the value the literature recommends for low-mileage runners — and that same exponent puts a 1:46:35 half at 3:55:54. His personal half-to-marathon fade coefficient, measured once, says his current half fitness is worth exactly what he already ran. The 47-minute gap between his 5 km and his marathon is not a VO2max deficit; the largest published study of recreational runners found short-race extrapolation 'dramatically underestimates marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners'.

Worse, he is not at May fitness now. His 42-day training-load average has fallen 28% from its early-August peak, he took a zero week three weeks ago, and his last four complete weeks were 27/35/0/15 km against a six-month average of 24.4. Six weeks is not enough to rebuild chronic load AND express it. Two of the six are taper, leaving four loading weeks.

So the physiology available to move is small, and almost all the accessible minutes are execution rather than fitness. Adding the top five levers at honest values, with the overlaps netted out rather than summed: fuelling 5-9, pacing 3-9 (sharing mechanism with fuelling — together realistically 8-12, not 14-18), taper 2-6, carbohydrate loading 2-5 (sharing glycogen currency with fuelling — realistically 2-3 net), intervals 1-3, volume 0-5. Netted: roughly 6 minutes at the pessimistic end, 16 at the optimistic end. That is 3:40 to 3:50 on paper.

Then subtract what the paper version ignores. He has never held 60 km for a week, let alone 100. He will be running six evenings plus weekends on a body that has averaged 24 km. The probability that some week in the next six goes badly wrong — illness, a niggle, work, a genuinely dead pair of legs — is not small, and one lost week alone costs 10-13 minutes. That asymmetry is why the honest central estimate lands at 3:50-3:53 rather than at the arithmetic 3:44.

What would have to go right for 3:44 or better: he is currently underfuelling badly (taking two or three gels rather than eight or nine) and the fuelling change is therefore real rather than marginal; he went out too fast in May and paces this one honestly; he executes a disciplined taper instead of panic-running in week five; and he completes all six weeks without missing more than two or three consecutive days. Note that three of those four are execution, not training. The training in this block is close to a rounding error next to them.

What would make it slower than May: he runs the 100 km week and either breaks (a 7-13 day gap costs 10-13 min, more than the taper, the intervals and the long runs combined), gets ill (the overreached group in the relevant trial had a 70% infection rate against 10% in controls), or arrives at the start line carrying fatigue he has not dissipated. Or he does everything right in training and then hits the wall — a 28-40% base rate for a man in the years before a personal best, costing 31.5 minutes when it happens.

One thing that should genuinely update this: the 12 September half. It is three days away and it is the only new information anyone will get. Run it with the exact fuelling, shoes and breakfast he intends to use in October. Its finish time re-anchors everything above; his gut tolerance at 75 g/h tells him whether the top-ranked lever is executable; and his pace over the last 5 km tells him whether his limiter is fuel or fitness. If he runs 1:44 or faster, shift the whole range down 3-4 minutes. If he runs 1:50 off a disrupted August, shift it up.
ranking.biggestLevers:
1. Eat, to a written plan, more than you think. Roughly a gel every 20-25 minutes from 40 minutes in — about eight or nine gels, 75 g of carbohydrate an hour, with water to thirst. The average recreational marathoner takes 35 g an hour, half the low end of what World Athletics recommends, and the one controlled trial in runners like him found that switching from freely-chosen eating to a prescribed practised protocol was worth nearly eleven minutes. Start practising it on every long run from this week, because the gut takes two weeks to adapt and it is the only lever here with a hard lead time.

2. Do not run the 100 km week. Peak around 65-70 instead. His biggest week ever is 57 and his last complete week was 15. A single week lost to injury or illness in the next six costs about twelve minutes — more than the taper, the intervals and the long runs are worth put together — and there is no randomised evidence that any amount of extra volume in six weeks buys anything at all. The whole block is only worth running if he gets to the start line healthy, and the peak week is the thing most likely to stop that.

3. Go out slower than feels right, and taper properly. About one man in three at his level hits the wall, and it costs half an hour when it happens; the risk peaks in exactly his situation — chasing a personal best. Pace the first half at what the 12 September half justifies, not at what the goal time demands. Then for the last two weeks cut the mileage roughly in half while keeping one hard session a week and still running most days: cut the volume, never the pace, and never the number of runs.
ranking.thingsToSkip:
Start strength or plyometric training. It works, but not on this timescale: the head-to-head evidence broken out by duration shows the effect only becomes reliably non-zero at 10-14 weeks — at 6-8 weeks the confidence interval crosses zero and at 4-6 weeks for plyometrics it is nothing at all. Four separate trials in recreational runners at his exact VO2max, run for eight to eleven weeks, all found no economy change despite 35-40% strength gains, including one done DURING a marathon build. The only study anywhere in that literature that reported an actual marathon finishing time (720 first-time NYC marathoners) found the strength group three minutes slower. Meanwhile a resistance session raises the oxygen cost of easy running for up to 48 hours until about the third session — landing precisely in the weeks he is ramping. Do it in the next block, starting in January.

A third hard session per week. The trained-athlete difference is 1.0% with a confidence interval running from half a minute slower to five minutes faster; the pooled figure usually cited in its favour is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be a statistical artefact. Two quality sessions is the ceiling in a block that is also adding volume.

Long interval sessions with lots of repetitions. Every repetition beyond the fifth cost 0.2% in trained athletes. Five by 1000 m beats twelve by 400 m, and the difference is worth about two minutes.

HRV-guided daily decisions. A six-week randomised trial in 28 recreational distance runners — the exact population, the exact timeframe — found no difference between HRV-guided, heart-rate-based and race-pace prescription, and the race-pace group got both the time-trial improvement and the most consistent response. Its mechanism is removing hard sessions, which is the last thing this block needs.

Compression garments. 51 studies, 899 runners, on race time: SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.22 to 0.09. That brackets any real effect at roughly minus one to plus half a minute.

Massage, foam rolling, ice baths, static stretching, electrical stimulation. None of them has ever been shown to improve an endurance performance outcome. Massage's largest analysis (29 randomised studies, 1,012 participants) found no benefit to endurance, strength, sprint or fatigue. The reason these feel effective is that they genuinely change how sore and tired you feel, which is a different measurement from what you can do. Keep any of them if you enjoy them; do not budget minutes for them.

Salt tablets. Sodium intake varied fifteen-fold across finishers of a 161 km race in 39C heat and was unrelated to cramping, nausea or hyponatraemia. The 2015 international consensus names over-drinking, not sodium loss, as the cause of race-day hyponatraemia.

Chasing 120 g/h of carbohydrate. No running trial has ever shown a faster race at 120 than at 60-90. The trail-marathon trial everyone cites found p=0.063 — no difference. The elite-marathoner study showing better oxidation at 120 measured no performance at all and found GI symptoms worst at that dose.

A depletion run in race week. Maximal glycogen is reached in 24 hours on a high-carbohydrate diet with rest; the depletion phase costs freshness and buys nothing.

Any run longer than about 32 km, and any long run at all inside the final 14 days. Beyond 30-35 km the measured return disappears entirely (-4.86 min adjusted, CI -13.5 to +3.8), and a long run in the last fortnight makes the evidenced taper volume arithmetically impossible.

Cutting caffeine for a week beforehand to 'resensitise'. The evidence is equivocal and the withdrawal headache in race week is certain.
citationsRejected: DROPPED (misattributed identifier) — Bacon, Carter, Ogle & Joyner 2013, 'VO2max Trainability and High Intensity Interval Training in Humans', cited with PMID 24023823. That identifier resolves to a paper about visual stimuli in human auditory cortex. It was carrying the ceiling on how much VO2max is trainable (+0.51 L/min, 0.86 SD). The real paper exists (PMID 24066036) and the numbers quoted from it were accurate — but the audit also found the researcher omitted the paper's own publication-bias correction, which cuts the estimate 27% lower to 0.37 L/min. Claim dropped; the conclusion it supported (that his VO2max headroom is modest) survives on the HERITAGE family study, which verified clean.

DROPPED (misattributed identifier) — Llanos-Lagos et al. 2024, 'The Effect of Strength Training Methods on Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Athletic Performance', cited with PMID 39023740. That identifier resolves to an oncology podcast paper about advanced urothelial cancer. It was carrying the entire positive case for strength training improving running PERFORMANCE (ES -0.469 for high-load, -1.035 for combined methods) and the null on VO2max. The companion paper by the same authors on running ECONOMY verified clean and survives. Losing the performance meta-analysis materially weakens the case for lifting, which was already ranked skip-this-block on duration grounds.

DROPPED (incomplete author list — will not verify as written) — Düking et al. 2021, HRV-guided endurance training meta-analysis in J Sci Med Sport. Two authors (Trabelsi K and Kunz P) were omitted from the byline. It was carrying the pooled finding that HRV-guided training has no significant performance benefit. The verdict survives independently on Ranieri 2025 — a six-week randomised trial in 28 recreational distance runners, which is a better-matched piece of evidence anyway. Also worth knowing: the audit found the researcher omitted the one pro-HRV finding in that same abstract (fewer non-responders on performance).

DROPPED (findings attributed to the wrong paper) — Piñero et al. 2024 cold-water-immersion meta-analysis. The paper is real but measures muscle hypertrophy only. The findings attributed to it — negative effects on 1RM, isometric strength, strength endurance and ballistic power, plus no effect on endurance adaptations — belong to Malta et al. 2021, which appeared in the researcher's own search log and was then dropped from the citation. Claim dropped as sourced. The practical conclusion (ice baths do not harm endurance adaptation, they just do not help) is actually better supported than was claimed, but not by the paper cited.

DROPPED (not found) — 'NCAA Interassociation Task Force, Interassociation recommendations on sleep.' The URL supplied points to an unrelated NCAA mental-health page. The likely real document is a 2019 BJSM paper by Kroshus et al., which is a different title in a different venue. Nothing rested on it; it was listed as an official source and the researcher had already flagged it as unretrieved.

REJECTED AS STATED (paper real, number wrong) — the claim that sleeping under 6 hours makes you 4.2 times more likely to catch a cold. The paper reports bands of under 5 hours (OR 4.50, 95% CI 1.08-18.69) and 5-6 hours (OR 4.24, CI 1.08-16.71) against a MORE-than-7-hour reference — and critically, 6.01-7 hours is NOT significant (OR 1.66, CI 0.40-6.95). There is no under-6-hour band and no 4.2. So a man sleeping 6.5 hours sits in the band the study found no elevated risk for, and the confidence intervals reach past 18 with lower bounds of 1.08 — barely clearing no-effect. The seven-hour threshold does have a source (Cohen 2009, 2.94x, tighter interval), which neither research pass found.

REJECTED AS STATED (arithmetic error, 40% understatement) — the derivation that his glycogen runs out at about 31 km, 'exactly where folklore puts it'. The calculation used a leg-muscle glycogen figure 39% smaller than the source paper's own, implying leg muscle is 11% of body mass when the paper states 21.4%. Corrected, the range is 36-66 km, midpoint ~51 km. The tidy coincidence with folklore was an artefact of the error. The corrected number actually strengthens the conclusion — glycogen is even less likely to be his binding constraint than claimed — but the specific figure was wrong. Separately, the claim that 'the paper reports no evidence that training changes glycogen storage capacity' is not in that paper; it is silent on the question.

REJECTED AS STATED (wrong estimate chosen from the right paper) — the running-economy-to-race-time transfer coefficient of 0.59. That was derived from a single data point whose standard deviation (1.36%) exceeds its mean (0.65%). The paper's own headline linear fit across all data gives 0.78% time per 1.11% metabolic cost = 0.70, and an independent point in the same paper gives 0.71. Every economy-to-minutes conversion built on 0.59 is about 19% too small. Corrected rule of thumb: 1% better running economy is worth about 0.7% of race time, or 1.7 minutes for him, not 1.4.

REJECTED AS STATED (confidence interval transcribed wrongly) — 'no difference between long intervals and sprint intervals (0.9%; 90% CI -0.1% to 1.9%)'. The published interval is -1.2% to 1.9%. The real data are compatible with sprint intervals being 1.2% BETTER, which the narrowed version conceals. The practical recommendation (long reps for a marathoner) survives on a separate and stronger finding, but the null was made to look one-sided.

REJECTED AS PRESENTED (result ordering inverted) — the 24-hour recovery figures from the 120 vs 90 vs 60 g/h trail-marathon trial. The numbers were transcribed correctly but sequenced 60/90/120 immediately after a sentence sequenced 120/90/60. Read in the stated order, 120 g/h appears to have wrecked recovery on every measure; the paper found the exact opposite. This changes no recommendation here (the race-time result was null either way) but it is the clearest example in the whole record of how a summary can invert a source without misquoting a single digit.

REJECTED AS APPLIED (right paper, wrong subgroup) — the reassurance that his 10-day August training gap cost little because 'athletes with higher trained-state VO2max lose significantly more, and at 53 he is at the shallow end'. That modifier (Q=4.24, p=0.03) was established for LONG-term detraining only; the paper explicitly states training status did not modify the short-term effect. His gap was short-term. The reassurance may still be right — the dominant short-term mechanism is plasma volume, restored within days of resuming — but not for the reason given. And a large within-runner analysis found a 7-day-plus gap costs 4.25-5.4% of marathon time, which cuts hard the other way.

REJECTED AS A COMPARISON (between-group tests omitted) — the taper dose-response claim that a 41-60% volume cut beats a 21-40% cut and that holding intensity beats dropping it. The source paper's own between-subgroup tests are non-significant: volume p=0.32, intensity p=0.10, frequency p=0.42. Only taper DURATION (p=0.02) shows a genuine between-band difference. The within-band estimates were transcribed perfectly; the comparisons between them are not supported. Compounding this, a verified trial in distance runners found an 85% volume cut improved 5 km time by 3% (p<0.005), directly contradicting the 'never cut more than 60%' rule that two of the seven research passes assert.

REJECTED AS APPLIED (wrong subgroup) — caffeine worth 1-3 minutes to him. The pooled running time-trial estimate of -0.71% comes from a paper whose own recreational-runner subgroup is g = -0.082, p = 0.141, and which states caffeine was not ergogenic in long-distance time trials. The commonly quoted 2-3% figure is from a cycling-dominated pool. Honest expected value for a recreational runner over four hours is closer to zero than to two minutes.

REJECTED AS FRAMED (study design misdescribed) — 'the closest thing to a randomised experiment on training volume found nothing'. The trial in question is titled and designed as a high- versus low-INTENSITY comparison in which volume was yoked to intensity; volume and intensity are perfectly confounded, so it cannot isolate a volume effect in either direction. It was also middle-distance runners doing a middle-distance test, at two to three times his current weekly volume. The claim that randomised evidence says volume buys nothing does not survive. The honest position is that no randomised trial has ever assigned recreational marathoners to different weekly volumes with finish time as the outcome — the question is untested, not answered.

REJECTED AS A MINUTES FIGURE (kept as a direction) — the 2.6% penalty for arriving at the taper functionally overreached, converted to 'about 6 minutes lost'. The source states that figure came from magnitude-based inference with no p-value, and the outcome was cycling performance in trained triathletes over an 8-week laboratory protocol. Setting it head-to-head against a Strava-derived marathon finish-time percentage, as though the two were the same currency, is a rhetorical construction dressed as arithmetic. The direction is right and the recommendation (do not run the 100 km week) survives on the disruption-cost evidence, which is far better designed.

REJECTED AS GENERALISED — the entire cost-side case against adding strength training, resting on a study showing submaximal running economy degraded for 48 hours after a resistance session. The citation was given without its title; the actual title identifies it as a study of thermoregulatory measures in the HEAT in heat-acclimatised men. The 48-hour penalty may well generalise to temperate conditions, but it has not been shown to here.

REJECTED (internally broken coefficient, correctly refused by the researcher and repeated here as a warning) — the published finding that each extra 1 km/week in the final four months before Boston improves marathon time by about 13 minutes. The reported effect is beta -0.22 with a 95% CI of (-0.48, -0.34) that does not contain its own point estimate, and 13 minutes per km/week implies 130 minutes off a marathon for +10 km/week. This is in a peer-reviewed 2025 Sports Medicine paper and is now in circulation. It is the exact shape of number an AI plan-generator would swallow whole.

REJECTED AS APPLIED (adolescent data applied to an adult) — that sleeping under 7-8 hours multiplies an adult athlete's injury risk by 1.7. Both the 1.7x and the pooled 1.58 odds ratio come from athletes aged 12-18, whose sleep requirement is 8-10 hours and whose injury profile includes growth-plate pathology that does not exist at 27. The 1.7x confidence interval's lower bound is exactly 1.0. No adult replication of comparable quality exists, and almost nobody quoting this statistic says so.

REJECTED AS SOURCED (number survives, attribution does not) — 'the taper is worth 2-3%' attributed to the 2007 taper meta-analysis. That paper reports standardised effect sizes, not percentages. The 0.5-6% range centring on 3% comes from a different 2003 paper that was never cited. The 2-3% figure itself holds up because a completely independent study of 158,117 recreational marathoners found 2.6% — but on the athlete's specific question of provenance, the single best-supported number in the entire exercise was, as written, unsourced.

COULD NOT BE VERIFIED AT ALL (recorded as absence, not as fabrication) — no document from World Athletics, UK Athletics, England Athletics, USATF or ACSM was located prescribing marathon interval structure, long-run distance, weekly volume progression, or a taper protocol. Four separate research passes searched for these and none found one. UK Athletics conditioning material sits behind a coach login and could not be opened. The practical consequence: any coach, app or plan claiming to follow 'the official protocol' for any of those things is citing a document nobody in this exercise could find. The genuine official prescriptions that DID verify verbatim are narrow — World Athletics' distance-running consensus on carbohydrate ('75-90 g/hr in the longest races'), the ACSM/Dietitians position stand on carbohydrate loading and pre-event meals, the 2015 international consensus on drinking to thirst, and the IOC consensus naming rapid changes in training load as a modifiable injury risk factor.
ranking.evidenceQualityStatement:
He asked how we know this is any good rather than invented. Here is the answer, split by how much each part is actually worth.

WHAT RESTS ON META-ANALYTIC EVIDENCE. The taper (27 controlled studies pooled, replicated by a second meta-analysis of 14 studies and 174 athletes, and independently reproduced at 2.6% in 158,117 recreational marathoners — two designs that share no assumptions landing on the same number is the strongest signal in this whole exercise). Interval programming (29 studies, 491 participants, mean VO2peak 52.0 against his 53.0, intervention window 2-10 weeks — the single best population-and-timeframe fit anywhere in the record). Carbohydrate feeding during exercise (136 studies). Training-intensity distribution (a network meta-analysis of individual participant data, 13 studies, 348 athletes — the strongest design in that literature, and its answer is that polarised versus pyramidal makes no measurable difference). And, importantly, the nulls: compression garments (51 studies, 899 runners, measured on race time), massage (29 randomised studies, 1,012 participants, measured on endurance), foam rolling, stretching, electrostimulation. The nulls are often better evidenced than the positives.

WHAT RESTS ON SINGLE TRIALS. The biggest positive number in the entire report — the fuelling protocol — is one controlled trial of 28 runners, matched-pairs rather than randomised, unreplicated in twelve years. The only marathon-distance running trial with a finish-time outcome anywhere in these seven literature passes has n=7. The only endurance sleep-extension study is 9 cyclists doing a 58-minute time trial. The only test of a shorter versus longer long run is a single observational cohort of 441 runners whose relevant confidence interval touches zero. When someone tells you 'the science says' about the long run or about sleep for endurance, this is what is behind it.

WHAT RESTS ON EXPERT PRACTICE WITH NO TRIAL EVIDENCE AT ALL. No randomised trial has ever manipulated long-run distance. Zero trials exist on marathon-pace segments inside a long run — a full-index search of the biomedical literature returned no records. No trial on back-to-back medium-long runs. No trial on where to place the final long run. No trial on the Hansons-style long-run cap. And every 'peak week' number in every published plan: a content analysis of 92 commercial sub-elite marathon plans found the authors converge on a ~30 km long run regardless of surrounding volume, and its own authors state there is 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated'. That sentence describes essentially the entire consumer marathon-plan industry.

WHAT NOBODY KNOWS. Whether interval gains measured over 5-60 minute time trials transfer to a 235-minute race — the longest outcome in that entire literature is about a quarter of his race duration. Whether a six-week volume ramp does anything: no randomised trial has ever assigned recreational marathoners to different weekly volumes with marathon finish time as the outcome, not one. How running economy behaves at hour three. Whether he personally responds: the HERITAGE family study put 481 people through an identical 20-week programme and individual gains ran from essentially zero to over 1000 mL/min, 47% of it familial, with no pre-test predictor. Any plan promising him a specific outcome is promising something the literature cannot deliver.

THE POPULATION-VALIDITY PROBLEM, which is the part most advice hides. The interval evidence base is 34 cycling groups to 27 running groups. The 78 g/h carbohydrate optimum is a cycling time trial. The taper evidence is competitive athletes over events an order of magnitude shorter than a marathon. The strength-and-economy meta-analysis required VO2max above 60 as an inclusion criterion — he is 53, below the entry threshold of every study in it. The sleep-injury statistic everyone quotes is 12-18-year-olds. The block-periodisation result is trained cyclists, who cannot get a stress fracture. The durability trial is sedentary cyclists at half marathon intensity. And a detail nobody flagged in seven research passes: participant body mass across the recovery and plyometric trials runs 61-79 kg. He is 85.5 kg. Not one participant in any cited study approaches his mass, which matters specifically for jumping and impact loading. The one dataset that genuinely matches him on sex, ability and finish time is the Strava corpus (mean finish 3:50 against his 3:55) — and it is observational, so it can establish that faster runners train more but not that training more makes you faster.

WHAT THE AUDIT ITSELF TELLS HIM. Seven independent literature passes were checked citation by citation. Five citations failed outright — three with identifiers pointing at entirely unrelated papers (an auditory-cortex study, an oncology podcast), one with findings attributed to a paper that does not contain them, one that could not be found at all. Beyond those, roughly fifteen further claims had a real paper behind them but a number that was misread, misapplied to the wrong subgroup, derived from the noisiest data point, or in one case sequenced so that it inverted the source's finding. Every single correction ran in the same direction: towards smaller effects. That is not a reason to distrust the whole exercise — it is what checking looks like, and the underlying transcription accuracy was in fact high. But it is a reason to distrust any confident, unchecked summary of this literature, including one produced by an AI.

HOW HE VALIDATES IT ON HIMSELF, which is the only validation that matters. Two measurements cost nothing and resolve the two biggest unknowns in this report. First, the 12 September half: run it with the exact gels, shoes and breakfast he intends to use on 24 October. Its finish time re-anchors the entire marathon prediction with fresh data; whether he tolerates 75 g/h for 105 minutes tells him whether the top-ranked lever is executable; and his pace over the final 5 km tells him whether his limiter is fuel or fitness. Second, wear the watch overnight for five consecutive nights — five nights is the established minimum for a reliable estimate of habitual sleep in adults his age — which converts the sleep row from a 0-to-4-minute guess into a number. Beyond that, the honest test of this whole report is the race itself, and it is a sample of one.
