interventions.intervention: Interval training (HIIT) instead of continuous moderate training, head-to-head — the actual size of the 'HIIT is better' effect on VO2max
interventions.effect: HIT beat continuous endurance training by +1.2 mL/kg/min (95% confidence limits ±0.9), which the authors classify as a 'possibly SMALL' beneficial effect. Against no-exercise controls the two modalities were nearly equal: endurance training +4.9 mL/kg/min (±1.4), HIT +5.5 mL/kg/min (±1.2). Modifiers of the HIT-over-endurance advantage: longer HIT repetitions +2.2 (±2.1), older subjects +1.8 (±1.7), longer interventions +1.7 (±1.7), greater work:rest ratio +1.6 (±1.5), lower baseline fitness +0.8 (±1.3).
interventions.population: 28 controlled trials, 723 participants, healthy adults 18–45 y. Mean age 25.1 ± 5 y, mean BASELINE VO2max 40.8 ± 7.9 mL/kg/min — i.e. untrained-to-recreationally-active, roughly 12 mL/kg/min BELOW this athlete. Not runners specifically; mixed modalities.
interventions.citation: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M. Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials. Sports Medicine 2015;45(10):1469–81. PMID 26243014, DOI 10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0
interventions.duration: Included trials ≥2 weeks; 'longer duration' was a positive modifier for both modalities
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Partially. Six weeks is at the short end of the included range and the meta-analysis explicitly found LONGER interventions produced larger effects for both modalities (+2.2 mL/kg/min for endurance, +3.0 for HIT), so a 6-week block sits below the dose where the pooled effects were measured.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: +1.2 mL/kg/min on a VO2max of 53.0 = +2.26%. Under the Joyner (1991) model, if fractional utilisation and running economy are held constant, race pace scales with VO2max, so a 2.26% VO2max gain buys 2.26% off the time: 235.9 min × 0.0226 = 5.3 min. BUT this must be discounted hard, and I would put the honest figure at UNDER 2 minutes: (a) the population's baseline VO2max was 40.8, and both this meta-analysis and Rosenblat 2021 show the effect shrinks sharply with training status; (b) the ±0.9 confidence limit means the true effect could be as small as +0.3 mL/kg/min (1.3 min); (c) the whole conversion assumes VO2max is this athlete's binding constraint, and his own data say it is not — see the Joyner row.

interventions.intervention: An interval-training block, as a driver of time-trial performance — the effect broken out BY TRAINING STATUS (this is the single most decision-relevant paper in the domain)
interventions.effect: Trained individuals improved time-trial performance by approximately 2%; less-trained individuals by up to 6%. Formally: active participants gained 2.0% MORE than trained (95% CI 0.6 to 3.4, p=0.006) from HIIT; for sprint interval training, inactive gained 2.6% more than active (95% CI 1.1 to 4.1) and 3.4% more than trained (95% CI 1.8 to 4.9). Dose-response in trained individuals: +0.21% per additional HIIT session (95% CI 0.07 to 0.35, p=0.003) and +0.09% per unit total work (95% CI 0.03 to 0.16, p=0.006). Work-bout INTENSITY had no effect on TT change; work-bout DURATION did, but only in trained participants (beta=0.37% per extra minute, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.69, p=0.019 — longer intervals better). Optimal recovery in trained ≈ 50% of work-bout duration (beta=-0.63, 95% CI -1.13 to -0.14, p=0.012). Every interval repetition beyond the first five COST 0.2% in trained (beta=-0.14, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.04, p=0.006) and 1.0% in active participants (beta=-0.97, 95% CI -1.32 to -0.62, p<0.001). Sex had no effect. Baseline VO2max had no effect once training status was accounted for.
interventions.population: 29 studies, 67 groups, 491 participants (400 male, 91 female), mean age 25 y (range 19–45), MEAN VO2peak 52 mL/kg/min (range 32–70) — this athlete's measured 53.0 sits almost exactly on the sample mean. Training status: 75 inactive, 146 active, 258 trained. Modes: 34 cycling, 27 running, 6 rowing groups. Time trials 1.6–40.0 km.
interventions.citation: Rosenblat MA, Lin E, da Costa BR, Thomas SG. Programming Interval Training to Optimize Time-Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine 2021;51(8):1687–1714. PMID 33826121, DOI 10.1007/s40279-021-01457-2. (Full text of the identical analysis is open-access as Chapter 5 of Rosenblat's 2021 University of Toronto PhD thesis, hdl 1807/106260.)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this is the one meta-analysis whose intervention window (2–10 weeks) actually matches a 6-week block, and whose participants match this athlete's VO2max. It is the best-fitting evidence in the entire domain for this decision.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working, two routes. (1) Category estimate: trained-status improvement ≈2% of 235.9 min = 4.7 min. (2) Dose estimate: a 6-week block with 2 quality sessions/week, minus the last 2 weeks reduced for taper, ≈ 10 HIIT sessions × 0.21%/session = 2.1% (95% CI 0.7% to 3.5%) = 5.0 min (95% CI 1.7 to 8.3 min). Both routes agree on ~5 min. THREE DISCOUNTS APPLY: (a) the longest time trial in the sample was 40 km cycling (~60 min); the marathon is roughly four times longer, so it is dominated by fuelling, thermoregulation and durability that these trials never tested — I would halve the estimate to ~2–3 min for a marathon; (b) heterogeneity was extreme (I²=89.8%) and Egger's test showed small-study bias specifically in the trained subgroup (p=0.002), meaning the trained ~2% is more likely an over- than an under-estimate; (c) this athlete's marathon is already 47 min slower than his 5 km equivalent predicts, which says the marathon-specific limiter is not the one intervals train.

interventions.intervention: Long intervals (≥4 min work bouts) rather than short sprints, as the interval format
interventions.effect: No overall difference between HIIT and sprint interval training on time-trial performance (0.9%; 90% CI -0.1% to 1.9%, p=0.18). But subgroup analysis by work-bout duration showed long-HIIT (≥4 min) produced a 2% GREATER time-trial improvement than sprint interval training, and a moderate effect (ES=0.70) in favour of HIIT for maximal aerobic power/velocity. No difference in VO2max change between formats. This aligns with the independent finding in Rosenblat 2021 that longer work bouts help specifically in trained athletes (beta=0.37%/min, 95% CI 0.06–0.69).
interventions.population: 6 randomised or pair-matched trials, at least moderately trained males and females (~3 h/week of activity), aged 18–45
interventions.citation: Rosenblat MA, Perrotta AS, Thomas SG. Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training Versus Sprint Interval Training on Time-Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine 2020;50(6):1145–61. PMID 32034701, DOI 10.1007/s40279-020-01264-1
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. This is a session-design choice, not an adaptation timescale — it costs nothing to apply from week 1.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: 2% of 235.9 min = 4.7 min, but this is 2% RELATIVE TO CHOOSING SPRINTS, not 2% on top of doing nothing. For a marathoner nobody would prescribe 30-second sprints anyway, so the realistic decision this informs is 5×1000 m / 4×8 min at threshold-to-VO2max pace versus 10-16×400 m. Combining with the repetition-count penalty below, choosing 5×1000 m over 12×400 m is worth roughly 1.5-2 min. Only 6 studies, so treat the 2% as indicative.

interventions.intervention: Adding a third weekly quality session instead of two, in an already-trained athlete
interventions.effect: NO significant difference. In the trained subgroup (24 studies at 2 sessions/week, 9 at 3 sessions/week) the weighted mean difference was 1.0% in favour of three sessions, 95% CI -0.2 to 2.2, p=0.115 — not statistically significant. The headline pooled result across all training statuses (3 sessions better by 1.5%, 95% CI 0.5 to 2.5, p=0.005) is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be an artefact: all five 'active' subgroup studies happened to use three sessions per week, which skewed the pooled comparison. Separately, the number of interval REPETITIONS within a session showed clear negative returns: -0.2% per rep beyond five in trained athletes, -1.0% per rep beyond five in active athletes.
interventions.population: Trained subgroup of the 29-study meta-analysis, n=258 trained participants, mean VO2peak 52 mL/kg/min
interventions.citation: Rosenblat MA, Lin E, da Costa BR, Thomas SG. Programming Interval Training to Optimize Time-Trial Performance. Sports Medicine 2021;51(8):1687–1714. PMID 33826121 — section 5.3.5.2.4 (Interval Repetitions) and 5.3.5.2.5 (Intensity Distribution)
interventions.sampleSize: 33 trained-group comparisons (24 at 2/wk, 9 at 3/wk); n=258 trained
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it matters most here. In a 6-week block with a large simultaneous volume increase, the evidence gives no justification for a third weekly quality session — the confidence interval crosses zero — while every extra hard session adds injury and overreaching risk (see Aubry row).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: The point estimate for a third session is 1.0% = 2.4 min, but the 95% CI runs from -0.2% (0.5 min SLOWER) to +2.2% (5.2 min faster). Honest reading: NOT CONVERTIBLE to a positive expected gain — the evidence cannot distinguish a third weekly session from doing nothing. The repetition finding IS convertible: cutting a session from 12 reps to 6 reps recovers 6 × 0.14% = 0.84% = 2.0 min.

interventions.intervention: Reorganising which interval format falls in which week (4×16 → 4×8 → 4×4, the reverse, or mixed) at matched total load
interventions.effect: All three groups improved 5–10% in mean power during a 40-min all-out trial, in peak power output and in VO2peak, with NO significant difference between the three periodisation orderings (p>0.05). An individual-response analysis found the same likelihood of large, moderate or non-responses in each group (p>0.05). The interval sessions were prescribed as maximal session efforts and produced mean blood lactate of 4.7, 9.2 and 12.7 mmol/L for 4×16, 4×8 and 4×4 respectively — i.e. genuinely different physiological stimuli that nonetheless produced the same outcome.
interventions.population: 63 cyclists, VO2peak 61.3 ± 5.8 mL/kg/min — well-trained, notably fitter than this athlete
interventions.citation: Sylta Ø, Tønnessen E, Hammarström D, Danielsen J, Skovereng K, Ravn T, Rønnestad BR, Sandbakk Ø, Seiler S. The Effect of Different High-Intensity Periodization Models on Endurance Adaptations. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2016;48(11):2165–74. PMID 27300278, DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000001007
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: The null result applies immediately — it says the ordering question does not need answering. The 5–10% magnitude does NOT apply, because it came from 24 sessions over 12 weeks; six weeks buys roughly half that dose.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: The comparison itself converts to ZERO minutes — that is the finding. The absolute 5–10% on a 40-min all-out cycling trial is not transferable to a marathon (different mode, trained cyclists, one-hour effort), so: not convertible. Its value here is that it removes an entire category of plan-design agonising.

interventions.intervention: Choosing a polarised training-intensity distribution over a pyramidal one (i.e. how the easy/moderate/hard split is arranged around the intervals)
interventions.effect: NO significant difference. Using the time-in-heart-rate-zone approach: VO2max SMD = -0.06 (p=0.68) and time-trial performance SMD = -0.05 (p=0.34) between polarised and pyramidal. No statistically significant difference between polarised and ANY other distribution model. The one signal was a subgroup interaction: the VO2max response differed between recreational and competitive athletes (SMD = -0.63, p<0.05), with competitive athletes possibly favouring polarised and RECREATIONAL athletes possibly favouring PYRAMIDAL. This is a network meta-analysis of individual participant data — the strongest available design in this literature, and it supersedes the earlier, more enthusiastic polarised-training meta-analyses including the authors' own.
interventions.population: 13 studies, 348 endurance athletes (296 male, 52 female): 150 recreational, 198 competitive. Mean age 17.6–41.5 y; VO2max 46.6–68.3 mL/kg/min across studies — this athlete's 53.0 falls inside the range, in the recreational half.
interventions.citation: Rosenblat MA, Watt JA, Arnold JI, Treff G, Sandbakk ØB, Esteve-Lanao J, Festa L, Filipas L, Galloway SD, Muñoz I, Ramos-Campo DJ, Schneeweiss P, Sellés-Pérez S, Stöggl T, Talsnes RK, Zinner C, Seiler S. Which Training Intensity Distribution Intervention will Produce the Greatest Improvements in Maximal Oxygen Uptake and Time-Trial Performance in Endurance Athletes? A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Individual Participant Data. Sports Medicine 2025. PMID 39888556, DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02149-3
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as a null — it removes the pressure to adopt any particular branded distribution. Note the recreational-athlete signal points toward PYRAMIDAL (more moderate-intensity work, fewer maximal sessions), which is also what elite marathoners actually do (Casado 2022).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero — that is the finding. Choosing polarised over pyramidal is worth no measurable time. The recreational-athlete subgroup signal (SMD -0.63) is a subgroup interaction on VO2max in a 13-study network and is not robust enough to convert.

interventions.intervention: Keeping a large fraction of total volume genuinely easy (80% below threshold) rather than pushing more of it into the moderate zone, while holding hard-training volume constant
interventions.effect: Both groups improved substantially on a simulated 10.4 km cross-country race, but the low-intensity-emphasis group improved significantly MORE: -157 ± 13 s versus -121.5 ± 7.1 s (p=0.03), a difference of ~36 s on a ~40 min effort (~1.5%). Achieved distributions: Z1 group 80.5 ± 1.8% zone 1 / 11.8 ± 2.0% zone 2; Z2 group 66.8 ± 1.1% / 24.7 ± 1.5%. Critically, HIGH-intensity (zone 3) volume was held EQUAL at 8.3 ± 0.7% vs 8.5 ± 1.0% — so this is not an argument about intervals, it is an argument about what the other 90% of the week looks like.
interventions.population: 12 sub-elite endurance runners (5000 m track specialists who also race 9–12 km cross-country). Small sample; substantially more trained than this athlete.
interventions.citation: Esteve-Lanao J, Foster C, Seiler S, Lucia A. Impact of training intensity distribution on performance in endurance athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 2007;21(3):943–9. PMID 17685689, DOI 10.1519/R-19725.1
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO — this effect was produced over five months of accumulated distribution difference. Six weeks cannot reproduce it. What it DOES license in six weeks is the negative instruction: do not let the easy running drift into the moderate zone, because that is what the losing arm did.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: the between-group difference was 36 s on ~2340 s = 1.5%. On 235.9 min that would be 3.5 min — but the intervention ran 5 months, n=12 (6 per arm, which is very small), and the improvements in BOTH arms (2–2.6 min on a 10.4 km race) are so large that these runners were clearly not near their ceiling. For a 6-week block I would call this NOT CONVERTIBLE to a positive number; treat it as a constraint on how the easy days are run, not as a source of minutes.

interventions.intervention: Intervals as a route to running economy specifically (as opposed to VO2max)
interventions.effect: HIIT improved running economy significantly more than moderate-intensity continuous training: SMD = 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.72, Z=3.01). For VO2max the pooled mean difference was +2.48 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.61 to 3.34, Z=5.60), with the paper noting the VO2max effect was more pronounced with MICT — i.e. the two modalities split the work: intervals buy economy, continuous work buys VO2max.
interventions.population: Endurance runners across the included randomised controlled trials (search completed March 2024). The abstract as indexed does not state total n or study count — I could not verify those figures and am not going to guess them.
interventions.citation: Feng Y, Li D, Liu Y, Tang D. High-Intensity Interval Training and Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training Affect Running Economy in Endurance Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Human Kinetics 2026. PMID 41766811, DOI 10.5114/jhk/205427
interventions.sampleSize: Not stated in the indexed abstract — unverified
interventions.duration: Not stated in the indexed abstract — unverified
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Probably. Economy changes are among the faster-responding adaptations and have been shown to shift over 6-week interventions, but this specific meta-analysis does not report its duration range, so I cannot confirm it.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working, with an explicit weak link. SMD 0.44 must be converted to a percentage using the between-subject SD of running economy, which is typically ~5% of the mean in trained runners: 0.44 × 5% ≈ 2.2% economy improvement (95% CI 0.15×5% = 0.75% to 0.72×5% = 3.6%). Hoogkamer et al. measured that a 1.11% metabolic-cost change produced a 0.65% time change, i.e. a 0.59 transfer coefficient. So 2.2% × 0.59 = 1.3% faster (95% CI 0.44% to 2.1%) = 3.1 min (95% CI 1.0 to 5.0 min). THE WEAK LINK is the assumed 5% SD — the meta-analysis reports a standardised effect, not a percentage, and if the true pooled SD is smaller the whole estimate shrinks proportionally. Treat 3 min as an upper-ish estimate, not a forecast.

interventions.intervention: The transfer coefficient itself: how a change in running economy converts to a change in race time (the conversion machinery every other row depends on)
interventions.effect: Adding mass to shoes increased metabolic rate at 3.5 m/s by 1.11% per 100 g per shoe (95% CI 0.88% to 1.35%). The corresponding 3000 m time trials were 0.65% ± 1.36% slower with +100 g and 2.37% ± 2.09% slower with +300 g. So a 1% worsening in economy costs roughly 0.6–0.8% in race time — the relationship is close to, but slightly less than, one-for-one.
interventions.population: 18 male sub-20-minute 5 km runners. This athlete's 5 km equivalent is 19:39 — he is inside this population's performance band, which is unusual and makes the transfer coefficient more credible for him than most sports-science numbers are.
interventions.citation: Hoogkamer W, Kipp S, Spiering BA, Kram R. Altered Running Economy Directly Translates to Altered Distance-Running Performance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2016;48(11):2175–80. PMID 27327023, DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000001012
interventions.duration: Acute (single-session manipulations), not a training study
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as a conversion tool. It is not itself an intervention.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: This IS the conversion rule: 1% economy = ~0.6% time = 1.4 min on a 235.9 min marathon. Caveat: measured at 3000 m, a ~10-minute effort. Extrapolating to a 4-hour effort is an assumption, not a measurement — at marathon duration, substrate availability and the drift in economy over hours plausibly change the coefficient, and nobody has measured it there.

interventions.intervention: Pushing training load hard enough in the weeks before a race to induce functional overreaching (directly relevant to a 60/80/100/80/60 km block in an athlete whose largest-ever week is 57.1 km)
interventions.effect: After a 3-week overload period, 11 of 23 trained triathletes (48%) were diagnosed functionally overreached — performance DECREASED with concomitant high perceived fatigue. During the subsequent 4-week taper, the acutely-fatigued (non-overreached) group achieved a peak performance supercompensation that was 2.6% ± 1.1% GREATER than the functionally-overreached group and 2.6% ± 1.6% greater than controls. VO2max increased significantly from baseline at peak performance ONLY in the control and acutely-fatigued groups — the overreached group's VO2max did not recover. Infection rates during the study: 70% in the functionally-overreached group, 20% acutely fatigued, 10% control.
interventions.population: 33 trained male triathletes (23 overload, 10 normal training). Trained, not elite; overload was a controlled training-load increase over 3 weeks.
interventions.citation: Aubry A, Hausswirth C, Louis J, Coutts AJ, Le Meur Y. Functional overreaching: the key to peak performance during the taper? Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2014;46(9):1769–77. PMID 25134000, DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000000301
interventions.duration: 8 weeks: 1 week moderate + 3 weeks overload + 4 weeks taper
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Emphatically yes, and this is the row that should govern the block design. Three weeks of overload was enough to overreach half a trained cohort. This athlete's ratified block is a 6-week ramp from a 15 km week to 100 km — a ~4x increase into a peak he has never touched, in a man whose 42-day training-load fitness metric has fallen from 72.3 to 52.2. The base rate of overreaching under this plan should be assumed higher than 48%, not lower.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: -2.6% ± 1.1% of 235.9 min = 6.1 min SLOWER (±2.6 min), plus a 70% infection rate that risks losing the race entirely. This single negative number is LARGER than every positive interval-training effect in this domain combined. In expectation terms: if the block overreaches him with probability ~0.5, the expected cost is ~3 min, against an expected interval-training gain of ~2–5 min. The plan's volume ramp is fighting its own interval work for the same minutes.

interventions.intervention: Concentrating five hard sessions into one week then backing off (block periodisation), versus spreading two hard sessions per week evenly
interventions.effect: 4-week study: block periodisation increased VO2max +4.6 ± 3.7%, peak power +2.1 ± 2.8%, power at 2 mmol/L lactate +10 ± 12% (all p<0.05), while the traditional 2-sessions-per-week group changed on NOTHING. Effect sizes for block over traditional: 1.34 (VO2max), 0.85 (Wmax), 0.71 (power at 2 mmol/L). Replicated over 12 weeks by the same group: block +8.8 ± 5.9% VO2max versus traditional +3.7 ± 2.9% (p<0.05), with a trend for power at 2 mmol/L (22 ± 14% vs 10 ± 7%, p=0.054). Total HIT and low-intensity volume were matched between groups in both studies.
interventions.population: 4-week study: 19 trained cyclists (VO2max 62–63 mL/kg/min). 12-week study: 15 well-trained cyclists. Both CYCLISTS, both fitter than this athlete, and both with very small n.
interventions.citation: Rønnestad BR, Hansen J, Ellefsen S. Block periodization of high-intensity aerobic intervals provides superior training effects in trained cyclists. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2014;24(1):34–42. PMID 22646668, DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2012.01485.x. Replication: Rønnestad BR, Ellefsen S, Nygaard H, Zacharoff EE, Vikmoen O, Hansen J, Hallén J. Effects of 12 weeks of block periodization on performance and performance indices in well-trained cyclists. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2014;24(2):327–35. PMID 23134196
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — the 4-week version fits inside the window. But note the direct conflict with the row above: concentrating five hard sessions into one week is exactly the load spike that produced functional overreaching in Aubry's triathletes, and Rønnestad's cyclists were fitter, non-weight-bearing (no impact injury risk) and NOT simultaneously doubling their weekly volume. I would not stack this on top of a 15→100 km ramp.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: the 4-week VO2max advantage of block over traditional was 4.6 percentage points; at constant economy and fractional utilisation that is 4.6% off race pace = 10.9 min. That number is almost certainly not real for this athlete: n=19 cyclists, the comparison group improved on nothing at all (which is itself odd), the impact-loading and injury risk of running is absent from the cycling model, and the effect has never been tested in runners doing a concurrent volume ramp. Honest call: NOT CONVERTIBLE. Cite it as evidence that hard-session frequency can be safely varied within a block, not as a source of ten minutes.

interventions.intervention: How fast VO2max actually moves — the time course, which determines whether six weeks is enough
interventions.effect: VO2max increased 5% (p<0.05) during the FIRST WEEK and rose linearly across 10 weeks, averaging +0.12 L/min per week, for a total of +16.8 mL/kg/min (+44%). Endurance, VO2max and time to peak heart rate all increased linearly with no plateau over 10 weeks. Protocol: 40 min/day, 6 days/week — three days of 6×5 min intervals at VO2max with 2 min recovery at 50–60% VO2max, three days of 40 min continuous running.
interventions.population: 8 untrained subjects. This is the classic landmark, and its magnitude is a pure untrained-population artefact — a 44% VO2max gain is not available to anyone who already trains.
interventions.citation: Hickson RC, Bomze HA, Holloszy JO. Linear increase in aerobic power induced by a strenuous program of endurance exercise. Journal of Applied Physiology 1977;42(3):372–6. PMID 838658, DOI 10.1152/jappl.1977.42.3.372
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes for the TIME COURSE claim — measurable VO2max change begins within the first week and does not need months. Absolutely NOT for the magnitude: these were untrained subjects.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. The +44% figure applies to sedentary people; this athlete has trained consistently for six months and sits at 53.0 mL/kg/min. The transferable content is the shape of the curve (fast onset, no early plateau), not its height.

interventions.intervention: The ceiling question: how much VO2max is trainable at all, and how variable the response is
interventions.effect: Mean VO2max increase ≈ 400 mL/min after a standardised 20-week programme, with CONSIDERABLE heterogeneity: some individuals gained little or nothing, others gained more than 1000 mL/min. ANOVA found 2.5 times more variance BETWEEN families than within families; maximal heritability of the VO2max training response was 47%. Corroborating magnitude from an independent meta-analysis of 37 HIIT studies (40 groups, 334 subjects, 18–45 y, 6–13 weeks, ≥3 days/week): mean VO2max increase 0.51 L/min (95% CI 0.43–0.60), standardised effect 0.86 SD (95% CI 0.72–0.99); the subset using longer 3–5 min intervals (9 studies, 72 subjects) reached 0.8–0.9 L/min.
interventions.population: HERITAGE: 481 SEDENTARY adult Caucasians from 98 two-generation families. Bacon: 334 healthy sedentary or recreationally active adults under 45. Both are untrained baselines — this bounds what is trainable from scratch, not what remains available to a trained runner.
interventions.citation: Bouchard C, An P, Rice T, Skinner JS, Wilmore JH, Gagnon J, Pérusse L, Leon AS, Rao DC. Familial aggregation of VO2max response to exercise training: results from the HERITAGE Family Study. Journal of Applied Physiology 1999;87(3):1003–8. PMID 10484570. And: Bacon AP, Carter RE, Ogle EA, Joyner MJ. VO2max Trainability and High Intensity Interval Training in Humans: A Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE 2013;8(9):e73182. PMID 24023823, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073182
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Only as a bound. Bacon's 6–13 week window brackets a 6-week block at its floor; HERITAGE's 20 weeks does not.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: 0.51 L/min on an 85.5 kg athlete = 6.0 mL/kg/min, which on a base of 53.0 is +11.3% — that would be 26.6 min on a marathon if it applied. IT DOES NOT APPLY: both samples started sedentary. The transferable content is the SHAPE OF THE UNCERTAINTY, not a number: response to an identical programme ranged from zero to >1000 mL/min, and 47% of that variation is familial. Any single-point prediction of what this block will produce for this specific athlete is therefore false precision — the honest statement is a wide distribution with a real probability mass at 'no measurable VO2max change'.

interventions.intervention: Higher intensity as a way to convert NON-responders into responders, at matched total energy expenditure
interventions.effect: After 10 weeks of moderate training, 16 of 31 participants (52%) were VO2max responders. Sixteen further weeks of continued moderate training produced NO further increase in the number of responders. In contrast, an energy-equivalent progression (8 weeks at 70% heart-rate reserve, then 8 weeks of 4×4 min intervals) raised responders to 13 of 15 (87%, p=0.031), and beat continued moderate training on responder rate (p=0.012). VO2max change over 26 weeks: +3.4 ± 2.7 mL/kg/min (intensity-increase) vs +0.4 ± 2.9 (continued moderate), p=0.020.
interventions.population: 31 healthy UNTRAINED participants, aged 46 ± 8 y, BMI 25.4 ± 3.3, baseline VO2max 34 ± 4 mL/kg/min. Two decades older and 19 mL/kg/min less fit than this athlete. Small n, and the group split happened after 10 weeks.
interventions.citation: Reuter M, Rosenberger F, Barz A, Venhorst A, Blanz L, Hecksteden A, Meyer T. Does Higher Intensity Increase the Rate of Responders to Endurance Training When Total Energy Expenditure Remains Constant? A Randomized Controlled Trial. Sports Medicine – Open 2023;9(1):37. PMID 37209213, DOI 10.1186/s40798-023-00579-3
interventions.duration: 26 weeks total; the intensity contrast ran for the final 16
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No. The responder conversion took 16 weeks after a 10-week base. The mechanism is interesting; the timeline is not available here.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. The population is untrained 46-year-olds; the finding is about escaping a plateau after a long moderate-training phase, which is not this athlete's situation (he has done six months of varied training and has never plateaued at a high volume — his fitness metric fell because he stopped, not because he adapted).

interventions.intervention: A 2-week taper — the highest-certainty, fastest-acting performance intervention available inside a 6-week window
interventions.effect: Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper with training volume exponentially reduced by 41–60%, intensity and frequency unchanged. Overall effect 0.59 ± 0.33 (standardised mean difference, p<0.05), pooled across 27 of 182 screened studies in competitive athletes using actual competition or field-based criterion performance. Independently replicated in a 2023 meta-analysis of 14 studies: significant pre-to-post-taper improvement in time-trial performance (SMD = -0.45), with a ≤21-day taper reducing volume 41–60% without changing intensity or frequency identified as effective, and tapers preceded by overload training producing larger gains than conventional tapers.
interventions.population: Bosquet: competitive athletes across endurance sports, 27 studies. Wang: endurance athletes, 14 studies. Not marathon-specific.
interventions.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2007;39(8):1358–65. PMID 17762369, DOI 10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0. Replication: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y. Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS ONE 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0282838
interventions.duration: 2-week taper is the optimum; ≤21 days effective
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — and it consumes a third of the block. A 6-week block that ends with a proper 2-week taper has only 4 weeks of actual loading, which changes every dose calculation above: 4 loading weeks × 2 quality sessions = 8 sessions, not 12.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: NOT CONVERTIBLE from the abstracts I verified. Both papers report standardised effect sizes (0.59 ± 0.33; -0.45), not percentages, and converting an SMD to minutes requires the pooled within-athlete performance SD, which neither abstract gives. The commonly quoted '2–3% from a taper' figure is widely repeated but I did not verify it in either source and will not assert it. What IS assertable: the taper is the only intervention here with a large, replicated effect that fully expresses itself inside two weeks, and the direction is unambiguous.

interventions.intervention: What elite and highly trained distance runners actually do — the expert-practice benchmark, offered as practice rather than proof
interventions.effect: Highly trained and elite distance runners typically follow a PYRAMIDAL intensity distribution: volume decreasing from zone 1 (at or below first threshold) through zone 2 (between thresholds) to zone 3 (above second threshold). Continuous-tempo runs or threshold intervals in zone 2, and short/anaerobic intervals in zone 3, were EACH used at least once per week — i.e. two quality sessions per week, one threshold-flavoured and one faster. Marathoners specifically used more pyramidal approaches; 1500 m runners more polarised. The authors' recommendation is traditional periodisation on a hard-day/easy-day basis, shifting from pyramidal in the preparatory phase toward polarised in the competition phase.
interventions.population: 10 studies of highly trained and elite middle- and long-distance runners. Descriptive of what elites do, with no control group and no causal claim — elites' training is confounded with their genetics, their volume and their decade of accumulated adaptation.
interventions.citation: Casado A, González-Mohíno F, González-Ravé JM, Foster C. Training Periodization, Methods, Intensity Distribution, and Volume in Highly Trained and Elite Distance Runners: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 2022;17(6):820–33. PMID 35418513, DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2021-0435
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: The structure applies immediately (two quality sessions, one threshold, one faster, hard/easy alternation). The volumes do not — elite marathoners run 160–200 km/week; this athlete has never run 60.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. This is an observational description of practice, not a controlled comparison — there is no counterfactual, so no effect size exists to convert. Its value is that the elite pattern (two quality sessions per week, pyramidal for marathoners) independently converges on what Rosenblat's meta-analysis found in trials, and that convergence is itself informative.

myths: 'HIIT is dramatically superior to continuous training.' The largest head-to-head meta-analysis puts the advantage at +1.2 mL/kg/min (95% confidence limits ±0.9) — the authors' own words are 'possibly SMALL'. Against no exercise the two are nearly indistinguishable (endurance +4.9, HIT +5.5). The popular framing inflates a small effect measured in untrained 25-year-olds into a training philosophy.

'There is an optimal interval format — 4×4, or 30/30, or whatever is fashionable.' Rosenblat 2021 found NO effect of work-bout intensity on time-trial change following HIIT. Sylta 2016 randomised 63 cyclists to three different orderings of 4×16 / 4×8 / 4×4 at matched load and found no difference on any outcome, despite the sessions producing blood lactates of 4.7, 9.2 and 12.7 mmol/L — genuinely different stimuli, identical results. The one format variable with support is work-bout DURATION in already-trained athletes, where LONGER is better (+0.37% per extra minute, 95% CI 0.06–0.69) — the opposite of the short-sharp-interval fashion.

'More intervals in a session means more adaptation.' Every repetition beyond the first five was associated with a 0.2% WORSE time-trial outcome in trained athletes (95% CI -0.24 to -0.04, p=0.006) and 1.0% worse in active ones (95% CI -1.32 to -0.62, p<0.001). Five to six long reps, not twelve short ones.

'Three quality sessions a week beat two.' In the trained subgroup the difference was 1.0% with a 95% CI of -0.2 to 2.2 and p=0.115 — not significant. The frequently cited pooled figure favouring three sessions (1.5%, 95% CI 0.5–2.5) is acknowledged BY THE AUTHORS to be an artefact of all five 'active' studies happening to use three sessions.

'Polarized training is proven superior.' The 2025 network meta-analysis of individual participant data (13 studies, 348 athletes) found no difference between polarised and pyramidal on VO2max (SMD -0.06, p=0.68) or time trial (SMD -0.05, p=0.34), and no significant difference between polarised and any other distribution. The subgroup signal actually points the other way for this athlete's level: RECREATIONAL athletes may respond better to PYRAMIDAL. The earlier, more enthusiastic polarised meta-analyses have been superseded — including by the same lead author.

'Adding easy continuous mileage dilutes your interval gains — the meta-analysis says so.' Rosenblat did find that trained groups doing intervals ALONE improved time trials more than those adding continuous training (HIIT WMD 1.4%, 95% CI 0.3–2.4; SIT 2.6%, 95% CI 0.9–4.4), and this gets quoted as licence to drop long runs. It does not survive contact with the context: the outcome was a ≤40 km time trial (≈60 minutes), the interventions ran 2–10 weeks, the intensity of the added continuous training was not consistently reported (the authors flag this themselves), and it directly contradicts Esteve-Lanao's 5-month RCT where the group with MORE low-intensity volume improved significantly more. For a marathon — an event where the limiter is durability over four hours — reading this as 'skip the long run' is the most dangerous misreading in the domain.

'VO2max is what makes you faster.' Joyner's model, and this athlete's own data, say otherwise for the marathon. His 5 km equivalent of 19:39 predicts a ~3:08 marathon by Riegel extrapolation; his half marathon of 1:46:35 predicts ~3:42; he ran 3:55:54. The 47-minute gap between his short-distance fitness and his marathon is not a VO2max deficit — it is fractional utilisation, durability and fuelling. Interval training attacks the capacity he already has in surplus.

'The 10% rule for weekly mileage increases.' The 874-runner prospective cohort that tested it found NO statistically significant difference in injury rate across <10%, 10–30% and >30% weekly progression groups. The only signal was a non-significant hazard ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, p=0.07) for distance-related injuries above 30% over a two-week period. The 10% rule is folklore with a fig leaf; the >30%-over-two-weeks threshold is the closest thing to an evidence-based line, and it is weak.

'Everyone who does the work gets the adaptation.' In HERITAGE, 481 sedentary adults did an identical 20-week programme: mean gain ~400 mL/min, but individual responses ran from essentially zero to more than 1000 mL/min, with 47% maximal heritability. Any plan that promises a specific VO2max outcome is promising something the literature cannot deliver.

'Overreaching before a taper produces supercompensation — you have to dig the hole to climb out of it.' The study most often cited for this actually found the opposite. Triathletes who were merely acutely fatigued out-performed the functionally-overreached group by 2.6% ± 1.1% at peak, VO2max rose from baseline only in the non-overreached groups, and 70% of the overreached group got sick versus 10% of controls. Overload before a taper helps; crossing into functional overreaching costs more than it buys.
unknowns: There is no randomised controlled trial of interval prescription with THE MARATHON as the outcome. Every effect size in this domain comes from time trials of 1.6–40 km (roughly 5–60 minutes). The longest outcome measured is about a quarter of this athlete's race duration. Whether interval-training gains at 60 minutes transfer to 235 minutes is an assumption the literature has never tested.

Nobody has studied a 6-week interval block combined with a simultaneous 4x increase in weekly volume. The interval-programming literature and the training-load/injury literature do not intersect anywhere. The Rosenblat dose-response numbers come from studies where volume was held roughly constant; applying them to a plan that also ramps 15 km/week to 100 km/week is extrapolation into an empty cell.

Whether two or three quality sessions per week is better for a trained runner is genuinely unresolved, not resolved-in-favour-of-two. The 95% CI is -0.2% to +2.2% — wide enough to contain both 'slightly harmful' and 'meaningfully helpful'. The trial that would settle it has not been run.

The trained-athlete effect sizes are probably inflated. Egger's test found significant small-study bias specifically in the trained subgroup (p=0.002), and heterogeneity was I²=89.8%. The true trained-athlete time-trial gain from an interval block may be materially below 2%.

Nothing predicts an individual's response in advance. HERITAGE established 47% heritability of VO2max trainability and a response range from zero to >1000 mL/min, but no usable pre-test predictor has emerged. Whether this specific athlete is a responder is unknowable before the block, and the only way to find out is to measure.

How economy and its transfer coefficient behave over four hours is unmeasured. Hoogkamer's 0.6-time-per-1-economy relationship was established over 3000 m. Economy drifts during prolonged running, and whether the same transfer holds at hour three of a marathon has not been established.

No governing body publishes a quantified interval prescription for marathon training. I verified the ACSM position stand on quantity and quality of exercise (health-oriented, not performance-oriented) and the IOC consensus statements on training load and injury/illness risk. I did NOT verify — and will not invent — any World Athletics, UK Athletics or USATF document that prescribes interval structure, session count or volume progression for marathon preparation, and my web-search budget was exhausted before I could complete that search. Treat 'the official body says X about intervals' as unverified until someone reads the actual coaching syllabus.

The block-periodisation result (five hard sessions in one week, then back off) has been shown twice in small cohorts of trained CYCLISTS and never in runners. Non-weight-bearing exercise removes the impact-injury mechanism that dominates running, so the transferability is unknown and the risk profile is certainly different.

Whether an athlete whose training-load fitness metric has fallen 28% in six weeks (72.3 to 52.2) responds to a hard block like a trained athlete (~2%) or a detrained one (~4–6%) is not addressed anywhere. He is in a transitional state that the training-status categories in these meta-analyses do not have a bin for.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine
officialSources.document: ACSM Position Stand: Quantity and Quality of Exercise for Developing and Maintaining Cardiorespiratory, Musculoskeletal, and Neuromotor Fitness in Apparently Healthy Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43(7):1334–59. PMID 21694556
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: ≥150 min/week moderate, OR ≥75 min/week vigorous (≥20 min/day on ≥3 days), OR a combination reaching 500–1000 MET·min/week; resistance training 2–3 days/week; explicit instruction that programmes be modified to individual habitual activity and that GRADUAL progression of intensity and volume reduces exercise risk. Note honestly: this is a health-and-fitness prescription for the general adult population. It contains no marathon-specific or interval-structure guidance and should not be cited as endorsing any competitive training plan.

officialSources.body: International Olympic Committee (consensus expert group)
officialSources.document: How much is too much? (Part 1) IOC consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med 2016;50(17):1030–41. PMID 27535989. And Part 2, on load and risk of illness. Br J Sports Med 2016;50(17):1043–52. PMID 27535991
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Guidelines for prescribing and monitoring training and competition load, athlete well-being and injury/illness surveillance. Names RAPID CHANGES in training load as a major modifiable risk factor for both injury and illness, and recommends load monitoring rather than fixed volume targets. This is the most directly relevant official document to a plan that ramps from a 15 km week to a 100 km week in four weeks; it is a consensus statement, so its evidence grade is expert synthesis, not trial data.

officialSources.body: Not found — stated explicitly rather than fabricated
officialSources.document: World Athletics / UK Athletics / USATF coaching syllabus prescribing marathon interval structure
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: I could not verify that such a document exists with a quantified interval prescription, and my web-search budget ran out before the search completed. I am not going to cite one I have not read. As far as this research pass established, the quantified prescriptions in this domain come from the peer-reviewed literature (above), not from governing-body coaching manuals — and the elite-practice benchmark is best sourced from Casado et al. 2022's systematic review of what elite runners actually do, which is descriptive rather than official.

check.domain: Interval versus continuous training — quantified evidence, and what a 6-week block can plausibly move on a 3:55 marathon

citationChecks.citation: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M. Effectiveness of HIT and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements. Sports Med 2015;45(10):1469-81. PMID 26243014
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact (authors, journal, vol 45(10), pp 1469-81, 2015). Abstract confirms every number quoted: 28 studies, n=723, age 25.1±5 y, baseline VO2max 40.8±7.9, ET vs control +4.9 (±1.4), HIT vs control +5.5 (±1.2), HIT vs ET +1.2 (±0.9) described by the authors as 'possibly small', and all five modifiers of the HIT-over-ET advantage (longer reps +2.2±2.1, older +1.8±1.7, longer duration +1.7±1.7, work/rest +1.6±1.5, lower baseline fitness +0.8±1.3). ONE SELECTIVE OMISSION: in the HIT-vs-CONTROL model the same abstract reports longer HIT repetitions as a NEGATIVE modifier (-1.8 ±2.7). The researcher reports only the +2.2 from the HIT-vs-ET model, which is the half that supports their 'longer intervals are better' convergence with Rosenblat. Also worth noting the abstract's own conclusion is the opposite in tone to the researcher's myth-bust: 'gains in VO2max being greater following HIT when compared with endurance training.'

citationChecks.citation: Rosenblat MA, Lin E, da Costa BR, Thomas SG. Programming Interval Training to Optimize Time-Trial Performance. Sports Med 2021;51(8):1687-1714. PMID 33826121
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. I downloaded the open-access thesis (tspace.library.utoronto.ca/bitstream/1807/106260/1/, 187 pp) and text-extracted it. Every full-text-only coefficient the researcher quoted is verbatim correct: active 2.0% greater than trained (95% CI 0.6-3.4, p=0.006); SIT inactive 2.6% (1.1-4.1) over active, 3.4% (1.8-4.9) over trained; sex null (WMD 0.1%, p=0.904); baseline VO2max null (p=0.157); work-bout intensity no effect; work-bout duration in trained beta=0.37 (0.06-0.69, p=0.019); optimal recovery ~50% of work bout beta=-0.63 (-1.13 to -0.14, p=0.012); reps beyond five -0.97 (-1.32 to -0.62, p<0.001) active and -0.14 (-0.24 to -0.04, p=0.006) trained; sessions/wk pooled 1.5% (0.5-2.5, p=0.005) and the authors' own artefact explanation (all n=5 active studies used three/wk); trained subgroup 24 studies at 2/wk vs 9 at 3/wk, WMD 1.0% (-0.2 to 2.2, p=0.115); total HIIT sessions in trained beta=0.21 (0.07-0.35, p=0.003); total work in trained beta=0.09 (0.03-0.16, p=0.006); I²=89.8%; Egger's eliminated in active (p=0.174) but not trained (p=0.002). This is unusually accurate reporting. Trivial: TT range is 1.5-40.0 km, not 1.6-40.0.

citationChecks.citation: Rosenblat MA, Perrotta AS, Thomas SG. Effect of HIIT Versus SIT on Time-Trial Performance. Sports Med 2020;50(6):1145-61. PMID 32034701
citationChecks.note: Paper and metadata exact; the 2% long-HIIT (≥4 min) subgroup advantage over SIT, the ES=0.70 for MAP/MAV, the null on VO2max, the 6 included studies and the ~3 h/wk moderately-trained 18-45 y population are all confirmed. BUT the confidence interval is transcribed wrongly. Abstract: 'no difference in the change in TT performance when comparing all HIIT versus SIT (0.9%; 90% CI -1.2-1.9%, p=0.18)'. Researcher wrote '90% CI -0.1% to 1.9%'. The real lower bound is -1.2%, i.e. the data are compatible with SIT being 1.2% BETTER. The narrowed CI makes the overall null look more favourable to HIIT than it is.

citationChecks.citation: Sylta Ø, Tønnessen E, Hammarström D, et al. The Effect of Different High-Intensity Periodization Models on Endurance Adaptations. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(11):2165-74. PMID 27300278
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact (pages are 2165-2174). Abstract confirms 63 cyclists, VO2peak 61.3±5.8, 12 wk / 24 interval sessions, group sizes 23/20/20, blood lactates 4.7 / 9.2 / 12.7 mmol/L (p<0.001), all groups improved 5-10% in 40-min mean power / peak power / VO2peak, no between-group differences (p>0.05), and the individual-response analysis showing similar likelihood of large/moderate/non-responses. The researcher's null claim is exactly what the paper says.

citationChecks.citation: Rosenblat MA, Watt JA, Arnold JI, et al. Which Training Intensity Distribution Intervention...? Network Meta-analysis of Individual Participant Data. Sports Med 2025;55(3):655-673. PMID 39888556
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact including the full 17-author list and the March 2025 issue. Abstract confirms 13 studies, n=348 (296 male, 52 female), 150 recreational / 198 competitive, mean age range 17.6-41.5 y, VO2max range 46.6-68.3, POL vs PYR null on VO2max (SMD -0.06, p=0.68) and TT (SMD -0.05, p=0.34), no significant difference between POL and any other TID, and the recreational-vs-competitive subgroup interaction (SMD -0.63, p<0.05) with recreational athletes possibly favouring PYR. Correctly reported, including the direction of the subgroup signal.

citationChecks.citation: Esteve-Lanao J, Foster C, Seiler S, Lucia A. Impact of training intensity distribution on performance in endurance athletes. J Strength Cond Res 2007;21(3):943-9. PMID 17685689
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 12 sub-elite 5000 m/cross-country runners, 5 months, achieved distributions Z1 80.5±1.8 / 11.8±2.0 vs Z2 66.8±1.1 / 24.7±1.5, zone 3 held equal at 8.3±0.7 vs 8.5±1.0, and improvements -157±13 s vs -121.5±7.1 s (p=0.03). Minor: the abstract does not state the 6-vs-6 split the researcher asserts, only that 12 were randomly assigned to two programmes.

citationChecks.citation: Feng Y, Li D, Liu Y, Tang D. HIIT and MICT Affect Running Economy in Endurance Runners. J Hum Kinet 2026;100:113-134. PMID 41766811
citationChecks.note: Real paper, correct authors, J Hum Kinet vol 100, pp 113-134, Jan 2026, search completed March 2024. RE SMD 0.44 (95% CI 0.15-0.72, Z=3.01) confirmed; the abstract genuinely does not state study count, total n, or intervention durations, and the researcher was right to refuse to guess them. One presentational conflation: MD 2.48 (1.61-3.34, Z=5.60) is the MICT-OVER-HIIT advantage on VO2max, not a general pooled VO2max improvement; the researcher's sentence reads ambiguously, though their summary ('intervals buy economy, continuous work buys VO2max') gets the direction right.

citationChecks.citation: Hoogkamer W, Kipp S, Spiering BA, Kram R. Altered Running Economy Directly Translates to Altered Distance-Running Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(11):2175-80. PMID 27327023
citationChecks.note: Paper and all quoted raw numbers are correct: 18 male sub-20-min 5 km runners, +1.11% metabolic rate per 100 g per shoe (95% CI 0.88-1.35), times 0.65%±1.36% and 2.37%±2.09% slower at +100 g and +300 g. BUT the researcher derived their 0.59 transfer coefficient from the +100 g point alone — a point whose SD (1.36%) is larger than its mean (0.65%). The paper's own headline estimate, which the researcher did not report, is a linear fit across ALL the data: 3000-m time increased 0.78% per added 100 g per shoe (95% CI 0.52-1.04). Against 1.11% metabolic that is a coefficient of 0.70, not 0.59, and the +300 g point independently gives 2.37/3.33 = 0.71. The paper's stated conclusion is that performance degrades 'proportionally'. Every downstream minutes conversion built on 0.59 is ~19% too small.

citationChecks.citation: Aubry A, Hausswirth C, Louis J, Coutts AJ, Le Meur Y. Functional overreaching: the key to peak performance during the taper? Med Sci Sports Exerc 2014;46(9):1769-77. PMID 25134000
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 33 trained male triathletes (23 OT / 10 CTL), 1 wk moderate + 3 wk overload + 4 wk taper, 11 of 23 diagnosed F-OR, AF group's peak supercompensation greater than F-OR by 2.6%±1.1% and than CTL by 2.6%±1.6%, VO2max rising from baseline only in CTL and AF, and infection prevalence 70% / 20% / 10%. The researcher's myth-bust framing is fair and their caveat that 'overload before a taper helps, crossing into F-OR costs more than it buys' matches the paper's own first conclusion. Note the outcome was CYCLING performance in triathletes, not a run.

citationChecks.citation: Rønnestad BR, Hansen J, Ellefsen S. Block periodization of high-intensity aerobic intervals... Scand J Med Sci Sports 2014;24(1):34-42. PMID 22646668
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms n=10 BP (VO2max 62±2) + n=9 TRAD (63±2) = 19 trained cyclists, 4 weeks, BP week 1 = five HIT sessions then 3 wk of one weekly HIT, BP gains +4.6±3.7% VO2max / +2.1±2.8% Wmax / +10±12% power at 2 mmol/L (p<0.05), no changes in TRAD, and ES 1.34 / 0.85 / 0.71. One inference to flag: the paper reports 'BP showed relative improvements in VO2max compared with TRAD (P<0.05)' without a between-group point estimate; the researcher's '4.6 percentage point advantage' is their own subtraction, defensible only because TRAD changed on nothing. They label the row non-convertible anyway.

citationChecks.citation: Rønnestad BR, Ellefsen S, Nygaard H, et al. Effects of 12 weeks of block periodization... Scand J Med Sci Sports 2014;24(2):327-35. PMID 23134196
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms n=8 BP + n=7 TRAD = 15 well-trained cyclists, 12 weeks, VO2max +8.8±5.9% vs +3.7±2.9% (p<0.05), and power at 2 mmol/L 22±14% vs 10±7% (p=0.054, correctly reported as a trend).

citationChecks.citation: Hickson RC, Bomze HA, Holloszy JO. Linear increase in aerobic power... J Appl Physiol 1977;42(3):372-6. PMID 838658
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact (J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol). Abstract confirms n=8, 40 min/day 6 days/wk for 10 wk, six 5-min bouts at VO2max with 2-min recovery at 50-60%, VO2max +5% in week 1 (p<0.05), linear increase with no plateau, +0.12 L/min per week, total +16.8 mL/kg/min (44%). Minor misdescription: the alternate three days were 'ran as far as they could in 40 min' — maximal time trials, not the easy continuous running the researcher implies. That makes the programme harder than described and slightly weakens its use as a generic time-course reference.

citationChecks.citation: Bouchard C, An P, Rice T, et al. Familial aggregation of VO2max response to exercise training: HERITAGE. J Appl Physiol 1999;87(3):1003-8. PMID 10484570
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 481 sedentary adult Caucasians from 98 two-generation families, 20 weeks, mean increase ~400 mL/min, range from little/no gain to >1.0 L/min, 2.5 times more variance between than within families, maximal heritability 47%. Reported faithfully, including the honest 'this bounds what is trainable from scratch' caveat.

citationChecks.citation: Bacon AP, Carter RE, Ogle EA, Joyner MJ. VO2max Trainability and High Intensity Interval Training in Humans: A Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE 2013;8(9):e73182. PMID 24023823
citationChecks.note: THE PMID IS WRONG. PMID 24023823 is Smith E et al., 'Seeing is believing: neural representations of visual stimuli in human auditory cortex...', PLoS ONE 2013;8(9):e73148 — an auditory-cortex paper, nothing to do with VO2max. The Bacon paper is real and everything else in the citation is right: PMID 24066036, PLoS ONE 8(9):e73182, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073182. Content verified from the abstract and the PLoS full text: 37 studies, 40 training groups, 334 subjects (120 women), sedentary/recreationally active <45 y, 6-13 weeks, ≥3 d/wk, I²=70, +0.51 L/min (95% CI 0.43-0.60), subset of 9 studies with 72 subjects using longer intervals ~0.8-0.9 L/min. The standardised effect '0.86 SDs (95% CI 0.72 to 0.99)' is not in the abstract but IS in the full text, verbatim — the researcher genuinely read the paper. OMISSION: the very next sentence of that results paragraph reports publication bias and a Trim-and-Fill corrected estimate of 0.37 L/min (95% CI 0.28-0.4x), 27% smaller than the 0.51 the researcher quoted. That correction was not reported.

citationChecks.citation: Reuter M, Rosenberger F, Barz A, et al. Does Higher Intensity Increase the Rate of Responders...? Sports Med Open 2023;9(1):37. PMID 37209213
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact (article number 35 in the esummary vs 37 cited — a trivial discrepancy in how the e-locator is indexed). Abstract confirms 31 untrained participants, 46±8 y, BMI 25.4±3.3, baseline VO2max 34±4, 10 wk moderate then randomisation, 16 of 31 responders (52%) at 10 wk, no further increase in CON, INC to 13 of 15 (87%, p=0.031), INC beat CON on responder rate (p=0.012), and VO2max change +3.4±2.7 vs +0.4±2.9 (p=0.020). The researcher's 'not convertible, wrong population and wrong timeline' verdict is correct.

citationChecks.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39(8):1358-65. PMID 17762369
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 27 of 182 studies, competitive athletes, actual competition or field-based criterion performance, 2-week taper optimal (overall effect 0.59±0.33, p<0.001), volume exponentially decreased 41-60% (0.72±0.36), intensity unchanged (0.33±0.14), frequency unchanged (0.35±0.17). The researcher's refusal to convert the SMD to '2-3%' without the pooled within-athlete SD is methodologically correct and creditable.

citationChecks.citation: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y. Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes. PLoS ONE 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 14 studies, TT SMD -0.45 (p<0.05), TTE SMD 1.28, no improvement in VO2max or economy of movement, taper-plus-pre-taper-overload better than conventional taper (p<0.05), and ≤21-day taper with 41-60% volume reduction at unchanged intensity and frequency. Worth adding for the athlete's benefit: this paper found NO taper effect on VO2max or running economy — the taper's gain is performance-expression, not adaptation.

citationChecks.citation: Casado A, González-Mohíno F, González-Ravé JM, Foster C. Training Periodization, Methods, Intensity Distribution, and Volume in Highly Trained and Elite Distance Runners. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2022;17(6):820-33. PMID 35418513
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact. Abstract confirms 10 articles, pyramidal TID with volume decreasing z1>z2>z3, zone-2 tempo/threshold intervals and zone-3 short/anaerobic intervals each used at least once per week, marathoners more pyramidal and 1500 m runners more polarised, and the recommendation of traditional periodisation on a hard-day/easy-day basis shifting from pyramidal in preparation toward polarised in competition. Correctly labelled observational with no causal claim.

citationChecks.citation: Garber CE, Blissmer B, Deschenes MR, et al. ACSM Position Stand: Quantity and Quality of Exercise... Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43(7):1334-59. PMID 21694556
citationChecks.note: Metadata exact, ACSM corporate authorship present. The researcher's characterisation — a general-adult health-and-fitness prescription containing no marathon-specific or interval-structure guidance, and which should not be cited as endorsing any competitive plan — is the honest reading and is the right call.

citationChecks.citation: Soligard T, Schwellnus M, Alonso JM, et al. How much is too much? (Part 1) IOC consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med 2016;50(17):1030-41. PMID 27535989; and Part 2, risk of illness, 50(17):1043-52. PMID 27535991
citationChecks.note: Both PMIDs verified with correct titles, journal, volume, issue and page ranges. Correctly labelled as a consensus statement (expert synthesis, not trial data).

citationChecks.citation: [myths] The 874-runner prospective cohort on the 10% rule — no formal citation given in the research output
citationChecks.note: The researcher stated this without a citation. It is Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. 'Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury.' J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2014;44(10):739-47. PMID 25155475. Every number checks out: 874 runners, 202 injuries, no statistically significant difference in injury rates across <10% / 10-30% / >30% groups, and HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96-2.66, P=.07) for distance-related injuries above 30% over two weeks. TWO OMISSIONS THAT MATTER: (a) the cohort was 874 healthy NOVICE runners on self-structured regimens — see population mismatches; (b) the paper's own conclusion is cautionary, not permissive: 'novice runners may be well advised to progress their weekly distances by less than 30% per week over a 2-week period.' The researcher quotes the null and the fig-leaf line but not the recommendation.

citationChecks.citation: [uncited] 'the Joyner (1991) model' — used as the VO2max-to-race-pace conversion machinery in the Milanović row and invoked again in the myths section, but never listed as a citation
citationChecks.note: Not fabricated, but not cited either. It is Joyner MJ. 'Modeling: optimal marathon performance on the basis of physiological factors.' J Appl Physiol 1991;70(2):683-7. PMID 2022559. Since two of the researcher's marathon-minutes conversions rest on this model's assumption that race pace scales with VO2max at fixed economy and fractional utilisation, it should have appeared as a formal citation with that assumption stated. Joyner has also updated the model: 'Modeling the marathon and human endurance performances: some thoughts and what's new?' 2025, PMID 39947644.

populationMismatches: Nielsen 2014 (the 10% rule myth-bust) — 874 healthy NOVICE runners on self-structured beginner regimens, tracked for one year. The researcher does not flag this at all, and it is the single most consequential mismatch in the set because it is used to license the riskiest element of the plan: a ramp from a 15 km week to a 100 km week. Injury-rate data from beginners going from 0 to ~15 km/week does not transfer to a trained runner quadrupling an already-substantial volume into a peak he has never touched. The direction of the error is unknown but the confidence is unjustified either way.

Rosenblat 2021 — the pooled sample is 34 cycling groups, 27 running, 6 rowing, i.e. a majority-cycling evidence base being applied to a runner. The researcher lists the modes but never discounts for it, despite the same paper's own full text showing that training MODE significantly modified the SIT response and produced a 1.2% (95% CI -0.2 to 2.6, p=0.094) running-vs-cycling difference in trained individuals. The paper's cleanest match to this athlete is the running subgroup, not the pooled trained subgroup.

Milanović 2015 — mean baseline VO2max 40.8 mL/kg/min, mixed exercise modalities, untrained-to-recreationally-active 18-45 y. The researcher flags this well (roughly 12 mL/kg/min below the athlete) and discounts appropriately.

Sylta 2016 — 63 trained CYCLISTS at VO2peak 61.3, a non-weight-bearing mode with no impact-injury mechanism and 8 mL/kg/min fitter. Flagged by the researcher; the null result does transfer more readily than a magnitude would.

Rønnestad 2014 (both studies) — trained CYCLISTS at VO2max 62-63, n=19 and n=15. Flagged well, and the researcher explicitly refuses to convert the 4.6% and warns that concentrating five hard sessions in one week is the same load spike Aubry showed overreaches half a cohort.

Aubry 2014 — trained male TRIATHLETES, with CYCLING performance as the outcome, in a controlled 3-week overload. Flagged. The unflagged part: this athlete's overload is a running volume ramp with an impact-loading injury mechanism the cycling protocol did not carry, so the 48% overreaching base rate may understate his risk for reasons beyond the ones the researcher gives.
Esteve-Lanao 2007 — 12 sub-elite 5000 m track specialists over 5 months. Flagged, and correctly declared non-convertible for a 6-week window.

Hoogkamer 2016 — 18 male sub-20-minute 5 km runners. The researcher claims the athlete sits inside this band, which makes the transfer coefficient unusually credible for him. That claim rests on a 19:39 'equivalent' derived from a 5.04 km training run at 3:54/km with average HR 172 against a max of 201 — a submaximal effort, not a raced 5 km. Treating an extrapolated training-run pace as membership of a sub-20 racing cohort is an inference, not a measurement, and it is load-bearing because the whole economy-to-minutes conversion chain hangs off it. Separately, this was an ACUTE shoe-mass manipulation, not a training adaptation; the coefficient may not hold for economy gained through training.

Bacon 2013 and HERITAGE 1999 — both sedentary/untrained baselines (334 sedentary or recreationally active under 45; 481 sedentary adults). The researcher flags both emphatically and correctly refuses to convert the 26.6-minute figure.
Reuter 2023 — 31 untrained participants aged 46±8 with baseline VO2max 34±4, i.e. two decades older and 19 mL/kg/min less fit. Flagged, non-convertible.
Hickson 1977 — 8 untrained subjects. Flagged; only the time-course shape is claimed to transfer, which is the right call.
Casado 2022 — highly trained and elite runners on 160-200 km/week. Flagged, with volumes explicitly excluded from transfer.

Bosquet 2007 and Wang 2023 — competitive athletes across mixed endurance sports; neither is marathon-specific and neither taper meta-analysis used a >2-hour event as the criterion performance. The researcher notes 'not marathon-specific' but does not draw out that a 2-week taper's evidence base is dominated by events an order of magnitude shorter than his race.
Feng 2026 — population not verifiable from the indexed abstract. The researcher says so explicitly rather than guessing, which is the correct handling.
effectSizeErrors: HOOGKAMER TRANSFER COEFFICIENT IS WRONG, AND IT PROPAGATES. The researcher derived 0.59 (= 0.65% time / 1.11% metabolic) from the +100 g condition alone — a data point whose reported SD (±1.36%) exceeds its mean (0.65%), i.e. the noisiest single estimate in the paper. The paper's own headline result, in the same abstract, is a linear fit across ALL the data: 3000-m time increased 0.78% per added 100 g per shoe (95% CI 0.52-1.04). Against 1.11% that gives 0.70, and the +300 g condition independently gives 2.37/3.33 = 0.71. Using the paper's estimate, the Feng running-economy row becomes 2.2% × 0.70 = 1.54% = 3.6 min rather than 3.1 min, and the researcher's stated rule of thumb should be '1% economy ≈ 0.7% time ≈ 1.7 min', not 1.4 min.

THE ROSENBLAT '~5 MIN, TWO ROUTES AGREE' CONVERGENCE IS AN ARTEFACT — the two routes are not independent, they are the same quantity computed twice, and one of them is computed wrongly. Route 1 (category) uses the trained group's TOTAL improvement of ~2%. Route 2 (dose) takes the meta-regression slope beta=0.21% per HIIT session and multiplies it by 10 sessions to get 2.1%. But a meta-regression slope describes the marginal difference between studies within the observed range of session counts, not a line through the origin; there is no zero-session anchor, so '10 sessions × 0.21% = 2.1% total' is not a claim the model supports. It also contradicts the paper's own stated conclusion that 'increasing interval training dose beyond minimal requirements may not augment the training response'. The apparent agreement of the two routes should not be read as corroboration.

THE 2.0% QUOTED AS THE FORMAL VERSION OF 'TRAINED IMPROVE ~2%' IS A DIFFERENT STATISTIC. The thesis's 2.0% (95% CI 0.6-3.4, p=0.006) is the BETWEEN-GROUP difference (active minus trained), while the abstract's 'trained individuals only seeing improvements of approximately 2%' is the trained group's ABSOLUTE gain. These are two different 2%s that happen to coincide numerically, and the researcher presents the between-group CI as though it bounded the absolute effect. The conversion needs the absolute figure, whose confidence interval is not reported in either the abstract or the section of the thesis quoted.

ROSENBLAT 2020 CI TRANSCRIBED WRONGLY: '90% CI -0.1% to 1.9%' should be '-1.2% to 1.9%'. The true interval is compatible with SIT being 1.2% better than HIIT; the narrowed version makes the null look one-sided in HIIT's favour.

BACON'S PUBLICATION-BIAS CORRECTION OMITTED. The researcher quotes +0.51 L/min (95% CI 0.43-0.60) and 0.86 SDs (0.72-0.99) accurately from the full text, but the immediately following sentences report funnel-plot asymmetry and a Trim-and-Fill corrected estimate of 0.37 L/min — 27% lower. Given the researcher used Bacon to bound what is trainable, the corrected figure is the more conservative and more decision-relevant one, and its omission runs the same direction as the Egger's-test caveat they DID report for Rosenblat.

MILANOVIĆ MODIFIER REPORTED SELECTIVELY. 'Longer HIT repetitions' appears twice in that abstract with opposite signs: +2.2 (±2.1) in the HIT-vs-endurance comparison, and -1.8 (±2.7) in the HIT-vs-control comparison. Only the positive one is reported, and it is then used to build a 'longer intervals are better' convergence with Rosenblat's beta=0.37. Both estimates have confidence limits spanning zero.

ARITHMETIC ITSELF IS CLEAN — I re-derived every conversion and found no calculation errors. 3:55:54 = 235.9 min correct. +1.2 on 53.0 = 2.264%, × 235.9 = 5.3 min correct; the ±0.9 floor of +0.3 giving 1.3 min correct. 0.51 L/min ÷ 85.5 kg = 5.96 mL/kg/min = +11.25% = 26.5 min correct. 35.5 s / 2340 s = 1.5% = 3.5 min correct. 2.6% = 6.1 min correct. 4.6% = 10.9 min correct. 6 reps × 0.14% = 0.84% = 2.0 min correct. Dose CI 0.7%/3.5% = 1.65/8.26 min correct. Riegel checks also correct: 19:39 over 5 km projects 3:08:29 and 1:46:35 over the half projects 3:42:14 at exponent 1.06, giving the stated ~47-minute gap. The errors in this domain are in which number was chosen and what statistic it is, not in the multiplication.
missedEvidence: STRENGTH AND PLYOMETRIC TRAINING FOR RUNNING ECONOMY — an entire intervention class, meta-analytically supported, absent from the research. Balsalobre-Fernández C, Santos-Concejero J, Grivas GV. 'Effects of Strength Training on Running Economy in Highly Trained Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials.' J Strength Cond Res 2016;30(8):2361-8, PMID 26694507. And Eihara Y, Takao K, Sugiyama T, et al. 'Heavy Resistance Training Versus Plyometric Training for Improving Running Economy and Running Time Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.' 2022, PMID 36370207. This matters more than any interval-format question the research answers: it targets the same economy channel as the Feng row, it fits inside six weeks, it is done in highly trained RUNNERS rather than cyclists, and critically it does not compete with running volume for the athlete's recovery budget the way a third quality session does. A domain review that concludes 'intervals buy economy' without mentioning the strength-training economy literature has left out the better-evidenced half of that claim.

ZANINI M, FOLLAND JP, WU H, BLAGROVE RC. 'Strength Training Improves Running Economy Durability and Fatigued High-Intensity Performance in Well-Trained Male Runners: A Randomized Controlled Trial.' 2025, PMID 40016936. A 10-week RCT in 28 well-trained male runners (VO2max 58.6, 10 km 39:02 — a close population match) measuring running economy across 90 minutes at MARATHON race intensity, plus fatigued high-intensity performance. This directly attacks the durability limiter the researcher identifies as this athlete's actual binding constraint, and it partly FALSIFIES their listed unknown that 'how economy and its transfer coefficient behave over four hours is unmeasured'.

ZANINI M, FOLLAND JP, BLAGROVE RC. 'Regular Long Runs and Higher Training Volumes Are Associated with Better Running Economy Durability in Performance Matched Well-Trained Runners.' 2026, PMID 40878015. Two performance-MATCHED groups of 13 male runners differing only in whether they did regular ≥90 min long runs, compared on economy decay over a 90-min run. This is the closest published evidence to the question 'does the long run and the volume buy anything for a marathoner, holding fitness constant' — the question the entire 60/80/100/80/60 ramp is premised on — and it cuts against the 'skip the long run' misreading the researcher rightly identifies as dangerous, with data rather than with argument.

THE DURABILITY LITERATURE GENERALLY, declared unmeasured but extant: Zanini et al. 'Durability of Running Economy: Differences between Quantification Methods and Performance Status in Male Runners' 2024, PMID 38857519 (44 male runners, VO2max 62.4); Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D. 'Durability of Parameters Associated With Endurance Running in Marathoners' 2025, PMID 41128270; Zanini M, Jones AM, Nybo L. 'Defining physiological resilience and durability in the context of endurance performance modeling' 2025, PMID 41396096; Meixner BJ, Joyner MJ, Sperlich B. 'Durability, fatigability, repeatability, and resilience in endurance sports' 2025, PMID 40590809. The researcher's unknown #6 overstates the emptiness of this field.

KENNEALLY M, CASADO A, SANTOS-CONCEJERO J. 'The Effect of Periodization and Training Intensity Distribution on Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review.' Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2018, PMID 29182410. A running-specific systematic review of exactly the TID and periodisation question the researcher answered with a cycling-heavy meta-analysis and an elite-practice description. Also Kenneally et al. 2021, PMID 32449500, on race-pace versus physiological TID quantification in world-class distance runners — which matters because how you define the zones changes which distribution you appear to be doing.

CARBOHYDRATE INTAKE DURING EXERCISE — the largest evidence base in the domain, on a limiter the researcher explicitly names and then supplies nothing for. Ramos-Campo DJ et al. 'The ergogenic effects of acute carbohydrate feeding on endurance performance: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression.' 2024, PMID 37449467 — 136 studies. And Vandenbogaerde TJ, Hopkins WG. 'Effects of acute carbohydrate supplementation on endurance performance: a meta-analysis.' Sports Med 2011, PMID 21846165 — 88 randomised crossover studies, 155 effect estimates. The research states three times that this athlete's marathon-specific limiter is 'fractional utilisation, durability and fuelling' and that his 47-minute gap is not a VO2max deficit, then produces zero evidence on fuelling. It is the best-evidenced, fastest-acting, lowest-injury-risk lever available inside six weeks, and it is the one the plan can adopt without fighting the volume ramp for recovery.

BACON'S OWN TRIM-AND-FILL CORRECTION (0.37 L/min, down from 0.51) — not missed literature but missed content inside a paper the researcher had open in full text. It cuts the same way as the Egger's finding they did report.

JOYNER MJ. 'Modeling: optimal marathon performance on the basis of physiological factors.' J Appl Physiol 1991;70(2):683-7, PMID 2022559 — invoked twice as the conversion model but never cited, so its central assumption (race pace scales with VO2max only when economy and fractional utilisation are held constant) is never put in front of the athlete as an assumption. Joyner's own 2025 update, PMID 39947644, revisits it.

domains.title: Training volume and the dose-response curve for marathon time

research.domain: Training volume and the dose-response curve for marathon time — quantified, with the causal question addressed head-on
