Full-text retrieval: PMC12441744 (Boston 2022 cohort), PMC7496388 (Fokkema 2020), PMC5000509 (Vickers 2016), PMC11065819 (Knopp 2024), repository.londonmet.ac.uk/9883 (Muniz-Pumares 2025 accepted manuscript PDF)

interventions.intervention: Higher habitual weekly mileage — cross-sectional coefficient (the number most often quoted at recreational runners)
interventions.effect: Marathon time difference between training 50 vs 30 miles/week (80.5 vs 48.3 km/wk) = 25 min 32 s for men (31 min 41 s for women), adjusted for age, BMI, sex, interval training and tempo running. That is 0.79 min per km/week, i.e. ~7.9 min per extra 10 km/week. p<0.0005. Modelled with cubic splines, so the coefficient is local to the 30–50 mi/wk range.
interventions.population: 2,303 recreational runners (1,022 with marathon data), median age 35, 61% male, median weekly mileage 40 mi (64 km) among marathoners, median male marathon 3:28. Only 7 of 2,303 hit an Olympic qualifying standard — a genuinely recreational sample, the closest published population to this athlete.
interventions.citation: Vickers AJ, Vertosick EA. An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2016;8:26. doi:10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y (PMID 27570626, PMC5000509)
interventions.duration: Cross-sectional survey — 'typical weekly training mileage', i.e. habitual volume, not a six-week block
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO, not as stated. The coefficient describes runners whose bodies were built at that volume over months-to-years, not runners who arrived at it six weeks ago. The authors themselves hedge in the paper: 'If these associations are seen to be causal, then we could say that…'. Nothing in the design licenses reading it as what happens when one runner adds mileage.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Naive application: his six-month average is 24.4 km/wk; the ratified block averages (60+80+100+80+60)/5 = 76 km/wk. Δ = +51.6 km/wk × 0.79 min = 41 min → 3:15. This number is almost certainly wrong and is the single most over-claimable figure in this domain. Three reasons it fails: (a) it extrapolates below the 30 mi/wk spline anchor, where his 24 km/wk (15 mi/wk) sits; (b) it prices habitual volume, not six weeks of it; (c) the one randomised test of the same contrast found nothing (see Enoksen row). A defensible ceiling from his OWN data is much smaller — see the Riegel-gap row.

interventions.intervention: Volume category in a real marathon-preparation cohort of recreational runners (Rotterdam)
interventions.effect: Versus the 40–65 km/wk reference: training >65 km/wk associated with a finish time 14.09 min faster (95% CI −22.47 to −5.72); training <40 km/wk associated with 6.33 min slower (95% CI +0.18 to +12.48). A longest run <25 km: 13.44 min slower (95% CI 5.34 to 21.55). Notably, NO association was found between training volume or long-run distance and running-related injury.
interventions.population: 441 recreational marathon runners preparing for the Rotterdam Marathon; mean weekly volume 43.6 ± 27.3 km, longest run 29.1 ± 8.5 km, training pace 5:41/km, mean finish 4:17:54 ± 0:37:14, mean age 42, 65% male. This is the closest published cohort to this athlete in ability and volume.
interventions.citation: Fokkema T, van Damme AADN, Fornerod MWJ, de Vos R-J, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, van Middelkoop M. Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2020;30(9):1692–1704. doi:10.1111/sms.13725 (PMC7496388)
interventions.duration: Prospective, three questionnaires across the preparation period and immediately post-race
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: PARTIALLY. The exposure is the preparation block itself, not lifetime habit, which makes it more relevant than Vickers. But it is still between-runner: the runners in the >65 km/wk group chose that volume and could sustain it. It does not say what happens to a 24 km/wk runner dropped into 80 km/wk with six weeks to go.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Moving from the <40 km/wk category to the >65 km/wk category = 6.33 + 14.09 = 20.4 min, with a combined uncertainty range of roughly 6–35 min. On 3:55:54 that is 3:35 (range 3:21–3:50). Halve it if you believe only half the association is causal; the honest answer is that nobody knows the fraction.

interventions.intervention: Habitual weekly running distance in the 12–4 months before the race (Boston Marathon cohort)
interventions.effect: Each +1 km/week of running distance in the 12–4 month window: race time improved ~0.6 min (β −0.01 h, 95% CI −0.02 to −0.005, p<0.001). Each +1 running session/week: ~3.6 min (β −0.06, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.02). Each +1 quality (hard) session/week: ~16.2 min (β −0.27, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.10). Model R² = 0.485. Separately, runners who DECREASED running sessions/week in the final 4 months ran faster (β −0.05, 95% CI −0.09 to −0.003, p=0.035).
interventions.population: 917 registrants of the 2022 Boston Marathon, mean age 47±14, 95% classified tier-2 'trained/developmental'. Males: 3:35 ± 0:39 off 67.6 ± 26.2 km/wk. Females: 3:53 ± 0:37 off 64.4 ± 24 km/wk.
interventions.citation: DeJong Lempke AF, Ackerman KE, Stellingwerff T, et al. Training Volume and Training Frequency Changes Associated with Boston Marathon Race Performance. Sports Medicine. 2025. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02304-4 (PMC12441744)
interventions.duration: Retrospective self-report over two windows: 12–4 months and 4–0 months pre-race; recall bias acknowledged by the authors
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO for the volume coefficient — the window it prices (12–4 months out) is October 2025 to June 2026 and is already spent; his actual habitual volume across it was ~24 km/wk. YES for the frequency finding, which points the other way: the runners who cut sessions in the final months ran faster, which is evidence against a late ramp.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0.6 min per km/wk of habitual volume — so the ~24 km/wk he actually ran in that window, versus a counterfactual 60 km/wk, is worth ~22 min. That is a verdict on the last year, not on the next six weeks. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON THIS PAPER: the 4–0 month coefficient it reports (β −0.22, '~13 min faster per 1 km/week', 95% CI '−0.48, −0.34') is internally broken — the CI does not bracket the point estimate, and 13 min per km/week implies 130 min off a marathon for +10 km/wk. Do not use that figure. I flag it because it is the sort of number a plan-generating tool would happily swallow.

interventions.intervention: Weekly training volume across performance levels — the 119,452-runner Strava analysis (the '90% of variance' dataset)
interventions.effect: Whole dataset: 45.1 ± 26.4 km/wk over the 16 weeks pre-race, 3.6 ± 1.7 sessions/wk, weekly long run 19.6 ± 9.6 km, mean finish 230.2 ± 41.9 min (3:50). By finish band: 2:00–2:30 ≈ 107 km/wk (n=620); 2:30–3:00 ≈ 67 km/wk (derived from the paper's stated '~60% higher than the next group'); 4:30–5:00 ≈ 35 km/wk (n=8,798). Correlations between marathon time and volume markers computed on GROUP MEANS: R² ≥ 0.90. Individual-level OLS: adjusted R² = 0.596, with total distance β = −0.3317 min/km (SE 0.0010) and total training time β = +0.0581 min/min (SE 0.0002).
interventions.population: 119,452 recreational Strava runners, 151,813 marathons, 2014–2017, 76% male, mean age 39.5. Mean finish 3:50 — this athlete sits almost exactly at the dataset mean.
interventions.citation: Muniz-Pumares D, Hunter B, Meyler S, Maunder E, Smyth B. The Training Intensity Distribution of Marathon Runners Across Performance Levels. Sports Medicine. 2025;55(4):1023–1035. doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7 (PMID 39616560; accepted manuscript at repository.londonmet.ac.uk/9883)
interventions.duration: 16 weeks of training data preceding each marathon
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO. It measures the whole 16-week block, of which he has six weeks left, and it is entirely between-runner.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Two answers, and the gap between them is the point. (a) From the binned group means: 35 → 67 km/wk spans 4:45 → 2:45, i.e. 3.75 min per km/wk; 67 → 107 km/wk spans only 30 min, i.e. 0.75 min per km/wk. The curve is steepest exactly where he sits and flattens hard above ~70 km/wk. (b) From the paper's own individual-level regression, adding 10 km/wk for 16 weeks = +160 km and, at his easy pace of ~6:15/km, +1,000 min of training time: −0.3317×160 + 0.0581×1000 = −53.1 + 58.1 = +5.0 min SLOWER. At a 5:30/km training pace it is −2.0 min faster. Net: essentially zero. The multivariable model, which holds training TIME constant, says volume per se buys almost nothing — the apparent volume effect is carried by pace and by the collinearity between distance and time. Neither coefficient is individually interpretable, but the contrast between (a) and (b) is a clean demonstration of how much of the headline correlation is an artefact of aggregation.

interventions.intervention: Randomly assigning trained runners to HIGHER weekly volume (the closest thing to an experiment)
interventions.effect: 70 km/wk low-intensity vs 50 km/wk higher-intensity, 10 weeks, matched on pretest and randomly assigned. NO significant between-group differences on VO2max, velocity at VO2max, running economy, lactate-threshold velocity, or the performance test, before OR after. Both groups improved running economy; the LOWER-volume group had the larger gains in vVO2max and vLT. Performance-test progress: high-volume group 218 ± 546 m, low-volume group 301 ± 886 m — indistinguishable, and the error bars swamp the means.
interventions.population: 26 well-trained male middle-distance runners, Norwegian School of Sport Sciences, precompetition period
interventions.citation: Enoksen E, Shalfawi SAI, Tønnessen E. The effect of high- vs. low-intensity training on aerobic capacity in well-trained male middle-distance runners. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(3):812–818. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181cc2291 (PMID 20647950)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: This is the most important row in the table. A 40% volume difference, randomly assigned, in already-trained runners, over a window nearly twice as long as his block, produced no measurable performance advantage. The cross-sectional coefficient (Vickers) predicts 50 → 70 km/wk should be worth ~16 min on a marathon; the randomised comparison found an effect indistinguishable from zero.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0 min (95% CI not reported; with n=26 and a between-group SD of ~700 m on the performance test, this trial could not have detected anything smaller than a large effect — absence of evidence, but it is the only randomised evidence that exists). The outcome was a middle-distance performance test, not a marathon, so it does not rule out a marathon-specific volume effect operating through fuelling and durability.

interventions.intervention: A sudden large volume increase in already-trained athletes — the direct test of a ramp
interventions.effect: Training distance DOUBLED (4,266 → 8,970 m/day) for 10 consecutive days at ~95% VO2max. No significant change in any performance measure (365.8 m maximal swim, two 22.9 m sprints, semi-tethered power). Pre-exercise cortisol rose 17.5 → 20.6 µg/dl and creatine kinase rose 56.2 → 119.0 U/l (both p<0.05). Estimated plasma volume rose 11.4 ± 2.7%.
interventions.population: 12 male collegiate competitive swimmers
interventions.citation: Kirwan JP, Costill DL, Flynn MG, Mitchell JB, Fink WJ, Neufer PD, Houmard JA. Physiological responses to successive days of intense training in competitive swimmers. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 1988;20(3):255–259. (PMID 3386504)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Directly. It is the only published test of 'what happens when a trained athlete abruptly doubles training volume', and the answer over ~1.5 weeks was: nothing to performance, measurable stress-marker elevation, and a fast plasma-volume expansion. Swimming, not running, so the mechanical-loading cost of the same manoeuvre in running is missing (and it is the cost that matters most here).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0 min from the volume itself in the short term. The plasma-volume expansion (+11%) is real and fast (days), and does transfer — it raises stroke volume and heat tolerance — but it is not a 'volume' adaptation so much as a fluid one, and it reverses within days of stopping.

interventions.intervention: CUTTING volume sharply in trained runners (the mirror-image test)
interventions.effect: Replacing ~45 km/wk of endurance training with 8–12 × 30 s sprints plus easy running (total 15.6 km/wk — a 65% volume cut) for 4 weeks: 10-km performance time UNCHANGED, VO2max unchanged, citrate synthase and HAD activity unchanged, capillary-to-fibre ratio unchanged. Submaximal oxygen uptake fell 5.7–7.6% at 11–16 km/h (p<0.05), i.e. running economy improved.
interventions.population: 17 endurance-trained runners (9 intervention, 8 control), Copenhagen
interventions.citation: Iaia FM, Hellsten Y, Nielsen JJ, Fernström M, Sahlin K, Bangsbo J. Four weeks of speed endurance training reduces energy expenditure during exercise and maintains muscle oxidative capacity despite a reduction in training volume. Journal of Applied Physiology. 2009;106(1):73–80. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.90676.2008 (PMID 18845781)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Directly, and it is the strongest evidence that inside a 4–6 week window volume is not the lever. Existing aerobic machinery is not lost, and is not obviously gained, on that timescale.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0 min lost from a 65% volume cut over 4 weeks in trained runners. Caveat: the outcome was 10 km, and marathon-specific durability (glycogen storage, fat oxidation, connective-tissue tolerance of 3.5 hours of ground contact) was not measured, and is precisely the thing a marathon block is supposed to build.

interventions.intervention: Tapering — the one volume manipulation with high-grade evidence that fits inside six weeks
interventions.effect: Meta-analysis: optimal taper = 2 weeks, training volume reduced exponentially by 41–60%, intensity and frequency UNCHANGED. Overall effect size 0.59 ± 0.33 for a 2-week taper (p<0.001); 0.72 ± 0.36 for the 41–60% volume reduction specifically. Typical performance gains from tapering in the underlying literature are 0.5–6%, centred around 2–3%.
interventions.population: 27 studies of competitive athletes across endurance sports (from 182 screened)
interventions.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2007;39(8):1358–1365. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0 (PMID 17762369)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES — this is the highest-confidence performance lever available inside his block, and it is a within-subject, pre-post effect rather than a between-runner association.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 2–3% of 235.9 min = 4.7 to 7.1 min. Working: 235.9 × 0.02 = 4.7; × 0.03 = 7.1. On 3:55:54 that is 3:48:48 to 3:51:11. This is real minutes, purchasable in the last two weeks, and it is directly threatened by a plan whose fourth and fifth weeks are 80 and 60 km — those need to be the taper, not 'still building'.

interventions.intervention: Taper discipline, measured in recreational marathoners at scale
interventions.effect: A strict 3-week taper (progressively decreasing weekly distance) vs a minimal taper: median finish-time saving 5 min 32.4 s, or 2.6% (Kruskal-Wallis H(7) ≥ 521.11, p<0.001; post-hoc Dunn with Bonferroni, p<0.001). Longer tapers up to 3 weeks beat shorter ones; strict beat relaxed. 64% of recreational runners taper less disciplinedly than optimal.
interventions.population: 158,000+ recreational marathon runners (Strava)
interventions.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2021;3:735220. doi:10.3389/fspor.2021.735220 (PMC8506252)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES. Between-runner, so subject to the same confounding caveat as every registry number — but it replicates the controlled-trial finding (Bosquet) in exactly this athlete's population, which is the kind of convergence that should move belief.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 2.6% of 235.9 = 6.1 min. Consistent with the Bosquet-derived 4.7–7.1 min. Two independent designs agreeing on ~5–7 min makes this the best-supported number in the whole domain for this athlete.

interventions.intervention: Avoiding a training disruption (within-runner natural experiment — the design that actually addresses confounding)
interventions.effect: Comparing the SAME runners' disrupted vs undisrupted marathons: a training disruption of ≥7 days costs 5–8% of finish time. Disruptions late in training cost 5.2% vs 4.4% for early ones. Male runners lose 5% vs 3.5% for females; faster runners lose 5.4% vs 2.6% for slower ones.
interventions.population: 300,000 recreational marathon runners, >15 million activities, 2014–2017; analysis restricted to runners with at least one disrupted and one undisrupted marathon
interventions.citation: Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A. Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2023;4:1096124. doi:10.3389/fspor.2022.1096124 (PMC9871827)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES, and it is the risk side of the ledger. Each runner is his own control, which removes the between-runner selection problem that ruins the cross-sectional coefficients. It is the best-designed number in this domain.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: A ≥7-day break late in the block costs 5.2% × 235.9 = 12.3 min. He already took one zero-kilometre week three weeks ago. A second one — which is the modal outcome of a 24 → 60 → 80 → 100 km/wk ramp — wipes out roughly twice the entire taper benefit. Expected-value framing: if the ramp raises the probability of a ≥7-day layoff by even 25 percentage points, that is 0.25 × 12.3 = 3.1 min of expected loss against a volume benefit that the randomised evidence puts at zero.

interventions.intervention: Rate of volume progression and injury risk
interventions.effect: Progressing weekly running distance by >30% over a 2-week period vs <10%: hazard ratio 1.59 for distance-related injuries (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, gluteus medius injury, trochanteric bursitis, TFL injury, patellar tendinopathy), 95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, p=0.07. Across ALL injury types there were no significant differences between the <10%, 10–30% and >30% groups.
interventions.population: 874 healthy novice runners on self-structured programmes, GPS-tracked for 1 year; 202 sustained a running-related injury
interventions.citation: Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):739–747. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164 (PMID 25155475)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES, and it is the constraint the ratified block violates most severely. Novices, not a 5-month-trained runner, so transfer is imperfect — but note the direction of the bias: a runner whose all-time peak week is 57.1 km is a novice with respect to 100 km.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not directly convertible; convertible only through the disruption cost. His week 1 is 24 → 60 km/wk, a +150% jump (or +212% against his last four weeks' 19.25 km/wk average). Weeks 2 and 3 are +33% and +25%, both at or above the 30% threshold, on top of a body that has never held 60 km. Note the honesty requirement: the hazard ratio's CI crosses 1 (0.96–2.66) and p=0.07 — this is a suggestive association, not a demonstrated one, and the authors themselves call the study exploratory and call for RCTs.

interventions.intervention: What experienced coaches actually prescribe (expert practice, quantified)
interventions.effect: Across 92 publicly available sub-elite 12-week marathon plans: mean weekly volume in the final 12 weeks was 107.7 km (high-volume plans), 58.5 km (middle), 42.9 km (low). Peak-week thresholds defining those bands: >90, 65–90, <65 km/wk. Longest run 35.2 km (high) to 30.9 km (low). Intensity distribution pyramidal in every band: 13.2% zone 1, 65.6% zone 2, 15.1% zone 3, 3.0% zone 4, 3.0% zone 5.
interventions.population: 92 published marathon training plans aimed at sub-elite/recreational runners
interventions.citation: Knopp M, Appelhans D, Schönfelder M, Seiler S, et al. Quantitative Analysis of 92 12-Week Sub-elite Marathon Training Plans. Sports Medicine – Open. 2024;10:50. doi:10.1186/s40798-024-00717-5 (PMC11065819)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: As a benchmark, yes. The authors are explicit about the limitation: 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated'. It tells you what is conventional, not what works.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — no outcome data attached to the plans. Its value here is calibration: his ratified block averages 76 km/wk and peaks at 100 km, which places it between the 'middle' (58.5 km) and 'high' (107.7 km) bands of plans written for sub-elite runners. That is a plan shape designed for someone whose baseline is 60 km/wk, not 24.

interventions.intervention: Meta-regression across the whole marathon training literature (the widest-scope estimate)
interventions.effect: Univariate random-effects meta-regressions found a negative association between marathon finish time and every one of: average weekly running distance, number of weekly runs, maximum single-week distance, number of runs ≥32 km in the pre-marathon block, average training pace, longest-run distance, and weekly running hours (R² 0.38–0.81, p<0.001). Marathon non-finish rate: 7.27% (95% CI 6.09–8.65%).
interventions.population: 137 cohorts of elite and recreational marathon runners (25% female) from 85 studies
interventions.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B. An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020;23(2):182–188. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2019.09.013 (PMID 31704026)
interventions.duration: Pooled across observational and interventional studies of varying length
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO. The unit of analysis is the cohort, not the runner — this is a meta-regression across study-level means, so it is an ecological analysis and inherits every confound of its inputs plus aggregation bias. Every training variable is 'significant' because they are all proxies for one another and for fitness.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to this athlete without the per-unit coefficients, which the abstract does not report and which I could not retrieve (the full text is paywalled at ScienceDirect; ResearchGate returned 403). I am flagging that rather than inventing a coefficient. Treat this paper as establishing direction and consistency, not magnitude.

interventions.intervention: Elite reference points (what the top of the curve looks like — included because it is the source of most transferred-and-wrong advice)
interventions.effect: 2004 US Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers: men ran 145.3 ± 25.6 km/wk over 8.7 ± 2.8 sessions/wk; women 116.0 ± 26.5 km/wk over 7.1 ± 2.5. Elite women (<2:40) ran 135.8 ± 31.5 km/wk vs national-class 111.3 ± 23.3. Men ran 75% and women 68% of weekly distance below marathon race pace. Weekly distance correlated with marathon time for WOMEN but the relationship was weaker for men. 49% of men and 31% of women had no coach. Separately, in top-class marathoners (<2:11 men), higher weekly kilometres and higher training velocity distinguished top-class from high-level, and VO2peak predicted 59% of the variance in marathon time.
interventions.population: 93 US Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers (37 M, 56 W) of 255 contacted — a 36% response rate; and 20 top-class/high-level international marathoners
interventions.citation: Karp JR. Training characteristics of qualifiers for the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2007;2(1):72–92. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2.1.72 (PMID 19255456). And: Billat VL, Demarle A, Slawinski J, Paiva M, Koralsztein JP. Physical and training characteristics of top-class marathon runners. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2001;33(12):2089–2097. (PMID 11740304)
interventions.duration: The training year preceding the Trials (Karp); 8 weeks before Olympic trials (Billat)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO, and it should not be applied at all to this athlete. Karp's own conclusion is the useful one: 'Among U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers, there is no consensus as to how to prepare for the marathon beyond running at a pace slower than race pace.' If the best-selected marathon population in the United States shows no consensus, a prescriptive volume number for a 24 km/wk recreational runner is not derivable from elite practice.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. These athletes reached 145 km/wk after 12.2 ± 5.3 years of training; the volume is a consequence of the physiology as much as a cause of it.

interventions.intervention: Reading his own data instead of the registry: the Riegel gap as a volume-attributable ceiling
interventions.effect: Vickers & Vertosick found the Riegel formula (time_y/time_x = (dist_y/dist_x)^k) is well-calibrated up to the half marathon but 'dramatically underestimates marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners', and that weekly mileage predicts the correct value of k for an individual. Riegel's own k values: 1.08 elite, 1.05–1.06 male recreational aged 40–70.
interventions.population: 2,303 recreational runners as above; validated on a held-out set of 721
interventions.citation: Vickers AJ, Vertosick EA. An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2016;8:26. doi:10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: This is the most defensible way to bound what volume could buy HIM specifically, because it uses his own measured short-race fitness as the anchor rather than a between-runner regression.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: his half PB 1:46:35 = 106.58 min. Riegel with k=1.06: 106.58 × 2^1.06 = 106.58 × 2.0851 = 222.2 min = 3:42:15. He actually ran 3:55:54 = 235.9 min. His shortfall against his own half-marathon fitness is 13.7 min. His 5 km equivalent (19:39) predicts 188.5 min = 3:08:30, i.e. a 47-minute shortfall — but the Vickers result says Riegel systematically overshoots from short races, so the 5 km figure is not a real target. The 13.7 min from the half is the honest size of his 'endurance gap' — the portion of his marathon time attributable to insufficient marathon-specific preparation rather than to aerobic power. That is the realistic ceiling for what a volume-and-long-run block could return, versus the 41 min the raw cross-sectional coefficient implies. Note his half is being re-run on 2026-09-12, three days from now, which will re-anchor this estimate with fresh data.

myths: 'Weekly mileage explains more than 90% of marathon performance.' This is the single most-repeated number from the 119,452-runner Strava study and it is a misreading. The R² ≥ 0.90 figures are correlations computed on GROUP MEANS after binning runners into 30-minute finish-time bands — an ecological correlation, which inflates R² by averaging away all within-group variance. In the same paper, the individual-level regression has adjusted R² = 0.596, and the volume coefficient is entangled with a training-time coefficient of the opposite sign. Source: Muniz-Pumares et al. 2025, Table 2 and Figure 5.

'Increase volume by no more than 10% per week and you won't get injured.' The 10% rule has been tested in a randomised controlled trial and failed. GRONORUN randomised 532 novice runners to a graded 13-week programme built on the 10% rule versus a standard 8-week programme: injury incidence 20.8% vs 20.3% (chi-square 0.016, p=0.90). Source: Buist I et al., American Journal of Sports Medicine 2008;36(1):33–39. The nearest thing to an evidence-based threshold is Nielsen's >30% over two weeks, and even that had a CI crossing 1 (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96–2.66, p=0.07).

'Higher mileage causes injuries, so a big block is dangerous because of the volume itself.' In the cohort closest to this athlete — 997 runners preparing for the Rotterdam half and full marathon — no association was found between weekly training volume or longest-run distance and running-related injuries, despite a 55% injury rate in the marathon group. Source: Fokkema et al. 2020. The risk in his block is the RATE OF CHANGE and the absolute novelty of 100 km, not high mileage as such.

'Peak week volume is what determines your marathon.' The Boston Marathon cohort found that runners who DECREASED running sessions per week in the final 4 months ran faster than those who maintained or increased them (β −0.05, 95% CI −0.09 to −0.003, p=0.035), while it was habitual volume 12–4 months out that carried the association with performance. Source: DeJong Lempke et al. 2025.

'Faster runners train more, so training more will make you faster.' The inference runs backwards at least as strongly as forwards. Karp's Olympic Trials qualifiers reached 145 km/wk after 12.2 ± 5.3 years of training. Being able to absorb 100 km/wk without breaking is itself a phenotype — high VO2max, good running economy, injury-resistant tissue — and that phenotype causes both the volume and the finish time. No published study has instrumented or randomised its way past this.

'Six weeks is enough to build the aerobic base.' The only randomised comparison of high versus low volume in trained runners ran for 10 weeks at a 40% volume difference and found nothing (Enoksen 2011). Doubling volume for 10 days in trained athletes produced zero performance change and raised cortisol and creatine kinase (Kirwan/Costill 1988). Cutting volume by 65% for 4 weeks in trained runners cost nothing in 10 km time or muscle oxidative capacity (Iaia 2009). The volume dial does not move performance on a six-week timescale in an already-trained runner, in either direction.

'A 5 km time predicts your marathon.' Riegel extrapolation from short races 'dramatically underestimates marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners' (Vickers & Vertosick 2016). His 19:39 5 km implies 3:08 and that number is meaningless. The half-marathon extrapolation is the one that is well-calibrated.

'Elite training distributions are the model to copy.' The fastest runners in the 119,452-runner recreational dataset ran ~67% (men) and ~57% (women) of training time in zone 1, well short of the ~80% reported in elites — and the authors attribute the discrepancy to the volume difference (107 vs 160–220 km/wk), i.e. the elite distribution is a consequence of elite volume, not a template that transfers downward.
unknowns: No randomised controlled trial has ever assigned recreational marathon runners to different weekly training volumes with marathon finish time as the outcome. Not one. The entire dose-response literature for marathon time is observational; the closest randomised evidence is Enoksen 2011 (n=26 middle-distance runners, 70 vs 50 km/wk, 10 weeks, no difference on a middle-distance performance test). Every minutes-per-kilometre figure in this report — including the ones I computed — rests on that gap.

What fraction of the volume–performance association is causal is genuinely unquantified. No published marathon study uses instrumental variables, sibling/twin designs, or a within-runner volume-change design. The one within-runner design that exists (Feely 2023) prices training DISRUPTION, not training INCREASE, and its answer — that losing a week costs 5–8% — is not symmetric evidence that gaining volume returns 5–8%.

Whether a volume ramp inside a six-week window improves marathon time at all is untested. No study has randomised trained recreational runners to ramp versus hold in the final six weeks and measured finish time. The mechanistic evidence is ambiguous: plasma volume expands within days (+11.4% in 10 days, Kirwan 1988) and running economy can improve in 4 weeks even on reduced volume (Iaia 2009), but connective-tissue and bone remodelling operate on months, and no one has measured which of these is rate-limiting for a 3:55 marathoner.

Where the dose-response curve saturates for an individual is unknown. The between-runner curve appears to flatten above ~70 km/wk (from ~3.75 min per km/wk between 35 and 67 km/wk down to ~0.75 min per km/wk between 67 and 107 km/wk in the Strava data) but that shape is contaminated by selection at every point on it, and the individual curve may have a completely different shape or an individual-specific ceiling.

How much volume is required for a given finish time cannot be answered as a threshold, because the between-runner spread swamps the between-band differences. The Strava dataset's volume SD is 26.4 km/wk against a mean of 45.1 — the spread within the population is 59% of the mean. Anchors that ARE defensible: sub-4:00 ≈ 45 km/wk (dataset mean 45.1 ± 26.4 km/wk at a mean finish of 3:50); sub-3:45 ≈ 60–65 km/wk (Boston female mean 3:53 at 64.4 ± 24 km/wk); sub-3:30 ≈ 65–70 km/wk (Boston male mean 3:35 at 67.6 ± 26.2 km/wk; Vickers male marathoners median 3:28 at a median 64 km/wk). Every one of those has an SD of roughly ±25 km/wk, meaning plenty of sub-3:30 runners train on 40 km/wk and plenty of 4:30 runners train on 90.

Individual trainability is unpredictable in advance. VO2max responses to identical standardised training programmes range from essentially zero to +100% across individuals, and age, sex and ethnicity explain almost none of that heterogeneity; familial/genetic factors explain a substantial part (Bouchard & Rankinen, HERITAGE Family Study, MSSE 2001;33(6 Suppl):S446–451). There is no way to know which end of that distribution this athlete sits at before running the block.

What the correct peak-week volume is RELATIVE to an athlete's own training history has not been studied. All the registry data reports absolute kilometres. Whether 100 km/wk means something different to a runner whose all-time peak week is 57.1 km than to one whose peak is 120 km is exactly the question, and it is unaddressed in the literature.

The Doherty & Keogh 2020 meta-regression's per-unit coefficients could not be retrieved (paywalled; the pre-proof on ResearchGate returns 403). If a precise pooled minutes-per-km/week figure is wanted, that full text is the place to get it, and I have not seen it — I am not going to quote a number I could not read.

One published coefficient in this literature is demonstrably wrong and is now in circulation: DeJong Lempke et al. 2025 report that each +1 km/week in the final 4 months improves race time by ~13 min, with β −0.22 and a 95% CI of (−0.48, −0.34) that does not contain its own point estimate. Whether the intended figure was per 10 km, a standardised coefficient, or something else cannot be determined from the published text.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)
officialSources.document: Position Stand: Quantity and Quality of Exercise for Developing and Maintaining Cardiorespiratory, Musculoskeletal, and Neuromotor Fitness in Apparently Healthy Adults. Garber CE et al., Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2011;43(7):1334–1359
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: ≥150 min/week moderate or ≥75 min/week vigorous cardiorespiratory exercise, 500–1000 MET·min/week, with explicit advice on 'gradual progression of exercise intensity and volume' to reduce risk. It prescribes nothing about marathon training volume, and is a health-fitness document, not a performance one. It is the only ACSM position stand that bears on progression rate at all, and it gives no numerical progression limit.

officialSources.body: World Athletics (via New Studies in Athletics, its coaching-science journal)
officialSources.document: Republication of Karp JR, 'Training characteristics of US Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers' (hosted at worldathletics.org/download/downloadnsa)
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Nothing prescriptive. It is a descriptive survey of 93 US Olympic Trials qualifiers, and its stated conclusion is that among that population 'there is no consensus as to how to prepare for the marathon beyond running at a pace slower than race pace'. The most important fact about official sources in this domain is what this document represents: the governing bodies publish descriptions of what elites do, not prescriptions of weekly volume for recreational marathoners.

officialSources.body: No governing body (finding, not a source)
officialSources.document: None located
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: I could not verify any document from World Athletics, UK Athletics, England Athletics, USATF or ACSM that prescribes a weekly training volume for a recreational marathon runner, or that sets a maximum safe rate of volume progression. If such a document exists I did not find it, and I am recording that as an absence rather than filling it with something plausible-sounding. The de facto standard in this space is expert practice — quantified by Knopp et al. 2024's analysis of 92 published plans (peak weeks of 43 / 59 / 108 km/wk for low / middle / high volume plans), whose own authors note there is 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated'.

check.domain: Training volume and the dose-response curve for marathon time

citationChecks.citation: Vickers AJ, Vertosick EA. An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2016;8:26. PMID 27570626
citationChecks.note: Checked against PubMed record and PMC5000509 full text. Every specific claim holds: 'The difference in marathon time for training 50 vs. 30 miles per week was 25:32' (men) and 31:41 (women); cubic splines were used for age, BMI and weekly mileage; n=2303, 1022 with marathon times, median age 35, 61% male; marathon subgroup median mileage 40 mi/wk (IQR 30-50) — so the 30-vs-50 contrast is exactly the IQR and the 'coefficient is local' caveat is correct; median male marathon 3:28:02; 'Only 3 men and 4 women reported a time that met Olympic qualifying standards' = the report's 7 of 2303; the causal hedge 'if these associations are seen to be causal' is verbatim; Riegel 'dramatically underestimates marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners' is verbatim from the abstract. One discrepancy: the paper's own Riegel exponent is k=1.07, not the k=1.06 the report uses downstream.

citationChecks.citation: Fokkema T, et al. Training for a (half-)marathon... Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2020;30(9):1692-1704. PMID 32421886, PMC7496388
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms all four coefficients verbatim: <40 km/wk beta 6.33 (0.18;12.48); >65 km/wk beta -14.09 (-22.47;-5.72); longest run <25 km beta 13.44 (5.34;21.55); and 'No associations between training characteristics and RRIs were identified.' n=441 marathoners plus 556 half-marathoners confirmed. NOT verified: the cohort descriptives the report gives (43.6+/-27.3 km/wk, longest run 29.1+/-8.5 km, pace 5:41/km, finish 4:17:54+/-0:37:14, age 42, 65% male, 55% injury rate) — these are full-text-only and PMC returned a reCAPTCHA wall. They are plausible but I could not confirm them, and the 'closest published cohort' claim rests on them.

citationChecks.citation: DeJong Lempke AF, et al. Training Volume and Training Frequency Changes Associated with Boston Marathon Race Performance. Sports Medicine. 2025. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02304-4, PMC12441744
citationChecks.note: MINOR MISATTRIBUTION of the year/volume: the paper is Sports Med. 2026 Jan;56(1):243-256, Epub 2025 Sep 6 (PMID 40913707). Everything substantive checks out against the full text: 12-4 month running distance beta -0.01 (-0.02, -0.005) p<0.001; running sessions -0.06 (-0.13, -0.02) p=0.010; quality sessions -0.27 (-0.42, -0.10) p<0.001; model R2 0.485; TFC finding 'decreased their number of weekly running sessions in 4-0 months had faster official race times by an average of 3 min (beta -0.05 [-0.09, -0.003]; p=0.035)'. CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY: the broken 4-0 month coefficient the report flags is printed exactly as '-0.22 (-0.48, -0.34); p<0.001' — a CI that does not bracket its own point estimate. The report is right to refuse to use it. Unverified: the report's 'mean age 47+/-14, 95% classified tier-2 trained/developmental'.

citationChecks.citation: Muniz-Pumares D, Hunter B, Meyler S, Maunder E, Smyth B. The Training Intensity Distribution of Marathon Runners Across Performance Levels. Sports Med. 2025;55(4):1023-1035. PMID 39616560
citationChecks.note: Verified against the accepted manuscript (repository.londonmet.ac.uk/9883). Table 2 prints exactly what the report quotes: Total distance (km) -0.3317 (0.0010)*, Total time (min) 0.0581 (0.0002)*, Adjusted R2 = 0.596. Descriptives confirmed: 45.1+/-26.4 km/wk, 3.6+/-1.7 sessions/wk, weekly long run 19.6+/-9.6 km, finish 230.2+/-41.9 min, mean age 39.5, sex split 91,334 M / 28,118 F = 76.5% male, 119,452 runners / 151,813 marathons. Bins confirmed: fastest 120-150 min at ~107 km/wk, n=620; 270-300 min at ~35 km/wk, n=8,798; and the text does say 107 was '~60% higher than the training volume of runners within the next performance group', which is where the report's derived 67 km/wk comes from (it declares the derivation). ONE INFERENCE, NOT A QUOTE: the report's myth-busting claim that the R2>=0.90 correlations were 'computed on GROUP MEANS after binning into 30-minute bands' is not stated in the Statistical Analysis section, which says only that Pearson coefficients were calculated. It is a very strong inference (the paper bins everything else in 30-min bands, and an individual-level R2 of 0.596 in the same paper makes 0.90 across 119k runners impossible), but it is inferred. Also note the abstract says R2>=0.90 while the results text says R2>=0.85.

citationChecks.citation: Enoksen E, Shalfawi SAI, Tonnessen E. The effect of high- vs. low-intensity training on aerobic capacity in well-trained male middle-distance runners. J Strength Cond Res. 2011;25(3):812-818. PMID 20647950
citationChecks.note: The paper exists and the numbers are exact (n=26, matched then randomly assigned, 70 km low-intensity vs 50 km high-intensity, no significant between-group differences before or after, progress 301+/-886 m vs 218+/-546 m). But the report's framing is wrong in a way that matters: the study is titled and designed as a HIGH- vs LOW-INTENSITY comparison in which volume is the yoked variable, not as a volume trial. Volume and intensity are perfectly confounded, so it cannot isolate 'randomly assigning trained runners to HIGHER weekly volume' — the report's own row title. The report calls this 'the most important row in the table' and hangs the '0 minutes from volume' verdict on it; the design will not carry that weight. It is also a middle-distance performance test in middle-distance runners, and the authors' own conclusion is the opposite emphasis: runners 'improved in vVO2max and vLT more when they train around LT'.

citationChecks.citation: Kirwan JP, Costill DL, et al. Physiological responses to successive days of intense training in competitive swimmers. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1988;20(3):255-259. PMID 3386504
citationChecks.note: Numbers exact: 12 male collegiate swimmers, 4,266+/-264 to 8,970+/-161 m/day for 10 d at ~95% VO2max, no significant performance change (365.8 m swim, two 22.9 m sprints, semi-tethered power), cortisol 17.5->20.6 ug/dl and CK 56.2->119.0 U/l both p<0.05, plasma volume +11.4+/-2.7%. One grading error: the report labels this 'controlled-trial'. It is a single-group pre-post design with no control group and no randomisation.

citationChecks.citation: Iaia FM, et al. Four weeks of speed endurance training... J Appl Physiol. 2009;106(1):73-80. PMID 18845781
citationChecks.note: Exact: 17 endurance-trained runners (9 SET, 8 Con), ~45 km/wk replaced by 5.7+/-0.1 km/wk of sprints plus 9.9+/-0.3 km/wk easy = 15.6 km/wk (the report's 65% cut checks out), submaximal VO2 lower by 6.6/7.6/5.7/6.4% at 11/13/14.5/16 km/h, 10-km time, VO2max, citrate synthase, HAD and capillary-to-fibre ratio all unaltered. Worth noting the report soft-pedals: the intervention was not merely 'cutting volume' — it substituted frequent maximal sprint sessions, a stimulus this athlete's plan does not contain.

citationChecks.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-1365. PMID 17762369
citationChecks.note: Exact: 27 of 182 studies, 2-wk taper overall effect 0.59+/-0.33 p<0.001, volume decreased exponentially 41-60% giving 0.72+/-0.36, intensity and frequency unchanged. However the '0.5-6%, centred around 2-3%' figure — which is the number the report actually converts into minutes — is NOT in Bosquet and is left uncited. Its real source is Mujika & Padilla 2003 (MSSE 35(7):1182-7): 'Performance usually improves by about 3% (usual range 0.5-6.0%)'. Given the athlete's whole question is provenance, an unsourced number doing the load-bearing work is a real defect, even though the number itself is right.

citationChecks.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Front Sports Act Living. 2021;3:735220. PMID 34651125
citationChecks.note: Exact: >158,000 recreational marathon runners, Kruskal-Wallis H(7)>=521.11 p<0.001, post-hoc Dunn with Bonferroni, strict 3-week taper vs minimal taper = 'a median finish-time saving of 5 min 32.4 s or 2.6%', and 64% of runners adopt less disciplined tapers. All as reported.

citationChecks.citation: Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A. Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;4:1096124. PMID 36704260
citationChecks.note: Exact: >15 million activities from 300,000 recreational runners 2014-2017; >=7-day disruption costs 5-8%; late disruptions 5.2% vs early 4.4%; males 5% vs females 3.5%; faster runners 5.4% vs slower 2.6%. One inflation: the report's sampleSize says 'n ~ 300,000 runners (within-runner paired comparisons)'. 300,000 is the parent dataset; the paired analysis is restricted to runners with at least one disrupted AND one undisrupted marathon, a subset whose size the report does not give and the abstract does not state.

citationChecks.citation: Nielsen RO, et al. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2014;44(10):739-747. PMID 25155475
citationChecks.note: Exact, including the honesty the report insists on: 874 novice runners, 202 injuries, HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96, 2.66), P=.07, no significant differences across the <10% / 10-30% / >30% groups for all injury types, and the authors' own call for RCTs given the exploratory design.

citationChecks.citation: Knopp M, Appelhans D, Schonfelder M, Seiler S, et al. Quantitative Analysis of 92 12-Week Sub-elite Marathon Training Plans. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:50. PMID 38695978
citationChecks.note: Volumes confirmed (abstract: 108 / 59 / 43 km per week for high / middle / low; bands >90, 65-90, <65 km/wk) and consistent with the report's more precise 107.7 / 58.5 / 42.9. The authors' own limitation, 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated', is verbatim. UNVERIFIED DETAIL: the report gives a single pooled intensity distribution '13.2% zone 1, 65.6% zone 2, 15.1% zone 3, 3.0% zone 4, 3.0% zone 5'. The abstract prints per-band distributions of 15-67-10-5-3, 14-63-18-2-3 and 12-67-17-2-2, none of which is the report's figure; it looks like an unweighted mean across bands, presented as if quoted. Longest-run figures (35.2 / 30.9 km) are also full-text-only and unchecked. Full author list is Knopp, Appelhans, Schonfelder, Seiler, Wackerhage.

citationChecks.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B. An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression. J Sci Med Sport. 2020;23(2):182-188. PMID 31704026
citationChecks.note: Exact, including author order: 85 studies, 137 cohorts, 25% female, univariate random-effects meta-regressions with R2 0.38-0.81 p<0.001 across all seven training variables, non-finish rate 7.27% (95% CI 6.09-8.65%). The report's refusal to invent a per-unit coefficient it could not read is correct behaviour; the abstract genuinely does not report one.

citationChecks.citation: Karp JR. Training characteristics of qualifiers for the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2007;2(1):72-92. PMID 19255456
citationChecks.note: Every number exact: 104 men + 151 women contacted, 93 responded (37 M, 56 W); men 145.3+/-25.6 km/wk over 8.7+/-2.8 sessions, women 116.0+/-26.5 over 7.1+/-2.5; elite women 135.8+/-31.5 vs national-class 111.3+/-23.3; 75% / 68% below marathon pace; 49% / 31% without a coach; 12.2+/-5.3 years training (men). The quoted conclusion 'there is no consensus as to how to prepare for the marathon beyond running at a pace slower than race pace' is verbatim, and the sex asymmetry ('Weekly training distance seems to influence women's marathon performance more than it does men's') is stated as the report says.

citationChecks.citation: Billat VL, Demarle A, Slawinski J, Paiva M, Koralsztein JP. Physical and training characteristics of top-class marathon runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2001;33(12):2089-2097. PMID 11740304
citationChecks.note: Exact: n=20 (5 top-class and 5 high-level per sex), TC defined as <2:11 men / <2:32 women, VO2peak inversely correlated with marathon time r=-0.73 predicting 59% of variance, and 'TC marathon runners trained for more total kilometers per week and at a higher velocity'. Omitted nuance that cuts against a naive volume story: top-class MEN were significantly LESS economical (212+/-17 vs 195+/-14 mL/km/kg).

citationChecks.citation: Buist I, et al. No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Sports Med. 2008;36(1):33-39. PMID 17940147
citationChecks.note: Exact: GRONORUN, N=532 novice runners, graded 13-week programme 'based on the 10% training rule' vs standard 8-week, injury incidence 20.8% vs 20.3%, chi2=0.016, df=1, P=.90. The report's myth-busting of the 10% rule is correctly sourced.

citationChecks.citation: Bouchard C, Rankinen T. Individual differences in response to regular physical activity. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2001;33(6 Suppl):S446-451. (HERITAGE)
citationChecks.note: Verbatim support: 'VO2max responses to standardized training programs have ranged from almost no gain up to 100% increase in large groups of sedentary individuals', and 'age, sex, and race have little impact on interindividual differences in training responses', with familial aggregation significant. The report's use is faithful — but note the population qualifier in the source sentence: SEDENTARY individuals.

citationChecks.citation: Garber CE, et al. ACSM Position Stand: Quantity and Quality of Exercise... Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(7):1334-1359. PMID 21694556
citationChecks.note: Confirmed: >=150 min/wk moderate or >=75 min/wk vigorous, 500-1000 MET.min/wk, apparently healthy adults, explicitly a health-fitness prescription with nothing about marathon volume — as the report says. COULD_NOT_CHECK on one sub-claim: the specific 'gradual progression of exercise intensity and volume' wording sits beyond the truncated abstract. The report's own conclusion (no numerical progression limit anywhere in it) is consistent with everything I could see.

populationMismatches: Enoksen 2011 — the report's single most load-bearing row ('the closest thing to an experiment', verdict: 0 minutes). Population: 26 well-trained male MIDDLE-DISTANCE runners at the Norwegian School of Sport Sciences, already training 50-70 km/wk (two to three times this athlete's 24.4 km/wk). Outcome: a middle-distance performance test, not a marathon. And volume was confounded with intensity by design. Concluding 'volume buys nothing' for a 24 km/wk recreational marathoner from a 50-vs-70 km/wk intensity trial in trained 1500m-5000m men is a double extrapolation — wrong population and wrong event.

Kirwan/Costill 1988 — 12 male collegiate SWIMMERS, 10 days. Swimming is non-weight-bearing; the entire cost of a running volume ramp is mechanical loading of bone and connective tissue, which this design cannot see. The report acknowledges this, then still marks it 'Directly' applicable.

Iaia 2009 — endurance-trained runners at ~45 km/wk in Copenhagen, outcome 10-km time. Two mismatches: the event is 10 km, not a marathon (the durability, fuelling and 3.5-hour ground-contact demands are exactly what is not measured), and the intervention added 8-12 x 30 s maximal sprints three times a week, a stimulus absent from this athlete's plan. Reading it as 'a 65% volume cut costs nothing' for a marathoner drops both.

Bosquet 2007 — 27 studies of COMPETITIVE athletes across endurance sports: swimmers, cyclists, runners, many at national or international level, with race durations from minutes to a couple of hours. The 2-3% taper gain is not a marathon-specific, recreational-runner number. It survives here only because Smyth & Lawlor 2021 independently reproduces ~2.6% in 158,000 recreational marathoners — the convergence is what makes the 5-7 minutes defensible, not Bosquet alone.

Nielsen 2014 and Buist 2008 — NOVICE runners (Danish and Dutch beginners on self-structured or event-preparation programmes, many previously sedentary, mean age mid-to-late 30s). This athlete has run consistently for six months, has a 3:55 marathon, a 1:46 half and a 57.1 km peak week. The report argues the bias runs in the safe direction ('a runner whose all-time peak week is 57.1 km is a novice with respect to 100 km') — that is a reasonable argument, but it is an argument, not a measurement, and it is presented as if it settled the transfer.

Bouchard & Rankinen 2001 (HERITAGE) — previously SEDENTARY adults on a standardised 20-week cycle-ergometer programme. The 0-to-+100% VO2max response range is the response of untrained people to starting exercise. It says nothing about how much an already-trained 27-year-old runner with a VO2max estimate of 53 gains from adding running volume; his position on that distribution is not even the relevant distribution.

DeJong Lempke 2025 (Boston) — 2022 Boston Marathon registrants, mean age 47, a population selected by having run a Boston-qualifying time (or charity equivalent), training 64-68 km/wk. The 0.6 min per km/wk coefficient comes from older, faster, self-selected runners. This athlete is 27 and at 3:55 is not a Boston qualifier; the report applies the coefficient to his last 12 months to produce '~22 min', which imports the selection of that cohort wholesale.

Fokkema 2020 — Rotterdam recreational marathoners, mean age ~42, mean finish 4:17:54. Older and slower than this athlete, and the >65 km/wk group self-selected into that volume. The report calls it 'the closest published cohort to this athlete in ability and volume'; on finish time the Strava dataset (mean 3:50 vs his 3:55) is closer, and on age Vickers (median 35) is closer.

Karp 2007 and Billat 2001 — elite (sub-2:15 men, sub-2:40 women; sub-2:11 top-class), 12.2 +/- 5.3 years of training. The report flags this correctly and refuses to transfer anything, which is the right call and worth saying explicitly since these are the two citations most often misused at recreational runners.

Knopp 2024 — the units of analysis are 92 DOCUMENTS, not athletes. No outcomes, no runners, no evidence of effectiveness. Used correctly as calibration, but it can support no claim about what this athlete's body will do.

Muniz-Pumares 2025 — the best population match on ability (dataset mean finish 3:50 vs his 3:55) and sex mix (76% male). The mismatch is at the top of the curve: the ~107 km/wk figure belongs to 2:00-2:30 runners, a group two hours faster than him. The report does not transfer it, correctly.

Vickers 2016 — closest overall (median age 35, recreational, 61% male, median male marathon 3:28). The mismatch is at the bottom: his 24.4 km/wk is 15 mi/wk, below the marathon subgroup's interquartile range of 30-50 mi/wk, so he sits off the bottom end of the fitted spline. The report identifies this, and it is the reason the 41-minute figure is unusable.
effectSizeErrors: Riegel exponent swap. The report computes his 'endurance gap' as 13.7 min using k=1.06, but the paper it cites for the Riegel finding (Vickers & Vertosick) uses k=1.07. Re-derived: 106.58 x 2^1.07 = 223.8 min = 3:43:47, giving a 12.1 min gap, not 13.7. Separately, the report justifies k=1.06 as 'Riegel's own k values: 1.08 elite, 1.05-1.06 male recreational aged 40-70' — that age band is 40-70 and this athlete is 27, so even taking the claim at face value it is the wrong row of the table. I could not verify those Riegel age-group exponents from any source in this check.

Fokkema confidence intervals added end-to-end. The report sums the two category coefficients (6.33 + 14.09 = 20.4 min, correct, both are vs the same 40-65 km/wk reference) but then sums the CI bounds (0.18+5.72 to 12.48+22.47) to get 'roughly 6-35 min'. Coefficients from one regression covary; the combined standard error is sqrt(SE1^2 + SE2^2 + 2cov), not the sum of half-widths. The direction of the error is conservative (the true interval is almost certainly narrower), but the method is wrong and the interval should not be quoted as if computed.

The Strava individual-level calculation is arithmetically right and structurally hollow. I re-derived it: -0.3317 x 160 = -53.1; +0.0581 x 1000 = +58.1; net +5.0 min. Correct. But Table 2 also contains 'Number of long runs' at +2.6964 min each and 'Number of active days' at -0.0505 each, and the report holds both constant while adding 10 km/wk for 16 weeks — which cannot happen in reality. The report concedes the coefficients are not individually interpretable and then uses the result as its headline 'essentially zero'. Two of those three sentences can be true, not all three.

Taper: the effect size never converts to the minutes. ES 0.59 is a standardised mean difference; the 2-3% that becomes 4.7-7.1 minutes comes from a different source entirely (Mujika & Padilla 2003, '~3%, usual range 0.5-6.0%'), which the report does not cite. The number survives because Smyth & Lawlor independently give 2.6% in the right population — but as written, the single best-supported figure in the report is derived from an uncited source.

The 3.75 min per km/wk 'steep part of the curve' figure is two derivations deep. It uses bin midpoints (4:45 and 2:45) against 35 km/wk (published) and 67 km/wk (which the report itself derived by dividing 107 by 1.6 from a prose sentence, '~60% higher than the next performance group'). I confirmed both source facts in the manuscript, and the arithmetic (120 min / 32 km = 3.75) is right, but it is a slope between two binned midpoints, one of whose x-values was reverse-engineered from a sentence. It should not be quoted to three significant figures.

Everything else I re-derived checks out: 25:32 over 32.19 km/wk = 0.793 min per km/wk; 2-3% of 235.9 = 4.72-7.08 min; 2.6% of 235.9 = 6.13 min; 5.2% of 235.9 = 12.27 min; beta -0.01 h = 0.6 min per km/wk and 36 x 0.6 = 21.6 min; 6.33 + 14.09 = 20.42 min; Riegel from 5 km, 19.65 x 8.439^1.06 = 188.5 min = 3:08:30; 20 km/wk x 0.79 = 15.8 min for the Enoksen contrast. No fabricated conversions found.

Missing conversion the report should have made: Tanda & Knechtle's published equation for recreational MALE marathoners gives, for 24.4 -> 76 km/wk at constant training pace, 98.46[exp(-0.0053x24.4) - exp(-0.0053x76)] = 86.5 - 65.8 = 20.7 min. That is a fourth independent estimate, in the right population and inside its stated validity range (165-266 min; he is 235.9), and it lands almost exactly on Fokkema's 20.4 min. Its absence lets the report present a wider spread of estimates (0 to 41 min) than the evidence actually supports.
missedEvidence: Tanda G, Knechtle B. Marathon performance in relation to body fat percentage and training indices in recreational male runners. Open Access J Sports Med. 2013;4:141-9 (PMID 24379719). THE BIGGEST GAP. n=126 recreational male marathoners, Basel 2010-2011, r=0.81, and it publishes a closed-form equation: marathon time (min) = 11.03 + 98.46 x exp(-0.0053 x mean weekly training km) + 0.387 x mean training pace, explicitly validated over 165-266 min — this athlete's 235.9 min sits inside that window. It is the only published dose-response function in exactly his population, it models saturation explicitly rather than assuming linearity, and it yields ~20.7 min for his ramp. The report ran fourteen searches and did not find it.

Tanda G, Knechtle B. Effects of training and anthropometric factors on marathon and 100 km ultramarathon race performance. Open Access J Sports Med. 2015;6:129-36 (PMID 25995653). CONTRADICTS THE REPORT'S FRAMING: same authors, larger cohort, and the finding is that for the MARATHON, mean training PACE mattered more than training volume, while volume dominated only at 100 km. That inverts the report's entire volume-centric axis and points at a lever (training pace) that is actually manipulable inside six weeks. Its absence is why the report's option set is narrower than the evidence.

Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sorensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen R. Progression in Running Intensity or Running Volume and the Development of Specific Injuries in Recreational Runners: Run Clever, a Randomized Trial Using Competing Risks. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2018;48(10):740-748 (PMID 29895234). RANDOMISED evidence directly on the report's weakest row: 447 recreational runners, 24 weeks, randomised to a volume-progression schedule or an intensity-progression schedule; 80 injuries; no difference in risk (all risk differences straddle zero). The report says of the progression-rate question that 'the authors themselves call for RCTs' — an RCT exists, in recreational (not novice) runners, and it is null.

Damsted C, Glad S, Nielsen RO, Sorensen H, Malisoux L. Is there evidence for an association between changes in training load and running-related injuries? A systematic review. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2018;13(6):931-942 (PMID 30534459). Conclusion: 'Very limited evidence exists supporting that a sudden change in training load is associated with increased risk of running-related injury.' It also surfaces a study finding no difference between a 10% and a 24% average weekly volume increase (HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6-1.3). The report leans on Nielsen 2014's HR 1.59 (p=0.07) as 'the constraint the ratified block violates most severely'; the systematic review covering that literature is more sceptical than the report is.

Mujika I, Padilla S. Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(7):1182-7 (PMID 12840640). The actual origin of the '0.5-6%, about 3%' taper gain the report converts into its best-supported number, plus the operational detail the report's taper advice needs: maintain intensity, reduce volume 60-90%, reduce frequency by no more than 20%, progressive nonlinear rather than step. Given the athlete's question is specifically about provenance, quoting the percentage without this citation is the exact failure mode he is worried about.

Knechtle B, Barandun U, et al. Prediction of half-marathon race time in recreational female and male runners. Springerplus. 2014;3:248 (PMID 24936384), and the related Knechtle/Rust recreational-runner prediction series. In recreational runners these models find running SPEED during training plus percent body fat as the predictors (men adj r2 = 0.41; women 0.68), with weekly volume not entering the model. Relevant twice over: his half marathon is three days away and will re-anchor everything, and body mass — 85.5 kg, untouched in his profile since March — appears as a predictor in Tanda/Knechtle and as BMI in Vickers' adjusted model, yet appears nowhere in the report's fifteen interventions.

One negative finding that supports the report: I searched independently and found no randomised trial assigning recreational marathon runners to different weekly volumes with finish time as the outcome. The report's central 'unknown' claim is, as far as I can establish, true.
