interventions.intervention: Longest training run of 30–35 km vs <25 km before the marathon (the headline long-run dose question)
interventions.effect: Adjusted finish time +13.44 min slower for a longest run <25 km compared with the 30–35 km reference group (95% CI +5.34 to +21.55 min, p<0.01). Unadjusted group means: <25 km 4:37:43 (n=91), 25–30 km 4:25:07 (n=111), 30–35 km 4:15:26 (n=200), >35 km 3:50:18 (n=38). Model adjusted for age, sex, BMI, running experience, prior injury, weekly volume and training pace, so it is not simply 'fitter runners run further'.
interventions.population: 441 recreational marathon runners recruited via Dutch mass-participation events; 70% male, mean age 41.4 y, median weekly volume 40 km [IQR 30–50], median longest run 32.0 km [IQR 27.0–35.0], mean finish 4:17:54. Closely matched to this athlete on volume and finish time; he is younger and faster than the mean.
interventions.citation: Fokkema T, van Damme AADN, Fornerod MWJ, de Vos R-J, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, van Middelkoop M. Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2020;30(9):1692–1704. doi:10.1111/sms.13725 (PMC7496388)
interventions.sampleSize: n=441 marathoners (341 finishers analysed for finish time); half-marathon arm n=556
interventions.duration: Training characteristics captured 2–6 weeks pre-race; single race outcome
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as a decision rule — the choice of long-run ceiling is made inside this block. But the association is measured across whole training histories, so it partly reflects months of training the six weeks cannot recreate.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: +13.44 min in a cohort whose mean finish was 257.9 min = +5.21%. Applied proportionally to this athlete's 235.9 min (3:55:54): ~+12.3 min if his long run fell below 25 km. He will not be below 25 km, so this is the penalty he is avoiding, not the one he faces.

interventions.intervention: Longest run of 25–30 km vs 30–35 km — THE ATHLETE'S ACTUAL QUESTION (27–29 km this block vs 30.11 km last block)
interventions.effect: Adjusted finish time +6.40 min slower (95% CI −0.04 to +12.82 min). The confidence interval touches zero: in the only dataset that has ever binned long-run distance this finely, 25–30 km is NOT statistically distinguishable from 30–35 km. Point estimate favours the longer run; the evidence cannot rule out zero difference. Note his 27–29 km sits at the top of the 25–30 bin, so the true point estimate for him is likely below 6.4 min. Separately, longest run showed NO association with in-race pace decline in marathoners (25–30 vs 30–35: +0.21%, 95% CI −4.04 to +4.55) — i.e. the shorter long run did not predict a bigger fade.
interventions.population: Same 441 recreational marathoners (see above). Directly transferable: same ability band, same weekly volumes, same race distance.
interventions.citation: Fokkema T et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2020;30(9):1692–1704, Table 3. doi:10.1111/sms.13725
interventions.sampleSize: n=111 in the 25–30 km group vs n=200 reference (30–35 km)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this is exactly the decision in front of him and the number is measured on runners like him.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: +6.40 min on a cohort mean of 257.9 min = +2.48%. Proportionally on 235.9 min → +5.9 min. Bin-position correction: 27–29 km is in the upper half of the 25–30 bin, so halve it → roughly +3 min. Honest answer: expected cost ≈ 3–6 minutes, 95% interval roughly 0 to +12 minutes. It is the smallest lever in his block, not the binding one.

interventions.intervention: Longest run >35 km vs 30–35 km (does going even longer buy anything?)
interventions.effect: Adjusted −4.86 min (95% CI −13.51 to +3.79), NOT significant. Beyond ~30–35 km the measured return on extra long-run distance disappears. The raw >35 km group was much faster (3:50:18) but that difference vanishes once volume, pace, age, sex and BMI are adjusted for — a clean demonstration that raw long-run/finish-time correlations are mostly fitness confounding.
interventions.population: n=38 recreational marathoners running >35 km as their longest run, within the same 441-runner cohort
interventions.citation: Fokkema T et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2020;30(9):1692–1704, Table 3. doi:10.1111/sms.13725
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Moot — he cannot reach >35 km. Relevant only as reassurance that the ceiling he is missing sits in flat territory of the dose-response curve.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to a reliable number: CI spans −13.5 to +3.8 min, i.e. anywhere from a 13-minute gain to a 4-minute loss. Treat as 'no measurable effect'.

interventions.intervention: Number of runs ≥32 km completed in the pre-marathon training block
interventions.effect: Univariate random-effects meta-regression found a negative association with finish time (faster times with more ≥32 km runs), alongside weekly distance, weekly runs, peak week, training pace, longest run and weekly hours. R² across the seven covariate models ranged 0.38–0.81, all p<0.001. IMPORTANT: the published abstract reports only the R² RANGE across all seven covariates, not per-covariate coefficients — I could not obtain the full text (paywalled, 403) so I cannot tell you how much of that 0.38–0.81 belongs to long-run count specifically. Do not let anyone quote a per-run minute figure from this paper; it is not in the accessible record.
interventions.population: 85 studies, 137 cohorts of marathon runners (25% female), spanning elite and recreational. Heterogeneous — cohort-level meta-regression, so ecological: it relates group means to group means, not individuals.
interventions.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B. An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 2020;23(2):182–188. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2019.09.013
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Partially. In six weeks with a 27–29 km ceiling he can fit roughly 3–4 long runs. He cannot fit any ≥32 km run. This covariate is one he simply cannot buy.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — the accessible record gives no per-unit coefficient, only that the association exists and is negative. Anyone converting this to minutes is inventing a number.

interventions.intervention: Longest endurance run >21 km vs 15–21 km before a HALF marathon (directly relevant to his 2026-09-12 tune-up)
interventions.effect: Adjusted half-marathon finish time −3.87 min faster (95% CI −6.31 to −1.44, p<0.01), AND less in-race pace decline: −1.89 percentage points (95% CI −3.65 to −0.12, p<0.05). Note the contrast with the marathon arm: in the half, the long run predicted better pace-holding; in the marathon it did not.
interventions.population: 556 recreational half-marathon runners, 61% male, mean age 42.8 y, median weekly volume 26 km, mean finish 2:00:05
interventions.citation: Fokkema T et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2020;30(9):1692–1704, Table 3. doi:10.1111/sms.13725
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: His half is in 3 days; the long runs that would have driven this are already banked (best continuous half 1:46:35). Use the half as a fitness probe, not as a training stimulus.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: −3.87 min on a 120.1 min cohort mean = −3.2%. On his 106.6 min half → ~−3.4 min. Not directly a marathon number.

interventions.intervention: Durability / resilience: resisting the deterioration of physiological capacity during the second half of the race — the quality the long run is actually supposed to build
interventions.effect: Internal-to-external workload decoupling (%HRmax relative to speed as a fraction of critical speed) averaged 1.16 ± 0.22, first detected at 25.2 ± 9.9 km. Runners in the LOW decoupling third (34.5% of the sample) first decoupled at 33.4 ± 9.0 km and finished in 217.3 ± 33.1 min; the HIGH decoupling third first decoupled at 19.1 ± 6.8 km and finished in 238.5 ± 30.7 min — a 21.2-minute spread. Adding decoupling magnitude and onset to a critical-speed model cut marathon prediction error from 6.45% to 5.16%. Males decoupled more (1.17 vs 1.12) and earlier (25.0 vs 26.3 km) than females.
interventions.population: 82,303 recreational marathon runners (13,125 female) with heart-rate and split data — the largest durability dataset in existence, and squarely this athlete's population
interventions.citation: Smyth B, Maunder E, Meyler S, Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D. Decoupling of Internal and External Workload During a Marathon: An Analysis of Durability in 82,303 Recreational Runners. Sports Medicine 2022;52(9):2283–2295. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01680-5
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: The MEASUREMENT applies immediately — he has HR and pace on every run, so he can compute his own decoupling on each long run and on race day. Whether the underlying quality can be moved in six weeks is a separate, unanswered question (see Jones & Kirby below).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: The 21-minute gap between low- and high-decoupling groups is NOT a treatment effect — decoupling is confounded with fitness (the low group also ran at 88% of critical speed vs 82%). Not convertible. Use it as a monitoring variable, not a promise.

interventions.intervention: Training durability deliberately: prolonged sessions, race-pace bouts late in long runs, progressive intensity into fatigue
interventions.effect: No quantified effect exists. The current authoritative review states plainly that 'data are scant' and that the available evidence 'suggests that training consistency and the accumulation of relatively large volumes of training over the longer-term (i.e., several years) might promote resilience', with regular prolonged sessions — 'especially when these include bouts of high-intensity exercise at race pace or above or a progressive increase in intensity in the face of developing fatigue' — as a plausible but unproven stimulus. Every verb in the source is conditional.
interventions.population: Narrative review across endurance athletes; no single population, no intervention data
interventions.citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS. Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2025;35(3):e70032. doi:10.1111/sms.70032
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: The review's own answer is: probably not. It attributes resilience to multi-YEAR volume accumulation and training consistency. Six weeks is the wrong timescale for the primary mechanism it names.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — no effect size exists anywhere in the literature for this intervention.

interventions.intervention: Endurance training as a durability intervention (the only controlled trial that has tested it)
interventions.effect: 10 weeks of either low-intensity (6.8 ± 0.7 h/wk) or high-intensity (1.6 ± 0.2 h/wk) cycling improved averaged durability similarly in both groups (time × group p=0.42; LIT p=0.03, g=0.49; HIT p=0.01, g=0.62). HIT reduced both drift magnitude (8.8 ± 7.9% → 5.4 ± 6.7%, p=0.03, g=0.49) and delayed drift onset (108 ± 54 → 137 ± 57 min, p=0.03, g=0.61); LIT's drift changes did not reach significance (magnitude p=0.09; onset 106 → 131 min, p=0.08). VO2max rose only with HIT (g=1.51). The authors' own caution: 'a 10-week intervention did not alter drifts and their onsets in a large amount'.
interventions.population: 35 SEDENTARY and recreationally active men (n=16) and women (n=19), cycling, tested over 3 h at 48% of pre-training VO2max. Major transfer problem: untrained, cycling not running, and an intensity far below marathon effort. An athlete already at VO2max 53 with five months of running has already banked most of what a sedentary person gains in 10 weeks.
interventions.citation: Matomäki P, Heinonen OJ, Nummela A, Laukkanen J, Auvinen E-P, Pirkola L, Kyröläinen H. Durability is improved by both low and high intensity endurance training. Frontiers in Physiology 2023;14:1128111. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1128111
interventions.sampleSize: n=35 (allocated to two groups; not blinded, no non-training control)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Partially — six weeks is 60% of the protocol, and the effect appeared as drift onset moving ~25–29 min later. But in an untrained population; expect materially less in a trained runner.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. The outcome was physiological drift during sub-marathon-intensity cycling, never a race time. Converting g=0.5 on a drift measure into marathon minutes would be fabrication.

interventions.intervention: Strength + plyometric training to protect running economy late in a long effort (the best-evidenced durability intervention, and it is not a long run)
interventions.effect: 10 weeks of twice-weekly maximal strength and plyometric training, added to habitual running: running economy at 90 min of heavy-intensity running improved −2.1% in the strength group vs +0.6% in controls (group × time p=0.003, ηp²=0.13); time to exhaustion at 95% VO2max immediately after the 90-min run changed +35% (strength) vs −8% (control), group × time p=0.004, ηp²=0.28.
interventions.population: 28 well-trained MALE runners, VO2max 58.6 ml/kg/min, 10 km 39:02. Faster than this athlete (VO2max 53, 5 km ~19:39) but the same sex, the same broad training background, and running rather than cycling — the closest transferable population in the durability literature.
interventions.citation: Zanini M, Folland JP, Wu H, Blagrove RC. Strength Training Improves Running Economy Durability and Fatigued High-Intensity Performance in Well-Trained Male Runners: A Randomized Control Trial. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2025;57(7):1546–1558. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003685
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Partially — six weeks is 60% of the protocol and neuromuscular adaptations arrive early, but adding heavy strength work in the final six weeks of a marathon block carries its own fatigue and soreness cost. Realistic ceiling: keep it light, expect a fraction of the effect.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working, and treat it as an upper bound: a 2.1% improvement in oxygen cost at 90 min, IF it held across the whole marathon and translated 1:1 to speed, would be 2.1% of 235.9 min ≈ 5 min. It almost certainly does not hold across 3h56 in someone doing an abbreviated protocol. Say 0–5 min, most likely at the low end.

interventions.intervention: The 'wall' as a fuel-limited event — what a shorter long run actually threatens
interventions.effect: Modelled carbohydrate stores: liver glycogen ~270 mmol/kg typical (~350 kcal) rising to ~500 mmol/kg supercompensated (~650 kcal); muscle glycogen ~110 mmol/kg in trained athletes (~80 kcal/kg muscle) rising to ~200 mmol/kg supercompensated (~144 kcal/kg muscle). For a typical 70 kg male: 1,600–2,920 kcal total carbohydrate. Distance to depletion = [liver glycogen + leg-muscle glycogen] / [carbohydrate fraction of energy × energy cost per km] — it rises with leg muscle mass and glycogen density and falls steeply with intensity, because carbohydrate's share of fuel rises supralinearly with speed. Critically for this question: the paper reports NO evidence that training changes glycogen STORAGE CAPACITY itself; training acts through aerobic capacity and substrate use.
interventions.population: Computational model calibrated on published human physiology; validated against marathon performance distributions rather than an experimental cohort
interventions.citation: Rapoport BI. Metabolic factors limiting performance in marathon runners. PLoS Computational Biology 2010;6(10):e1000960. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000960
interventions.sampleSize: n/a — computational model, not a trial
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, but mostly as a fuelling instruction rather than a training one. If the mechanism the long run is supposed to defend is glycogen, and glycogen storage capacity is not trainable, then in-race carbohydrate intake substitutes for the missing kilometres more directly than the kilometres do.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: DERIVED, not measured — my arithmetic on Rapoport's model for THIS athlete, flagged as such: 85.5 kg; energy cost ~0.95 kcal/kg/km → ~81 kcal/km. At 5:31/km, VO2 ≈ 0.2×181.3 + 3.5 ≈ 39.8 ml/kg/min ≈ 75% of his 53 VO2max, so carbohydrate ≈ 67% of fuel → ~54 kcal/km from carbohydrate. Rapoport's 70 kg runner has 975–1,785 kcal in liver + LEG muscle; scaled to 85.5 kg → 1,190–2,180 kcal. Unfuelled range to depletion = 22–40 km, midpoint ~31 km — the wall lands exactly where folklore puts it. Ingesting 60 g/h for 3.9 h = 234 g ≈ 940 kcal ≈ 17 extra km of glycogen equivalent. That single intervention dwarfs the 2–3 km he is missing off his long run.

interventions.intervention: Carbohydrate ingestion during prolonged exercise preserves the physiological capacity that deteriorates late (the substitute lever)
interventions.effect: Clark 2019: end-test power (a critical-power proxy) was unchanged after 40 and 80 min of heavy cycling but fell 9% after 2 h (260 ± 37 → 236 ± 47 W, p<0.05); 60 g/h carbohydrate NEGATED that fall (254 ± 49 W), while having no effect on W'. Norte 2026: after 3 h of moderate cycling, critical power fell from 277 ± 27 W to 236 ± 30 W on water, 257 ± 28 W on 60 g/h, and 266 ± 29 W on 120 g/h — a dose-dependent rescue (p<0.05 between all three).
interventions.population: Clark 2019: n=16 participants, cycling. Norte 2026: n=16 endurance-trained cyclists/triathletes, VO2max 51.8 ± 6.8 ml/kg/min — almost exactly this athlete's aerobic capacity (53), though cycling not running.
interventions.citation: Clark IE, Vanhatalo A, Thompson C, Joseph C, Black MI, Blackwell JR, Wylie LJ, Tan R, Bailey SJ, Wilkins BW, Kirby BS, Jones AM. Dynamics of the power-duration relationship during prolonged endurance exercise and influence of carbohydrate ingestion. Journal of Applied Physiology 2019;127(3):726–736. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00207.2019 — and — Norte BR, Slinn MM, Johnson KO, Mahon E, Shepherd SO, Strauss JA, Louis JB. Graded Carbohydrate Ingestion up to 120 g·h−1 Attenuates the Reduction in Critical Power Following 3 h of Moderate-Intensity Exercise in a Dose-Dependent Manner. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 2026;36:e70326. doi:10.1111/sms.70326
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, fully, and it is the highest-certainty lever in this whole domain. It needs six weeks only to practise gut tolerance at 60–120 g/h on the long runs — which is itself a reason to run the long runs, independent of their length.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to marathon minutes from these papers — the outcome is critical power in cycling, not a race time, and I found no verified dose-response trial converting in-race carbohydrate rate to marathon minutes in recreational runners. State the mechanism, not a fabricated minute count.

interventions.intervention: Metabolic adaptations to prolonged endurance sessions — the time course, i.e. can six weeks of long runs do anything at all?
interventions.effect: Phillips 1996: after only 5 DAYS of training, muscle lactate accumulation, phosphocreatine hydrolysis and GLYCOGEN DEPLETION during a 90-min exercise challenge were all reduced (p<0.01) — the glycogen-sparing adaptation is fast. Further training to 31 days reduced them further, and only by 31 days did succinate dehydrogenase (mitochondrial oxidative potential) rise +41% (p<0.01) and VO2peak +10% (p<0.05). Talanian 2007: seven interval sessions over 2 WEEKS raised whole-body fat oxidation during a 60-min ride by 36% (15.0 ± 2.4 → 20.4 ± 2.5 g), raised β-HAD +32% and citrate synthase +20%, raised plasma-membrane FABP +25%, and reduced net glycogen use — with resting muscle glycogen content UNCHANGED.
interventions.population: Phillips 1996: 7 healthy untrained men, 2 h/day cycling at 59% VO2peak, 5–6×/wk. Talanian 2007: 8 moderately active women, VO2peak 2.36 l/min. Both are untrained/moderately-active cyclists — the transfer to a trained 53-VO2max runner is weak, and the effect sizes in a trained athlete will be much smaller.
interventions.citation: Phillips SM, Green HJ, Tarnopolsky MA, Heigenhauser GJ, Grant SM. Progressive effect of endurance training on metabolic adaptations in working skeletal muscle. American Journal of Physiology 1996;270(2 Pt 1):E265–72. doi:10.1152/ajpendo.1996.270.2.E265 — and — Talanian JL, Galloway SDR, Heigenhauser GJF, Bonen A, Spriet LL. Two weeks of high-intensity aerobic interval training increases the capacity for fat oxidation during exercise in women. Journal of Applied Physiology 2007;102(4):1439–1447. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.01098.2006
interventions.sampleSize: n=7 and n=8 — both very small, neither replicated in trained marathon runners
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this is the one genuinely encouraging finding for a six-week block. Glycogen sparing and fat-oxidation capacity move within days to two weeks; the slower mitochondrial and VO2max changes need ~4+ weeks and he has 6. Note also that BOTH studies found the adaptation WITHOUT any single session approaching 30 km.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. These are muscle-biopsy and substrate-oxidation outcomes in untrained cyclists; no race-time arm exists. The useful inference is directional: the metabolic machinery the long run targets responds to repeated prolonged sessions, not to one maximal-distance session.

interventions.intervention: Marathon-pace or fast-finish segments inside the long run, vs the same distance run easy
interventions.effect: NO QUANTIFIED EFFECT EXISTS. A Europe PMC full-index search for abstracts containing both 'marathon pace' and 'long run' returned ZERO records. No trial has randomised long-run composition. The strongest defensible statement in the literature is the conditional one from Jones & Kirby 2025: prolonged sessions 'especially when these include bouts of high-intensity exercise at race pace or above or a progressive increase in intensity in the face of developing fatigue, MIGHT also represent an effective means of enhancing resilience'. Everything else — the fast-finish long run, the marathon-pace long run, Pfitzinger's 'LT within the long run' — is coaching practice with a plausible mechanism and no controlled test.
interventions.population: n/a — the intervention has never been tested in any population
interventions.citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS. Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scand J Med Sci Sports 2025;35(3):e70032. doi:10.1111/sms.70032 (for the conditional claim); absence established by Europe PMC index search returning 0 hits for ABSTRACT:'marathon pace' AND ABSTRACT:'long run'
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as a practice — a 26 km run with 8–10 km at marathon pace at the end is deliverable inside his ceiling and is the most defensible way to make a shorter long run harder without making it longer. But he should know he is buying a mechanism, not a measured effect.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — no effect size exists. Any number offered for this is invented.

interventions.intervention: Capping the long run (Hansons' 16-mile / 3-hour rule)
interventions.effect: No published trial supports OR refutes the cap. The Hansons rationale — that runs beyond ~3 hours deplete too much glycogen and risk overtraining — is asserted in a commercial book that contains no research references. The nearest empirical evidence: Fokkema's >35 km group showed no significant benefit over 30–35 km (−4.86 min, CI −13.51 to +3.79), which is consistent with a plateau but is not a test of a cap; and Fokkema found NO association between longest run and running-related injury in either the marathon or half-marathon arm, which undercuts the injury half of the cap's rationale (though a null in n=441 with 55% injury incidence is weak evidence of safety, not proof).
interventions.population: n/a for the cap itself; Fokkema's 441 recreational marathoners for the adjacent evidence
interventions.citation: Fokkema T et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2020;30(9):1692–1704 (the >35 km null and the injury null). The Hansons cap itself: Humphrey L, Hanson K, Hanson K. Hansons Marathon Method (VeloPress) — trade book, no primary-source citations for the cap.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — and conveniently, his 27–29 km ceiling at ~6:00/km easy pace is roughly 2:45–2:55, i.e. he lands inside the capped philosophy whether he chooses it or not. He can frame the constraint as a method rather than a deficit, and that framing is as evidence-based as the alternative.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — no trial has compared capped against uncapped long runs at matched weekly volume.

interventions.intervention: What published training plans actually prescribe (the de-facto standard, and what it is worth)
interventions.effect: Across 92 commercial sub-elite plans, the single longest run was 35.2 ± 3.3 km (high-volume plans, >90 km peak week), 32.5 ± 3.8 km (middle, 65–90 km) and 30.9 ± 4.1 km (low, <65 km). Strikingly, the PEAK-WEEK long run did not differ significantly across volume bands: 32.2 ± 6.2 / 31.2 ± 3.1 / 29.7 ± 4.9 km, F=1.9, p=0.16 — plan authors converge on ~30–32 km regardless of how much running surrounds it. Average weekly long run over the last 12 weeks was 27.4 / 23.0 / 19.9 km. The authors state the limitation themselves: 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated'.
interventions.population: 92 publicly available marathon training plans aimed at sub-elite recreational runners — the source of nearly all the advice this athlete will encounter online
interventions.citation: Knopp M, Appelhans D, Schönfelder M, Seiler S, Wackerhage H. Quantitative Analysis of 92 12-Week Sub-elite Marathon Training Plans. Sports Medicine – Open 2024;10:50. doi:10.1186/s40798-024-00717-5 (PMC11065819), Tables 3 and 4
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as a benchmark: his 27–29 km ceiling sits ~2–4 km below the low-volume plan norm of 30.9 km and ~1–3 km below the peak-week convergence point of ~29.7 km. He is a rounding error away from what the entire commercial-plan corpus recommends for his volume band.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — this is a content analysis of documents, not an outcome study. It tells you what coaches believe, with zero information about whether they are right.

interventions.intervention: Elite practice as a check on the long-run orthodoxy
interventions.effect: Among 2004 US Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers, marathon performance correlated with years training, average and peak weekly distance, number of weekly runs, and number of runs ≥32 km — but the ≥32 km correlation held FOR WOMEN ONLY. Men ran 145.3 ± 25.6 km/wk, women 116.0 ± 26.5 km/wk; men and women ran 75% and 68% of weekly distance below marathon race pace. The author's conclusion is the useful one: 'there is no consensus as to how to prepare for the marathon beyond running at a pace slower than race pace'. 49% of men and 31% of women had no coach.
interventions.population: 93 respondents (37 men, 56 women) of 255 US Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers — elite and national class. Transfer to a 3:55 recreational runner on 24 km/wk is very weak; included as evidence about the STATE of the field, not as a prescription.
interventions.citation: Karp JR. Training characteristics of qualifiers for the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 2007;2(1):72–92. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2.1.72
interventions.sampleSize: n=93 (36% response rate — substantial non-response bias risk)
interventions.duration: Retrospective questionnaire on a training block
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No — irrelevant as a prescription. Relevant only as evidence that even at the top of the sport there is no agreed long-run doctrine.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — correlations in a homogeneous elite sample, and the ≥32 km relationship failed to appear in men.

interventions.intervention: Context: what actually causes late-race collapse, and how much it costs
interventions.effect: In 2,179,221 race records, 28% of male and 17% of female runners hit the wall (defined as ≥25% slowdown sustained ≥5 km after 20 km; odds ratio 1.43, p<0.01). It began at 29.6 km (males) / 29.3 km (females), lasted 10.72 / 9.61 km, with a 40% / 37% pace reduction, and cost 31.50 min (males) / 33.20 min (females). Prevalence rose from ~15% among 3:00 finishers to over 40% among 5:00+ finishers. Risk was HIGHEST in the three years BEFORE a personal best (40% of males) versus 26% in earlier years — i.e. chasing a PB with aggressive pacing is itself the dominant risk factor.
interventions.population: 717,940 unique recreational runners across 270 marathons in 38 cities, 2005–2019. Directly this athlete's population, and he is in the highest-risk profile: male, chasing a PB, in the years before his best time.
interventions.citation: Smyth B. How recreational marathon runners hit the wall: A large-scale data analysis of late-race pacing collapse in the marathon. PLOS ONE 2021;16(5):e0251513. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0251513
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — but the actionable lever it identifies is PACING and fuelling on race day, not long-run distance. A 31-minute collapse dwarfs the 3–6 minute long-run question by a factor of five to ten.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 31.5 min for a male who hits the wall — measured, not modelled. For this athlete the expected value of avoiding it (if his baseline risk is ~28%) is roughly 0.28 × 31.5 ≈ 9 min of expected finish time, which is larger than the entire long-run effect he is worried about.

interventions.intervention: Context on the binding constraint: a ≥7-day training gap (he already had a 0 km week)
interventions.effect: Runners who lost 7–13 consecutive days of training in weeks 3–12 pre-race finished 4.25% slower than the same runners' own undisrupted marathons. Longer gaps cost progressively more (5–8%). Late disruptions (3–7 weeks out) cost 5.2% vs 4.4% for early (8–12 weeks). A 21–27 day late disruption cost ~10%. Faster runners (PB ≤240 min) paid more (5.4%) than slower ones (2.6%). Each runner served as their own control, which removes most fitness confounding.
interventions.population: 292,323 recreational marathon runners, 509,979 marathons, 15,697,711 activities, 2014–2017; 80% male, mean age ~39–40. Exactly this athlete's population and he is in the 'faster runner' band that pays the larger penalty.
interventions.citation: Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A. Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 2023;4:1096124. doi:10.3389/fspor.2022.1096124 (PMC9871827)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and urgently — the six weeks remaining ARE the 'late disruption' window that carries the higher penalty. Consistency over the next six weeks matters demonstrably more than the last 3 km of any single long run.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 5.4% (the faster-runner figure) × 235.9 min = +12.7 min for a single 7–13 day gap in this window. Compare: the 27–29 km vs 30 km long-run question is worth ~3–6 min. One missed week costs two to four times more than the long-run shortfall.

myths: 'You must run 32 km (20 miles) before a marathon or you will not finish.' The only study that has ever binned long-run distance against finish time in recreational marathoners found <25 km cost +13.4 min versus a 30–35 km reference (Fokkema 2020) — a time penalty, not a failure mode. Non-finish rate across 85 marathon studies was 7.27% (95% CI 6.09–8.65%, Doherty 2020), and no study attributes non-finishing to long-run distance.

'A 30 km long run is measurably better than a 25 km one.' In Fokkema 2020 the adjusted difference between the 25–30 km and 30–35 km groups was +6.40 min with a 95% CI of −0.04 to +12.82 — it fails to exclude zero. The raw between-group difference (4:25:07 vs 4:15:26) is roughly 10 min, but most of that vanishes once weekly volume, training pace, age, sex, BMI and experience are adjusted for. The honest verdict is 'probably a small benefit, not measurably established'.

'More is more — 35 km and beyond keeps helping.' Adjusted effect of >35 km versus 30–35 km: −4.86 min, 95% CI −13.51 to +3.79, not significant (Fokkema 2020). The dose-response flattens somewhere around 30 km in this population.

'A short long run means you will fade in the second half.' Fokkema 2020 measured in-race pace decline directly (5–10 km segment vs 35–40 km segment) and found NO association with longest run in marathoners (25–30 vs 30–35 km: +0.21 percentage points, 95% CI −4.04 to +4.55). It did find such an association in half-marathoners, which makes the marathon null more, not less, credible.

'Runs over three hours deplete too much glycogen to be worth doing.' This is the Hansons cap. It appears in a commercial trade book with no primary-source citations, and no controlled trial has ever compared a capped against an uncapped long run at matched weekly volume. It may well be right; it is not evidenced.

'The long run builds your glycogen stores.' Rapoport's model states explicitly that there is no evidence training changes glycogen STORAGE CAPACITY itself; training-induced improvement in the distance-to-depletion comes through aerobic capacity and substrate use. Talanian 2007 found resting muscle glycogen UNCHANGED after training that cut net glycogen use by 36% via fat oxidation. The long run does not make the tank bigger; it makes the engine sip.

'Fat adaptation from long slow runs takes months.' Phillips 1996 found reduced glycogen depletion during a 90-min challenge after just 5 DAYS of training, and Talanian 2007 found +36% whole-body fat oxidation after 2 weeks. Both in untrained/moderately-active cyclists, so the magnitude will not transfer — but the timescale argument against a six-week block is not supported.

'Time on feet is what matters, not distance.' Every dataset in this domain measured DISTANCE. Fokkema binned kilometres. Doherty's covariates were kilometres and hours-per-week, not long-run duration. Knopp's plan analysis converted time-based plans INTO distance. There is no study comparing time-matched against distance-matched long runs. The claim is untested in either direction, and repeating it as settled is folklore.

'The wall is a training-distance problem.' Smyth 2021 (n=2.18 million races) found wall risk was highest in the three years BEFORE a personal best (40% of males vs 26% in earlier years) — i.e. the dominant identified risk factor is aggressive PB-chasing pacing, not training shortfall. Prevalence also scales with ability (≈15% at 3:00 to >40% at 5:00+).

'Durability is a distinct quality you can train in a block.' The current review by the people who named it says 'data are scant' and attributes it primarily to training consistency and volume accumulated over SEVERAL YEARS (Jones & Kirby 2025). The only intervention trial (Matomäki 2023) was 10 weeks in sedentary/recreationally-active cyclists and its own authors note the drift changes were small.

'Long runs are the main injury risk in marathon training.' Fokkema 2020 found no statistically significant association between longest endurance run, weekly volume or training pace and running-related injury in either the marathon or half-marathon arm (55.1% of marathoners sustained a new injury during follow-up regardless). This is a null, not a safety guarantee — but it removes injury as a stated reason for capping the long run.
unknowns: No randomised controlled trial has ever manipulated long-run distance. Every quantitative claim in this domain — including the best one (Fokkema 2020) — is observational, and longest run is partly a marker of the fitness that produced it. The causal effect of adding 3 km to a long run is unmeasured and is very likely smaller than the observed association.

The shape of the dose-response curve between 25 and 35 km is unknown. Fokkema's bins (<25, 25–30, 30–35, >35) are the finest resolution that exists, and within-bin position — whether 29 km behaves like 26 km or like 31 km — cannot be recovered from binned data.

Whether time or distance is the correct prescription. No study has compared duration-matched with distance-matched long runs. This matters most for slower runners, for whom 30 km and 3 hours are the same session, and for whom the entire literature is therefore confounded between the two.

Whether marathon-pace or progressive-intensity segments inside a long run add anything over the same distance run easy. Zero trials. A Europe PMC index search for abstracts containing both 'marathon pace' and 'long run' returned zero records.
Whether back-to-back medium-long runs (e.g. 20 km Saturday + 18 km Sunday) substitute for a single 30 km run. Widely practised, never tested against a single-session comparator.

Whether durability/physiological resilience is trainable on a six-week timescale in an already-trained runner, or whether it is essentially a multi-year accumulation. Jones & Kirby (2025) say the data are scant and lean towards years.

Per-covariate effect sizes from the only meta-regression in the field. Doherty 2020 reports only that R² across seven separate univariate models ranged 0.38–0.81; the paper is paywalled and I could not obtain per-covariate coefficients. Anyone quoting a minutes-per-long-run figure from it is extrapolating beyond the accessible record.
Whether the >35 km null in Fokkema reflects a genuine plateau or the small subgroup (n=38) and its wide confidence interval.

How much of the 30 km long run's apparent benefit is the session itself versus the weekly volume and training consistency required to survive it. Fokkema adjusted for weekly volume, which is the best available attempt, but adjustment is not randomisation.

Whether any official governing body has ever published a quantitative long-run prescription. I verified that the one ACSM public page reachable in this session (distance-running form guidance) contains none, and my web-search budget was exhausted before I could check World Athletics, UK Athletics or England Athletics coaching materials. I could NOT verify the existence of any such official document, and I am not going to assert one exists or does not. What is verified is that the de-facto standard is commercial plans, quantified by Knopp 2024, whose authors state there is no evidence for their effectiveness.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)
officialSources.document: Healthy Habits for Distance Running (public guidance page)
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: CHECKED AND IT PRESCRIBES NOTHING RELEVANT. The page covers running form, cadence, posture and injury prevention. It contains no long-run distance, no long-run duration, and no weekly-mileage prescription. Recorded here as a verified negative: the one official body page I could reach in this session offers no long-run doctrine at all.

officialSources.body: Peer-reviewed corpus of published commercial training plans (the closest thing to an 'official' standard in this domain, and it is not official)
officialSources.document: Knopp M, Appelhans D, Schönfelder M, Seiler S, Wackerhage H. Quantitative Analysis of 92 12-Week Sub-elite Marathon Training Plans. Sports Medicine – Open 2024;10:50
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Longest single run 30.9 ± 4.1 km (plans peaking <65 km/wk), 32.5 ± 3.8 km (65–90 km/wk), 35.2 ± 3.3 km (>90 km/wk). Peak-week long run converges on ~29.7–32.2 km with NO significant difference across volume bands (F=1.9, p=0.16). Average weekly long run over the final 12 weeks 19.9 / 23.0 / 27.4 km. Pyramidal intensity distribution, 13.2/65.6/15.1/3.0/3.0% across zones 1–5. The authors state the caveat themselves: 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated'.

officialSources.body: Note on absence
officialSources.document: World Athletics / UK Athletics / England Athletics coaching materials — NOT VERIFIED
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: I was unable to verify, within this session's search budget, whether any of these bodies publishes a quantitative marathon long-run prescription. I am explicitly NOT claiming they do or do not. Treat any citation to a 'World Athletics long-run guideline' with suspicion unless someone produces the document.

check.domain: The long run in marathon training — distance, frequency, composition, and the cost of a 27–29 km long-run ceiling for a 3:55 recreational marathoner in a six-week block

citationChecks.citation: Fokkema T, van Damme AADN, Fornerod MWJ, de Vos R-J, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, van Middelkoop M. Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2020;30(9):1692-1704. doi:10.1111/sms.13725 (PMC7496388)
citationChecks.note: Pulled the full text (Europe PMC PMC7496388) and checked Tables 1-3 line by line. EVERY number the researcher reported is exact: <25 km beta 13.44 (5.34;21.55); 25-30 km 6.40 (-0.04;12.82); >35 km -4.86 (-13.51;3.79); marathon pace-decline for 25-30 vs 30-35 = 0.21 (-4.04;4.55); half >21 km -3.87 (-6.31;-1.44) and decline -1.89 (-3.65;-0.12); group n = 91/111/200/38; group finish times 4:37:43 / 4:25:07 / 4:15:26 / 3:50:18; cohort mean finish 4:17:54; age 41.4; 70.1% male; median weekly 40.0 [30.0;50.0]; median longest run 32.0 [27.0;35.0]; half median weekly 26.0; 341 marathon finishers; 55.1% injured; no training-injury association. The claimed adjustment set is also correct — the paper states all regressions were adjusted for sex, age, BMI, running experience and prior-12-month injury, with weekly volume, longest run and training pace all entered in the same multivariable model. This is the single load-bearing citation and it holds completely.

citationChecks.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B. An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression. J Sci Med Sport 2020;23(2):182-188. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2019.09.013
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms 85 studies, 137 cohorts, 25% female, the exact seven covariates including 'number of runs >=32km completed in the pre-marathon training block', R2 0.38-0.81 p<0.001 across separately conducted univariate random-effects models, and the non-finish rate 7.27% (95% CI 6.09-8.65%) used in the myths section. The researcher's self-imposed caveat is correct and unusually honest: the accessible record gives only the R2 RANGE across seven separate models, never a per-covariate coefficient, so no minutes-per-long-run figure can be derived from it. No overclaim here.

citationChecks.citation: Smyth B, Maunder E, Meyler S, Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D. Decoupling of Internal and External Workload During a Marathon: An Analysis of Durability in 82,303 Recreational Runners. Sports Med 2022;52(9):2283-2295. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01680-5 (PMC9388405)
citationChecks.note: Every figure matches the abstract verbatim: 82,303 runners (13,125 female); overall decoupling 1.16 +/- 0.22 first detected at 25.2 +/- 9.9 km; low group 34.5%, 88 +/- 6% CS, 217.3 +/- 33.1 min, onset 33.4 +/- 9.0 km; high group 32.8%, 82 +/- 7% CS, 238.5 +/- 30.7 min, onset 19.1 +/- 6.8 km; male vs female 1.17 vs 1.12 and 25.0 vs 26.3 km; prediction error reduced 6.45% -> 5.16%. The 21.2-min spread is correct arithmetic (238.5-217.3) and the researcher correctly refuses to treat it as a treatment effect, explicitly naming the relative-speed confound (88% vs 82% CS) that the abstract itself reports.

citationChecks.citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS. Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scand J Med Sci Sports 2025;35(3):e70032. doi:10.1111/sms.70032 (PMC11872681)
citationChecks.note: Both quoted passages are verbatim from the abstract: 'data are scant', 'training consistency and the accumulation of relatively large volumes of training over the longer-term (i.e., several years) might promote resilience', and the conditional on prolonged sessions 'especially when these include bouts of high-intensity exercise at race pace or above or a progressive increase in intensity in the face of developing fatigue'. The researcher's insistence that every verb is conditional is accurate. One omission rather than an error: the same abstract also concludes that 'resistance training, especially heavy strength and plyometric training, appears to have positive effects' — which strengthens the researcher's own strength-training recommendation and should have been quoted alongside Zanini.

citationChecks.citation: Matomaki P, Heinonen OJ, Nummela A, Laukkanen J, Auvinen E-P, Pirkola L, Kyrolainen H. Durability is improved by both low and high intensity endurance training. Front Physiol 2023;14:1128111. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1128111 (PMC9977827)
citationChecks.note: Exact match on all reported values: LIT 6.8 +/- 0.7 h/wk vs HIT 1.6 +/- 0.2 h/wk; n=16 men and n=19 women (35 total); time x group p=0.42; LIT p=0.03 g=0.49, HIT p=0.01 g=0.62; HIT drift magnitude 8.8 +/- 7.9% -> 5.4 +/- 6.7% (p=0.03, g=0.49) and onset 108 +/- 54 -> 137 +/- 57 min (p=0.03, g=0.61); LIT magnitude p=0.09 and onset 106 -> 131 min p=0.08 (both non-significant); VO2max only with HIT, g=1.51. The quoted author caution 'a 10-week intervention did not alter drifts and their onsets in a large amount' is verbatim from the conclusion. The transfer warnings the researcher attaches are the paper's own.

citationChecks.citation: Zanini M, Folland JP, Wu H, Blagrove RC. Strength Training Improves Running Economy Durability and Fatigued High-Intensity Performance in Well-Trained Male Runners: A Randomized Control Trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2025;57(7):1546-1558. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003685
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms n=28 well-trained male runners (14 per arm), VO2max 58.6 mL/kg/min, 10 km 39:02, 10 weeks of twice-weekly maximal strength and plyometric training; RE interaction P=0.003 etap2=0.13 with -2.1% (E+S) vs +0.6% (E) at 90 min, P=0.04; TTE interaction P=0.004 etap2=0.28 with +35% vs -8%. All exact. Note the RE outcome was measured at 79.7% VO2max (heavy-intensity domain), which is above this athlete's marathon intensity — the researcher's decision to treat 5 min as a hard upper bound is therefore well-judged.

citationChecks.citation: Rapoport BI. Metabolic factors limiting performance in marathon runners. PLoS Comput Biol 2010;6(10):e1000960. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000960
citationChecks.note: The paper exists and every value quoted FROM it is exact (liver 270 typical / 500 max mmol/kg = 350/650 kcal; muscle 110 typical / 200 max mmol/kg = 80/144 kcal per kg leg muscle; leg muscle ~21.4% of body mass; and the paper's own 70 kg figure of 1250-2270 kcal leg glycogen + 350-650 kcal liver = the researcher's quoted 1,600-2,920 kcal). TWO problems. (1) The DERIVED application then silently uses a different, 39%-smaller base (975-1,785 kcal) for the same 70 kg runner — see effectSizeErrors; this is the number that produces the headline 'the wall lands at ~31 km'. (2) The claim that 'the paper reports NO evidence that training changes glycogen STORAGE CAPACITY itself' is not something Rapoport states. I grepped the full text for it and found nothing; the paper simply models capacity as leg muscle mass x glycogen density and never addresses trainability of density. Attributing an absence-of-evidence claim to a source that is silent on the question is an overstatement, and it is load-bearing for myth #6.

citationChecks.citation: Clark IE, Vanhatalo A, Thompson C, Joseph C, Black MI, Blackwell JR, Wylie LJ, Tan R, Bailey SJ, Wilkins BW, Kirby BS, Jones AM. Dynamics of the power-duration relationship during prolonged endurance exercise and influence of carbohydrate ingestion. J Appl Physiol 2019;127(3):726-736. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00207.2019
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms exactly: EP unchanged after 40 min (268 +/- 39 W) and 80 min (260 +/- 40 W) vs control (260 +/- 37 W), but 9% lower after 2 h (236 +/- 47 W, P<0.05); 60 g/h CHO 'negated' that reduction (254 +/- 49 W) with no effect on W' (13.5 +/- 3.4 kJ). n=16. The researcher's verb 'negated' is the paper's own. Only gap: the researcher describes the sample as 'n=16 participants, cycling' without stating training status or sex, so the population match to this athlete is left unassessed.

citationChecks.citation: Norte BR, Slinn MM, Johnson KO, Mahon E, Shepherd SO, Strauss JA, Louis JB. Graded Carbohydrate Ingestion up to 120 g/h Attenuates the Reduction in Critical Power Following 3 h of Moderate-Intensity Exercise in a Dose-Dependent Manner. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2026;36:e70326. doi:10.1111/sms.70326 (PMC13282445)
citationChecks.note: I checked this one hardest because a 2026 citation is the classic shape of a fabrication. It is real and open-access. Abstract confirms n=16 endurance-trained cyclists/triathletes, VO2max 51.8 +/- 6.8 mL/kg/min; CP non-fatigued 277 +/- 27 W falling after 3 h to 236 +/- 30 W (water), 257 +/- 28 W (60 g/h), 266 +/- 29 W (120 g/h), dose-dependent, all pairwise p<0.05; W' unaffected. Every figure exact. Crossref gives volume 36 issue 6, so the citation's omission of the issue number is the only imperfection.

citationChecks.citation: Phillips SM, Green HJ, Tarnopolsky MA, Heigenhauser GJ, Grant SM. Progressive effect of endurance training on metabolic adaptations in working skeletal muscle. Am J Physiol 1996;270(2 Pt 1):E265-72. doi:10.1152/ajpendo.1996.270.2.E265
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms 7 healthy untrained men, 2 h/day cycling at 59% pretraining VO2peak 5-6x/wk; after 5 days muscle lactate, PCr hydrolysis and glycogen depletion during a 90-min challenge all reduced (P<0.01); further reduction by 31 days; succinate dehydrogenase +41% (P<0.01) and VO2peak +10% (P<0.05) only at 31 days. All exact, including the researcher's key inference that the fast adaptations preceded any rise in mitochondrial potential — the paper states precisely that.

citationChecks.citation: Talanian JL, Galloway SDR, Heigenhauser GJF, Bonen A, Spriet LL. Two weeks of high-intensity aerobic interval training increases the capacity for fat oxidation during exercise in women. J Appl Physiol 2007;102(4):1439-1447. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.01098.2006
citationChecks.note: Abstract confirms seven HIIT sessions over 2 weeks in 8 women (22.1 yr, VO2peak 2.36 L/min); whole-body fat oxidation during a 60-min ride +36% (15.0 +/- 2.4 -> 20.4 +/- 2.5 g); beta-HAD +32%; citrate synthase +20%; resting muscle glycogen and triacylglycerol UNAFFECTED; net glycogen use reduced. All exact. The one figure I could not confirm is 'plasma-membrane FABP +25%' — it is not in the abstract and the full text is paywalled; FABPpm changes are reported in this paper's results but I could not verify the magnitude. Treat that single number as unchecked rather than wrong.

citationChecks.citation: Knopp M, Appelhans D, Schonfelder M, Seiler S, Wackerhage H. Quantitative Analysis of 92 12-Week Sub-elite Marathon Training Plans. Sports Med Open 2024;10:50. doi:10.1186/s40798-024-00717-5 (PMC11065819)
citationChecks.note: Pulled full text and checked Tables 3 and 4. Longest run 35.2 +/- 3.3 / 32.5 +/- 3.8 / 30.9 +/- 4.1 km with F=15.2 — exact. Peak-week long run 32.2 +/- 6.2 / 31.2 +/- 3.1 / 29.7 +/- 4.9 km, F=1.9, p=0.16 — exact, and the researcher's point that plan authors converge on ~30 km regardless of surrounding volume is a fair reading of a genuine null. Average weekly long run 27.4 / 23.0 / 19.9 km — exact. The intensity distribution 13.2/65.6/15.1/3.0/3.0% is not a per-band row but the paper's own aggregate summary sentence, quoted correctly. The caveat 'no evidence for the effectiveness of the training plans investigated' is verbatim from the abstract.

citationChecks.citation: Karp JR. Training characteristics of qualifiers for the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2007;2(1):72-92. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2.1.72
citationChecks.note: Abstract (via OpenAlex) confirms 104 men + 151 women invited, 93 responded (37 men, 56 women) = 36.5% response; men 145.3 +/- 25.6 vs women 116.0 +/- 26.5 km/wk; 75% and 68% of weekly distance below marathon race pace; 49% of men and 31% of women had no coach; and the quoted conclusion 'there is no consensus as to how to prepare for the marathon beyond running at a pace slower than race pace' is verbatim. One reading caveat: the abstract's list is 'correlated to ... years training, average and peak weekly distance, number of weekly runs, and number of runs >= 32 km for women'. The researcher reads 'for women' as attaching only to the >=32 km item. That reading supports their claim, but the paper's own conclusion ('Weekly training distance seems to influence women's marathon performance more than it does men's') suggests 'for women' may qualify more of the list. Their specific claim survives either reading.

citationChecks.citation: Smyth B. How recreational marathon runners hit the wall: A large-scale data analysis of late-race pacing collapse in the marathon. PLOS ONE 2021;16(5):e0251513. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0251513 (PMC8133477)
citationChecks.note: Full text checked. 28% male vs 17% female, OR 1.43 — exact. Slowdown onset 29.6 km male / 29.3 km female; duration 10.72 / 9.61 km; relative slowdown 0.40 / 0.37; cost 31.50 / 33.20 min — all exact. The definition is exactly as stated: degree-of-slowdown threshold 0.25 and length-of-slowdown threshold 5 km, applied to segments after the 20 km mark. The male-specific PB figure is exact and is the harder-to-find one: '1-3 years before achieving an overall PB, 40% of male runners hit the wall, compared to just under 26% in the 4-9 year period'. The paper also states 'more than 40% of male runners with slower PBs do hit the wall', supporting the ability gradient. One trivial slip: the 28%/17% comparison has chi-square N = 1,928,813; the 2,179,221 figure the researcher attaches to it is the size of the repeaters dataset (717,940 unique runners, 270 races, 38 cities, 2005-2019 — all correct).

citationChecks.citation: Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A. Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance. Front Sports Act Living 2023;4:1096124. doi:10.3389/fspor.2022.1096124 (PMC9871827)
citationChecks.note: Full text checked. 292,323 runners, 509,979 marathons, 15,697,711 activities, 2014-2017, 80% male — all exact. 7-13 day disruption = 4.25% increase in finish time — exact. Faster runners 5.4% vs slower 2.6%; late 5.2% vs early 4.4%; males 5% vs females 3.5% — all exact. The late/early definitions the researcher used are the paper's own: late = 3-7 weeks from race day, early = 8-12 weeks, with the final 3 taper weeks excluded — which is why 'weeks 3-12' is the right framing. Within-runner paired design confirmed. The only figure I could not verify in text is the '~10%' for a 21-27 day late disruption, which appears to be read off Figure 3 rather than stated; the 21-27 day bucket exists (n=2,411 pairs) and the abstract's 5-8% range is confirmed.

citationChecks.citation: Humphrey L, Hanson K, Hanson K. Hansons Marathon Method (VeloPress) — cited as a trade book with no primary-source citations for the 16-mile / 3-hour long-run cap
citationChecks.note: The book is real and the attribution is correct, but I did not obtain a copy and cannot confirm the claim that it 'contains no research references' for the cap. The researcher presents this as a verified negative about the book's contents; it should be presented as an unverified impression unless someone opens the book. The surrounding reasoning does not depend on it — the substantive point (no controlled trial has compared a capped against an uncapped long run at matched weekly volume) is one I also could not falsify.

citationChecks.citation: American College of Sports Medicine, 'Healthy Habits for Distance Running' — https://www.acsm.org/distance-running-form-tips/ — cited as a verified negative (contains no long-run prescription)
citationChecks.note: I did not re-fetch this page (session web-search budget exhausted before I reached it). I note only that the researcher's own framing is appropriately narrow — it claims one page, checked, containing nothing, and explicitly refuses to assert anything about World Athletics, UK Athletics or England Athletics. That refusal is the correct behaviour and I found no evidence contradicting it. But a single ACSM form-tips page is weak grounds for any statement about official doctrine, and the athlete should not read it as 'the ACSM has no position'.

effectSizeErrors: MATERIAL ERROR — the Rapoport glycogen derivation understates the athlete's fuel by ~40%, and that error is what manufactures the tidy '31 km' conclusion. The report states correctly, from Rapoport's own text, that a typical 70 kg male holds 1,600-2,920 kcal in liver plus leg-muscle glycogen (the paper says 1250-2270 kcal leg glycogen + 350-650 kcal liver — I confirmed both halves verbatim). Two paragraphs later the same 70 kg runner is given '975-1,785 kcal in liver + LEG muscle' — a different, 39%-smaller number, inconsistent with the report's own figure. Reverse-engineering it, the second calculation assumes leg muscle is ~11% of body mass; Rapoport's stated value is 21.4%. Everything downstream inherits it. Corrected: scaling 1,600-2,920 kcal by 85.5/70 gives 1,954-3,566 kcal; at the report's own 54.4 kcal/km that is 36-66 km to depletion, midpoint ~51 km — not '22-40 km, midpoint ~31 km'. Even refusing to scale at all (treating leg muscle mass as absolute, which is more defensible for a heavier runner whose extra mass may not be muscle) gives 29-54 km. The direction matters: the report's version has the wall landing 'exactly where folklore puts it', which reads as confirmation and is not what the source supports. The correction actually strengthens the report's overall conclusion — glycogen is even less likely to be the binding constraint — but the specific number is wrong and the coincidence it produces is an artefact.

Compounding the above: liver glycogen is scaled linearly with body mass. Rapoport derives 350-650 kcal from a fixed 1.8 kg liver; liver mass does not track body mass at anything like 1:1, so multiplying the liver term by 85.5/70 is not justified. Small in absolute terms (~75-140 kcal) but it is the same category of error.

The 'bin-position correction: 27-29 km is in the upper half of the 25-30 bin, so halve it' step has no basis and is arithmetically shaky on its own logic. The bin's midpoint is 27.5 km; the athlete's 27-29 km centres on 28 km, barely above it. Halving a coefficient for a 0.5 km displacement inside a 5 km bin is not interpolation, it is a guess dressed as one — and the report's own unknowns section correctly says within-bin position cannot be recovered from binned data. The two statements contradict each other. The defensible answer is the unmodified +6.4 min with a 95% interval of roughly 0 to +12.8, not '~+3 min'.

Rescaling Fokkema's beta from minutes into a percentage and re-applying it to a faster runner is a modelling choice that should be stated, not assumed. Beta is an absolute minutes coefficient from a linear regression on finish time; the model as fitted says +6.40 minutes for anyone in that bin. Converting to 2.48% of the cohort mean and re-multiplying by 235.9 min shrinks it to +5.9 — a systematically conservative bias applied to every conversion in the report (the <25 km figure, the half-marathon figure). The direction is towards understating the penalty, i.e. towards the answer the athlete wants to hear. Not wrong, but it should be flagged as an assumption rather than presented as 'working'.

Minor: the 28%-of-males / 17%-of-females wall prevalence is attached to '2,179,221 race records'. That figure is the repeaters dataset; the chi-square for that comparison reports N = 1,928,813. Does not change any conclusion.

The report's Europe PMC null search — ABSTRACT:'marathon pace' AND ABSTRACT:'long run' returning 0 hits — reproduces exactly, and I confirmed it. But it is a single singular-form query carrying a very strong claim ('NO QUANTIFIED EFFECT EXISTS'). Switching to 'long runs' returns 5 records; none is a long-run-composition trial, so the substantive conclusion survives, but a zero-hit result from one phrasing is thin evidence for the non-existence of a literature.
populationMismatches: Talanian 2007 — the sex mismatch is unflagged. The sample is 8 WOMEN, mean age 22.1, moderately active, VO2peak 2.36 L/min, on a cycle ergometer. The report flags 'untrained/moderately-active cyclists' but never mentions that every subject was female. This paper carries the entire '+36% fat oxidation in 2 weeks' claim and the 'resting muscle glycogen unchanged' claim that anchors myth #6, for a 27-year-old male at VO2max 53. Sex differences in substrate utilisation during exercise are among the better-established findings in this literature — women oxidise proportionally more fat at matched relative intensities — which makes a female-only fat-oxidation result a poor basis for a male-specific inference.

Fokkema 2020 is described as 'closely matched to this athlete on volume'. On current volume it is not. The cohort's median weekly training distance was 40 km [IQR 30-50]; this athlete's six-month average is 24.4 km/week and his last four complete weeks were 27 / 35 / 0 / 15 km. He sits in Fokkema's <40 km/week band, where the paper reports +6.33 min (95% CI 0.18-12.48) versus the 40-65 km reference — an effect the report never applies to him despite quoting the neighbouring >65 km coefficient. He is being compared to the long-run bins of runners who were training roughly twice as much as he currently is. He is also 27 against a cohort mean of 41.4 years. The ratified 60/80/100/80/60 km plan would move him into the cohort's range, but the plan is aspirational and he has never run a 60 km week; the evidence is being applied to a version of him that does not yet exist.

Rapoport 2010 models a LEAN 70 kg male assumed to be 45% skeletal muscle with half of that in the legs. This athlete is 85.5 kg with a 3:55 marathon and a weight field untouched since March, so his body composition is unknown and unlikely to match a lean elite-model runner. Scaling the whole glycogen store by 85.5/70 assumes the extra 15.5 kg is muscle distributed in the same proportion. If any meaningful part of it is not, leg glycogen stays near the 70 kg absolute value while energy cost per km rises with total mass — which cuts both the numerator and worsens the denominator. This is a genuine mismatch on top of the arithmetic error above.

Matomaki 2023 is the only controlled durability trial cited and its population is the furthest from this athlete of anything in the report: SEDENTARY and recreationally active men and women, cycling, tested at 48% of pre-training VO2max — roughly half his marathon intensity — and mixed-sex. The report flags this clearly and refuses to convert it to minutes, which is the correct call. Worth restating to the athlete: a 10-week effect in untrained cyclists at half marathon intensity is close to uninformative about what six weeks does to a runner already at VO2max 53 after five months of training.

Phillips 1996 — 7 untrained men, 2 h/day of cycling at 59% VO2peak, 5-6 days/week. That is roughly 12 hours a week of cycling in previously untrained men. The report uses it to argue the metabolic machinery moves fast enough for a six-week block, and flags the untrained/cycling problem. But the training dose itself is also mismatched: this athlete will not be doing 12 h/week, and the '5-day' adaptation was produced by an extreme stimulus in people with everything to gain.

Clark 2019 and Norte 2026 are both CYCLING studies with critical-power outcomes, n=16 each. Norte's participants (VO2max 51.8) are a good aerobic match; Clark's training status and sex are not stated in the report at all. Neither measured a running outcome and neither measured a race time. The report is explicit that no marathon-minutes conversion is possible from them, which is right — but the confidence rating of 'high' on this intervention rests on mechanism plus dose-response consistency across two cycling crossovers, not on any evidence in runners.

Zanini 2025 — well-trained MALE runners at VO2max 58.6 and 10 km 39:02, versus this athlete at VO2max 53 with a 5 km equivalent of 19:39 (roughly 41 min for 10 km). The report calls them 'faster than this athlete', which is true but understates the closeness: this is actually the best population match in the entire durability section, and the effect was measured in runners, not cyclists. If anything the report is over-cautious here relative to how confidently it treats the cycling carbohydrate work.

Karp 2007 — elite and national-class US Olympic Trials qualifiers running 145 km/week (men). That is six times this athlete's current volume. The report correctly rules it out as a prescription and uses it only as evidence about the state of the field, which is the right use.

Doherty 2020 — 137 cohorts spanning elite and recreational, 25% female, and cohort-level meta-regression, so every association relates group means to group means. The report names the ecological-inference problem explicitly. Correct handling.
missedEvidence: Hagan RD, Smith MG, Gettman LR. Marathon performance in relation to maximal aerobic power and training indices. Med Sci Sports Exerc 1981;13(3):185-189. doi:10.1249/00005768-198103000-00007 — THE MOST IMPORTANT MISS, because it CONTRADICTS the report's framing. In 50 male marathoners with 9 weeks of daily training diaries, average distance per workout correlated with faster times univariately (r = -0.64) — but in the multiple-regression model the coefficient on km per workout is POSITIVE: MPT (min) = 525.9 + 7.09(km/workout) - 0.45(workout speed) - 0.17(total km over 9 wk) - 2.01(VO2max) - 1.24(age), R2 = 0.71. Read literally, once total volume, training pace, VO2max and age are held constant, doing that volume in FEWER, LONGER runs predicted a slower marathon by about 7 minutes per extra km of average run length. That is an independent dataset showing the sign flip Fokkema only hints at, and it is the closest thing in the literature to empirical support for a Hansons-style cap — which the report explicitly says does not exist ('No published trial supports OR refutes the cap'). Caveats are real: average run length is not the long run, n=50, VO2max range 52.7-88.6, ages 21-61. But it belongs in the answer and it cuts against the report's point estimate.

Hagan R, Upton S, Duncan JJ, et al. Marathon performance in relation to maximal aerobic power and training indices in female distance runners. Br J Sports Med 1987;21(1):3-7. doi:10.1136/bjsm.21.1.3 — 35 female marathoners, 12-week diaries. The best predictors were mean km/day (r = -0.77) and mean km/week (r = -0.74); the final prediction equation contains only mean km/day and training pace. No long-run term survives. Second independent confirmation that the signal lives in weekly volume and pace, not in single-session length.

Tanda G. Prediction of marathon performance time on the basis of training indices. J Hum Sport Exerc 2011;6(3):511-520. doi:10.4100/jhse.2011.63.05 — 22 runners, 46 marathons, daily diaries. Marathon pace is predicted from just two variables, mean weekly distance K and mean training pace P, with a standard error of about 4 minutes. This is the widely-used 'Tanda formula' and it contains NO long-run term at all. It is arguably the single best piece of supporting evidence for the report's own conclusion and it was not found — a notable gap given the report's central claim is that the long run is the smallest lever.

Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Front Sports Act Living 2021;3:735220. doi:10.3389/fspor.2021.735220 — 158,000+ recreational marathoners. A strict 3-week taper was associated with a median finish-time saving of 5 min 32 s (2.6%) versus a minimal taper, p<0.001, with strict tapers beating relaxed tapers and longer beating shorter up to 3 weeks. This is the same research group and dataset family the report already cites three times, it is the same magnitude as the entire long-run question the athlete is agonising over, and it sits entirely inside his six remaining weeks. Missing it is a practical omission, not just a bibliographic one.

Maunder E, Seiler S, Mildenhall MJ, Kilding AE, Plews DJ. The Importance of 'Durability' in the Physiological Profiling of Endurance Athletes. Sports Med 2021;51(8):1619-1628. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01459-0 — the paper that named and defined durability, and the direct antecedent of both Smyth 2022 (Maunder is a co-author) and Jones & Kirby 2025. The report's own searchesRun list shows it looked for this and it does not appear in any citation. The durability section rests on the review and the observational study without the foundational conceptual paper.

Haugen T, Sandbakk O, Seiler S, Tonnessen E. The Training Characteristics of World-Class Distance Runners: An Integration of Scientific Literature and Results-Proven Practice. Sports Med Open 2022;8:46. doi:10.1186/s40798-022-00438-7 — relevant to two claims the report treats as evidence-free. It documents that marathon specialists run 160-220 km/week in mid-preparation and that the difference from track runners 'is mainly explained by more running kilometers on each session', and that 'volume of race-pace running increases as the main competition approaches'. That is results-proven practice bearing directly on the marathon-pace-in-the-long-run question, which the report declares has zero evidence of any kind. It is not a trial and does not overturn the 'no controlled test' verdict, but 'no trial' and 'no evidence' are different claims and the report blurs them.

Casado A, Hanley B, Santos-Concejero J, Ruiz-Perez LM. World-Class Long-Distance Running Performances Are Best Predicted by Volume of Easy Runs and Deliberate Practice of Short-Interval and Tempo Runs. J Strength Cond Res 2019. doi:10.1519/jsc.0000000000003176 — elite population, so not prescriptive here, but it is another independent analysis in which easy-run VOLUME, not long-run distance, carries the predictive weight. Consistent with the report's conclusion and would have strengthened it.

Emig T, Peltonen J. Human running performance from real-world big data. Nat Commun 2020;11:4936. doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18737-6 — a physiological model fitted to large-scale real-world training and racing data, relevant to the durability/endurance-decay framing and to individualised performance prediction. Not directly about the long run, but it is the other major big-data physiology paper in this space and the report's evidence base is heavily concentrated in one research group (Smyth/Lawlor/Caulfield/Feely account for four of its citations).

UNRESOLVED, and it undercuts one of the report's stated myths: myth #6 asserts that 'training does not make the tank bigger' and attributes to Rapoport a finding that there is no evidence training changes glycogen STORAGE CAPACITY. I could not find that statement in Rapoport, and I could not, within this session's exhausted search budget, find a source that settles the question either way. It runs against standard exercise-physiology teaching that endurance-trained muscle holds higher resting glycogen concentrations than untrained muscle — a difference that would be a change in habitual stored quantity, and arguably capacity. Talanian 2007 found resting glycogen unchanged after 2 weeks in previously moderately-active women, which is a much narrower claim than 'capacity is not trainable'. This myth should be softened to what is actually supported: the long run's benefit is unlikely to run primarily through enlarging glycogen stores, and in-race carbohydrate intake is a more direct lever than extra kilometres. Stated as it is, it is an unsourced physiological assertion sitting in a section whose whole purpose is to debunk unsourced physiological assertions.
