interventions.intervention: CONVERSION BASIS (read first — every marathon-minutes figure below uses this). Kipp, Kram & Hoogkamer quantified how a % improvement in running economy translates into % faster running velocity, accounting for the non-linear VO2–velocity relation and air resistance. Below ~3.0 m/s the velocity gain is slightly LARGER than the economy gain; above it, smaller; at 5.5 m/s (world-record marathon pace) it is ~2/3.
interventions.effect: At 5.5 m/s, a 3% RE improvement → 1.97% faster velocity. The ratio (%velocity gain ÷ %RE gain) rises as velocity falls and crosses ~1.0 at approximately 3 m/s.
interventions.population: Modelling/collation study — five published VO2–velocity equations compared across a wide velocity range. Not an intervention trial, no participants.
interventions.citation: Kipp S, Kram R, Hoogkamer W. Extrapolating Metabolic Savings in Running: Implications for Performance Predictions. Frontiers in Physiology. 2019;10:79. doi:10.3389/fphys.2019.00079. PMID 30804807
interventions.sampleSize: n/a — modelling paper collating 5 existing VO2–velocity equations
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it is the arithmetic, not an adaptation.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: WORKING FOR THIS ATHLETE: marathon 3:55:54 = 14,154 s = 235.9 min. Pace 5:31/km = 331 s/km → race velocity 1000/331 = 3.02 m/s. That sits almost exactly on Kipp's ~3 m/s pivot, so for him %velocity gain ≈ %RE gain (ratio ~1.0; use 0.9 if he races nearer 3:35, i.e. 3.28 m/s). Therefore 1% RE improvement ≈ 2.36 minutes off his marathon. This assumes (a) the treadmill RE gain persists over 42 km, and (b) nothing else is degraded to buy it — both assumptions are load-bearing and only (a) has any direct evidence (Zanini 2025, below).

interventions.intervention: Concurrent strength/explosive training added to endurance running, any modality — pooled effect on running economy expressed as a percentage
interventions.effect: RE improved by 3.93% ± 1.19% (mean ± 95% confidence limit) versus control, p<0.001. Broken down: explosive/plyometric training 4.83% ± 1.53% (p<0.001); heavy weight training 3.65% ± 2.74% (p=0.009); isometric training 2.20% ± 4.37% (p=0.324, NOT significant). Meta-regression: the magnitude of the RE improvement was LARGER for longer training duration (β = −0.83 ± 0.72, p=0.02).
interventions.population: Endurance running athletes. 20 effects from 16 studies, published to Aug 2015. Mixed training status (moderately trained to elite); the review explicitly modelled training status as a covariate.
interventions.citation: Denadai BS, de Aguiar RA, de Lima LCR, Greco CC, Caputo F. Explosive Training and Heavy Weight Training are Effective for Improving Running Economy in Endurance Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2017;47(3):545–554. doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0604-z. PMID 27497600
interventions.sampleSize: 16 studies, 20 effects (participant total not reported in abstract)
interventions.duration: Interventions varied; the duration term was a significant positive moderator
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Partly. This is the headline number people quote, but the meta-regression itself says the effect scales with duration — so six weeks buys the bottom of the range, not the mean. The authors' own conclusion is that effects appear 'within a few weeks' but that 'long-term training programs seem to be necessary when the largest possible improvement in RE is desired.'
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Central estimate 3.93% RE × 2.36 min/% = 9.3 min off 3:55:54. 95% CL range 2.74–5.12% → 6.5 to 12.1 min. THIS IS THE FULL-DURATION FIGURE AND IS NOT WHAT SIX WEEKS BUYS. Applying the duration moderator and the 6–8-week subgroup data from Eihara 2022 (below), a realistic six-week ceiling is roughly 0–2% → 0 to 4.7 min, before subtracting any fatigue cost.

interventions.intervention: Strength training (low-to-moderate resistance loads 40–70% 1RM plus plyometrics, 2–4 lower-body exercises, up to 200 jumps and 5–10 short sprints), 2–3×/week for 8–12 weeks, added to endurance training
interventions.effect: Standardised mean difference on running economy = −1.42 (95% CI −2.23 to −0.60). A 'large' beneficial effect. Note the CI is wide and the lower bound (−0.60) is only a moderate effect.
interventions.population: Competitive, high-level middle- and long-distance runners with VO2max >60 mL/kg/min — an explicit inclusion criterion. This athlete's VO2max estimate is 53.0, so he is BELOW the entry threshold of every study in this meta-analysis.
interventions.citation: Balsalobre-Fernández C, Santos-Concejero J, Grivas GV. Effects of Strength Training on Running Economy in Highly Trained Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(8):2361–2368. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001316. PMID 26694507
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No. The shortest included intervention was 8 weeks; the prescription the authors endorse is explicitly '2–3 times per week for 8–12 weeks'. Six weeks is below the evidenced window.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not directly convertible — SMD, not %. Converting an SMD to minutes requires the outcome SD, which in a homogeneous elite sample is small and produces a misleadingly large minute figure. Use Denadai's % change instead. What this study contributes is the DOSE (2–3×/wk, 8–12 weeks) and the population boundary (VO2max >60), not a time saving.

interventions.intervention: Strength training by method, effect on running ECONOMY, with running speed and VO2max as moderators
interventions.effect: High-load training (≥80% 1RM): small improvement, ES = −0.266, p=0.039, at speeds 8.64–17.85 km/h. Combined methods (two or more): moderate, ES = −0.426, p=0.018, at 10.00–14.45 km/h. Plyometric: small improvement but ONLY at speeds ≤12.00 km/h, ES = −0.307, p=0.028 (speed moderator β1=0.470, p=0.017). Submaximal-load (40–79% 1RM): no improvement (p>0.131). Isometric: no improvement (p>0.131). Moderators: higher running speed (β1=−0.117, p=0.027) and higher VO2max (β1=−0.040, p=0.020) both AMPLIFY the high-load effect.
interventions.population: 195 moderately trained, 272 well trained, 185 highly trained middle- and long-distance runners (652 total across the RE analyses). No sex or level restriction. GRADE certainty: moderate for high-load, submaximal, plyometric and isometric; low for combined.
interventions.citation: Llanos-Lagos C, Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Sáez de Villarreal E. Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(4):895–932. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01978-y. PMID 38165636
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: At the very bottom edge — 6 weeks was the minimum included duration, so six weeks is the shortest thing this evidence base speaks to at all, and the pooled effect is dominated by longer programmes.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Two things matter for THIS athlete and they point opposite ways. (1) His marathon pace is 10.9 km/h, which is inside the ≤12 km/h band where plyometrics work — so plyometrics are the right-shaped tool for his speed. (2) But the high-load effect is amplified by higher VO2max, and at 53.0 he is at the low end — so he sits in the part of the moderator space where high-load lifting delivers least. Net: no reliable minute figure; the ES values (−0.27 to −0.43) correspond loosely to RE changes of roughly 1–3% in these samples, i.e. 2.4–7.1 min at full duration, not at six weeks.

interventions.intervention: Strength training by method, effect on running PERFORMANCE (time trial and time to exhaustion) and on the physiological determinants
interventions.effect: Running performance: high-load ES = −0.469 (moderate, p=0.029); combined methods ES = −1.035 (large, p=0.036); plyometric ES = −0.210 (p=0.064, NOT significant). NONE of the methods improved VO2max, velocity at VO2max, maximum metabolic steady state, or sprint capacity (all p>0.072). Critically: subject moderators (sex, age, body mass, height, VO2max, performance level, strength-training experience) and intervention moderators (weeks, sessions/week, TOTAL SESSIONS) had NO effect on outcomes (all p>0.166).
interventions.population: 324 moderately trained, 272 well trained, 298 highly trained middle- and long-distance runners (894 total). GRADE certainty: very low to moderate.
interventions.citation: Llanos-Lagos C, Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Sáez de Villarreal E. The Effect of Strength Training Methods on Middle-Distance and Long-Distance Runners' Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(7):1801–1833. doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02018-z. PMID 39023740
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Ambiguous, and honestly so. The null moderator result for 'weeks' and 'total sessions' could mean short programmes work as well as long ones — or it could mean the moderator analysis was underpowered across a lumpy 6-to-40-week range. Denadai 2017 and Eihara 2022 both found duration DID matter, so I read this null as low-information rather than as evidence that six weeks suffices.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. The pooled performance outcome mixes 1500 m to 10 km time trials and time-to-exhaustion tests; there is no marathon in it. An SMD of −0.469 on a 3 km TT does not license a marathon minute figure.

interventions.intervention: Heavy resistance training versus plyometric training as an adjunct to running, head-to-head on running economy and time-trial performance
interventions.effect: Running economy: heavy resistance g = −0.32 (95% CI −0.55 to −0.10, small); plyometric g = −0.13 (95% CI −0.47 to 0.21, trivial, CI crosses zero). Time trial: heavy resistance g = −0.24; plyometric g = −0.17 (95% CI −0.27 to −0.06, trivial). Load matters: ≥90% 1RM g = −0.31 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.02) versus <90% 1RM g = −0.17 (95% CI −1.05 to 0.70, trivial, CI crosses zero). DURATION SUBGROUP — the key number for a six-week question: heavy resistance 10–14 weeks g = −0.45 (95% CI −0.83 to −0.08) versus 6–8 weeks g = −0.21 (95% CI −0.56 to 0.15, CI CROSSES ZERO); plyometric 8–10 weeks g = −0.26 versus 4–6 weeks g = −0.06 (trivial, CI crosses zero).
interventions.population: Long-distance runners across 22 studies; training status mixed.
interventions.citation: Eihara Y, Takao K, Sugiyama T, Maeo S, Terada M, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Heavy Resistance Training Versus Plyometric Training for Improving Running Economy and Running Time Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine – Open. 2022;8:138. doi:10.1186/s40798-022-00511-1. PMID 36370207
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: NO — and this is the single most decisive finding for the question asked. At 6–8 weeks the heavy-resistance effect on running economy is g = −0.21 with a confidence interval that crosses zero (−0.56 to 0.15). At 4–6 weeks the plyometric effect is g = −0.06, i.e. nothing. The effect only becomes reliably non-zero at 8–14 weeks. A six-week block sits in the part of the dose-response curve where the meta-analytic estimate is statistically indistinguishable from no effect.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: At 6–8 weeks: the point estimate g = −0.21 with a CI spanning zero means the honest answer is 'between 0 and roughly 2 minutes, and it may be nothing'. At 10–14 weeks: g = −0.45 corresponds to roughly a 2–3% RE change in these samples → 4.7 to 7.1 minutes. The lesson is that the 7-to-9-minute prize is real but it is priced in weeks he does not have before 24 October.

interventions.intervention: Strength training (any modality) added to endurance training, effect on middle- and long-distance performance across running, cycling, cross-country skiing and swimming
interventions.effect: Performance: net SMD = 0.52 (95% CI 0.33–0.70), moderate. Energy cost of locomotion: 0.65 (95% CI 0.32–0.98). Maximal force: 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.18). Maximal power: 0.50 (95% CI 0.34–0.67). Maximal-force (heavy) training produced greater improvements than other intensities. Subgroup analysis: the benefit was CONSISTENT irrespective of the athletes' performance level.
interventions.population: 28 studies from 554 screened; endurance athletes across four sports, mixed levels, both sexes.
interventions.citation: Berryman N, Mujika I, Arvisais D, Roubeix M, Binet C, Bosquet L. Strength Training for Middle- and Long-Distance Performance: A Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(1):57–63. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2017-0032. PMID 28459360
interventions.duration: 'A strength-training mesocycle' — durations varied by study
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Not established. The unit of analysis is a mesocycle, and duration was tested as a subgroup but the abstract does not report a short-duration result. The level-independence finding is the useful part: it argues the effect is not confined to elites.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — the performance outcome pools four sports and multiple event distances. The energy-cost SMD of 0.65 is the closest analogue to the RE literature and is consistent with Denadai's ~4%, i.e. ~9 min at full duration.

interventions.intervention: Supplementary maximal-strength plus plyometric training, twice weekly for 10 weeks, tested for effect on running economy DURABILITY over 90 minutes at marathon intensity and on fatigued high-intensity performance
interventions.effect: Running economy at the 90-minute mark: −2.1% in the strength group versus +0.6% in the running-only control (interaction p=0.003, ηp²=0.13, large; between-group p=0.04 at 90 min). Time to exhaustion at 95% VO2max immediately after the 90-minute run: +35% in the strength group versus −8% in control (interaction p=0.004, ηp²=0.28, large).
interventions.population: 28 well-trained male runners, VO2max 58.6 mL/kg/min, 10 km time 39:02. Faster and fitter than this athlete (his 5 km equivalent is 19:39, implying roughly 41–42 min for 10 km), but this is the closest population in the literature to a male marathon runner and the ONLY study that tests the effect at marathon intensity for marathon-relevant duration.
interventions.citation: Zanini M, Folland JP, Wu H, Blagrove RC. Strength Training Improves Running Economy Durability and Fatigued High-Intensity Performance in Well-Trained Male Runners: A Randomized Control Trial. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2025;57(7):1546–1558. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003685. PMID 40016936
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No — 10 weeks, and the design gives no interim measurement, so there is no way to know when in those 10 weeks the durability effect appeared.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: This is the study that licenses the treadmill-to-marathon transfer assumption at all. A 2.1% RE advantage sustained at 90 minutes → 2.1% × 2.36 = 5.0 minutes for this athlete, IF he could get the 10-week adaptation. It is also the strongest single argument for doing this work in his NEXT block: the benefit lands specifically in the back half of the race, which is where a 3:55 marathoner loses time.

interventions.intervention: Plyometric training added to normal running, 6 weeks — the shortest CONTROLLED intervention that produced a measurable running-economy improvement in a non-elite population
interventions.effect: Running economy improved significantly (p<0.05). Group means, averaged across three treadmill speeds: experimental 5.14 ± 0.39 → 5.26 ± 0.39 m·mL⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (+2.3%); control 5.10 ± 0.36 → 5.06 ± 0.36 (−0.8%). Between-group difference ≈ 3%. VO2max unchanged. Notably, jump height and elastic-energy indices did NOT change, so the mechanism was not demonstrated.
interventions.population: 18 'regular but not highly trained' distance runners, mean age 29 ± 7. This is the closest published population to the athlete in question, which is why it carries weight despite its age and size.
interventions.citation: Turner AM, Owings M, Schwane JA. Improvement in running economy after 6 weeks of plyometric training. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2003;17(1):60–67. doi:10.1519/1533-4287(2003)017<0060:IIREAW>2.0.CO;2. PMID 12580657
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES — this is the existence proof that six weeks CAN be enough, in roughly this population, with plyometrics rather than heavy lifting. It is a single small trial from 2003 and its effect is at the edge of the measurement noise (between-day RE coefficient of variation is ~2%; see Alda-Blanco 2026), so it should not be weighted against the meta-analytic duration data.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: ~3% between-group RE difference × 2.36 = ~7 minutes. Do NOT bank this. n=18, 2003, no mechanism demonstrated, effect size roughly 1.5× the day-to-day measurement error of the outcome, and the meta-analytic 4–6-week plyometric estimate (Eihara g = −0.06) is essentially zero. Treat Turner as the optimistic tail, not the expectation.

interventions.intervention: Plyometric jump training, 8 sessions over 4 weeks, on hard versus soft surfaces — one of the two shortest interventions to report a running-economy change
interventions.effect: 2–7% improvement in treadmill and off-trail running economy, independent of jumping surface and independent of the running velocity assessed. Changes in time-trial performance were associated with changes in RE. Drop-jump force development was UNCHANGED, so again no mechanism was demonstrated.
interventions.population: 19 orienteers (11 women, 8 men), mean age 21 ± 5.8, body mass 61.1 ± 7.3 kg. Much lighter and younger than this athlete; orienteering, not road marathon.
interventions.citation: Lännerström J, Nilsson LC, Cardinale DA, Björklund G, Larsen FJ. Effects of Plyometric Training on Soft and Hard Surfaces for Improving Running Economy. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2021;79:187–196. doi:10.2478/hukin-2021-0071. PMID 34400998
interventions.sampleSize: n=19, randomly stratified to two plyometric conditions
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes on duration. But the design has NO non-plyometric control group — both arms jumped, only the surface differed — so the 2–7% improvement is a within-subject pre-post change that cannot be separated from ongoing running training, learning effects, or regression to the mean. Weak design for the question 'does adding plyometrics help'.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 2–7% would be 4.7 to 16.5 minutes, which is not credible from 8 jump sessions and is the clearest illustration in this whole domain of why uncontrolled pre-post designs mislead. Report as 'not convertible — no control group'.

interventions.intervention: Four weeks of plyometric training at sea level, added to normal endurance training, in a controlled design
interventions.effect: Running economy, reactive strength index and 2 km time-trial all improved significantly (p<0.05) in the plyometric group; VO2max unchanged in both groups. Control group showed no improvement in reactive strength and a WORSE 2 km time trial.
interventions.population: 23 participants (11 plyometric, 12 control). The abstract does not report VO2max or training status, and the sea-level control-group 2 km times reported (10.3 → 9.02 min) are internally confusing, which lowers my confidence in the reporting.
interventions.citation: Andrade DC, Beltrán AR, Labarca-Valenzuela C, et al. (incl. Ramírez-Campillo R). Effects of Plyometric Training on Explosive and Endurance Performance at Sea Level and at High Altitude. Frontiers in Physiology. 2018;9:1415. doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.01415. PMID 30364035
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes on duration — it is one of only two 4-week studies reporting an RE effect. But it is small, the primary purpose was an altitude question, and the effect magnitudes for RE are not given as percentages in the abstract.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — RE change not quantified as a percentage or effect size in the available abstract, and the outcome distance (2 km) is not marathon-relevant.

interventions.intervention: One strength session per week for 8 weeks, plyometric versus dynamic weight training, on the energy cost of running — the lowest-frequency dose that produced a clear effect
interventions.effect: Plyometric group: energy cost 218 ± 16 → 203 ± 13 mL/kg/km, a 6.9% reduction. Dynamic weight training: 207 ± 15 → 199 ± 12, a 3.9% reduction. Control unchanged. Group × time interaction p<0.05. Plyometrics beat dynamic weight training. Pre-post change in energy cost correlated with INITIAL energy cost (r=−0.57, p<0.05) — i.e. the less economical you start, the more you gain. All three groups (including control) improved 3000 m time.
interventions.population: 35 moderately-to-well-trained male endurance runners. Closer to this athlete than the elite samples.
interventions.citation: Berryman N, Maurel DB, Bosquet L. Effect of plyometric vs. dynamic weight training on the energy cost of running. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2010;24(7):1818–1825. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181def1f5. PMID 20543734
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Almost — 8 weeks, one session weekly. The single-session-per-week dose is the genuinely useful finding: it is the lowest fatigue cost per unit of adaptation anyone has demonstrated, which matters enormously when running volume is being ramped simultaneously.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 6.9% plyometric energy-cost reduction × 2.36 = 16.3 min; 3.9% dynamic weight training = 9.2 min. Both figures are larger than the meta-analytic mean, so treat this trial as an optimistic outlier. The r=−0.57 correlation with baseline economy is the transferable point: a 3:55 marathoner has more headroom than a 2:30 one.

interventions.intervention: Replacing 32% of total training volume with explosive-strength training, volume-matched, for 9 weeks — the landmark trial that established the effect
interventions.effect: 5 km time, running economy and maximal velocity in an anaerobic treadmill test all improved (p<0.05) in the experimental group with NO change in VO2max. 20 m sprint speed and 5-jump both increased in the experimental group (p<0.01) and DECREASED in the control group (p<0.05). VO2max increased in CONTROL only (p<0.05). Change in 5 km velocity correlated with change in RE (r=−0.54) and with change in maximal anaerobic running velocity (r=0.55).
interventions.population: 18 well-trained endurance athletes (10 experimental, 8 control), Finnish.
interventions.citation: Paavolainen L, Häkkinen K, Hämäläinen I, Nummela A, Rusko H. Explosive-strength training improves 5-km running time by improving running economy and muscle power. Journal of Applied Physiology. 1999;86(5):1527–1533. doi:10.1152/jappl.1999.86.5.1527. PMID 10233114
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No, and its design is actively hostile to this athlete's situation: it REPLACED nearly a third of running volume with strength work. He is trying to add running volume, not substitute it. Applying Paavolainen's protocol to a marathon build would mean cutting his running by a third.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — 5 km outcome, volume-substitution design. Its value is mechanistic: it is the study that established that RE and neuromuscular power, not VO2max, are the channel through which strength work makes runners faster.

interventions.intervention: 40 weeks of strength training in competitive distance runners — the longest intervention, showing the ceiling and the time-course
interventions.effect: Significant improvements in maximal and reactive strength, running economy, and velocity at VO2max at BOTH 20 weeks (p≤0.05) and 40 weeks (p≤0.05). Control group showed no significant change at either time point. No significant change in body mass, fat mass, overall lean mass or leg lean mass in either group.
interventions.population: 20 competitive distance runners (11 intervention, mean age 29.5 ± 10.0, 72.8 ± 6.6 kg; 9 control).
interventions.citation: Beattie K, Carson BP, Lyons M, Rossiter A, Kenny IC. The Effect of Strength Training on Performance Indicators in Distance Runners. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(1):9–23. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001464. PMID 27135468
interventions.duration: 40 weeks, with measurements at 0, 20 and 40 weeks
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No — the earliest measurement point is 20 weeks. This study cannot tell you anything about week 6, which is itself informative about how the field thinks about the time-course.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — RE change not reported as a percentage in the abstract. Its contribution is the body-composition null (no hypertrophy at 40 weeks in runners) and the confirmation that gains persist and extend over a full season.

interventions.intervention: NULL RESULT, and the closest match in the literature to this athlete's exact situation: 8 weeks of concurrent strength training (2 sessions/week, 120 min total, trunk endurance plus high-intensity leg work) DURING marathon preparation in recreational runners
interventions.effect: NO significant difference between groups and no time × intervention interaction for VO2 at defined marathon running velocities (2.4 and 2.8 m/s), nor at 2.0, 3.0 or 4.0 mmol/L lactate thresholds. Stride length and stride frequency unchanged. Body mass unchanged. This was NOT a failure of the strength stimulus: maximal isometric knee-extension force rose from 4.6 ± 1.4 to 6.2 ± 1.0 N/kg (p<0.01), a 35% increase. They got much stronger and no more economical.
interventions.population: 22 recreational runners (14 men, 8 women), mean age 40.0 ± 11.7, BMI 22.6 ± 2.1, VO2peak 52.0 and 51.1 mL/kg/min in the two groups — essentially this athlete's VO2max (53.0). Tested at 2.4 and 2.8 m/s, i.e. 8.6 and 10.1 km/h, which brackets his 10.9 km/h marathon pace. During an actual marathon build.
interventions.citation: Ferrauti A, Bergermann M, Fernandez-Fernandez J. Effects of a concurrent strength and endurance training on running performance and running economy in recreational marathon runners. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2010;24(10):2770–2778. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181d64e9c. PMID 20885197
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: It is the eight-week version of the question being asked, in the right population, in the right context, and it found nothing. The authors attribute the null to possible underpowering or too short an intervention — but note the strength group also ran LESS (240 vs 276 min/week), which is exactly the trade this athlete would be making.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero minutes, measured at his pace, in his population, in his situation, over a period two weeks LONGER than he has.

interventions.intervention: NULL RESULT: 8 weeks of resistance training targeting hip extensors, knee extensors and ankle plantar flexors in recreational runners, measured on level and uphill running economy
interventions.effect: Despite a significant group × time interaction for plantar-flexor strength (p=0.026), running economy, joint work and joint stiffness were NOT significantly affected at any grade (level, 5%, 10%; all p>0.05). Some individuals did exceed the smallest worthwhile change in RE, but the change in RE was NOT correlated with change in strength or biomechanics (p>0.05). Author conclusion: 'coaches, health care providers, and athletes may need to explore other interventions to change RE or biomechanics.'
interventions.population: 25 recreational runners (12 female), mean age 34.2 ± 13.2, mass 70.4 ± 13.0 kg. Recreational, mixed-sex, close to this athlete's age.
interventions.citation: Robinson RM, Hahn ME. The Effect of Resistance Training on Uphill Running Economy and Biomechanics. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2026 [online ahead of print]. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000005567. PMID 42413900
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Another eight-week null in recreational runners, and the most recent. The individual-responder observation with no strength correlate is the honest state of play: some people respond, nobody can predict who.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero minutes at the group level.

interventions.intervention: NULL RESULT: 11 weeks of heavy strength training (4 leg exercises, 3 × 4–10RM, twice weekly) added to endurance training in well-trained female endurance athletes
interventions.effect: 1RM rose 40 ± 15%, countermovement jump +6 ± 6%, squat jump +9 ± 7% (all p<0.05), with muscle fibre cross-sectional area up 13 ± 7% (type I) and 31 ± 20% (type II). Despite all that: NO change in running economy, NO change in fractional utilisation of VO2max, NO change in VO2max, and NO change in distance covered in a 40-minute all-out run. Patellar tendon stiffness unchanged — the hypothesised mechanism did not occur.
interventions.population: 19 well-trained female endurance athletes, VO2max 53 ± 3 mL/kg/min (the same as this athlete's 53.0), 5.8 h/week endurance training.
interventions.citation: Vikmoen O, Raastad T, Seynnes O, Bergstrøm K, Ellefsen S, Rønnestad BR. Effects of Heavy Strength Training on Running Performance and Determinants of Running Performance in Female Endurance Athletes. PLoS ONE. 2016;11(3):e0150799. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0150799. PMID 26953893
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No — 11 weeks, and still null. The value here is that it rules out 'they just did not train hard enough' as an explanation for nulls: this group got 40% stronger and hypertrophied, and it bought them nothing in running economy. Female sample, so sex is a confound when generalising to this athlete.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero minutes, over nearly twice the time available.

interventions.intervention: MINIMUM-DOSE TEST: 30 minutes or 60 minutes of strength training per week for 10 weeks, substituted for running time, in female recreational runners
interventions.effect: Both concurrent groups significantly improved maximal treadmill test performance (30 min/wk group: 168.5 ± 43.2 → 191.3 ± 43.8 s; 60 min/wk group: 203.1 ± 47.8 → 249.3 ± 49.7 s). But NO significant differences between or within groups for running economy, VO2max, body composition or standing long jump power. Author conclusion: 30–60 min/week was 'sufficient to increase maximal running performance, however it did not lead to improvement in running economy or aerobic capacity.'
interventions.population: 41 female recreational runners randomised three ways (running only n=14; running + 1×30 min n=14; running + 2×30 min n=13).
interventions.citation: Štohanzl M, Baláš J, Draper N. Effects of minimal dose of strength training on running performance in female recreational runners. Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2018;58(9):1211–1217. doi:10.23736/S0022-4707.17.07124-9. PMID 28462571
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: No — 10 weeks. But it is the only deliberate minimum-dose trial, and it dissociates performance from economy: a small dose moved a maximal treadmill test while leaving running economy untouched, which means the mechanism was not the running-economy pathway.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero minutes via the running-economy route. The treadmill-performance gain is on a maximal incremental test, which does not transfer to a marathon.

interventions.intervention: TRAINING CESSATION / TAPER: 4 weeks of complete explosive-strength training cessation following an 8-week concurrent block, running maintained
interventions.effect: Energy cost of running improved −5.75% (95% CI −8.47 to −3.03) after the 8-week block, and was FULLY MAINTAINED after 4 weeks of no strength work (−6.31%, 95% CI −10.30 to −2.32 versus baseline). Neuromuscular performance was likewise maintained. 3000 m time trial improved −2.40% (95% CI −4.65 to −0.16) after the block and improved FURTHER to −4.43% (95% CI −6.83 to −2.03) after cessation. Authors: 'short-term explosive strength training cessation might be beneficial and could be considered as a taper strategy.'
interventions.population: 8 middle-distance runners (4 plyometric, 4 dynamic weight training).
interventions.citation: Berryman N, Mujika I, Bosquet L. Effects of Short-Term Concurrent Training Cessation on the Energy Cost of Running and Neuromuscular Performances in Middle-Distance Runners. Sports (Basel). 2020;9(1):1. doi:10.3390/sports9010001. PMID 33374897
interventions.sampleSize: n=8 — very small; the authors themselves flag this
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it is the directly relevant taper evidence — but it says the opposite of what an add-now plan wants. It says strength work is what you REMOVE in the last month, and that removing it is when the performance gain fully expresses. n=8, so weak, and it is the only study of its kind.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not a gain to add — a scheduling instruction. For this athlete it means: had he built strength in July–August, the right move now would be to stop. Starting now inverts the only evidenced periodisation of this intervention.

interventions.intervention: THE FATIGUE COST: acute and repeated-bout effects of a lower-body resistance session on subsequent running performance
interventions.effect: After a 6RM lower-body session: delayed-onset muscle soreness up (ES 1.41–10.53), countermovement jump down (ES −0.79 to −1.41) for 48 h, and the PHYSIOLOGICAL COST OF SUBMAXIMAL RUNNING INCREASED for up to 48 h post-exercise (p<0.05, ES 0.50–0.84). In the repeated-bout study: submaximal running performance only recovered to a protected state after the THIRD resistance bout (improved 1.9% versus bout two); maximal running performance after the third bout was still 12–20% BELOW baseline. Authors: 'submaximal running sessions should be avoided for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout, although a greater recovery period may be required for maximal running sessions.'
interventions.population: Resistance-UNTRAINED men. Study 1: n=10, age 27.4 ± 4.1, mass 76.8 ± 9.9 kg, VO2peak 48.2 ± 7.0. Study 2: n=12, age 24 ± 4, mass 79.3 ± 10.9, VO2peak 48.2 ± 6.5, 6RM squat 71.7 ± 12.2 kg. This is a near-exact demographic match to a 27-year-old, 85.5 kg man with no established lifting habit.
interventions.citation: Doma K, Nicholls A, Gahreman D, Damas F, Libardi CA, Sinclair W. Sports Medicine – Open. 2019;5:21. doi:10.1186/s40798-019-0195-y (PMID 31165339). AND Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D. Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism. 2017;42(9):978–985. doi:10.1139/apnm-2017-0214 (PMID 28553994).
interventions.duration: Acute — measured at 24 h and 48 h across three bouts
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES, IMMEDIATELY, AND IT IS THE COST SIDE OF THE LEDGER. The economy benefit takes 8–14 weeks to arrive; the economy PENALTY arrives within 24 hours of the first session and lasts 48 hours, and takes about three sessions to fade. In a 6-week block that is weeks 1–2 compromised out of 6, and those are the weeks he is jumping from 15 km to 60 and 80 km.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Negative, and not cleanly quantifiable. Practically: 2 sessions/week × 48 h of degraded submaximal running economy leaves roughly 3 clean days a week for quality running during the highest-volume weeks of his life. The transient increase in the oxygen cost of submaximal running (ES 0.50–0.84) is the same physiological quantity the intervention is meant to improve, moving the wrong way, now, with certainty.

interventions.intervention: Strength training as primary prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries
interventions.effect: Risk ratio 0.338 (95% CI 0.238–0.480) — roughly a two-thirds reduction in injury risk. Consistent across robustness tests, high strength of evidence, no publication bias detected. Dose-dependent: a 10% increase in strength-training volume reduced injury risk by more than four percentage points.
interventions.population: 7,738 participants aged 12–40 across 6 RCTs, 5 different interventions, 4 distinct injury outcomes; 177 acute or overuse injuries. Mixed sports, not runners specifically.
interventions.citation: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(24):1557–1563. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099078. PMID 30131332
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Not demonstrated at six weeks, and the dose-dependence means a short low-volume programme sits at the weak end. The 'strength training prevents injury, so start now to survive the ramp' argument is intuitive but does not have six-week evidence behind it — and the one trial that ran it inside a marathon build found nothing (Toresdahl 2020, next entry).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to minutes — but injury is the dominant risk in a 15 → 60 → 80 → 100 km ramp, and a DNS is infinite minutes. This is the strongest reason to do strength work, and the strongest reason to have started it in June.

interventions.intervention: DIRECT TEST OF THE 'START STRENGTH TRAINING BEFORE A MARATHON' HYPOTHESIS: a 10-minute self-directed programme (quadriceps, hip abductors, core), 3×/week, starting 12 weeks before the New York City Marathon
interventions.effect: NULL on both outcomes. Overuse injury causing marathon non-completion: 7.1% in the strength group versus 7.3% in observation (risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.57–1.63, p=0.90). Mean finishing time: 5h01 ± 60 min in the strength group versus 4h58 ± 55 min in observation (p=0.35) — numerically slightly SLOWER. Overall major-injury incidence 8.9%, minor-injury incidence 48.5%.
interventions.population: 720 FIRST-TIME marathon runners aged 18+, mean age 35.9 ± 9.4, 69.4% female; 583 started, 579 finished. By far the largest sample in this whole evidence base, and the population is recreational marathoners in a build.
interventions.citation: Toresdahl BG, McElheny K, Metzl J, Ammerman B, Chang B, Kinderknecht J. A Randomized Study of a Strength Training Program to Prevent Injuries in Runners of the New York City Marathon. Sports Health. 2020;12(1):74–79. doi:10.1177/1941738119877180. PMID 31642726
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: It tested TWICE the window this athlete has, in his population, and found no injury benefit and no time benefit. Caveat that fairly limits how far this generalises: the dose was tiny (10 minutes, self-directed, bodyweight-level, no heavy loading, adherence not verified) — which is precisely the dose that Llanos-Lagos 2024 shows does NOT improve running economy. So this is strong evidence against LOW-DOSE strength work in a marathon build, and silent on heavy loading.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Measured directly: −3 minutes, i.e. the strength group finished 3 minutes slower on average, p=0.35, so indistinguishable from zero. This is the only study in the domain that reports an actual marathon finishing time as its outcome.

interventions.intervention: ACUTE (same-day) plyometric warm-up before running, versus a resistance warm-up and a control warm-up
interventions.effect: Plyometric warm-up improved running economy versus control by 6.2% at 7 km/h (ES 0.355), 9.1% at 8 km/h (ES 0.513), 4.5% at 9 km/h (ES 0.346) and 4.4% at 10 km/h (ES 0.463). Leg stiffness increased 20% (p=0.039, ES 0.90) and correlated with the RE improvement at 8 km/h (r=0.475, p=0.041). The RESISTANCE warm-up produced no RE change at any velocity. No change in time to exhaustion, perceived race readiness, or VO2max.
interventions.population: 12 healthy university students (3 male, 9 female), age 20 ± 2, VO2max 38.4 ± 6.4 mL/kg/min, doing under 5 h/week of endurance exercise. Substantially less fit and less trained than this athlete — this is the study's main weakness.
interventions.citation: Wei C, Yu L, Duncan B, Renfree A. A Plyometric Warm-Up Protocol Improves Running Economy in Recreational Endurance Athletes. Frontiers in Physiology. 2020;11:197. doi:10.3389/fphys.2020.00197. PMID 32226393
interventions.sampleSize: n=12, counterbalanced crossover with Latin-square arrangement
interventions.duration: Acute — single session, trials separated by 48 h
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: YES, and it is the ONLY intervention in this entire domain whose mechanism can fire on race day itself, because it requires no chronic adaptation at all. It needs no training block, adds no cumulative fatigue, and can be rehearsed in his tune-up half on 12 September before being used on 24 October.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Taken at face value at his marathon pace (10.9 km/h, so interpolating the 10 km/h value of 4.4%): 4.4% × 2.36 = 10.4 minutes. DO NOT BELIEVE THAT NUMBER. n=12, untrained participants with VO2max 38, measured over short steady-state stages only, and there is no evidence whatsoever that a warm-up-induced stiffness change survives 3 hours 55 minutes of running. Realistic honest estimate: unknown, plausibly 0–1%, i.e. 0–2.4 minutes. Its actual merit is that the cost is zero and it is testable in the 12 September half marathon.

interventions.intervention: MEASUREMENT-ERROR FLOOR (needed to judge every effect above): test-retest reliability of running economy
interventions.effect: Within-session reliability excellent (ICC 0.917–0.948, CV ~1%). BETWEEN-DAY reliability good but noisier: oxygen cost ICC 0.819, metabolic cost ICC 0.849, CV rising to ~2%. Day-to-day variability significantly affected oxygen and metabolic cost independent of condition. In well-trained marathon runners during a 90-minute run, energy cost and oxygen cost had ICCs 0.96–0.99 with typical errors of 0.7–1.4% and CVs of 0.6–1.2%.
interventions.population: Alda-Blanco: 13 trained male runners, age 27.6 ± 8.2, mass 64.4 ± 6.1 kg, tested at 13 km/h. Zanini: 14 male marathon runners, VO2max 63.1 ± 5.8, marathon 2:47 ± 0:10.
interventions.citation: Alda-Blanco A, González-Mohíno F, Valero F, Rodríguez-Barbero S, Salinero JJ. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2026;21(6):792–799. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2025-0649 (PMID 41764993). AND Zanini M, Folland JP, Blagrove RC. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025;35(5):e70080. doi:10.1111/sms.70080 (PMID 40421635).
interventions.duration: Reliability studies — 4 sessions over 3 weeks, and 2 × 90-min runs respectively
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: n/a — this is the yardstick, not an intervention.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: n/a. But it sets the scepticism threshold: a single-runner, single-test RE change below ~2% is inside the day-to-day noise. Turner's 2003 six-week 2.3% within-group change sits barely above it. This is why the meta-analytic pooled estimates, not any individual short trial, should drive the decision.

myths: 'Strength training will make a runner heavier and slower.' Blagrove's systematic review of 24 controlled trials states explicitly that measures relating to body composition are NOT negatively impacted by strength training interventions in distance runners (Blagrove 2018, Sports Med 48:1117–1149). Beattie 2017 ran 40 weeks of strength training in competitive runners and found no significant change in body mass, fat mass, overall lean mass or leg lean mass. The one trial that DID produce hypertrophy (Vikmoen 2016: type I +13%, type II +31%) also found no change in running economy or 40-min performance — it neither helped nor hurt.

['Strength training raises VO2max.'] It does not. Llanos-Lagos 2024 (894 runners) found NO method improved VO2max, velocity at VO2max, maximum metabolic steady state, or sprint capacity (all p>0.072). Paavolainen 1999 found VO2max increased in the CONTROL group and not the explosive-training group. Whatever benefit exists arrives entirely via running economy and neuromuscular power. Anyone selling strength work as an aerobic-capacity intervention is wrong.

'Light, high-repetition circuits build running-specific strength endurance and improve economy.' Llanos-Lagos 2024 tested exactly this: submaximal loads (40–79% 1RM) produced NO improvement in running economy versus control (p>0.131), while loads ≥80% 1RM did. Eihara 2022 sharpened it further: ≥90% 1RM gave g = −0.31 (CI excludes zero) versus <90% 1RM at g = −0.17 (CI −1.05 to 0.70, crosses zero). The gym work that looks most like running is the gym work that does least.

'Isometrics improve running economy.' Two independent meta-analyses say no. Denadai 2017: −2.20% ± 4.37%, p=0.324. Llanos-Lagos 2024: no improvement versus control, p>0.131, at moderate GRADE certainty. Šuc 2022's narrative review floats isometrics as a low-fatigue option during high-load periods, but that is a hypothesis about tolerability, not a demonstrated economy effect.

'Plyometrics are the best strength modality for runners.' Head-to-head, heavy resistance beats plyometrics on both outcomes: running economy g = −0.32 versus −0.13, time trial g = −0.24 versus −0.17 (Eihara 2022, 22 studies). And plyometric training alone did not significantly improve running performance in Llanos-Lagos 2024 (ES −0.210, p=0.064). The nuance that saves plyometrics for THIS athlete: they work specifically at speeds ≤12 km/h (Llanos-Lagos 2024, speed moderator p=0.017), and his marathon pace is 10.9 km/h. So the myth is the universal claim, not the method.

'Core training improves running economy.' The evidence is thin and split. Stanton 2004: 6 weeks of Swiss-ball training improved core stability with NO change in running economy, VO2max or running posture (n=18). Hung 2019: 8 weeks of core training reduced VO2 at only the fourth of four treadmill stages (52.4 → 50.0 mL/kg/min, p=0.019) in 21 college athletes with no correction for multiple comparisons. This is 'widespread practice, essentially no controlled support', which is worth saying plainly.

'A 1% improvement in running economy makes you 1% faster.' Only at slow speeds. Kipp 2019 shows the relation is non-linear: above ~3 m/s the velocity gain is smaller than the economy gain, and at world-record marathon pace (5.5 m/s) it is roughly two-thirds. This athlete's 3.02 m/s race pace happens to sit almost exactly on the pivot where the ratio is ~1.0 — so for him the folk rule is accidentally right, which is not the same as it being right.

'Strength training prevents running injuries, so it will protect a big volume ramp.' The population-level meta-analysis is genuinely strong (Lauersen 2018: RR 0.338, 95% CI 0.238–0.480, no publication bias, high strength of evidence). But the only RCT that tested it inside an actual marathon build found nothing: 720 first-time NYC marathoners, 12-week programme, injury RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.57–1.63), finishing times identical (Toresdahl 2020). The gap is dose — 10 self-directed minutes is not the intervention Lauersen pooled — but it means 'start lifting to survive the ramp' is currently an inference, not a finding.

'You must keep lifting right up to race week or you lose the adaptations.' Berryman 2020 stopped explosive strength training entirely for 4 weeks after an 8-week block: the energy-cost improvement was fully retained (−5.75% after the block, −6.31% after cessation) and the 3000 m time trial got BETTER after stopping (−2.40% → −4.43%). n=8, so hold it loosely — but the direction of the only available evidence is that strength work is what you remove in the final month, not what you add.

'The 4% running-economy improvement from strength training is what you get.' Denadai's own meta-regression found the effect scales with duration (β = −0.83 ± 0.72, p=0.02), and Eihara's duration subgroups make the price explicit: heavy resistance at 6–8 weeks gives g = −0.21 with a confidence interval crossing zero, versus g = −0.45 at 10–14 weeks; plyometrics at 4–6 weeks give g = −0.06, versus −0.26 at 8–10 weeks. The headline number is a 10-to-14-week number quoted as though it were unconditional.
unknowns: No randomised trial has ever tested ADDING strength or plyometric training inside the final six weeks of a marathon build. Every inference here about the six-week window is extrapolated from 4-week studies in other contexts (Turner 2003, Andrade 2018, Lännerström 2021), duration subgroups within meta-analyses (Eihara 2022), and a cessation study run backwards (Berryman 2020). The specific question asked has zero direct evidence.

Why the recreational-runner trials keep coming back null while trained-runner trials come back positive is genuinely unresolved. Ferrauti 2010 (n=22, VO2peak 51–52, during marathon prep), Vikmoen 2016 (n=19, VO2max 53), Štohanzl 2018 (n=41) and Robinson & Hahn 2026 (n=25) are all null for running economy at 8–11 weeks despite large strength gains, while Balsalobre-Fernández's meta-analysis restricted to VO2max >60 found SMD −1.42. Competing explanations — insufficient statistical power in small recreational samples, lower training-quality ceiling, larger measurement noise relative to effect, or a real population boundary — have not been separated. This athlete (VO2max 53.0) sits on the wrong side of that unexplained line.

Individual responsiveness is unpredictable. Robinson & Hahn 2026 found some participants exceeded the smallest worthwhile change in running economy while the group mean did not move, and the change was NOT correlated with change in strength or in running biomechanics. Nobody can currently identify in advance who will respond.

Whether treadmill running-economy gains transfer to 42 km at recreational pace is untested. Zanini 2025 is the only study to follow economy into fatigue, and it goes to 90 minutes, in well-trained men running 2:47-level marathons — under half the duration this athlete will be running and a very different athlete.

There has never been a dose-finding trial. Berryman 2010 got a 6.9% energy-cost reduction from ONE session per week; Balsalobre-Fernández's included studies used 2–3; Llanos-Lagos's ranged 1–4 with no moderator effect. The minimum effective frequency, the minimum total sessions, and the shape of the dose-response curve are all unknown.

No trial has manipulated strength training and running volume simultaneously, which is exactly this athlete's situation — a roughly 4× volume increase (15 km last week to a planned 100 km peak) with strength work layered on top. The concurrent-training literature holds running volume constant or, in Paavolainen's case, cuts it by a third. The interaction is unmeasured.

Optimal cessation timing before a marathon is unknown. The only evidence is Berryman 2020: n=8, middle-distance runners, 3000 m outcome, 4-week cessation. Whether 2, 4 or 6 weeks is right before a marathon has never been studied.

The mechanism is still not established. Turner 2003 improved economy with NO change in jump height or elastic-energy indices; Lännerström 2021 improved economy with NO change in drop-jump force development; Vikmoen 2016 found no change in patellar-tendon stiffness. Three separate studies improved (or failed to improve) running economy without the hypothesised neuromuscular mediator moving, which means programming choices are being made without knowing what is actually being trained.

Whether the acute plyometric warm-up effect (Wei 2020) survives marathon duration is entirely unknown — it was measured over short steady-state stages in 12 low-fitness students, and no study has carried it past an hour.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)
officialSources.document: ACSM Position Stand: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults — An Overview of Reviews. Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Fiatarone Singh MA, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, Steen JP, Thomas GA, Triplett NT, Washington TA, Werner TJ, Phillips SM. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2026;58(4):851–872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897. PMID 41843416. Synthesises 137 systematic reviews and over 30,000 participants; first update to the 2009 position stand.
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: For voluntary STRENGTH: loads ≥80% 1RM, full range of motion, 2–3 sets, performed at the BEGINNING of a training session, ≥2 sessions per week. For POWER: moderate loads 30–70% 1RM, low-to-moderate volume (≤24 reps × sets), fast concentric phase, Olympic-style lifting. For HYPERTROPHY (which a marathon runner does not want): ≥10 sets per muscle group per week plus eccentric overload — note this is a different prescription, so a runner should deliberately stay below it. Explicitly found that training to momentary muscle failure, equipment type, exercise complexity, set structure, time under tension, blood-flow restriction and periodisation did NOT consistently affect outcomes. IMPORTANT LIMITATION: this document is about healthy adults and does not address endurance athletes, aerobic performance, running economy or concurrent training. It tells you HOW to lift, not whether a marathon runner should. Its eligibility criterion was interventions of ≥6 weeks.

officialSources.body: British Journal of Sports Medicine (peer-reviewed journal, not a governing body) — the nearest thing to a consensus practice summary for this specific question
officialSources.document: Lima LCR, Blagrove R. Infographic: Strength training-induced adaptations associated with improved running economy — potential mechanisms and training recommendations. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;54(5):302–303. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2019-100840. PMID 31362926. This is the practice-facing distillation of Blagrove's 2018 systematic review (Sports Medicine 48:1117–1149).
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: The underlying systematic review's recommendation: 'The addition of two to three ST sessions per week, which include a variety of ST modalities, are likely to provide benefits to the performance of middle- and long-distance runners.' Modalities reviewed were heavy resistance training, explosive resistance training and plyometric training, with a minimum intervention length of 4 weeks and runners with ≥6 months' experience.

officialSources.body: England Athletics / UK Athletics
officialSources.document: Youth Endurance Resource (Part 5 covers running economy and conditioning), authored by Dr Matt Long with Spencer Duval (National Endurance Lead) and Scott Grace; plus 'Conditioning for runners with Mark Brace' on the Athletics Hub coaching platform.
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: NOT VERIFIED — I could not access the content of these documents. What I can confirm from the England Athletics website is that they exist, that the Youth Endurance Resource is aimed at young athletes (not adult marathoners), and that the conditioning material sits behind the Athletics Hub coach login. I am listing them so the gap is visible rather than implying I checked them. Treat any claim about UK Athletics' prescriptive position on adult endurance strength training as unsourced until someone opens these. No World Athletics document on this topic was found either.

check.domain: Strength and plyometric training for distance running — the running-economy effect, and whether it is worth starting six weeks before a marathon

citationChecks.citation: Kipp S, Kram R, Hoogkamer W. Extrapolating Metabolic Savings in Running. Front Physiol. 2019;10:79. PMID 30804807
citationChecks.note: Europe PMC record matches exactly. Abstract verbatim confirms the ~3 m/s pivot, the <3 m/s velocity-gain-greater-than-RE-gain direction, and 'At 5.5 m/s... ~2/3rds' plus the worked 3% RE -> 1.97% velocity example. Modelling paper collating five VO2-velocity equations, no participants, as claimed.

citationChecks.citation: Denadai BS et al. Explosive Training and Heavy Weight Training are Effective for Improving Running Economy. Sports Med. 2017;47(3):545-554. PMID 27497600

citationChecks.citation: Balsalobre-Fernandez C, Santos-Concejero J, Grivas GV. Effects of Strength Training on Running Economy in Highly Trained Runners. J Strength Cond Res. 2016;30(8):2361-2368. PMID 26694507

The researcher's population caveat (this athlete at VO2max 53.0 is below every included study's entry threshold) is correct and important.

citationChecks.citation: Eihara Y et al. Heavy Resistance Training Versus Plyometric Training for Improving Running Economy and Running Time Trial Performance. Sports Med Open. 2022;8:138. PMID 36370207

citationChecks.citation: Doma K, Nicholls A, Gahreman D, Damas F, Libardi CA, Sinclair W. Sports Med Open. 2019;5:21. PMID 31165339
citationChecks.note: The paper exists and every number quoted is right (n=10, age 27.4+/-4.1, mass 76.8+/-9.9, VO2peak 48.2+/-7.0, resistance-untrained; DOMS ES 1.41-10.53; CMJ ES -0.79 to -1.41 for 48 h; submaximal running cost up to 48 h post, ES 0.50-0.84). It is a heat-stress study in heat-acclimatised participants, presented here as a generic acute-fatigue study. That context is material — the 48-hour economy penalty is the researcher's entire cost-side argument — and omitting the title is what let it pass unexamined.

The abstract reports control 2-km at altitude 9.02+/-0.64 min against a pre-training 10.3+/-0.8 min — numerically FASTER, not worse. citationChecks.citation: Hung 2019, 8 weeks core training, 21 college athletes, VO2 52.4 -> 50.0 ml/kg/min p=0.019 (cited in myths)
citationChecks.note: Hung KC, Chung HW, Yu CC, Lai HC, Sun FH. PLoS One 2019;14(3):e0213158, PMID 30849105. The researcher's criticism — a single significant stage out of four with no multiple-comparison correction — is fair.

citationChecks.citation: Suc A 2022 narrative review floating isometrics as a low-fatigue option (cited in myths without full reference)
citationChecks.note: Suc A, Sarko P, Plesa J, Kozinc Z. 'Resistance Exercise for Improving Running Economy and Running Biomechanics and Decreasing Running-Related Injury Risk: A Narrative Review.' Sports (Basel) 2022;10(7):98, PMID 35878109. Real, and the researcher's characterisation of it as a hypothesis about tolerability rather than a demonstrated economy effect is consistent with a narrative review whose own conclusion favours combined strength and plyometric work.

citationChecks.citation: England Athletics / UK Athletics Youth Endurance Resource and 'Conditioning for runners with Mark Brace' (Athletics Hub)
citationChecks.note: Behind a coach login, and I had no search budget left to attempt independent confirmation. The researcher labelled this NOT VERIFIED in the submission itself and told the reader not to treat any UK Athletics prescriptive position as sourced. That is the correct handling and I am not marking it against them.

effectSizeErrors: THE MINUTES CONVERSION IS SYSTEMATICALLY INFLATED, ALWAYS IN THE OPTIMISTIC DIRECTION. The researcher converts with minutes = %RE x 2.36, treating a percentage velocity gain as a percentage time saving. It is not: time = T/(1+x), so the saving is T x (1 - 1/(1+x)), always smaller. Re-derived against his 235.9-minute marathon: Denadai 3.93% is 8.92 min, not 9.3; the CL bounds 2.74% and 5.12% are 6.29 and 11.49 min, not 6.5 and 12.1; Berryman 2010's 6.9% is 15.23 min, not 16.3; 3.9% is 8.85 min, not 9.2; Wei's 4.4% is 9.94 min, not 10.4; Turner's ~3% is 6.87 min, not 7. The error is 4-7% relative and grows with effect size. Every single instance overstates the prize, and none understates it.

RACE VELOCITY DERIVED FROM AN INCONSISTENT INPUT RATHER THAN THE ACTUAL RESULT. 3:55:54 over 42.195 km is 335.4 s/km (5:35/km) and 2.98 m/s. The athlete's logged 5:31/km implies a 3:52:47 marathon — the two do not describe the same race, most likely because the watch measured long. The researcher took 5:31 at face value and got 3.02 m/s. Immaterial to the conclusion (both sit on Kipp's ~3 m/s pivot) but it is an inherited inconsistency passed through unexamined, in a piece whose whole value proposition is checking arithmetic.

KIPP'S MODEL IS APPLIED OUTSIDE THE ASSUMPTION THAT MAKES IT WORK. The %RE-to-%velocity conversion assumes the runner races at a fixed fraction of VO2max, so that a cheaper stride cashes out as a faster one. That is a reasonable model for a 2:04 marathoner, which is the case Kipp works. For a 3:55 marathoner running at roughly 70% VO2max, the binding constraint over 42 km is far more likely to be glycogen, durability, thermoregulation and pacing than steady-state oxygen cost. The researcher notes assumption (a) — that treadmill gains persist over 42 km — as load-bearing, but does not note that the conversion itself presupposes a VO2-limited runner. Every marathon-minutes figure in the submission inherits this.

EIHARA'S PUBLISHED CIs WERE TIDIED WITHOUT DISCLOSURE. The Sports Med Open abstract renders two intervals incoherently (heavy-resistance time trial g=-0.24 with '95% CI -1.04 to -0.55'; plyometric 8-10 wk g=0.26 with '-0.67 to 0.15'). The researcher reported clean, sensible versions. The load-bearing claim — that the 6-8 week heavy-resistance interval crosses zero — is correct and independently confirmed, so this changes no conclusion, but silently repairing a source's numbers is the wrong reflex in a document whose purpose is to show its working.

THE 'ES -0.27 TO -0.43 CORRESPONDS TO ROUGHLY 1-3% RE' STEP IS UNSOURCED. Llanos-Lagos reports standardised effect sizes; converting them to percentages requires the outcome standard deviation in those samples, which the researcher does not have and does not cite. He correctly refuses this conversion for Balsalobre-Fernandez on exactly this ground, then performs it anyway for Llanos-Lagos and again for Eihara ('g=-0.45 corresponds to roughly a 2-3% RE change'), producing 2.4-7.1 and 4.7-7.1 minute figures. Same objection, inconsistently applied.
populationMismatches: BODY MASS IS NEVER MENTIONED ANYWHERE IN THE SUBMISSION, AND IT IS THE MOST RELEVANT UNADDRESSED MISMATCH. This athlete is 85.5 kg. The cited trials used runners at 61.1 kg (Lannerstrom orienteers), 62.5 kg (Stanton), 64.4 kg (Alda-Blanco), 70.2-72.8 kg (Beattie), 76.8 kg (Doma 2019) and 79.3 kg (Doma 2017). Not one participant population approaches 85.5 kg. This matters specifically for the intervention being recommended: plyometric ground-reaction forces scale with body mass, so the eccentric loading and the injury exposure of 'up to 200 jumps' are materially larger for him than for anyone in whom the effect was measured — in the same six weeks he is ramping from 15 km/week to a planned 100 km peak.

BALSALOBRE-FERNANDEZ (SMD -1.42) REQUIRED VO2max >60; THIS ATHLETE IS 53.0. The researcher flags this clearly and correctly, and declines to convert it to minutes. Credit where due — this is the single best population call in the submission.

ZANINI 2025, THE STUDY THAT LICENSES THE WHOLE TREADMILL-TO-MARATHON TRANSFER, USED RUNNERS AT VO2max 58.6 RUNNING 39:02 FOR 10 KM. This athlete's 5 km equivalent implies roughly 41-42 min for 10 km. The researcher flags the gap. What he does not flag: the 90-minute test is 38% of this athlete's race duration, and the durability decline he is trying to prevent happens after minute 150, not minute 90. The 5.0-minute figure is extrapolated well past where it was measured.

WEI 2020 (THE PLYOMETRIC WARM-UP, AND THE ONLY RACE-DAY-ACTIONABLE ITEM) USED 12 UNIVERSITY STUDENTS, NINE OF THEM FEMALE, AT VO2max 38.4, DOING UNDER 5 h/WEEK. That is a substantially untrained, predominantly female sample being used to advise a trained 27-year-old man. The researcher flags it and explicitly says not to believe the 10.4-minute figure — but he prints the number first and disclaims it after, which is precisely the order that makes an anchor stick.

VIKMOEN 2016 AND STOHANZL 2018 ARE BOTH ALL-FEMALE. Flagged in both entries. Worth adding that the researcher leans on Vikmoen to rule out 'they didn't train hard enough' as an explanation for the null results — a load-bearing inferential move made on a female sample and generalised to a male athlete without argument.

STANTON 2004, USED TO DISMISS CORE TRAINING, STUDIED 15.5-YEAR-OLD BOYS. Not disclosed anywhere. Adolescent athletes are a different population for any neuromuscular adaptation claim, and the myth entry reads as though it were adults.

LANNERSTROM 2021 IS 19 ORIENTEERS, 11 OF THEM WOMEN, MEAN AGE 21, MEAN MASS 61.1 kg, RUNNING OFF-TRAIL. Sex and sport are flagged; the 24 kg body-mass gap is not, and it is the gap that matters most for a jumping intervention.

DOMA 2019 — THE ENTIRE COST-SIDE ARGUMENT — IS A HEAT STUDY IN HEAT-ACCLIMATISED MEN. The 48-hour degradation of submaximal running economy (ES 0.50-0.84) was measured under heat stress. The demographic match on age (27.4) and mass (76.8) is genuinely close, which is what the researcher emphasises, but a thermally stressed protocol is not the condition under which this athlete would run his October training. The 48-hour penalty may be real and may generalise; it has not been shown in temperate conditions here.

LAUERSEN 2018 (RR 0.338) POOLS SIX RCTs ACROSS MIXED SPORTS, AGES 12-40, NOT RUNNERS. Flagged. The researcher also correctly pairs it with Toresdahl's null inside an actual marathon build, which is the right way to handle it.

THE ACSM 2026 POSITION STAND IS ABOUT HEALTHY ADULTS AND SAYS NOTHING ABOUT ENDURANCE ATHLETES, AEROBIC PERFORMANCE, RUNNING ECONOMY OR CONCURRENT TRAINING. The researcher states this limitation explicitly and does not over-claim from it. This is handled correctly and is the strongest 'official source' discipline in the submission.

PAAVOLAINEN 1999 REPLACED 32% OF RUNNING VOLUME WITH STRENGTH WORK IN WELL-TRAINED FINNISH ATHLETES. Flagged, and the researcher's observation that applying it here would mean cutting his running by a third is the correct practical read.
missedEvidence: EIHARA Y ET AL. 2024, Eur J Sport Sci, PMID 39523854 — 'The effects of plyometric versus resistance training on running economy and 5-km running time in middle-aged recreational runners.' THIS IS THE BIGGEST MISS IN THE SUBMISSION. Same lead author as the 2022 meta-analysis the researcher leans on hardest, running the actual RCT in the population this athlete belongs to: 20 middle-aged recreational runners, 10 weeks, twice weekly. BOTH plyometric and resistance training improved oxygen cost by ~2.0% (p=0.001) at all velocities, with NO significant difference between them, and NEITHER changed 5-km time (p>=0.259). It cuts three ways at once: it is a positive running-economy result in the recreational population the researcher characterises as uniformly null; it contradicts his myth entry that 'heavy resistance beats plyometrics' by finding them equivalent in exactly this population; and it reinforces his scepticism by showing an economy gain that did not become a performance gain. Missing it while citing the same author's meta-analysis is the kind of gap that undermines the claim of a systematic search.

STOREN O, HELGERUD J, STOA EM, HOFF J. 'Maximal strength training improves running economy in distance runners.' Med Sci Sports Exerc 2008;40:1087-1092, PMID 18460997. One of the most-cited trials in this entire literature, and absent. EIGHT weeks — near the researcher's decision boundary — 3x/week, 4x4RM half squats, 17 well-trained runners (9 male, 8 female): RE +5.0%, 1RM +33.2%, rate of force development +26.0%, time to exhaustion at maximal aerobic speed +21.3%, with no change in VO2max or body weight. This is a short-duration positive result with a large effect, and its absence makes the 'you need 10-14 weeks' case look tidier than the evidence actually is.

PIACENTINI MF ET AL. 'Concurrent strength and endurance training effects on running economy in master endurance runners.' J Strength Cond Res 2013;27(8):2295-2303, PMID 23207882. Sixteen regularly-training MASTER MARATHON runners (mean age ~44), randomised to maximal strength training, resistance training, or control. The maximal strength group improved 1RM +16.34% and RUNNING ECONOMY +6.17% AT MARATHON PACE, with body composition unchanged. This is the only trial I found that measures running economy at marathon pace in non-elite adult marathoners — which is precisely the measurement the researcher says does not exist. He writes that 'whether treadmill running-economy gains transfer to 42 km at recreational pace is untested' and that Zanini is the only marathon-relevant study; Piacentini is a direct counterexample he did not find.

DAMASCENO MV ET AL. 'Effects of resistance training on neuromuscular characteristics and pacing during 10-km running time trial.' Eur J Appl Physiol 2015;115:1513-1522, PMID 25697149. EIGHT weeks of strength training: 1RM +23%, drop jump +12.7%, peak treadmill speed +2.9%, and 10-km performance +2.5% against -0.7% in controls, with the gain concentrated in the FINAL 2.8 km — the authors conclude it 'counteracts fatigue during the last parts of a 10-km running race'. That is a durability finding at eight weeks, in a distance-running time trial, which materially weakens the framing that durability benefits (Zanini) require ten weeks and are unavailable to him.

TROWELL D, VICENZINO B, SAUNDERS N, FOX A, BONACCI J. 'Effect of Strength Training on Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Variables in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.' Sports Med 2020;50:133-150, PMID 31541409. DIRECTLY CONTRADICTING ON MECHANISM, and 25 studies strong. Concurrent training reliably increases knee flexion, ankle plantarflexion and squat strength, but 'there is no evidence to suggest these adaptations transfer from strength exercises to running.' The researcher lists 'the mechanism is still not established' as an unknown and supports it with three individual trials; this meta-analysis is the systematic version of that same point and would have made it far stronger. Not finding it means the unknowns section is under-evidenced rather than wrong.

DESAI P, JUNGMALM J, BORJESSON M, ET AL. 'Effectiveness of an 18-week general strength and foam-rolling intervention on running-related injuries in recreational runners.' Scand J Med Sci Sports 2023, PMID 36630577. High-compliance runners showed an 85% injury reduction and a 57-day delay in injury onset versus controls. This is the counterweight the injury section needed: the researcher pairs Lauersen's population-level RR 0.338 against Toresdahl's null and concludes 'start lifting to survive the ramp' is an inference rather than a finding. Desai is a recreational-runner trial with a real dose and a large protective effect, and it moves that conclusion.

STENERSON LR, MELTON BF, BLAND HW, RYAN GA. 'Running-Related Overuse Injuries and Their Relationship with Run and Resistance Training Characteristics in Adult Recreational Runners.' J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2023, PMID 37754962. Cross-sectional, adult recreational runners: 84.4% injury history, weekly mileage above ~19 miles raised injury prevalence, and resistance-training participation showed NO protective effect overall. Weaker design than Desai, but it is a second contradicting datapoint on the injury argument and it points the other way. Note also the mileage finding, which speaks directly to the 15-to-100 km ramp.

PATOZ A, BREINE B, THOUVENOT A, ET AL. 'Does Characterizing Global Running Pattern Help to Prescribe Individualized Strength Training in Recreational Runners?' Front Physiol 2021, PMID 33815141. Matching plyometric or dynamic weight training to a runner's individual running pattern gave NO additional running-economy benefit over non-matched concurrent training. This bears directly on the researcher's 'individual responsiveness is unpredictable' unknown — it is a failed attempt to predict responders, which is more informative than the observation that responders vary.

SEDANO S, MARIN PJ, CUADRADO G, REDONDO JC. 'Concurrent training in elite male runners: the influence of strength versus muscular endurance training on performance outcomes.' J Strength Cond Res 2013;27(9):2433-2443, PMID 23287831. Eighteen well-trained male runners, 12 weeks: both concurrent groups improved maximal strength, running economy and peak velocity, with the strength-focused group advantaged in the 3-km time trial and no disruption to VO2 kinetics. A clean positive with a modality comparison, absent from the review.

BARNES KR, KILDING AE. 'Strategies to Improve Running Economy.' Sports Med 2015;45(1):37-56, PMID 25164465. The researcher lists a search for exactly this paper and then reports no result from it. It exists, it is the standard narrative review of the whole running-economy intervention space (endurance training, resistance and plyometric work, altitude, nutrition), and it is the natural document for placing strength training against the alternatives available in a six-week window. A search that ran and returned nothing usable should be reported as such rather than left silently empty.

CONTEXT, NOT A MISS: I checked whether a newer meta-analysis supersedes Llanos-Lagos 2024 and Eihara 2022. Running-economy meta-analyses published 2025-2026 cover hypoxic training (PMID 42302183, null), advanced footwear (PMID 40527489), stretching (PMID 40442558, null), footwear (PMID 39893208) and HIIT versus continuous training (PMID 41766811) — none on strength or plyometrics. The researcher's meta-analytic base is current.
