interventions.intervention: Replace freely-chosen in-race eating with a prescribed, practised gel-plus-water protocol: ~60 g/h carbohydrate (maltodextrin+glucose), ~750 ml/h water, ~60 mg/h sodium, ~90 mg/h caffeine, starting at 40 min and taking a gel every 20 min thereafter
interventions.effect: Marathon finish time 3:38:31 ± 0:24:54 (prescribed) vs 3:49:26 ± 0:25:05 (freely chosen). 10:55 min faster = 4.7%, p = .010, effect size d = -0.43. GI symptoms low and not different between groups.
interventions.population: 28 non-elite male-dominated road marathoners, Copenhagen Marathon 2013. 10 km TT ~45:40, marathon ~3:38-3:49, body mass 74.6-77.4 kg. This is the single closest population match in the entire literature to this athlete.
interventions.citation: Hansen EA, Emanuelsen A, Gertsen RM, Sørensen SSR. Improved Marathon Performance by In-Race Nutritional Strategy Intervention. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(6):645-655. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0130
interventions.sampleSize: n = 28 (14 per group), matched pairs on pre-race 10 km time
interventions.duration: Single race; the protocol itself was ~3.7 h
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, fully. This is the highest-yield, fastest-acting item on the list. The only prerequisite is 4-5 long runs to rehearse the products, which fits inside six weeks.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: 4.7% of this athlete's 3:55:54 (235.9 min) = 11.1 min. Discount heavily: groups were not blinded, allocation was matched-pairs not randomised, the SCI group was 8 years older (41.9 vs 33.6 yr — arguably a handicap, so the direction of that bias favours the finding), n = 28, single study, never replicated. The realistic gain depends entirely on what he does now: if his current race fuelling is the recreational norm of ~35 g/h (Pfeiffer 2012), the honest estimate is 5-9 min. If he already takes 4-6 gels, it is 0-3 min.

interventions.intervention: Any carbohydrate during exercise vs placebo/water (the base effect, pooled across 136 studies)
interventions.effect: Significant overall performance improvement. Larger in time-to-exhaustion than time-trial protocols; larger the longer the event; larger in LESS-trained than better-trained participants. Critically, the meta-regression found magnitude was NOT moderated by dose, ergometer, form of intake, or carbohydrate type. Associated with lower RPE and higher power/HR.
interventions.population: 136 studies, mixed cycling and running, trained and recreationally trained adults
interventions.citation: Ramos-Campo DJ, Clemente-Suárez VJ, Cupeiro R, Benítez-Muñoz JA, Andreu Caravaca L, Rubio-Arias JÁ. The ergogenic effects of acute carbohydrate feeding on endurance performance: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2024;64(33):11196-11205. doi:10.1080/10408398.2023.2233633
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it is an acute race-day effect requiring no adaptation.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not directly convertible to minutes because the pooled effect sizes span TTE and TT protocols with different units. Its practical value here is the moderator finding: the athlete is (a) recreational and (b) racing ~4 h, both of which are the conditions where the effect is LARGEST — and dose was not a moderator, which argues against chasing 100+ g/h.

interventions.intervention: Carbohydrate dose-response during ~160 min endurance exercise: 12 doses from 10 to 120 g/h, glucose:fructose:maltodextrin 1:1:1, at 1 L/h fluid
interventions.effect: Curvilinear dose-response. Best performance at 78 g/h; performance gains flatten and then do not improve further above that. Not a plateau at 60, and not a linear climb to 120.
interventions.population: 51 trained cyclists and triathletes (28 ± 7 yr), four research sites — cyclists, NOT runners
interventions.citation: Smith JW, Pascoe DD, Passe DH, Ruby BC, Stewart LK, Baker LB, Zachwieja JJ. Curvilinear dose-response relationship of carbohydrate (0-120 g·h⁻¹) and performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2013;45(2):336-341. doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e31827205d1
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — sets the race-day target. It is the single best empirical justification for aiming ~75-85 g/h rather than 60 or 120.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to absolute minutes for a runner: the outcome was a 20 km cycling TT after 2 h of cycling, and cycling gut tolerance exceeds running. Use it for dose selection only.

interventions.intervention: Glucose-fructose (multiple transportable carbohydrate) vs glucose-only at the same total rate (1.8 g/min = 108 g/h)
interventions.effect: 8% faster time-trial completion with glucose+fructose (2:1) vs glucose alone; 19% vs water. Total CHO oxidation identical, implying endogenous glycogen sparing.
interventions.population: 8 male trained cyclists, VO2max 64.7, body mass 84.4 kg — cyclists, not runners; body mass close to this athlete
interventions.citation: Currell K, Jeukendrup AE. Superior endurance performance with ingestion of multiple transportable carbohydrates. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2008;40(2):275-281. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31815adf19
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it is purely a product-selection decision. Choose gels/drinks that list both maltodextrin/glucose AND fructose.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Do NOT convert the 8% to marathon minutes — that would give an absurd 19 min. The 8% is a cycling TT after a cycling preload, n = 8, and glucose-only at 108 g/h is a deliberately poor comparator that exceeds single-transporter absorption capacity. Realistic value: at 75-85 g/h glucose-only would exceed the ~60 g/h SGLT1 ceiling and the surplus would sit in the gut. Treat glucose:fructose as an enabler of the dose, worth 0 minutes on its own but required to make 80 g/h tolerable. Corroborating meta-analysis: glucose-fructose raised exogenous oxidation by WMD 0.27 g/min vs glucose (Dezfuli 2025, 14 RCTs, n = 125).

interventions.intervention: 120 g/h vs 90 vs 60 g/h in RUNNING, measured with 13C stable isotope tracers
interventions.effect: 120 g/h (maltodextrin:fructose 1:1) produced greater whole-body and exogenous CHO oxidation and a lower O2 cost of running than 60 g/h (1:0) and 90 g/h (2:1). BUT: moderate-or-severe GI symptoms were common at every dose, and peak nausea, stomach fullness and abdominal cramps were greatest at 120 g/h. The authors state explicitly that the performance implications remain undetermined.
interventions.population: 8 ELITE male marathoners. Not recreational, not 85 kg, and gut-trained by career exposure.
interventions.citation: Ravikanti S, Silang KG, Martyn HJ, Johnson KO, Louis JB, Bampouras TM, Owens DJ, Jones AM, Morton JP, Pugh JN. 13C-labelled glucose-fructose show greater exogenous and whole-body CHO oxidation and lower O2 cost of running at 120 versus 60 and 90 g·h⁻¹ in elite male marathoners. J Appl Physiol. 2025;139(6). doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00665.2025
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Technically yes, but it should NOT be applied. A six-week gut-training runway starting from a recreational baseline is not enough to make 120 g/h safe at marathon effort, and the paper itself found GI symptoms worst at that dose in elite runners who were already adapted.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — no performance outcome was measured. This is the newest and most-cited-in-podcasts evidence for 120 g/h in running, and it explicitly does not show a faster race.

interventions.intervention: 120 g/h vs 90 vs 60 g/h during a real 42.195 km mountain marathon (~4000 m ascent), effect on race time and on 24 h recovery
interventions.effect: NO significant difference in race time: 271.7 ± 41.7 min (120 g/h) vs 284.1 ± 40.0 (90) vs 278.2 ± 43.6 (60), p = 0.063. Large differences in 24 h RECOVERY: countermovement jump height change -11.3% / -9.7% / +1.2% (p = 0.038); half-squat 1RM -15.3% / -13.8% / -2.4% (p = 0.041); run-to-exhaustion time -14.1% / -14.9% / +1.3% (p = 0.018). Internal load (TRIMP) lower at 120 g/h. Companion paper found lower CK/LDH/GOT at 120 g/h.
interventions.population: 20 ELITE male mountain/trail runners, >5 years ultra experience, who had completed a formal gut-training protocol first. 6 of 26 randomised withdrew, 3 of them for GI distress.
interventions.citation: Urdampilleta A, Arribalzaga S, Viribay A, Castañeda-Babarro A, Seco-Calvo J, Mielgo-Ayuso J. Effects of 120 vs. 60 and 90 g/h Carbohydrate Intake during a Trail Marathon on Neuromuscular Function and High Intensity Run Capacity Recovery. Nutrients. 2020;12(7):2094. doi:10.3390/nu12072094 — and companion: Viribay A, et al. Effects of 120 g/h of Carbohydrates Intake during a Mountain Marathon on Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage in Elite Runners. Nutrients. 2020;12(5):1367. doi:10.3390/nu12051367
interventions.sampleSize: n = 20 completers (6-7 per arm), parallel groups
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Not for this athlete. Parallel-group design with 6-7 per arm, elite trail runners on a 4000 m climb at ~4.6 h — a different physiological event. The 24 h recovery benefit is irrelevant to a one-off goal race.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero, by the study's own data — race time did not differ (p = 0.063). This trial is routinely cited as proof that 120 g/h makes you faster; it does not show that.

interventions.intervention: Gut training: 2 weeks of daily 1 h runs at 60% VO2max while consuming 90 g/h carbohydrate (2:1 glucose:fructose gel-discs), vs 0 g/h placebo
interventions.effect: After 2 weeks, in the repeat gut-challenge trial: reduced gut discomfort (p = .012), total GI symptoms (p = .009), upper (p = .015) and lower GI symptoms (p = .008), nausea (p = .05) in the CHO group only. Breath H2 peak (carbohydrate malabsorption marker) fell from 13 ± 6 to 6 ± 3 ppm in CHO (p = .004), unchanged in placebo. 1 h effort-bout distance rose 11.7 ± 1.5 → 12.3 ± 1.3 km (+5%, p = .035) in CHO only.
interventions.population: 18 endurance runners (companion trial n = 25). Trained runners, not elites — a reasonable match.
interventions.citation: Miall A, Khoo A, Rauch C, Snipe RMJ, Camões-Costa VL, Gibson PR, Costa RJS. Two weeks of repetitive gut-challenge reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms and malabsorption. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018;28(2):630-640. doi:10.1111/sms.12912 — companion: Costa RJS, Miall A, Khoo A, et al. Gut-training: the impact of two weeks repetitive gut-challenge during exercise on gastrointestinal status, glucose availability, fuel kinetics, and running performance. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2017;42(5):547-557. doi:10.1139/apnm-2016-0453 (GI symptoms -60% CHO-solid p=.008 and -63% CHO-food p=.046; distance test +5.2% and +4.3% vs -2.1% placebo)
interventions.sampleSize: n = 18 and n = 25, randomised, blinded to gel content
interventions.duration: 14 days of daily exposure — this is the measured time course, and it is why gut training has to start in week 1 of the six, not week 5
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, comfortably — 2 weeks is the demonstrated minimum and there are 6. But it MUST start now. Corroborating systematic review of 8 studies (durations 4-28 days) found gut discomfort down ~47% and carbohydrate malabsorption down 45-54% with 2-week protocols (Martinez IG, Mika AS, Biesiekierski JR, Costa RJS. Sports Med. 2023;53:1175-1200. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01841-0).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Do not convert the +5% distance figure to marathon minutes (that would imply ~12 min). The 5% was a 1 h effort bout inside a gut-challenge protocol, in a state where the placebo group was actively suffering GI symptoms. The correct framing: gut training buys the ABILITY to execute 75-85 g/h without a GI failure, and so it is the precondition for the Hansen-type gain, not an independent gain. Its own marathon-minutes value is best modelled as risk reduction: it lowers the probability that the fuelling plan collapses at 30 km, an event that costs 5-15 min when it happens.

interventions.intervention: Carbohydrate loading (7 days of extra carbohydrate: 566 g/day for 3 days then 452 g/day for 4 days, vs energy-matched extra fat/protein) before a 30 km treadmill time trial
interventions.effect: No overall group difference. BUT: the CHO group ran the last 5 km faster than in their own baseline trial (3.64 vs 3.44 m/s, p < .05), and the 6 MEN in the CHO group improved 30 km time from 131.0 ± 5.4 to 127.4 ± 4.9 min (-2.7%, p < .05), with no such change in controls.
interventions.population: 18 runners (12 men, 6 women), 30 km treadmill TT ~2h10 — pace and duration in the right neighbourhood for this athlete's back half
interventions.citation: Williams C, Brewer J, Walker M. The effect of a high carbohydrate diet on running performance during a 30-km treadmill time trial. Eur J Appl Physiol Occup Physiol. 1992;65(1):18-24. doi:10.1007/BF01466269. Landmark antecedent: Karlsson J, Saltin B. Diet, muscle glycogen, and endurance performance. J Appl Physiol. 1971;31(2):203-206. doi:10.1152/jappl.1971.31.2.203
interventions.sampleSize: n = 18 total; the significant finding rests on a subgroup of 6 men
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it happens in the final 36-48 h and needs one rehearsal.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: -2.7% applied to 235.9 min = 6.4 min. Discount hard — the result is a within-group pre-post change in a 6-man subgroup with no significant between-group effect, and the loading mechanism (glycogen) matters more the closer you get to depletion, which is exactly the 3:30-4:00 marathon. Honest estimate: 2-6 min, expressed mostly as reduced pace decay after 30 km rather than a faster first half. Note that this benefit and the in-race carbohydrate benefit are partly the same currency (both defend glycogen), so do not simply add the two.

interventions.intervention: 1-day carbohydrate loading: 10 g/kg/day high-glycaemic carbohydrate with physical inactivity, no depletion phase
interventions.effect: Maximal muscle glycogen contents achieved within 24 h; no glycogen-depleting exercise phase required. Supporting meta-analysis of 30 studies (n = 319): glycogen rose 269.7 ± 29.2 mmol/kg dw (95% CI 212.4-327.0) after cycling and 156.5 ± 48.6 (95% CI 61.3-251.7) after running — running achieves only ~58% of the cycling supercompensation. Supercompensation correlated with carbohydrate as a PERCENTAGE of energy, not with absolute g/kg/day.
interventions.population: 8 endurance-trained males (Bussau); meta-analysis 271 males / 48 females
interventions.citation: Bussau VA, Fairchild TJ, Rao A, Steele P, Fournier PA. Carbohydrate loading in human muscle: an improved 1 day protocol. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2002;87(3):290-295. doi:10.1007/s00421-002-0621-5 — and Solem K, Clauss M, Jensen J. Glycogen supercompensation in skeletal muscle after cycling or running followed by a high carbohydrate intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2025;16:1620943. doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1620943
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. It also kills the classic mistake — the depletion run in race week is unnecessary and costs freshness.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not separately convertible; it is the delivery method for the carbohydrate-loading effect quantified above, not an additional gain. Practical translation for 85.5 kg: 855 g/day at 10 g/kg. That is enormous; 8 g/kg = 684 g/day for 48 h is the realistic target, and Solem's finding that the % of energy matters more than absolute grams supports displacing fat and fibre rather than simply eating more.

interventions.intervention: Caffeine, 3 mg/kg in capsule form, ~60 min pre-race
interventions.effect: Running-specific meta-analysis (21 RCTs, n = 254, doses 3-9 mg/kg, 15-90 min pre): time-TRIAL performance improved by only -0.71% ± 0.83% (Hedges g = -0.101, p = .026); time-to-EXHAUSTION improved 16.97% ± 14.65% (g = 0.392, p < .001). Network meta-analysis (48 studies, n = 612) ranked LOW-dose capsules (~3 mg/kg) first for time-trial completion (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.06), ahead of moderate-dose capsules (SMD -0.31, 95% CI -0.45 to -0.17). Broader endurance meta-analysis (46 studies): TT completion time improved 2.22 ± 2.59% (ES 0.41 ± 0.2) at 3-6 mg/kg, but that pool is cycling-dominated.
interventions.population: Recreational and trained runners, 92.5% male. The running-specific pooling is the relevant one and it is notably smaller than the cycling-inclusive figure.
interventions.citation: Wang Z, Qiu B, Gao J, Del Coso J. Effects of Caffeine Intake on Endurance Running Performance and Time to Exhaustion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nutrients. 2022;15(1):148. doi:10.3390/nu15010148 — Xue R, Huang J, Chen B, Ding L, Guo L, Cao Y, Girard O. Effects of Caffeine Dose and Administration Method on Time-Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Nutrients. 2025;17(23):3792. doi:10.3390/nu17233792 — Southward K, Rutherfurd-Markwick KJ, Ali A. The Effect of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2018;48(8):1913-1928. doi:10.1007/s40279-018-0939-8
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. One caveat with a real time course: if he currently drinks coffee daily, the evidence on whether withdrawal for 3-7 days augments the effect is equivocal, and withdrawal headaches in race week are a real cost. Do not withdraw.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: the running-specific TT estimate of 0.71% applied to 235.9 min = 1.7 min (95% range from the ±0.83% SD spans roughly 0 to 3.6 min). If the cycling-inclusive 2.22% is used instead it gives 5.2 min, but the running-specific pooling is the honest number for a runner. Estimate: 1-3 min. Dose for 85.5 kg at 3 mg/kg = 257 mg. Note this is one of the few interventions here that acts on the LAST hour, when this athlete's 5:31/km fade historically occurs.

interventions.intervention: Pre-race carbohydrate meal: large carbohydrate feeding ~4 h before the start
interventions.effect: 312 g carbohydrate 4 h pre-exercise improved performance by 15% vs 0 g, despite elevated insulin at the start and a transient blood-glucose dip in the first 15 min. 45 g and 156 g produced no benefit over placebo — the effect was dose-dependent and only appeared at the highest dose.
interventions.population: Trained cyclists, small n, 95 min interval cycling then a performance trial. Cycling, and the comparator was a fasted state.
interventions.citation: Sherman WM, Brodowicz G, Wright DA, Allen WK, Simonsen J, Dernbach A. Effects of 4 h preexercise carbohydrate feedings on cycling performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1989;21(5):598-604. doi:10.1249/00005768-198910000-00017
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it is one of the cheapest changes available. Rehearse it before the long run twice.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Do not convert the 15% — the comparator was a fasted trial, which no marathoner replicates. Its value is that it sets the pre-race meal size: 312 g in that study is ~3.5-4 g/kg for their subjects. For 85.5 kg, 2 g/kg = 171 g carbohydrate ~3 h before is the defensible practical target (the position stands give 1-4 g/kg, 1-4 h prior). Estimated worth: 0 min if he already eats a proper breakfast, 3-8 min if he currently races on a banana and a coffee.

interventions.intervention: Drink to thirst rather than to a schedule; accept 2-4% body-mass loss
interventions.effect: Ad libitum drinking (505 ± 156 ml/h, -2.1% body mass) vs programmed drinking (1073 ± 247 ml/h, -1.0%): ad libitum was 0.98 ± 0.44% BETTER (95% CI 0.11-1.84%), which the authors call likely trivial. Separately: exercise-induced dehydration up to 4% body-mass loss did not alter self-paced TT performance (+0.06 ± 2.72%, p = .94); drinking to thirst beat drinking below thirst by +5.2 ± 4.6% (p = .01) and above thirst by +2.4 ± 5.0% (p = .40).
interventions.population: Goulet 2019: 7 publications, 82 subjects, cycling and running, 28 ± 6°C. Goulet 2011: 5 articles, 39 subjects, all cycling. Trained athletes.
interventions.citation: Goulet EDB, Hoffman MD. Impact of Ad Libitum Versus Programmed Drinking on Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2019;49(2):221-232. doi:10.1007/s40279-018-01051-z — Goulet EDB. Effect of exercise-induced dehydration on time-trial exercise performance: a meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2011;45(14):1149-1156. doi:10.1136/bjsm.2010.077966
interventions.duration: 1-2 h exercise bouts — shorter than a marathon, which is the main limitation
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, immediately. October in London is cool; sweat rates will be modest.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Approximately 0 minutes of upside — the honest conversion is that there is nothing to gain here, only something to lose. The value is avoiding two failure modes: (a) carrying an extra litre of unneeded fluid and the GI load that comes with it, and (b) over-drinking into hyponatremia. Budget ~400-600 ml/h in cool conditions, adjusted by thirst, and stop treating fluid as a performance lever.

interventions.intervention: Sodium supplementation (salt tablets/capsules) beyond what is in gels and sports drink
interventions.effect: NO effect. In a 161 km ultramarathon at up to 39°C, total sodium intake ranged 2541-38,338 mg and was unrelated to hyponatremia (10% of finishers), to muscle cramping (39%), or to nausea/vomiting (57%). Separately, in 72 distance runners there were no clinically significant differences in serum sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, osmolality or hydration status between crampers and non-crampers.
interventions.population: 20 ultramarathon finishers; 72 ultra-distance road runners. Extreme conditions — if sodium supplementation does nothing there, it does nothing in a cool 4 h London marathon.
interventions.citation: Hoffman MD, Stuempfle KJ, Valentino T. Sodium Intake During an Ultramarathon Does Not Prevent Muscle Cramping, Dehydration, Hyponatremia, or Nausea. Sports Med Open. 2015;1:39. doi:10.1186/s40798-015-0040-x — Schwellnus MP, Nicol J, Laubscher R, Noakes TD. Serum electrolyte concentrations and hydration status are not associated with exercise associated muscle cramping (EAMC) in distance runners. Br J Sports Med. 2004;38(4):488-492. doi:10.1136/bjsm.2003.007021 — Hew-Butler T, Rosner MH, Fowkes-Godek S, et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Clin J Sport Med. 2015;25(4):303-320. doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000000221
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it is a decision to NOT buy something.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0 minutes. Listed because it is the most reliably wasted item in a recreational marathoner's kit, and because the consensus statement identifies over-drinking of hypotonic fluid, not sodium loss, as the cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia. The ~60 mg sodium per gel used in the Hansen protocol was incidental, not therapeutic.

interventions.intervention: Maximal-availability strategy: 2 weeks of a high-carbohydrate diet PLUS gut training, then carbohydrate loading plus 90 g/h in-race, vs the lower end of current guidelines
interventions.effect: NEGATIVE / null result. Both groups improved performance by essentially the same amount (CON 39 s [95% CI 15-63]; MAX 36 s [13-59]; p = .002 for the improvement, no group difference), despite a three-fold increase in in-exercise carbohydrate intake in MAX. In the race-walker cohort, MAX was associated with MORE upper-GI symptoms in the second half (p < .01).
interventions.population: 18 highly trained male and female distance runners (35 km run: 28 km steady-state + 7 km TT), plus 19 elite male race walkers
interventions.citation: King AJ, Etxebarria N, Ross ML, Garvican-Lewis L, Heikura IA, McKay AKA, Tee N, Forbes SF, Beard NA, Saunders PU, Sharma AP, Gaskell SK, Costa RJS, Burke LM. Short-Term Very High Carbohydrate Diet and Gut-Training Have Minor Effects on Gastrointestinal Status and Performance in Highly Trained Endurance Athletes. Nutrients. 2022;14(9):1929. doi:10.3390/nu14091929
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — as a brake. This is the best available evidence that pushing beyond current guidelines does not add performance, and it is in RUNNERS.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 0 additional minutes above the guideline strategy. Include it explicitly in any honest account, because it is the counter-evidence to the whole 'maximal fuelling' narrative and the authors were the people best placed to find a positive result.

interventions.intervention: Chronic high daily carbohydrate availability around training (28 days), to raise the gut's exogenous oxidation capacity
interventions.effect: Exogenous glucose oxidation during 100 min steady-state cycling rose from 54.6 to 63.6 g (p < .01) in the high-carbohydrate group, unchanged in the energy-matched low-carbohydrate group. But the training-induced ~6% performance improvement was the SAME in both groups.
interventions.population: 16 endurance-trained cyclists/triathletes
interventions.citation: Cox GR, Clark SA, Cox AJ, Halson SL, Hargreaves M, Hawley JA, Jeacocke N, Snow RJ, Yeo WK, Burke LM. Daily training with high carbohydrate availability increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation during endurance cycling. J Appl Physiol. 2010;109(1):126-134. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00950.2009
interventions.duration: 28 days — fits inside six weeks with a week to spare
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it is the mechanism that makes the gut-training progression work. Note it also means the training-week diet must be carbohydrate-rich, not just the race-week diet.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not separately convertible — the study found no additional performance gain (the ~6% was from training, in both arms). Its role is to raise the ceiling on how much can be absorbed, i.e. it enables the 80 g/h target rather than adding minutes of its own.

interventions.intervention: Even a small carbohydrate dose during a full marathon-distance run: ~1.1 L of a 5.5% CHO-electrolyte solution (~61 g total, ~19 g/h) vs water
interventions.effect: 42.2 km treadmill time trial 190.0 ± 3.9 min (5.5% CHO) vs 193.9 ± 5.0 min (water) — 3.9 min / 2.0% faster, p < .05. Running speed was MAINTAINED throughout on the 5.5% drink, but decayed after 10 km on water and after 25 km on the 6.9% drink. The 6.9% solution (192.4 min) was not significantly better than water.
interventions.population: 7 endurance-trained runners, 42.2 km treadmill TT, ~3:10-3:14 — faster than this athlete but the only true marathon-distance running trial with a finish-time outcome
interventions.citation: Tsintzas OK, Williams C, Singh R, Wilson W, Burrin J. Influence of carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks on marathon running performance. Eur J Appl Physiol Occup Physiol. 1995;70(2):154-160. doi:10.1007/BF00361543. Supporting: Tsintzas OK, Williams C, Wilson W, Burrin J. Influence of carbohydrate supplementation early in exercise on endurance running capacity. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1996;28(11):1373-1379
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: 2.0% of 235.9 min = 4.7 min — from only ~19 g/h. n = 7, so the confidence interval is wide. Its real value is qualitative and directly on point for this athlete: the CHO trial preserved pace to the finish while the water trial faded from 10 km onward. A 3:55 marathoner's loss is almost entirely back-half fade, which is what carbohydrate defends.

myths: "Elite pros take 120 g/h, so I should push toward it." In RUNNING there is no trial showing a faster race at 120 g/h than at 60-90 g/h. The trail-marathon RCT that is always cited found race times of 271.7 vs 284.1 vs 271.7-284.1 min across 120/90/60 g/h with p = 0.063, i.e. no difference (Urdampilleta 2020). The 2025 elite-marathoner isotope study found better oxidation and running economy at 120 g/h but explicitly did not measure performance, and found peak nausea, stomach fullness and cramps WORST at 120 g/h (Ravikanti 2025). The 2026 Sports Medicine review concludes the best guidance for most athletes remains 60-90 g/h (Plews 2026), and the 2026 Journal of Nutrition review states the efficacy of 120-200 g/h 'is not yet substantiated by current scientific research' (Morton 2026).

"More carbohydrate is monotonically better." The 51-subject, 12-dose double-blind study found a CURVILINEAR relationship with best performance at 78 g/h and no further gain above it (Smith 2013). The 136-study meta-regression found dose was not a moderator of the performance effect at all (Ramos-Campo 2023).

"Sodium/salt tablets prevent cramp, dehydration and hyponatremia." Total sodium intake over a 161 km race varied 15-fold (2541-38,338 mg) and was unrelated to cramping, nausea or hyponatremia (Hoffman 2015). Serum electrolytes and hydration status do not differ between crampers and non-crampers (Schwellnus 2004). The 2015 international consensus identifies over-drinking of hypotonic fluid, not sodium loss, as the cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia (Hew-Butler 2015). Two-thirds of ultrarunners still believe otherwise (Hoffman 2020, n = 1152).

"Drink ahead of thirst; never let yourself get behind." Ad libitum drinking at half the programmed rate, producing -2.1% body mass, was 0.98% BETTER, not worse (Goulet 2019). Body-mass loss up to 4% did not impair self-paced performance (Goulet 2011). Drinking to thirst beat drinking below thirst by 5.2% and drinking above thirst by 2.4%.

"Body-mass loss during the race equals dehydration you must replace." A substantial share is metabolic water released from glycogen and substrate oxidation. This is why the 4% figure is tolerable rather than alarming.

"Carb loading requires a glycogen-depletion phase (the classic 3-days-low then 3-days-high)." Maximal muscle glycogen is reached in 24-36 h on 10 g/kg/day with rest and no depletion phase at all (Bussau 2002). The depletion run in race week costs freshness and buys nothing.

"Carbohydrate loading works the same for runners as for cyclists." Meta-analysis of 30 studies: glycogen supercompensation was 269.7 mmol/kg dw after cycling but only 156.5 after running — running achieves roughly 58% of the cycling response, plausibly because running causes muscle damage and depletes less completely (Solem 2025).

"Fat adaptation spares glycogen and therefore helps the marathon." A ketogenic low-carbohydrate high-fat diet raised fat oxidation as advertised but INCREASED the oxygen cost of moving at race velocities and impaired performance in elite endurance athletes, despite improving VO2peak (Burke 2017).

"Recreational marathoners already fuel adequately, so there is nothing to gain." Measured intake in a real marathon averaged 35 ± 26 g/h — barely half the low end of guidelines, and far below the Ironman figures of 62-71 g/h in the same study (Pfeiffer 2012). The gap between practice and guideline is where the minutes are.

"GI distress is the main reason marathoners underfuel." Serious GI symptoms were reported by only 4% of marathoners, versus ~31% in Ironman (Pfeiffer 2012). At marathon duration the limiting factor is more often plan, habit and carrying logistics than gut tolerance. That said, higher carbohydrate intake did correlate with more nausea and flatulence — and, in Ironman, with FASTER finishing times (r = -0.55 and -0.48).

"Stacking every fuelling strategy maximally will stack the gains." The best-designed test of exactly that — 2 weeks high-carbohydrate diet plus gut training plus carbohydrate loading plus 90 g/h in-race, versus the low end of guidelines — produced identical performance improvements in trained runners (King 2022).
unknowns: There is no randomised trial of 60 vs 90 g/h with MARATHON FINISH TIME as the outcome in recreational runners. Every dose-response finding above is extrapolated from cycling (Smith 2013), from oxidation tracers (Ravikanti 2025, Podlogar 2022), or from trail-running recovery markers (Urdampilleta 2020). The single most decision-relevant experiment for this athlete has not been run.

Whether >90 g/h improves running performance at all, as opposed to improving oxidation and running economy. Both 2026 reviews say the mechanistic case is incomplete and the performance case is unproven (Morton 2026; Plews 2026).

Whether carbohydrate targets should scale with body mass. Every guideline is an absolute rate in g/h. An 85.5 kg runner oxidises more carbohydrate per hour than a 60 kg runner at the same relative intensity, yet the intestinal transporter ceiling is believed to be absolute. Nobody has tested whether a heavier runner should take more. This is a real and unresolved gap for this specific athlete.

Whether the gut-training benefit (fewer GI symptoms, less malabsorption, more distance covered in a 1 h effort bout) translates into a faster marathon. The 2023 systematic review of 8 studies calls the performance evidence limited and inconclusive (Martinez 2023).

The optimal glucose:fructose ratio at high intake rates in running. Podlogar 2022 found 0.8:1 fructose:maltodextrin at 120 g/h beat 1:2 at 90 g/h for exogenous oxidation, but ratio and dose were confounded and it was cycling. Ravikanti 2025 confounded them again (1:0 at 60, 2:1 at 90, 1:1 at 120).
Whether gut training persists — how quickly the adaptation decays if high-carbohydrate exposure stops during a taper. No data. This matters directly for how much fuelling to do in the final week.

Whether carbohydrate loading benefits a 3:55 marathoner as much as a 2:30 one. The classic trials used faster runners at higher fractional intensity for shorter durations. A slower runner spends longer above the glycogen-dependence threshold but at a lower percentage of VO2max. The interaction is untested.

Whether caffeine habituation blunts the effect and whether withdrawal restores it. Reviews remain equivocal, and the running-specific time-trial effect (-0.71%) is small enough that habituation could plausibly erase it.

Whether the Hansen 2014 result (4.7% faster marathon from a prescribed nutrition strategy) replicates. It has not been repeated in the twelve years since publication, which for a finding of that magnitude and practical importance is itself informative.

Almost all of this evidence is in men (Wang 2022: 7.5% female; Solem 2025: 48 of 319 female). Irrelevant to this athlete's own decision, but it means the field's confidence intervals are narrower than they should be for general use.

officialSources.body: World Athletics (then IAAF) — consensus statement, 50 experts
officialSources.document: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):73-84. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Periodised guidelines for type, amount and timing of food and fluid across training and competition. Competition nutrition covers pre-event, within-event and between-event eating for carbohydrate and fluid replacement. A 'food first' policy, with a short evidence-based supplement list for which caffeine is named. This is the governing body's statement for the athlete's own sport.

officialSources.body: World Athletics (IAAF) — the distance-running chapter of the same consensus, and the most directly applicable official document to this athlete
officialSources.document: Burke LM, Jeukendrup AE, Jones AM, Mooses M. Contemporary Nutrition Strategies to Optimize Performance in Distance Runners and Race Walkers. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):117-129. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0004
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Explicitly: 'Beneficial CHO intakes range from small amounts, including mouth rinsing, in the case of shorter events to high rates of intake (75-90 g/hr) in the longest races.' Carbohydrate-rich eating in the hours-to-days before the event to store sufficient glycogen; in-race carbohydrate and fluid to offset losses; a personalised and PRACTISED race nutrition plan balancing benefit against 'the time, cost, and risk of gut discomfort'; caffeine (and possibly nitrate) as evidence-based supplements. The 75-90 g/h band is the official number this athlete's protocol should target.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine, Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada — joint position stand
officialSources.document: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2016;116(3):501-528. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2015.12.006
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: The reference guideline set for carbohydrate intake during exercise: up to 90 g/h from multiple transportable carbohydrates for exercise exceeding ~2.5-3 h; 60 g/h for 1-2.5 h; carbohydrate loading and pre-event meal targets in g/kg body mass. The 2026 Journal of Nutrition review (Morton et al.) treats this as the standing guideline it is proposing to revise upward toward 120 g/h — which tells you the 90 g/h ceiling is still the official position.

officialSources.body: Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference (Carlsbad, 2015) — the governing medical consensus on race-day hydration
officialSources.document: Hew-Butler T, Rosner MH, Fowkes-Godek S, et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Clin J Sport Med. 2015;25(4):303-320. doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000000221
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Drink according to thirst — no more, no less. Identifies overconsumption of hypotonic fluid, combined with non-osmotic AVP secretion, as the primary cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia. Drinking to thirst is stated to be sufficient to prevent BOTH dehydration and hyponatremia. This is the source that overrides the 'drink on a schedule' advice most marathon plans still contain.

officialSources.body: Contemporary expert reviews that set the current ceiling of the evidence (not governing bodies, but the papers the next guideline revision will be built from)
officialSources.document: Morton JP, Fell JM, Gonzalez JT, Hearris MA, Podlogar T, Pugh JN, Wallis GA. From Metabolism to Medals: Contemporary Perspectives and Revisiting Carbohydrate Guidelines for Fueling Endurance Athletes during Exercise. J Nutr. 2026;156(5):101442. doi:10.1016/j.tjnut.2026.101442 — and Plews DJ, Booth PD, Krieger T, Maunder E. Fuelled or Fooled? Examining the Evidence and Mechanisms Behind Ultra-High Carbohydrate Intake in Endurance Athletes. Sports Med. 2026. doi:10.1007/s40279-026-02462-z
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Morton et al. propose 30-60 g/h for 1-2.5 h and 90-120 g/h for 2.5-6 h in trained participants, while stating the efficacy of 120-200 g/h is not yet substantiated. Plews et al. conclude the best guidance for most athletes remains 60-90 g/h. Both note that marathon runners in the field average ~35 g/h versus 60-90 g/h in cyclists, and that GI symptoms are the binding constraint in running.

check.domain: Race fuelling and carbohydrate intake for a 27-year-old, 85.5 kg recreational male marathoner (3:55:54 PB, ~24 km/wk), Battersea Park Marathon 2026-10-24, six weeks out

citationChecks.citation: Hansen EA, Emanuelsen A, Gertsen RM, Sørensen SSR. Improved Marathon Performance by In-Race Nutritional Strategy Intervention. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(6):645-655. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0130
citationChecks.note: Crossref + Europe PMC. Every reported number is verbatim from the abstract: 3:49:26 ± 0:25:05 (freely chosen) vs 3:38:31 ± 0:24:54 (scientific), p=.010, effect size -0.43, 10:55 min = 4.7%. Group ages 33.6 ± 9.6 vs 41.9 ± 7.6 yr, masses 77.4 vs 74.6 kg, 10 km 45:40 vs 45:44 — all as stated. Protocol (0.750 L water, 60 g maltodextrin+glucose, 0.06 g sodium, 0.09 g caffeine per hour) matches. GI claim also accurate: 'overall, symptoms were low and not different between groups (p > .05)'. Searched Europe PMC for any replication or critique citing Hansen on marathon nutrition — none found, so the researcher's 'never replicated in twelve years' stands.

citationChecks.citation: Ramos-Campo DJ, et al. The ergogenic effects of acute carbohydrate feeding on endurance performance: systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2024;64(33):11196-11205. doi:10.1080/10408398.2023.2233633
citationChecks.note: Real, 136 studies. Abstract confirms every moderator claim verbatim: larger in TTE than TT, larger with longer events, 'higher effect of CHO intake in lower trained than in higher trained participants', and magnitude 'not affected by the dosage, ergometer used, the type of intake... and the type of CHO'; lower RPE, higher power and HR. One trivial citation slip: Crossref gives volume 64, issue 30, not issue 33.

citationChecks.citation: Smith JW, Pascoe DD, et al. Curvilinear dose-response relationship of carbohydrate (0-120 g/h) and performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2013;45(2):336-341. doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e31827205d1
citationChecks.note: n=51 cyclists and triathletes, 28 ± 7 yr, four sites, 12 double-blind beverages, 1:1:1 glucose-fructose-maltodextrin at 1 L/h, 2 h constant load + 20 km TT. Abstract: 'best performance occurring with a CHO ingestion rate of 78 g/h', with 'diminishing performance enhancement seen at CHO levels >78 g/h'. Incremental gains 1.0/2.0/3.0/4.0/4.7% at 9/19/31/48/78 g/h. Researcher's characterisation is exact, including the correct caveat that this is cycling.

citationChecks.citation: Currell K, Jeukendrup AE. Superior endurance performance with ingestion of multiple transportable carbohydrates. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2008;40(2):275-281. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31815adf19
citationChecks.note: n=8 male trained cyclists, 84.4 ± 6.9 kg, VO2max 64.7, 1.8 g/min, 2 h ride + ~1 h TT; 8% quicker vs glucose, 19% vs water; total CHO oxidation not different, implying endogenous sparing. All as claimed. Caveat the researcher did not flag: the published abstract's own raw times are internally inconsistent (GF 4022 s vs G 3641 s reads as GF being slower) — a known transposition in the abstract. The 8% direction matches the paper's stated conclusion, but anyone re-deriving from the abstract's seconds will get the opposite sign.

citationChecks.citation: Ravikanti S, et al. 13C-labelled glucose-fructose show greater exogenous and whole-body CHO oxidation and lower O2 cost of running at 120 versus 60 and 90 g/h in elite male marathoners. J Appl Physiol. 2025;139(6). doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00665.2025
citationChecks.note: Real; Crossref gives vol 139, issue 6, pp 1581-1595, all 10 authors matching. n=8 elite males, marathon PB 2:22:54 ± 5:37. Ratios 1:0 / 2:1 / 1:1 at 60/90/120 g/h as stated. 120 > 90 > 60 for whole-body and exogenous oxidation (P<0.01 all pairwise); running economy better at 120 (8.1 mL O2/kg/km lower than 60, P=0.039); 'incidence of moderate or severe GI symptoms was high in all trials, though peak symptoms of nausea, stomach fullness, and abdominal cramps were greatest for 120 g/h'. No performance outcome measured — the researcher's central caveat is correct.

citationChecks.citation: Urdampilleta A, et al. Effects of 120 vs. 60 and 90 g/h Carbohydrate Intake during a Trail Marathon on Neuromuscular Function and High Intensity Run Capacity Recovery. Nutrients. 2020;12(7):2094. doi:10.3390/nu12072094
citationChecks.note: Paper real; I pulled the PMC full text (PMC7400827). Race times are exact and correctly mapped: Table 1 gives LOW 278.2 ± 43.6, MED 284.1 ± 40.0, HIGH 271.7 ± 41.7, p = 0.063 — so 'no faster race at 120 g/h' is right, and in fact stronger than stated because race time is a BASELINE group-equivalence row in Table 1, not a designed outcome. Withdrawals verified verbatim: 26 randomised, '6 athletes withdrew during the race (3 with gastrointestinal discomfort–flatulence and/or reflux and 3 with injury)', 20 completers. BUT the recovery percentages are listed in an order that inverts the study's finding — see effectSizeErrors.

citationChecks.citation: Viribay A, et al. Effects of 120 g/h of Carbohydrates Intake during a Mountain Marathon on Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage in Elite Runners. Nutrients. 2020;12(5):1367. doi:10.3390/nu12051367
citationChecks.note: Companion paper confirmed. n=20 male elite runners 'who had previously undertaken nutritional and gut training' — corroborates the researcher's population caveat. Internal load lower in 120 g/h (3805 ± 281 vs 4688 ± 705 and 4692 ± 716 AU, p=0.019); CK (p=0.019), LDH (p<0.001) and GOT lower. As claimed.

citationChecks.citation: Miall A, Khoo A, Rauch C, Snipe RMJ, Camões-Costa VL, Gibson PR, Costa RJS. Two weeks of repetitive gut-challenge reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms and malabsorption. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018;28(2):630-640. doi:10.1111/sms.12912
citationChecks.note: n=18 endurance runners. Every p-value matches the abstract exactly: gut discomfort p=.012, total GI p=.009, upper p=.015, lower p=.008, nausea p=.05. Breath H2 peak 13 ± 6 → 6 ± 3 ppm on CHO, p=.004, unchanged on placebo. Effort-bout distance 11.7 ± 1.5 → 12.3 ± 1.3 km, p=.035, CHO only. Note the intervention was 1 h daily at 60% VO2max with 90 g/h — as stated.

citationChecks.citation: Costa RJS, Miall A, Khoo A, et al. Gut-training: two weeks repetitive gut-challenge... Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2017;42(5):547-557. doi:10.1139/apnm-2016-0453
citationChecks.note: n=25. Abstract confirms GI symptoms reduced 60% on carbohydrate-gel (p=0.008) and 63% on carbohydrate-food (p=0.046); distance test +5.2% (gel), +4.3% (food), -2.1% (placebo), trial x time p=0.009. Exactly as reported.

citationChecks.citation: Martinez IG, Mika AS, Biesiekierski JR, Costa RJS. The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status... Sports Med. 2023;53:1175-1200. doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01841-0
citationChecks.note: 8 studies included from 304 screened, durations 4-28 days, carbohydrate-only in 7. Abstract states gut discomfort decreased 'by an average of 47%' with a 2-week repetitive carbohydrate feeding protocol. The 45-54% malabsorption figure falls past the abstract truncation point but the rest is verbatim. The researcher's title paraphrase ('Two weeks of repetitive gut-challenge...') is loose — the actual title is 'The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status in Response to Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Literature Review'.

citationChecks.citation: Williams C, Brewer J, Walker M. The effect of a high carbohydrate diet on running performance during a 30-km treadmill time trial. Eur J Appl Physiol Occup Physiol. 1992;65(1):18-24. doi:10.1007/BF01466269
citationChecks.note: 18 runners (12 men, 6 women). 566 (29) g/day for 3 days then 452 (26) g/day for 4 days after a baseline of 334 (22) g. No overall group difference. CHO group faster over the last 5 km (3.64 vs 3.44 m/s, P<0.05) and the 6 men improved 131.0 → 127.4 min. All exact. Caveat: the paper reports SEM, not SD — the researcher writes '±' which reads as SD and makes the finding look tighter than it is.

citationChecks.citation: Karlsson J, Saltin B. Diet, muscle glycogen, and endurance performance. J Appl Physiol. 1971;31(2):203-206. doi:10.1152/jappl.1971.31.2.203
citationChecks.note: Record confirmed via Crossref with correct authors, journal, volume, issue and pages. Cited only as a 'landmark antecedent' with no specific numerical claim attached, so there is nothing to check.

citationChecks.citation: Bussau VA, Fairchild TJ, Rao A, Steele P, Fournier PA. Carbohydrate loading in human muscle: an improved 1 day protocol. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2002;87(3):290-295. doi:10.1007/s00421-002-0621-5
citationChecks.note: n=8 endurance-trained males, 10 g/kg/day high-glycaemic-index carbohydrate with physical inactivity, no depletion phase. Glycogen 95 (5) → 180 (15) mmol/kg wet mass after ONE day and stable thereafter; maximal in type I, IIa and IIb fibres at 24 h. Supports the 'no depletion run needed' claim exactly.

citationChecks.citation: Solem K, Clauss M, Jensen J. Glycogen supercompensation in skeletal muscle after cycling or running followed by a high carbohydrate intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2025;16:1620943. doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1620943
citationChecks.note: 30 studies, 319 participants (271 male, 48 female). Cycling +269.7 ± 29.2 mmol/kg dw (95% CI 212.4-327.0); running +156.5 ± 48.6 (95% CI 61.3-251.7). Supercompensation after cycling positively associated with percent carbohydrate in the diet. Every number exact. One framing problem: it is bundled under the '1-day carbohydrate loading' intervention, but the inclusion criterion was glycogen measured after 3-5 days of high-carbohydrate diet — it does not test a 1-day protocol and cannot corroborate Bussau's 24 h finding.

citationChecks.citation: Morton JP, Fell JM, Gonzalez JT, Hearris MA, Podlogar T, Pugh JN, Wallis GA. From Metabolism to Medals... J Nutr. 2026;156(5):101442. doi:10.1016/j.tjnut.2026.101442

The key quoted claim is verbatim: field intakes of '120-200 g/h... the efficacy of such doses is not yet substantiated by current scientific research', and 'the upper limit of CHO intake could increase from 90 to 120 g/h (at least for trained participants)'. The specific proposed bands (30-60 g/h for 1-2.5 h; 90-120 g/h for 2.5-6 h) sit past the abstract and I could not confirm them, but they are consistent with what the abstract says.

citationChecks.citation: Plews DJ, Booth PD, Krieger T, Maunder E. Fuelled or Fooled? Examining the Evidence and Mechanisms Behind Ultra-High Carbohydrate Intake in Endurance Athletes. Sports Med. 2026. doi:10.1007/s40279-026-02462-z
citationChecks.note: Paper is real (Crossref: Plews, Booth, Krieger, Maunder; Sports Medicine; 2026-06-08). The abstract supports the general thrust — 'the scientific literature supporting these practices remains limited', 'a disconnect between metabolic data and the real-world adoption of intakes far beyond established oxidation ceilings' — but it does NOT contain the two specific claims attributed to it: that 'the best guidance for most athletes remains 60-90 g/h', and that it notes marathoners average ~35 g/h versus 60-90 g/h in cyclists. Springer full text is paywalled and bot-blocked, with no PMC copy. That numeric attribution is unverified and is used twice, including as the load-bearing rebuttal to the 120 g/h claim in the myths section.

citationChecks.citation: Pfeiffer B, Stellingwerff T, Hodgson AB, Randell R, Pöttgen K, Res P, Jeukendrup AE. Nutritional intake and gastrointestinal problems during competitive endurance events. (cited as 'Pfeiffer 2012', no DOI given)
citationChecks.note: Real: Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2012;44(2):344-351, doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31822dc809, 221 athletes. Every figure used is verbatim: marathon 35 ± 26 g/h vs Ironman 62 ± 26 / 71 ± 25 / 65 ± 25 g/h; serious GI symptoms ~31% in Ironman vs 4% in marathon and 4% in cycling; carbohydrate intake positively correlated with nausea and flatulence and negatively with Ironman finishing time (r = -0.55 and -0.48). Range 6-136 g/h. Cited with no DOI despite carrying two of the eleven myth-busts.

citationChecks.citation: Dezfuli ZG et al. (cited only as 'Dezfuli 2025, 14 RCTs, n = 125', no journal, no DOI)
citationChecks.note: Real and the numbers are exact: Iran J Public Health. 2025;54(4):723-738, doi:10.18502/ijph.v54i4.18411. 14 RCTs, 125 endurance athletes; glucose-fructose increased exogenous carbohydrate oxidation by WMD 0.27 g/min versus glucose. Flagged because it is cited with no journal name: it is a low-visibility public-health journal, not a sports-science one, and a reader cannot locate it from the citation as given.

citationChecks.citation: Podlogar T (cited only as 'Podlogar 2022' in the unknowns: 0.8:1 fructose:maltodextrin at 120 g/h beat 1:2 at 90 g/h for exogenous oxidation)
citationChecks.note: Real: Podlogar T, Bokal Š, Cirnski S, Wallis GA. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122(11):2393-2401, doi:10.1007/s00421-022-05019-w. 11 highly trained male cyclists, 3 h at 95% gas exchange threshold, 120 g/h at 0.8:1 fructose:glucose-based vs 90 g/h at 1:2 — exactly the comparison described, and the point that ratio and dose are confounded is correct. Cited without journal or DOI, and there are at least two other 2022 Podlogar papers, so the bare 'Podlogar 2022' is ambiguous.

citationChecks.citation: Burke LM (cited only as 'Burke 2017': ketogenic LCHF raised the oxygen cost of race velocities and impaired performance despite improving VO2peak)
citationChecks.note: Real: Burke LM, Ross ML, Garvican-Lewis LA, et al. 'Low carbohydrate, high fat diet impairs exercise economy and negates the performance benefit from intensified training in elite race walkers.' J Physiol. 2017;595(9):2785-2807, doi:10.1113/JP273230. The 2020 PLoS ONE replication (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0234027) confirms the pattern: all groups raised VO2peak, LCHF raised fat oxidation to 1.3 g/min but also 'the oxygen cost of walking at race-relevant velocities', and LCHF was 2.3% slower over 10,000 m while high-carbohydrate improved 4.8%. Cited with no journal or DOI. Population is elite race walkers, not marathon runners.

citationChecks.citation: Hoffman MD (cited only as 'Hoffman 2020, n = 1152': two-thirds of ultrarunners still believe sodium supplements prevent hyponatraemia and cramping)
citationChecks.note: Real: Hoffman MD, White MD. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2020;45(1):118-122, doi:10.1139/apnm-2019-0238. 1152 ULTRA-study participants; 66.4% said sodium supplements should be available, on beliefs that they prevent exercise-associated hyponatraemia (65.5%) and cramping (59.1%). Exact. Again cited with no journal or DOI.

populationMismatches: Caffeine, the sharpest one. The 1-3 minute estimate rests on Wang 2022's pooled running time-trial effect of -0.71%. But inside that same paper the subgroup that IS this athlete returns nothing: recreational runners g = -0.082, 95% CI -0.190 to 0.027, p = 0.141; trained runners g = -0.140, p = 0.075; and 'caffeine was not ergogenic in middle-distance or long-distance time trials'. The submission quotes the pooled figure and omits the null subgroup. Honest expected value for a 27-year-old recreational runner over four hours is closer to 0 than to 1.7 minutes.

Caffeine, second layer. Xue 2025's network meta-analysis (SMD -0.34 for low-dose capsules) and Southward 2018 (2.22% faster time trials) pool overwhelmingly short cycling time trials. Nothing in either pool resembles a 235-minute road marathon by a 3:55 runner. The dose recommendation (257 mg) survives; the minutes attached to it do not.

Smith 2013, the source of the whole 75-85 g/h target: 51 trained cyclists and triathletes, 20 km cycling time trial after 2 h of seated cycling at 1 L/h fluid. Running gut tolerance is materially worse than cycling — acknowledged — yet 78 g/h is still promoted as 'the single best empirical justification' for this runner's race-day dose. It is a cycling number.

Currell 2008: n = 8 male trained cyclists, VO2max 64.7 against this athlete's estimated 53. Body mass matches (84.4 vs 85.5 kg) but nothing else does, and it is cycling. Correctly not converted to minutes.

Ravikanti 2025: 8 elite male marathoners with a mean personal best of 2:22:54, running at 94% of lactate turnpoint after a 24 h 8 g/kg carbohydrate diet, guts adapted by career exposure. This athlete is 93 minutes slower over the distance and has never gut-trained. Anything measured here about 120 g/h tolerance is measured in the most tolerant population that exists.

Urdampilleta 2020 / Viribay 2020: elite trail runners with >5 years ultra experience who had 'previously undertaken nutritional and gut training', racing 42.195 km with 4000 m of ascent in ~4.6 h. An eccentric-loading mountain event, not a flat London park marathon, with 6-7 per arm in a parallel-group design.

King 2022: 19 elite male race walkers and 18 highly trained male and female distance runners in a live-in training camp. Correctly used as a brake, but its null is a null in athletes already at the top of the guideline — it does not establish that a recreational runner currently on ~35 g/h gains nothing by moving up.
Cox 2010 and Sherman 1989: both cycling, both trained cyclists/triathletes. Sherman's 15% is also against a 0 g comparator, which the submission correctly refuses to convert.

Goulet 2011: five articles, 39 subjects, all cycling, 86 ± 34 min bouts at 26 °C. Goulet 2019: 96 ± 25 min bouts at 28 ± 6 °C. Both are 1-2 h protocols licensing a hydration strategy over four hours. The duration limitation is noted, but the conclusion 'approximately 0 minutes of upside' still reaches beyond the evidence's duration range.

Hoffman 2015 and Schwellnus 2004: a 161 km ultramarathon at up to 39 °C, and ultra-distance road runners. Cramping and hyponatraemia over 30 hours at 39 °C have different aetiology and different fluid volumes from a four-hour October marathon in London. The a fortiori argument is reasonable but it is an argument, not a measurement in this population.

Williams 1992: the significant result is a within-group pre-post change in a 6-man subgroup running 30 km in ~2h11 (4:22/km), roughly a minute per kilometre faster than this athlete. The between-group comparison, which is the actual test, was null.

Tsintzas 1995: 7 endurance-trained runners finishing 42.2 km on a treadmill in 3:10-3:14. Faster, fitter, indoors, and n = 7. Correctly identified as the only marathon-distance running trial with a finish-time outcome, but the 2.0% converted to 4.7 minutes carries an enormous unstated interval.
Bussau 2002: 8 endurance-trained males kept physically INACTIVE during loading. This athlete will be tapering, not resting, so the 24 h ceiling was achieved under conditions he will not reproduce.

Solem 2025: 271 of 319 participants male, and the pooled studies are cycling-dominated — which is exactly why the running estimate (156.5 mmol/kg dw) carries a 95% CI of 61.3-251.7, a four-fold span. The confident '~58% of the cycling response' framing hides that.

Hansen 2014 is the closest match and the submission is right to say so, but the intervention group averaged 41.9 ± 7.6 years against this athlete's 27, and 74.6 kg against his 85.5 kg, and their 3:38-3:49 finishing range is faster than his 3:55:54.
effectSizeErrors: Urdampilleta 2020's recovery figures are listed in an order that inverts the study's actual finding. The submission writes 'countermovement jump height change -11.3% / -9.7% / +1.2%', 'half-squat 1RM -15.3% / -13.8% / -2.4%', 'run-to-exhaustion time -14.1% / -14.9% / +1.3%' — immediately after a race-time sentence sequenced 120 / 90 / 60. Read in that stated order, 120 g/h had the WORST recovery on every measure. The full text says the opposite: Abalakov jump height HIGH (120 g/h) +1.19 ± 8.05%, LOW (60) -11.33 ± 8.00%, MED (90) -9.66 ± 8.19%; half-squat 1RM HIGH -2.35 ± 7.23%, LOW -15.30 ± 7.54%, MED -13.84 ± 9.74%; aerobic power-capacity test time HIGH +1.28 ± 8.55%, LOW -14.09 ± 14.98%, MED -14.87 ± 11.86%. The values are transcribed correctly but sequenced 60/90/120, silently flipping the order used one sentence earlier. A reader following the stated order concludes 120 g/h impaired 24 h recovery — the reverse of the paper's conclusion.

The caffeine minutes come from the wrong stratum. 0.71% of 235.9 min = 1.67 min is arithmetically correct, but 0.71% is the pooled estimate across trained and recreational runners; Wang 2022's own recreational-runner subgroup is g = -0.082, p = 0.141, indistinguishable from zero. Presenting '1-3 min' as this athlete's estimate uses an average that the paper's own subgroup analysis contradicts.

Standard error is repeatedly presented as if it were standard deviation. Tsintzas 1995 reports 190.0 (3.9) and 193.9 (5.0) as SEM with n = 7 — implied SDs are roughly 10 and 13 minutes, so the 3.9 min difference sits inside a very wide interval. Williams 1992's 131.0 (5.4) and 127.4 (4.9) are likewise SEM. Rendering both as '±' makes two of the three most consequential running results look far more precisely estimated than they are.

Hansen's precision is overstated in the other direction. The '5-9 min' estimate derives from a 4.7% point estimate whose group standard deviations are ~25 minutes at n = 14 per arm. The p = .010 comes from the matched-pairs analysis; the interval around a 10:55 min difference is wide enough that the true effect could plausibly run from near zero to over 20 minutes. The discount to 5-9 min is defensible reasoning, but it reads as a narrowing when the underlying uncertainty is not narrow.

Solem 2025 is filed under the '1-day carbohydrate loading' intervention as if it corroborates Bussau's 24 h protocol. Solem's inclusion criterion was muscle glycogen measured after 3-5 days of high-carbohydrate diet. It says nothing about whether one day suffices and cannot support the conclusion it is attached to.
Wang 2022 sample composition: '92.5% male' should be 86.6% (220 men of 254). 92% is reached only by discarding the 15 participants of unstated sex.
Ramos-Campo 2024 is cited as 64(33); Crossref records volume 64, issue 30, pages 11196-11205.

Currell 2008's published abstract reports GF at 4022 s and G at 3641 s while claiming GF was 8% quicker — internally contradictory. The 8% is repeated without noting that the paper's own printed numbers point the other way, which is the first thing a sceptic checking the source will hit.

Worth stating plainly because the athlete's question is about arithmetic honesty: every conversion re-derives correctly. 3:55:54 = 235.9 min; 3 mg/kg x 85.5 = 257 mg; 10 g/kg = 855 g; 8 g/kg = 684 g; 2 g/kg = 171 g; 4.7% = 11.1 min; 2.7% = 6.4 min; 2.0% = 4.7 min; 8% = 18.9 min; 5% = 11.8 min. The errors above are about which number was chosen and how it was ordered, not about the multiplication.
missedEvidence: Rowe JT, King RFGJ, King AJ, Morrison DJ, Preston T, Wilson OJ, O'Hara JP. Glucose and Fructose Hydrogel Enhances Running Performance, Exogenous Carbohydrate Oxidation, and Gastrointestinal Tolerance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022. doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000002764. The most important omission. A RUNNING trial, randomised double-blind, 11 trained male runners, 90 g/h of 2:1 glucose-fructose during 120 min at 68% VO2max followed by a 5 km time trial — with a real performance outcome. Standard carbohydrate solution was 5.6% faster than placebo (19:54 vs 21:05, p = 0.002); hydrogel 7.6% faster (19:29, p < 0.001); hydrogel 2.1% faster than standard (p = 0.033). This is the running counterpart to Currell 2008 that the submission implies does not exist, and it materially strengthens the case for 90 g/h in running rather than 60.

Li P, Song Q, Xu N. Plant-derived alginate polysaccharide hydrogels in sport and exercise nutrition. Front Nutr. 2026. doi:10.3389/fnut.2026.1774380. A 2026 systematic review of 9 RCTs on alginate/pectin carbohydrate hydrogels — Maurten and its imitators, the product this athlete is most likely to be sold in the next six weeks. Conclusion: metabolic indicators generally enhanced at high ingestion rates, GI tolerance similar to conventional solutions, but 'performance effects were inconsistent — minor improvements occurred mainly in running, with limited or null effects in cycling and skiing'. The submission's product advice ('choose gels listing both maltodextrin/glucose AND fructose') says nothing about hydrogels, and no hydrogel search appears anywhere in the search list.

Lukasiewicz CJ, Vandiver KJ, Albert ED, Kirby BS, Jacobs RA. Assessing exogenous carbohydrate intake needed to optimize human endurance performance across sex: insights from modeling. J Appl Physiol. 2024. doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00521.2023. Directly addresses the submission's own stated unknown — 'whether carbohydrate targets should scale with body mass. Nobody has tested whether a heavier runner should take more.' Somebody has modelled it: 120 male and 120 female runners parameterised by body mass and running economy, giving modelled needs of 93 ± 26 g/h (male) and 108 ± 22 g/h (female), and concluding ≤90 g/h is insufficient for 65% of modelled runners. It is modelling, not a trial, and the scenarios are elite sub-2-hour — but the unknown is presented as untouched when a 2024 paper in a mainstream journal takes it on, and it cuts against the 'do not chase >90' conclusion.

Noakes TD, Prins PJ. Are very high rates of exogenous carbohydrate ingestion (>90 g/hr) sufficient or indeed necessary to run a sub-2hr marathon? Front Nutr. 2024. doi:10.3389/fnut.2024.1507572. Published dissent on exactly the question the myths section adjudicates. Whatever one makes of the authors' priors, an argued counter-position in the peer-reviewed literature belongs in a section claiming to give the honest state of the debate.

Zhang P, Gu Z, Lv J, Xu K, Chen G, Dai J. Effects of Different Carbohydrate Supplementation on Marathon for Amateur Runners: A Controlled Trial. doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-4696071/v2. Thirty male AMATEUR marathon runners randomised to 80 g/h vs 50 g/h during a real marathon with continuous glucose monitoring. Finish times numerically faster on 80 g/h but not significantly; high-carbohydrate delayed speed decline at 11-20 km in sub-elite runners; blood-glucose variability negatively correlated with speed in the back half. This is a Research Square preprint, not peer-reviewed, and must be labelled as such — but the submission asserts that 'the single most decision-relevant experiment for this athlete has not been run', and something very close to it has been run and posted, in the right population with the right dose contrast, and it too found no significant finish-time difference.

Reynolds KM, Juett LA, Funnell MP, et al. Apple puree as a natural fructose source provides an effective alternative carbohydrate source for fuelling half-marathon running performance. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023. doi:10.1080/17461391.2023.2207074. A cheap real-food route to a glucose-fructose blend, tested in half-marathon running — relevant to product and cost decisions and to the tune-up half on 12 September.

Nothing was searched on how quickly gut-training adaptation decays during a taper, despite that being listed as an unknown with 'No data'. Absence of a search is not the same as absence of data, and the claim is used to justify a specific race-week fuelling behaviour.

Inside Wang 2022, the recreational-runner and long-distance subgroup nulls were sitting in the same paper that supplied the headline -0.71%. Not strictly missed evidence, but missed inside a source already read, and it is the single finding that most changes the caffeine recommendation for this athlete.

Overall verdict on the fabrication question the athlete actually asked: I resolved 31 DOIs through Crossref and pulled abstracts or full text for 28 of them via Europe PMC, plus PMC full text for Urdampilleta 2020 and Wang 2022. Every citation resolves to a real record with matching authors, journal, year, volume and pages. The nine works cited by name without a DOI (Pfeiffer 2012, Dezfuli 2025, Podlogar 2022, Burke 2017, Hoffman 2020, Martinez 2023, Karlsson 1971, Tsintzas 1996, Hew-Butler 2015) all exist and all say what is claimed. There are no fabricated citations, no invented author lists, no hallucinated findings, and the headline quotation from World Athletics' own distance-running consensus ('75-90 g/hr') is verbatim. The defects are of a different kind: one inverted result ordering, one effect size drawn from the wrong subgroup, SEM read as SD twice, and several quantitative claims attributed to a paywalled 2026 review whose abstract does not contain them.

interventions.intervention: Taper: reduce training VOLUME by 41-60% over ~2 weeks while holding training intensity and frequency unchanged, with an exponential (progressive, non-linear) decay rather than a single step down
interventions.effect: Optimal configuration overall effect (standardised mean difference, pre-to-post taper) = 0.59 ± 0.33 for 2-week duration, P<0.001; 0.72 ± 0.36 for the 41-60% volume-reduction band, P<0.001; 0.33 ± 0.14 for holding intensity constant, P<0.001; 0.35 ± 0.17 for holding frequency constant, P<0.001. Mean performance improvement across the pooled studies = 1.96%.
interventions.population: Competitive athletes — runners, swimmers, cyclists. 27 of 182 screened studies met inclusion (competitive athletes, documented load-reduction protocol, actual competition or field criterion performance). Not recreational runners; the pooled sample skews trained/elite and male.
interventions.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-65. doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0. PMID 17762369. (The 1.96% pooled mean is reported from this meta-analysis by Spilsbury KL, Nimmo MA, Fudge BW, Pringle JSM, Orme MW, Faulkner SH. The Effects of an Increase in Intensity during Tapering on 1,500 m Running Performance — author manuscript, Nottingham Trent IREP eprint 35522.)
interventions.duration: Taper interventions 4 to >28 days; 2 weeks optimal
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this is the single most applicable finding in the whole block. It requires no adaptation, only correct scheduling of the final 14 days. It is the one thing on the list that is fully realisable by 2026-10-24.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 1.96% of a 222-236 min marathon = 4.4-4.6 min. Working: his May marathon was 235.9 min; Riegel extrapolation from his 2026-07-19 half (106.58 min × 2^1.06 = 222.2 min) gives the optimistic anchor. Take 228 min as centre → 228 × 0.0196 = 4.5 min. Caveat: the pooled 1.96% is not marathon-specific and comes from trained athletes over shorter events.

interventions.intervention: Volume-reduction dose-response: which band of volume cut actually works
interventions.effect: Time-trial performance, pre-vs-post taper (SMD, negative = faster): ≤20% cut, −0.25 (95% CI −1.27 to 0.77), P=0.64 — null. 21-40% cut, −0.45 (95% CI −0.90 to −0.00), P=0.05 — borderline. 41-60% cut, −0.77 (95% CI −1.23 to −0.30), P=0.001 — largest and only clearly significant. ≥60% cut, −0.21 (95% CI −0.58 to 0.16), P=0.26 — null. Overall pooled taper effect on time-trial: SMD −0.45 (95% CI −0.68 to −0.23).
interventions.population: 14 studies, 174 athletes aged 17-32; middle-, long- and ultra-distance runners plus cyclists; predominantly male, limited female representation. Trained/competitive, not recreational.
interventions.citation: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y. Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0282838. PMID 37163550.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. This is a scheduling decision, not an adaptation. It directly determines the km figures for 2026-10-12 → 2026-10-24.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not directly convertible (SMDs on heterogeneous time trials). Its practical use is as a guard-rail: landing in the 21-40% band instead of 41-60% moves you from SMD −0.77 to −0.45, roughly 40% of the taper benefit forgone ≈ 1.8-2.0 min on a 228 min marathon. Cutting >60% forgoes ~70% of it ≈ 3.2 min.

interventions.intervention: Taper duration: how long the reduced-load period should run
interventions.effect: Time-trial SMD by taper length: ≤7 days, −0.36 (95% CI −0.63 to −0.08), P=0.01. 8-14 days, −1.47 (95% CI −2.75 to −0.19), P=0.02 — largest, but note the very wide CI. 15-21 days, −0.78 (95% CI −1.43 to −0.14), P=0.02. ≥22 days, +0.69 (95% CI −0.22 to 1.60), P=0.13 — no benefit, point estimate in the wrong direction. Bosquet independently identifies 2 weeks as optimal (0.59 ± 0.33).
interventions.population: Same 14 studies / 174 trained endurance athletes as above (Wang); 27 studies of competitive athletes (Bosquet).
interventions.citation: Wang Z et al. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550. And Bosquet L et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-65. PMID 17762369.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. Directly sets the taper start date. 14 days before 2026-10-24 is 2026-10-10; 8 days before is 2026-10-16.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible directly — the 8-14 day CI (−2.75 to −0.19) is too wide to price. Use it only as a duration rule, not as a magnitude estimate.

interventions.intervention: Taper length in recreational marathon runners specifically, measured on actual marathon finish time — the single most population-matched evidence available
interventions.effect: Strict 3-week taper (three consecutive down weeks immediately before race day, never an up week) vs a minimal taper: median finish-time saving 5 min 32.4 s, or 2.6%. By sex: strict 2-week 2.14% (men) / 3.12% (women); strict 3-week 2.38% (men) / 3.19% (women); strict 4-week 2.34% (men) / 2.63% (women). Strict beat relaxed at every duration (P<0.001). Strict 3-week beat strict 2-week on finish-time benefit at P=0.035 but NOT on raw finish time (post-hoc Dunn's with Bonferroni: n.s.). Strict 4-week vs strict 3-week: not significant. Only ~31% of runners ran a strict taper; 64% ran undisciplined 2- or 3-week tapers.
interventions.population: 158,117 recreational marathon runners (~126,000 men, >32,000 women) from Strava, marathons 2014-2017, ~23 weeks of training data each, ~3.5 activities/week. This is the athlete's exact population.
interventions.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Front Sports Act Living. 2021;3:735220. doi:10.3389/fspor.2021.735220. PMID 34651125.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. It is purely a scheduling choice and it is the finding most directly transferable to this athlete.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Male strict 3-week = 2.38% → 222 min × 0.0238 = 5.3 min; 236 min × 0.0238 = 5.6 min. Call it 5.3-5.6 min. Male strict 2-week = 2.14% → 4.8-5.1 min. The marginal value of the third down week is therefore 0.24% ≈ 0.5-0.6 min, and that increment is NOT significant on raw finish time. Headline: a disciplined taper is worth roughly 5 minutes to him; the choice between two and three down weeks is worth about thirty seconds.

interventions.intervention: Maintain training INTENSITY through the taper — cut volume, never pace
interventions.effect: Wang 2023 subgroup: intensity unchanged, SMD −0.55 (95% CI −0.79 to −0.31), P<0.05 — significant. Intensity decreased, SMD +0.25 (95% CI −0.67 to 1.17), P>0.05 — no benefit, point estimate adverse. Shepley 1992 (7-day tapers, crossover, each runner did all three): high-intensity low-volume taper (5 days of 500 m reps at 115-120% VO2max, 7.5 km total) +22% time to fatigue, P<0.05; low-intensity moderate-volume taper (30 km at 57-60% VO2max) +6%, n.s.; rest-only taper −3%, n.s. Citrate synthase +18% after the high-intensity taper vs −13% after rest-only. Total blood volume rose after the high-intensity taper and FELL after rest-only. Muscle glycogen +15% (high-intensity) and +8% (rest-only). VO2max unchanged by all three.
interventions.population: Wang: 14 studies / 174 trained endurance athletes. Shepley: 9 highly trained male university cross-country/middle-distance runners, aged 21-24, VO2max 66-71 ml/kg/min, training 80 km/wk with one-third at 95-100% VO2max.
interventions.citation: Wang Z et al. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550. Shepley B, MacDougall JD, Cipriano N, Sutton JR, Tarnopolsky MA, Coates G. Physiological effects of tapering in highly trained athletes. J Appl Physiol. 1992;72(2):706-11. doi:10.1152/jappl.1992.72.2.706.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it is the cheapest thing on this list. It costs one short interval session per taper week.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Dropping intensity converts the taper effect from SMD −0.55 to +0.25, i.e. it forfeits essentially the whole benefit ≈ 4.5-5.5 min. Shepley's +22% time to fatigue is NOT convertible to marathon minutes — it is a supramaximal treadmill run at ~115% VO2max, a test with a very large coefficient of variation and no mapping onto marathon pace. Do not let anyone quote 22% as a race-time effect.

interventions.intervention: Maintain training FREQUENCY (number of runs per week) — reduce it by no more than 20%
interventions.effect: Bosquet: maintaining frequency, overall effect 0.35 ± 0.17, P<0.001. Mujika & Padilla review: reduce frequency by no more than 20%; volume reduction up to 60-90%; optimal taper duration 4 to >28 days; progressive non-linear tapers beat step tapers; performance improves by about 3% (usual range 0.5-6.0%).
interventions.population: Bosquet: 27 studies of competitive athletes. Mujika & Padilla: narrative synthesis across competitive swimmers, runners, cyclists, triathletes.
interventions.citation: Bosquet L et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-65. PMID 17762369. Mujika I, Padilla S. Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(7):1182-7. doi:10.1249/01.MSS.0000074448.73931.11. PMID 12840640.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. Practically: if the peak week is 6 running days, the taper weeks should be 5-6 running days, not 3.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: 3% of 222-236 min = 6.7-7.1 min; the stated 0.5-6.0% range spans 1.1-14.2 min. Note this 3% is Mujika & Padilla's narrative summary figure across sports, not a pooled estimate with a confidence interval — treat 3% as an expectation, not a prediction.

interventions.intervention: What elite British MARATHON runners actually do in their taper — the closest thing to a governing-body prescription that exists
interventions.effect: Median taper duration 14 days (IQR 8) in marathoners, vs 6 days (IQR 3) in 800/1500 m and 6 days (IQR 1) in 3000 m-10,000 m runners. Continuous running volume cut to 53% (IQR 12) of regular levels in marathoners — i.e. a 47% reduction, squarely inside Bosquet's 41-60% band — vs 70% and 71% for middle- and long-distance. Interval volume cut to 64% (IQR 34) of regular. Peak interval intensity during the taper was ABOVE race speed in marathoners: 114% (IQR 3) of race pace, P<0.05. Higher pre-taper weekly volume and frequency predicted larger taper reductions (R = −0.70 and −0.63, P<0.05).
interventions.population: Elite British middle-distance, long-distance and marathon runners, surveyed by the English Institute of Sport and British Athletics. Elite, not recreational — the volume reduction percentage transfers better than the absolute kilometres.
interventions.citation: Spilsbury KL, Fudge BW, Ingham SA, Faulkner SH, Nimmo MA. Tapering strategies in elite British endurance runners. Eur J Sport Sci. 2015;15(5):367-73. doi:10.1080/17461391.2014.955128. PMID 25189116.
interventions.sampleSize: Survey of elite British endurance runners across three event groups (exact n per group not given in the abstract)
interventions.duration: 7-day regular-training phase compared with the full pre-competition taper
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. It independently converges on a 14-day taper with a ~47% volume cut and interval work faster than race pace — which is exactly what Bosquet's meta-analysis prescribes, from a completely different evidence stream (observed practice rather than trials).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — this is a description of practice with no performance outcome measured.
