Its value is corroborative: two independent lines (27 controlled studies, and what the best British marathoners actually do) land on the same 14 days / ~50% cut / above-race-pace intervals.

interventions.intervention: Pre-taper overload — go into the taper with a high training load, but do NOT arrive functionally overreached
interventions.effect: Wang 2023: taper combined with pre-taper overload training improved time-trial performance significantly more than conventional taper (P<0.05). Aubry 2014: of 23 triathletes doing a 3-week overload, 11 became functionally overreached (F-OR: performance decrement plus high perceived fatigue) and 12 were only acutely fatigued (AF). The AF group achieved 2.6% ± 1.1% greater peak performance supercompensation than the F-OR group, and 2.6% ± 1.6% greater than controls. VO2max rose from baseline at peak performance only in the control and AF groups, not in F-OR. Infection during the study: 70% of F-OR, 20% of AF, 10% of controls. Peak performance occurred within the first two weeks of taper in 83% of AF, 73% of F-OR, 60% of controls — peaking is NOT delayed by heavy loading immediately beforehand.
interventions.population: 33 trained male triathletes, 8-week study, cycling performance and VO2max. Trained but not elite; triathletes not runners. n=23 overload, n=10 control.
interventions.citation: Aubry A, Hausswirth C, Louis J, Coutts AJ, Le Meur Y. Functional overreaching: the key to peak performance during the taper? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2014;46(9):1769-77. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000301. PMID 25134000. And Wang Z et al. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550.
interventions.duration: 1 wk moderate + 3 wk overload + 4 wk taper
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and it is the finding that decides whether his ratified 100 km peak week is defensible. It is not. The 2.6% penalty for arriving overreached is the same magnitude as the entire 2.4-2.6% taper benefit — a peak week that tips him into F-OR cancels the taper exactly.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: The F-OR penalty of 2.6% ± 1.1% = 5.8-6.1 min lost on a 222-236 min marathon, with an uncertainty of ±2.4-2.6 min. Set against the strict-3-week taper's +5.3-5.6 min, arriving overreached converts a five-minute gain into approximately zero. Add the 70% infection rate, whose expected cost is not quantifiable but is bounded below by 'did not start'.

interventions.intervention: APPLIED — the taper this athlete should run (weeks and sessions), and where his ratified plan departs from the evidence
interventions.effect: His plan's SHAPE is right and his plan's NUMBER is wrong. Ratified: 60/80/100/80/60 km for weeks beginning 14 Sep, 21 Sep, 28 Sep, 5 Oct, 12 Oct, then an unspecified race week 19-24 Oct. Three consecutive down weeks (100→80→60→race week) is, in Smyth & Lawlor's taxonomy, a strict 3-week taper — the best-performing category out of eight in 158,117 recreational marathoners. Keep that. Three departures. (1) The 100 km peak week. His lifetime maximum week is 57.1 km and his last four complete weeks were 27/35/0/15 km; 100 km is 75% above his lifetime best and ~6.7x his last complete week. Every taper study in this list tapers an athlete off a load they had already absorbed for 3-8 weeks (Shepley 80 km/wk for 8 wk; Houmard 81 km/wk habitual; Spilsbury's marathoners off their own regular training). There is no evidence for tapering off a load never previously tolerated, and Aubry prices arriving F-OR at −2.6%. Recommended peak: 68 km in the week beginning 2026-09-28 (+19% on his lifetime max, reachable as 38 → 52 → 68). (2) The final 14 days are under-specified and, as written, too shallow. Bosquet/Spilsbury want the last two weeks averaging 41-60% below the peak week with an exponential decay. Off a 68 km peak: w/c 5 Oct = 54 km (−21%), w/c 12 Oct = 40 km (−41%), race week 19-24 Oct = 20 km of running plus the marathon (−71%). Final-14-day mean = 30 km = −56% from peak, mid-band. Off his ratified 100 km peak the equivalents are 80 / 58 / 29 km. (3) Intensity is not mentioned anywhere in the ratified plan. Every taper week must keep one hard session, and Spilsbury's elite marathoners ran their taper intervals at 114% of race pace. Concrete sessions — w/c 5 Oct: last long run 26-28 km on Sun 11 Oct (13 days out) with the final 8 km at goal marathon pace, plus 6 x 1000 m at 10 km-to-half pace. w/c 12 Oct: 5 x 1000 m at half-marathon pace (5:02/km) on Tue, 5 km at goal marathon pace inside an 8 km run on Thu, 13 km easy on Sun 18 Oct, nothing longer. Race week: 8 km with 6 x 400 m at 10 km pace (3:54/km, full recovery) on Tue 20 Oct, 5 km easy plus 6 x 100 m strides on Thu 22 Oct, 3 km shakeout or rest Fri, race Sat. Running frequency 6 / 5-6 / 4-5 days — never below 80% of peak frequency (Mujika & Padilla).
interventions.population: Prescription synthesised for a 27 y/o male recreational runner, 85.5 kg, 6-month mean 24.4 km/wk, lifetime-max week 57.1 km, marathon PB 3:55:54, half 1:46:35. The underlying evidence is drawn from trained/competitive athletes (Bosquet, Wang, Shepley, Spilsbury, Aubry) plus one very large recreational observational cohort (Smyth & Lawlor). No RCT exists in his exact population.
interventions.citation: Synthesis of: Bosquet L et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-65 (PMID 17762369); Wang Z et al. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838 (PMID 37163550); Smyth B, Lawlor A. Front Sports Act Living. 2021;3:735220 (PMID 34651125); Spilsbury KL et al. Eur J Sport Sci. 2015;15(5):367-73 (PMID 25189116); Aubry A et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2014;46(9):1769-77 (PMID 25134000); Mujika I, Padilla S. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(7):1182-7 (PMID 12840640).
interventions.duration: Peak week beginning 2026-09-28; taper 2026-10-05 to 2026-10-24 (three down weeks; the evidence-dense window is the final 14 days, 2026-10-11 to 2026-10-24)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this IS the six weeks. Nothing here depends on an adaptation that needs longer than the block allows.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Running this taper correctly instead of a minimal/relaxed one: +5.3-5.6 min (Smyth male strict-3-week, 2.38% of 222-236 min). Capping the peak at 68 km instead of 100 km: the taper literature gives no direct estimate, but avoiding F-OR protects the 5.8-6.1 min that Aubry's F-OR group forfeited, at the cost of an unquantified amount of forgone chronic-load adaptation. Net: the correctly-shaped, correctly-scaled taper is worth ~5 minutes; a 100 km peak week that tips him over is worth about −6 minutes, and the two are the same size.

interventions.intervention: APPLIED — recovery from a maximal half marathon on 2026-09-12, and whether starting a 60 km week on 2026-09-14 is defensible
interventions.effect: On the muscle-damage evidence the 48-hour turnaround into EASY running is defensible; the 60 km is not, and the 60 km has nothing to do with the half. Wang 2025 (simulated treadmill half, 36 recreational runners running 10-50 km/wk): immediately post-run, concentric knee extensor torque fell 2.19 → 2.00 Nm/kg and eccentric 2.44 → 1.96 Nm/kg (both P<0.001), knee joint position sense error rose 1.6° → 3.0° and hip 1.5° → 2.6° (both P<0.001), contact time rose and peak vertical GRF fell (P<0.001). Recovery: essentially every measure — knee torques, joint kinematics and kinetics, landing parameters — back to baseline within ONE day; hip joint position sense within TWO days; by day 2 thigh muscle torques showed supercompensation above baseline. Authors' own recommendation: avoid higher-intensity activity within two days. Child 2000 (14 male runners, two self-paced treadmill halves seven days apart): half-marathon time was statistically identical between the two runs in both groups (86.75 → 87.67 min normal training; 85.62 → 85.39 min tapered), i.e. a second maximal half seven days later cost nothing; the tapered group's post-race CK was 149% ± 22% of baseline vs 269% ± 55% in the normally-training group (P<0.05).
interventions.population: Wang 2025: 36 recreational runners (19 F / 17 M), mean age 28.5 ± 5.6, 10-50 km/wk, health/leisure runners — a close match to this athlete. Child 2000: 14 male trained runners, half-marathon ~86 min (faster than this athlete).
interventions.citation: Wang W, Xu S, Komnik I, Viellehner J, Zedler M, Potthast W. Biomechanical Changes and the Time Course of Recovery in Lower Extremities of Recreational Runners Following a Simulated Treadmill Half-Marathon. Sports Med Open. 2025;11(1):22. doi:10.1186/s40798-025-00824-x. PMID 40025365. And Child RB, Wilkinson DM, Fallowfield JL. Effects of a training taper on tissue damage indices, serum antioxidant capacity and half-marathon running performance. Int J Sports Med. 2000;21(5):325-31. doi:10.1055/s-2000-3778. PMID 10950440.
interventions.duration: Recovery tracked to 48 h (Wang); 7 days between halves (Child)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it settles the 2026-09-13/14 decision immediately. Prescription: Sun 13 Sep off or a walk; Mon 14 to Wed 16 Sep easy running only, 5-8 km per day; first hard session no earlier than Thu 17 Sep (day 5). Week total w/c 14 Sep: 36-40 km, not 60. The 60 km figure is unjustifiable not because of the half but because his last complete week was 15 km and his lifetime-best week is 57.1 km.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — these are recovery time-courses, not performance interventions. The number that matters is the downside: Nielsen 2014 found runners increasing weekly distance by >30% over two weeks had a hazard ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, P=0.07) for distance-related injuries. A 15 km → 60 km step is a 300% increase. An injury that removes him from the start line costs 100% of the marathon, which dominates every other number in this report.

interventions.intervention: CONTEXT — the 10-day training gap in late August: how much fitness was actually lost, and does it matter by 2026-10-24
interventions.effect: Short-term training cessation (≤30 days) reduces VO2max by a pooled effect size of −0.62 (95% CI −0.94 to −0.31, P<0.01; within-group I² = 35.3%), corresponding to a mean VO2max decline of 3.93%. Long-term cessation (>30 days) is far worse: ES −1.42 (95% CI −1.99 to −0.84), mean −9.43%; the difference between short and long is significant (Q = 6.5, P = 0.01). Coyle 1984 (n=7 highly trained, complete cessation): VO2max fell 7% over the first 21 days and stabilised at −16% by 56 days; the EARLY decline was attributable to reduced stroke volume (i.e. plasma/blood volume), the later decline to reduced a-vO2 difference; oxidative enzymes (citrate synthase, succinate dehydrogenase) declined with a half-time of 12 days; muscle capillarisation did not decline at all. Mujika & Padilla: in short-term detraining the VO2max fall is driven primarily by the loss of total blood and plasma volume, and 'these changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals'.
interventions.population: Zheng 2022: 21 studies from 3,315 screened, athletes across sports, no age/sex restriction; athletes with HIGHER trained-state VO2max lost significantly more (Q = 4.24, P = 0.03) — this athlete at VO2max ~53 is at the lower-loss end. Coyle 1984: 7 endurance-trained subjects, VO2max still 50.8 ml/kg/min after 84 days off vs 43.3 in never-trained controls. Mujika & Padilla: highly trained athletes, review.
interventions.citation: Zheng J, Pan T, Jiang Y, Shen Y. Effects of Short- and Long-Term Detraining on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Biomed Res Int. 2022;2022:2130993. doi:10.1155/2022/2130993. PMID 36017396. Coyle EF, Martin WH 3rd, Sinacore DR, Joyner MJ, Hagberg JM, Holloszy JO. Time course of loss of adaptations after stopping prolonged intense endurance training. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1984;57(6):1857-64. PMID 6511559. Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med. 2000;30(2):79-87. PMID 10966148.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, in the sense that the answer is: stop worrying about it. A 10-day gap in late August sits at the very shallow end of 'short-term cessation'. By race day it will be roughly eight weeks of retraining in the past, and the dominant mechanism (plasma volume) is restored within days of resuming training. What the gap actually cost is chronic training load, not physiology — and that is what the remaining block is for.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Upper bound if the loss had persisted: a 3.93% VO2max decline, if it translated one-for-one into pace at the same fractional utilisation, would be 8.7-9.3 min on a 222-236 min marathon. It has not persisted. Ten days is shorter than the 12-21 day windows in Coyle, his trained state is modest (which reduces the loss per Zheng's Q = 4.24 subgroup), and he has resumed training. Realistic residual cost on 2026-10-24: indistinguishable from zero. The correct concern is the 28% fall in his 42-day load average (72.3 → 52.2), which is an accounting fact about training done, not a measurement of anything physiological.

interventions.intervention: Reduced training does NOT cost fitness — the direct evidence against 'taper madness'
interventions.effect: Ten well-conditioned runners habituated to 81 ± 5 km/wk over 6 days/wk cut weekly volume by 70% to 24 ± 2 km/wk and frequency by 17% to 5 days/wk, holding the intensity distribution (17 km/wk at ~75% VO2max, 7 km/wk at ~95% VO2max), for THREE WEEKS. Result after 2 and 3 weeks: no significant change in 5 km race time, VO2max, body weight, body fat, muscular power (vertical leap, Margaria) or citrate synthase. Time to exhaustion in the VO2max test actually INCREASED by 9.5% (P<0.05). Maximal heart rate rose ~4 beats/min (P<0.05), associated with a 5.62 ± 0.43% fall in estimated plasma volume (P<0.01) — the only measurable cost. Houmard's 1991 review of this literature: maximal measures (VO2max, max HR, max speed/workload) are maintained for 10 to 28 days with weekly volume reductions of 70-80%; performance is improved or maintained with 60-90% volume reduction over 6-21 days provided frequency is cut by no more than 20%.
interventions.population: Houmard 1990: 10 well-conditioned distance runners, 81 km/wk, 6 days/wk — trained, running roughly 3.3x this athlete's six-month average. Houmard 1991: narrative review across endurance athletes.
interventions.citation: Houmard JA, Costill DL, Mitchell JB, Park SH, Hickner RC, Roemmich JN. Reduced training maintains performance in distance runners. Int J Sports Med. 1990;11(1):46-52. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1024761. PMID 2318562. And Houmard JA. Impact of reduced training on performance in endurance athletes. Sports Med. 1991;12(6):380-93. PMID 1784880.
interventions.duration: 3 weeks of reduced training after 4 weeks baseline
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it is the reassurance that lets him actually execute a deep taper instead of panicking in week 5 and running an extra 20 km. It also tells him the plausible upper bound on what a longer easy period costs, which is very little.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero, by construction — 5 km race time was unchanged. Its value is as a negative result: three weeks at 30% of normal volume cost nothing measurable, so the fear that motivates people to ruin their taper is not supported.

interventions.intervention: The taper's mechanism — what actually changes, so you know which levers exist
interventions.effect: Cardiorespiratory: VO2max may rise but this is NOT a prerequisite for taper-induced performance gain; submaximal VO2 can fall, more likely in less-skilled athletes; resting/max/submaximal HR unchanged unless the athlete was overreached beforehand. Haematological: increased blood and red cell volume, haemoglobin, haematocrit, reticulocytes; a positive haemolysis/erythropoiesis balance. Metabolic: muscle glycogen increases progressively; peak blood lactate rises; CK falls, indicating recovery from muscle damage. Neuromuscular: markedly increased muscular strength and power; oxidative enzyme activity can rise; positive changes in single muscle fibre size and contractile properties. Psychological: reduced total mood disturbance, reduced perception of effort, improved sleep quality. Confirmatory hard numbers from Shepley 1992: total blood volume rose significantly and red cell volume rose significantly after the high-intensity taper; muscle glycogen +15%; citrate synthase +18%; maximum voluntary knee-extensor strength rose significantly after all three tapers including rest-only. Confirmatory null: Wang 2023 found NO significant pre-to-post-taper change in VO2max or in economy of movement (both P>0.05).
interventions.population: Mujika 2004: review spanning competitive swimmers, runners, cyclists, triathletes and team-sport athletes since the 1980s. Shepley: 9 highly trained male runners. Wang: 174 trained endurance athletes.
interventions.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S, Pyne D, Busso T. Physiological changes associated with the pre-event taper in athletes. Sports Med. 2004;34(13):891-927. doi:10.2165/00007256-200434130-00003. PMID 15487904. Shepley B et al. J Appl Physiol. 1992;72(2):706-11. Wang Z et al. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — with one practical consequence: because the gains are haematological, glycogenic and neuromuscular rather than aerobic-capacity gains, the taper cannot be replaced by 'more training', and equally it will not show up as a better VO2max estimate on his Garmin. He should not judge the taper by the watch.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible individually. The mechanistic point that matters for a marathon is muscle glycogen: Shepley measured +15% after a high-intensity taper and +8% after complete rest, which compounds with race-week carbohydrate loading and is directly relevant to the last 10 km.

interventions.intervention: NEGATIVE RESULT — a deep 7-day taper that did not improve half-marathon performance
interventions.effect: Two matched groups of seven male runners each ran two self-paced treadmill half marathons seven days apart. One group maintained normal weekly volume; the other progressively cut weekly volume by 85%. No difference in running performance between the first and second half marathon within either group, or between groups: 86.75 ± 2.65 → 87.67 ± 2.87 min (normal training) vs 85.62 ± 2.81 → 85.39 ± 3.52 min (taper). The taper did reduce muscle damage — post-exercise CK was 149 ± 22% of baseline in the taper group vs 269 ± 55% in the normal group (P<0.05) — but the damage reduction did not convert into performance.
interventions.population: 14 male trained runners, treadmill half marathons ~86 min. Small, male, treadmill rather than road.
interventions.citation: Child RB, Wilkinson DM, Fallowfield JL. Effects of a training taper on tissue damage indices, serum antioxidant capacity and half-marathon running performance. Int J Sports Med. 2000;21(5):325-31. doi:10.1055/s-2000-3778. PMID 10950440.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, as a warning: an 85% volume cut sits in the ≥60% band that Wang 2023 found non-significant (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.58 to 0.16). Cutting harder is not cutting better. Aim for a 41-60% cut across the final fortnight, not 85%.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero — that is the point. This is the best single illustration that the taper is not a free lunch and that mis-dosing it produces literally nothing. It is also badly underpowered (n=7 per group), so it should be read as 'no detectable effect', not 'no effect'.

interventions.intervention: Volume progression into the peak week — how fast he can safely build to a peak worth tapering from
interventions.effect: Nielsen 2014 (874 healthy novice runners, GPS-monitored for one year, 202 running-related injuries): runners progressing weekly distance by more than 30% over a two-week period had a hazard ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, P = 0.07) for distance-related injuries (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, gluteus medius injury, greater trochanteric bursitis, TFL injury, patellar tendinopathy) compared with those progressing under 10%. There was NO significant difference in overall injury rate across the <10% / 10-30% / >30% groups. Damsted 2018 systematic review found only four eligible articles; three showed an association between load increase and injury, but one found no difference between a 10% and a 24% average weekly increase (HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.3). Conclusion: 'Very limited evidence exists.'
interventions.population: Nielsen: 874 novice runners, self-structured programmes, Denmark. Damsted: runners aged 18-65 across four studies. Novice-runner data transfers imperfectly to a runner with a 3:55 marathon, but it is the best controlled evidence available.
interventions.citation: Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2014;44(10):739-47. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164. PMID 25155475. And Damsted C, Glad S, Nielsen RO, Sørensen H, Malisoux L. Is there evidence for an association between changes in training load and running-related injuries? A systematic review. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2018;13(6):931-42. PMID 30534459.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — it constrains the ramp. From a 15 km week, weeks of 38 / 52 / 68 km are each roughly a 25-35% step, at or slightly above Nielsen's threshold; weeks of 60 / 80 / 100 are not achievable within any reading of this evidence. Note honestly that the evidence for the threshold itself is weak (HR 1.59 was not statistically significant, and the '10% rule' has essentially no support).
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to minutes — it is a risk, not a performance effect. The relevant expected-value calculation is that the whole taper is worth about 5 minutes, whereas a stress fracture in week 3 is worth the entire race.

myths: 'You lose fitness during the taper.' Ten runners habituated to 81 km/wk cut volume by 70% to 24 km/wk for three weeks, holding intensity, and 5 km race time, VO2max, muscular power and citrate synthase were all unchanged; time to exhaustion actually rose 9.5%. The only measurable cost was a 5.6% fall in estimated plasma volume (Houmard 1990, Int J Sports Med 11:46-52, PMID 2318562).

'The taper is a rest.' Reducing intensity during the taper produced SMD +0.25 (95% CI −0.67 to 1.17), i.e. no benefit and a point estimate in the wrong direction, versus −0.55 (95% CI −0.79 to −0.31) when intensity was held (Wang 2023, PMID 37163550). A rest-only 7-day taper made trained runners 3% WORSE on time to fatigue and dropped citrate synthase 13% and total blood volume, while an intensity-maintaining taper improved them 22% (Shepley 1992, J Appl Physiol 72:706-11).

'Cut as much volume as possible.' Volume cuts of ≥60% gave SMD −0.21 (95% CI −0.58 to 0.16, P=0.26) — statistically indistinguishable from nothing — versus −0.77 (95% CI −1.23 to −0.30, P=0.001) for the 41-60% band (Wang 2023). An 85% cut over 7 days produced no half-marathon improvement at all despite halving post-race CK (Child 2000, PMID 10950440).

'A good taper raises your VO2max.' Wang 2023 found no significant pre-to-post-taper change in VO2max or in economy of movement (both P>0.05) across 14 studies. Shepley 1992 found VO2max unaffected by all three taper types. Mujika 2004 states explicitly that a VO2max increase 'is not a necessary prerequisite for taper-induced gains in performance'. The taper's gains are haematological, glycogenic, neuromuscular and psychological. He should not expect his watch to show anything.

'Three weeks of taper is proven better than two.' The controlled literature says 8-14 days: Bosquet's optimum is 2 weeks (0.59 ± 0.33) and Wang's largest duration subgroup is 8-14 days. The 3-week claim rests on one observational Strava data set, where strict-3-week beat strict-2-week by 0.24% in men (2.38% vs 2.14%) — significant on the derived finish-time-benefit metric at P=0.035 but NOT on raw finish time after Bonferroni correction, and strict-4-week vs strict-3-week was not significant at all (Smyth & Lawlor 2021, PMID 34651125).

'Your peak week should be the biggest of your life.' Higher pre-taper load helps only if it does not tip you into functional overreaching. Overreached triathletes gained 2.6% ± 1.1% LESS supercompensation than merely fatigued ones, failed to raise VO2max at all, and had a 70% infection rate versus 20% and 10% (Aubry 2014, PMID 25134000). The F-OR penalty (2.6%) is the same size as the entire taper benefit (2.4-2.6%).

'Peaking is delayed if you train hard right up to the taper.' 83% of acutely-fatigued athletes and 73% of overreached athletes hit peak performance within the first two weeks of a four-week taper, versus 60% of controls (Aubry 2014). Loading heavily before the taper brought the peak forward, not back.

'The 10% rule.' Damsted 2018 (Int J Sports Phys Ther 13:931-42) reviewed the entire literature and found four eligible studies and 'very limited evidence'. Nielsen's own >30% threshold produced HR 1.59 with a 95% CI of 0.96 to 2.66 (P=0.07) — not statistically significant — and one study found no difference between a 10% and a 24% weekly increase (HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6-1.3). Progressive loading is still sensible; the specific numbers are folklore wearing a lab coat.

'A ten-day break destroyed my block.' Pooled short-term training cessation (≤30 days) costs a mean 3.93% of VO2max (ES −0.62, 95% CI −0.94 to −0.31), driven mainly by plasma volume loss which is restored within days of resuming training; athletes with higher trained-state VO2max lose significantly more (Q=4.24, P=0.03), so a VO2max-53 recreational runner sits at the shallow end (Zheng 2022, PMID 36017396). Muscle capillarisation did not decline at all even after 84 days off (Coyle 1984, PMID 6511559).

'You must not race within two weeks of a big training week.' The measurable neuromuscular and biomechanical cost of a half marathon in recreational runners is gone in 24 hours except hip proprioception, which recovers by 48 hours, and thigh muscle torque supercompensates above baseline by day 2 (Wang 2025, PMID 40025365). A second maximal half seven days after the first was run at an identical time (Child 2000). The problem with his 2026-09-14 week is the 60 km, not the 48-hour turnaround.

'Extra long runs late in the taper build confidence at no cost.' There is no controlled evidence either way — see unknowns. But it directly contradicts the one thing that IS established: the final 14 days must average 41-60% below the peak week (Bosquet 2007; Spilsbury 2015 measured elite British marathoners at 53% of regular continuous volume). A 30 km run inside the last fortnight makes hitting that band arithmetically impossible.
unknowns: There is no randomised controlled trial of tapering in recreational marathon runners at 25-70 km/week. The two meta-analyses rest on 27 studies of competitive athletes (Bosquet) and 14 studies / 174 trained athletes aged 17-32 (Wang), overwhelmingly male, mostly over time trials far shorter than a marathon. The only marathon-specific, recreational-population evidence is a single observational Strava analysis (Smyth & Lawlor 2021) which cannot establish causation — runners who taper strictly may simply be more disciplined, better coached, or fitter, and the authors do not adjust for training history beyond a 2-week baseline.

Whether Bosquet's '41-60% volume reduction' means the AVERAGE weekly volume across the taper or the END-POINT volume in the final week is not resolved in the primary sources. Spilsbury measured elite marathoners' taper volume as 53% of regular training averaged across the taper; Bosquet specifies an exponential decay, which by definition ends lower than its mean. The two readings differ by roughly 15-20 km/week for this athlete. The prescription above assumes the mean-across-the-final-fortnight reading and states it explicitly.

No study has tapered athletes off a peak training load they had never previously absorbed. Every trial in this evidence base tapers from an established habitual load — Shepley's runners had done 80 km/wk for 8 weeks, Houmard's 81 km/wk habitually, Spilsbury's elites off their own regular training. Whether a taper 'works' when the preceding block was itself an unabsorbed overload is untested, and the mechanism (dissipating accumulated fatigue while retaining adaptation) implies it would not, because there is no adaptation yet to retain.

The optimal taper for an athlete with a LOW chronic training load is unknown. Every taper study taper a well-loaded athlete; there is a plausible argument that someone carrying less accumulated fatigue needs a shorter and shallower taper, and an equally plausible argument that someone unaccustomed to the volume needs a longer one. Neither has been tested. Spilsbury's finding that higher pre-taper volume predicts larger taper reductions (R = −0.70) hints at the first, but it is a correlation among elites.

The effect of racing a maximal ROAD half marathon six weeks before a marathon, as a tune-up, has not been studied. The two relevant recovery studies used a simulated TREADMILL half at self-selected pace (Wang 2025) and self-paced treadmill halves (Child 2000). A flat-out road race in carbon-plated shoes involves more eccentric loading, greater pace variability and race-day arousal; the recovery time-course is plausibly longer than 48 hours and nobody has measured it.

How much of a marathon-specific gain the taper actually delivers is unresolved because the outcome measures diverge. The pooled 1.96% (Bosquet) and 3% (Mujika & Padilla) come from short time trials and pool across sports; the 2.38% (Smyth & Lawlor, men, strict 3-week) is an actual marathon finish time but observational. Nobody has run a controlled taper trial with marathon finish time as the endpoint.

Whether running economy improves during a taper is genuinely contested. Houmard 1994 found a 6% reduction in submaximal oxygen consumption at 80% VO2max after a 7-day run taper (PMID 8007812), but Wang's 2023 meta-analysis found no significant change in economy of movement across studies (P>0.05). For a marathon, economy matters more than VO2max, so this is not a small disagreement.

There is no validation of Garmin's 42-day exponentially-weighted training load ('fitness', 72.3 → 52.2) against marathon performance in any published literature I could find. It is a load-accounting number, not a physiological measurement, and its manufacturer has not published the algorithm or an outcome validation. Treating a 28% fall in it as a 28% fall in fitness is unjustified.

No governing body publishes a prescriptive taper protocol. I could find no taper document from World Athletics, UK Athletics, USATF or ACSM. The nearest thing to an official-body source is Spilsbury et al. 2015, co-authored by the English Institute of Sport and British Athletics, and that is a SURVEY of what elite British runners do, not guidance on what anyone should do. Any claim that 'the official recommendation is X' should be treated as fabricated until a document is produced.

The optimal placement and length of the final long run is entirely expert practice. The common '3 weeks out, 32 km' rule has no controlled trial behind it that I could locate. What IS established is the volume constraint on the final 14 days, which bounds the problem from the other direction.

Sex differences in taper response are large in the one large data set (female benefit 3.19% vs male 2.38% for a strict 3-week taper, P<0.001) and completely unexplained. This does not affect the present athlete but it demonstrates that taper effect sizes are population-dependent in ways the mechanistic literature does not predict, which should temper confidence in transferring any of these numbers.

This athlete has two nights of sleep data in six months and a body mass untouched since March. Sleep quality improvement is one of the reported taper effects (Mujika 2004) and nothing in his data can confirm or refute whether he is recovering. Any inference about his readiness during the taper will be made blind.

officialSources.body: British Athletics and the English Institute of Sport (via peer-reviewed publication, not a coaching document)
officialSources.document: Spilsbury KL, Fudge BW, Ingham SA, Faulkner SH, Nimmo MA. Tapering strategies in elite British endurance runners. European Journal of Sport Science. 2015;15(5):367-373.
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Does not prescribe — it documents. Elite British MARATHON runners tapered for a median of 14 days (IQR 8), cut continuous running volume to 53% of regular levels (IQR 12), cut interval volume to 64% (IQR 34), and ran their peak taper intervals at 114% of race speed (IQR 3), P<0.05. Middle-distance runners tapered only 6 days (IQR 3) with volume cut to 70%. Higher regular volume and frequency predicted larger taper cuts (R = −0.70 and −0.63). The paper publishes regression algorithms to prescribe an individual taper from an athlete's regular training load. This is the closest thing to a national-governing-body position that exists, and the marathon numbers land inside Bosquet's 41-60% band from a completely independent evidence stream.

officialSources.body: American College of Sports Medicine (as publisher of the field's two reference papers in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise — not as an institutional position stand)
officialSources.document: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of Tapering on Performance: A Meta-Analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-1365. And Mujika I, Padilla S. Scientific Bases for Precompetition Tapering Strategies. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(7):1182-1187.
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Bosquet: a 2-week taper in which training volume is decreased exponentially by 41-60%, with NO modification to training intensity or frequency (2-week duration effect 0.59 ± 0.33; 41-60% volume effect 0.72 ± 0.36; intensity unchanged 0.33 ± 0.14; frequency unchanged 0.35 ± 0.17; all P<0.001). Mujika & Padilla: maintain intensity, reduce volume (they say up to 60-90%), reduce frequency by no more than 20%, use a progressive non-linear rather than step reduction, expect about 3% improvement (range 0.5-6.0%). Note the two disagree on the volume ceiling: the later meta-analysis (2007) supersedes the earlier narrative review's 60-90% figure, and Wang 2023 confirms that cuts ≥60% are non-significant.

officialSources.body: No prescriptive taper document was found from World Athletics, UK Athletics, USATF or ACSM as an institutional position stand
officialSources.document: None located. UK Athletics' public coaching pages (uka.org.uk/coaching) list qualification pathways and course resources but expose no endurance tapering guidance. PubMed title searches for taper/tapering guidance in athletics returned only medical tapering (opioids, glucocorticoids, biologics) plus the sports-science primary literature already cited.
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Nothing. This is itself a finding worth stating plainly to the athlete: there is no official body that publishes 'the taper'. What exists is a peer-reviewed meta-analytic consensus (Bosquet 2007, replicated by Wang 2023), a documented record of elite practice (Spilsbury 2015), and one very large observational study in his exact population (Smyth & Lawlor 2021). Any coach or app claiming to follow an official taper protocol is citing something that does not exist.

check.domain: The taper — quantified taper prescription, detraining time-course, and post-half-marathon recovery for a 27 y/o male recreational marathoner racing Battersea Park Marathon 2026-10-24

citationChecks.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(8):1358-65. PMID 17762369.
citationChecks.note: Abstract retrieved verbatim via NCBI eutils. All four reported effect sizes match to the digit: 2-wk duration 0.59 +/- 0.33; volume exponentially decreased 41-60% 0.72 +/- 0.36; intensity unmodified 0.33 +/- 0.14; frequency unmodified 0.35 +/- 0.17; all P<0.001. '27 of 182 potential studies' confirmed, as is the competitive-athlete inclusion criterion and the requirement for actual competition or field-based criterion performance.

citationChecks.citation: The 1.96% pooled mean performance improvement attributed to Bosquet 2007, sourced via Spilsbury KL, Nimmo MA, Fudge BW, Pringle JSM, Orme MW, Faulkner SH. The Effects of an Increase in Intensity during Tapering on 1,500 m Running Performance. Nottingham Trent IREP eprint 35522.
citationChecks.note: Downloaded the IREP manuscript (irep.ntu.ac.uk/id/eprint/35522/1/13033_Faulkner.pdf) and extracted the text. Line 815-816 reads verbatim: 'In a meta-analysis of the available literature, Bosquet et al. (2007) reported a mean performance improvement of 1.96% in competitive runners, swimmers and cyclists.' The researcher correctly labelled this second-hand. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: 1.96% does NOT appear in Bosquet's abstract and Bosquet's full text is paywalled, so the number is verified only as a secondary quotation. The report's headline conversion (4.4-4.6 marathon minutes) therefore rests entirely on one sentence in another group's discussion section. The same paragraph also states 'In runners specifically, improvements in time trial or actual race performance have been reported in the range of 1.6-3.0%', which the report did not carry across.

citationChecks.citation: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y. Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838. PMID 37163550.
citationChecks.note: Extracted Table 2 in full from Europe PMC XML (PMC10171681). EVERY number the researcher quoted matches exactly: volume <=20% -0.25 (-1.27,0.77) P=0.64; 21-40% -0.45 (-0.90,-0.00) P=0.05; 41-60% -0.77 (-1.23,-0.30) P=0.001; >=60% -0.21 (-0.58,0.16) P=0.26; duration <=7d -0.36 (-0.63,-0.08) P=0.01; 8-14d -1.47 (-2.75,-0.19) P=0.02; 15-21d -0.78 (-1.43,-0.14) P=0.02; >=22d 0.69 (-0.22,1.60) P=0.13; intensity unchanged -0.55 (-0.79,-0.31) vs decreased 0.25 (-0.67,1.17); overall TT -0.45 (-0.68,-0.23). Transcription accuracy is exemplary. OVERSTATED because the report omits the between-subgroup P values that Table 2 also carries: P inter-group = 0.32 for volume, 0.10 for intensity, 0.42 for frequency. Only duration (0.02) shows a statistically significant difference BETWEEN bands. Wang therefore cannot support 'the 41-60% band beats the 21-40% band' or 'holding intensity beats dropping it' as comparisons — only as separate within-band estimates. Subgroup sizes are also very small and unreported by the researcher: 8-14 day duration n=18, >=22 days n=10, <=20% volume n=8.

citationChecks.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Front Sports Act Living. 2021;3:735220. PMID 34651125.
citationChecks.note: Full text pulled from Europe PMC (PMC8506252). Table 4 confirms verbatim: Strict 2w 2.14%M / 3.12%F; Strict 3w 2.38%M / 3.19%F; Strict 4w 2.34%M / 2.63%F (p=0.158, the only non-significant sex comparison); Relaxed 2w 1.29%M / 2.19%F; Relaxed 3w 1.76%M / 2.73%F. Table 3 confirms Strict 3w vs Strict 2w: p(FT) '-', p(FTE) '-', p(FTB) 0.035 — exactly as the researcher reported, and the researcher correctly noted it is significant only on the derived metric. '5 min 32.4 s or 2.6%', '31% adopt strict tapers', '64% adopt less disciplined 2- and 3-week tapers' all confirmed. One subtlety the report glosses: %FTB is defined (Eqs. 10-12) as the gap between actual finish time and a MODEL-PREDICTED untapered finish time derived from the runner's fastest 10 km training pace — not the difference against any actually-observed alternative taper.

citationChecks.citation: Spilsbury KL, Fudge BW, Ingham SA, Faulkner SH, Nimmo MA. Tapering strategies in elite British endurance runners. Eur J Sport Sci. 2015;15(5):367-73. PMID 25189116.
citationChecks.note: Abstract retrieved verbatim. Every figure matches: MAR taper 14 (8) days vs MD 6 (3) and LD 6 (1); continuous running volume reduced to 53 (12)% in MAR, 70 (16)% MD, 71 (24)% LD; interval volume MAR 64 (34)%; peak taper interval intensity above race speed in MAR 114 (3)% and LD 112 (27)%, not different in MD 100 (2)%; R = -0.70 and -0.63 for pre-taper volume/frequency predicting taper reduction; prediction algorithms generated. The researcher's caveat that n per event group is not in the abstract is correct and I could not obtain it from the paywalled full text. EIS/British Athletics affiliation is corroborated by the companion IREP manuscript's author affiliations (Spilsbury: English Institute of Sport; Fudge: British Athletics).

citationChecks.citation: Aubry A, Hausswirth C, Louis J, Coutts AJ, Le Meur Y. Functional overreaching: the key to peak performance during the taper? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2014;46(9):1769-77. PMID 25134000.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. n=33 (23 OT / 10 CTL), 11 F-OR / 12 AF, 2.6% +/- 1.1% vs F-OR and 2.6% +/- 1.6% vs CTL, VO2max rose only in CTL and AF, infections 70/20/10%, peak performance within first two weeks in 83% AF / 73% OR / 60% CTL — all confirmed exactly. OVERSTATED on two counts the report never surfaces. First, the abstract states the 2.6% figures come from 'qualitative statistical analysis' — magnitude-based inference, not a hypothesis test; there is no P value behind the number the report treats as a hard -6 minute penalty. Second, the outcome is CYCLING performance in trained male triathletes on an 8-week lab protocol, and the report converts it directly into marathon minutes and subtracts it from a Strava-derived marathon finish-time percentage.

citationChecks.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(7):1182-7. PMID 12840640.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. 'maintaining training intensity, reducing the training volume (up to 60-90%) and slightly reducing training frequency (no more than 20%)'; 'optimal duration ranges between 4 and more than 28 d'; 'Progressive nonlinear tapers are more beneficial to performance than step tapers'; 'Performance usually improves by about 3% (usual range 0.5-6.0%)'. All four claims match. The researcher also correctly flags this as a narrative synthesis figure with no confidence interval, and correctly notes the 60-90% volume figure conflicts with Bosquet's 41-60%.

citationChecks.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S, Pyne D, Busso T. Physiological changes associated with the pre-event taper in athletes. Sports Med. 2004;34(13):891-927. PMID 15487904.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. Confirms the exact quoted phrase 'this is not a necessary prerequisite for taper-induced gains in performance' regarding VO2max; submaximal VO2 decrease 'more likely to occur in less-skilled athletes'; unchanged resting/max/submaximal HR 'unless athletes show clear signs of overreaching before the taper'; increased blood and red cell volume, haemoglobin, haematocrit, reticulocytes; positive haemolysis/erythropoiesis balance; progressive muscle glycogen increase; increased peak blood lactate; reduced CK; markedly increased strength and power; improved sleep quality and reduced perception of effort. Every element of the researcher's mechanism list is present.

citationChecks.citation: Shepley B, MacDougall JD, Cipriano N, Sutton JR, Tarnopolsky MA, Coates G. Physiological effects of tapering in highly trained athletes. J Appl Physiol. 1992;72(2):706-11.
citationChecks.note: Located at PMID 1559951 (the researcher supplied no PMID for this one — the only citation in the report without one). Abstract confirms: n=9 male runners, crossover, three 7-day tapers, running time to fatigue +22% HIT, +6% LIT, -3% ROT; citrate synthase up with HIT and down with ROT; muscle glycogen up after ROT and HIT; total blood volume up after HIT and down after ROT; VO2max unaffected by all three; strength up after all three. The GRANULAR numbers could not be checked: +18% citrate synthase, +15%/+8% glycogen, 5 days of 500 m reps at 115-120% VO2max totalling 7.5 km, 30 km at 57-60% VO2max, ages 21-24, VO2max 66-71, 80 km/wk for 8 weeks. journals.physiology.org returned HTTP 403 and the quantifiedrowing.com PDF link returned HTML, not a PDF. Note the abstract says 'middle-distance runners' tested at 1,500 m velocity, not 'cross-country' runners.

citationChecks.citation: Wang W, Xu S, Komnik I, Viellehner J, Zedler M, Potthast W. Biomechanical Changes and the Time Course of Recovery... Following a Simulated Treadmill Half-Marathon. Sports Med Open. 2025;11(1):22. PMID 40025365.
citationChecks.note: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC11872820). Confirms n=36 (19 F / 17 M), mean age 28.5 +/- 5.6, 10-50 km/wk recreational definition, concentric extensors 2.19->2.00 Nm/kg and eccentric 2.44->1.96 (both P<0.001), knee JPS 1.6->3.0 deg and hip 1.5->2.6 deg (both P<0.001), increased contact time and reduced peak vGRF, recovery within one day except hip JPS within two, thigh torque supercompensation by day 2. The authors' recommendation is confirmed verbatim: 'we recommend that runners avoid engaging in higher-intensity physical activities within two days after completing the half marathon'. Two things the report omits: the run was maximal effort ('at their preferred speed, aiming to complete it as quickly as possible', male mean 1:53:20) which strengthens the researcher's case, and the authors explicitly state 'It is not possible to establish a full recovery until all parameters return to the baseline' — nothing was measured past 48 h.

citationChecks.citation: Child RB, Wilkinson DM, Fallowfield JL. Effects of a training taper on tissue damage indices, serum antioxidant capacity and half-marathon running performance. Int J Sports Med. 2000;21(5):325-31. PMID 10950440.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. Two matched groups of seven male runners, 85% progressive volume reduction, 86.75 +/- 2.65 -> 87.67 +/- 2.87 min (normal) vs 85.62 +/- 2.81 -> 85.39 +/- 3.52 min (taper), post-exercise CK 149 +/- 22% vs 269 +/- 55% baseline (P<0.05), 'half-marathon performance was not enhanced'. Every figure matches.

citationChecks.citation: Zheng J, Pan T, Jiang Y, Shen Y. Effects of Short- and Long-Term Detraining on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Athletes. Biomed Res Int. 2022;2022:2130993. PMID 36017396.
citationChecks.note: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC9398774). ES -0.62 (-0.94,-0.31) short-term and -1.42 (-1.99,-0.84) long-term, Q=6.5 P=0.01, I2 35.3%, 21 of 3315 studies — all confirmed. The 3.93% and 9.43% mean declines are confirmed in Section 4.1 verbatim. MISAPPLIED SUBGROUP: the researcher writes 'athletes with HIGHER trained-state VO2max lost significantly more (Q = 4.24, P = 0.03) — this athlete at VO2max ~53 is at the lower-loss end' and repeats it in the myths section, using it to reassure him about a 10-day (short-term) gap. The paper states Q=4.24 for LONG-term detraining only, and says explicitly: 'the effects of age, training status, and detraining format led to the differing impacts of detraining on VO2max in the long-term period but did not change in the short-term period.' The reassurance is drawn from a subgroup the paper says does not operate over his timescale.

citationChecks.citation: Coyle EF, Martin WH 3rd, Sinacore DR, Joyner MJ, Hagberg JM, Holloszy JO. Time course of loss of adaptations after stopping prolonged intense endurance training. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1984;57(6):1857-64. PMID 6511559.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. n=7, VO2max -7% over first 21 days stabilising at -16% by 56 days, 50.8 vs 43.3 ml/kg/min after 84 days vs never-trained controls, early decline attributable to reduced stroke volume and later to reduced a-vO2 difference, citrate synthase and succinate dehydrogenase half-time 12 days, 'Skeletal muscle capillarization did not decline with inactivity'. All match.

citationChecks.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: ... Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med. 2000;30(2):79-87. PMID 10966148.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim, including the exact quoted phrase 'These changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals' and the characterisation of short-term cardiorespiratory detraining as 'a rapid decline in maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) and blood volume'. The '<4 weeks' definition of short-term is confirmed.

citationChecks.citation: Houmard JA, Costill DL, Mitchell JB, Park SH, Hickner RC, Roemmich JN. Reduced training maintains performance in distance runners. Int J Sports Med. 1990;11(1):46-52. PMID 2318562.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. n=10, 81 +/- 5 km/wk 6 days/wk baseline, reduced 70% to 24 +/- 2 km/wk and frequency 17% to 5 days/wk for 3 weeks, intensity distribution preserved (17 km at ~75% and 7 km at ~95% VO2max), max HR +4 beats/min, estimated plasma volume -5.62 +/- 0.43% (P<0.01), time to exhaustion +9.5% (P<0.05), no significant change in 5 km race time, VO2max, body weight, body fat, vertical leap, Margaria power or citrate synthase. Every figure matches.

citationChecks.citation: Houmard JA. Impact of reduced training on performance in endurance athletes. Sports Med. 1991;12(6):380-93. PMID 1784880.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. 'Maximal exercise measures (VO2max, maximal heart rate, maximal speed or workload) are maintained for 10 to 28 days with reductions in weekly training volume of up to 70 to 80%'; 'Athletic performance is improved or maintained with a 60 to 90% reduction in weekly training volume during a 6 to 21 day reduced training period, provided that exercise frequency is reduced by no more than 20%'. Both claims match.

citationChecks.citation: Houmard JA, Scott BK, Justice CL, Chenier TC. The effects of taper on performance in distance runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1994;26(5):624-31. PMID 8007812.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. Run taper group: 85% volume reduction plus high-intensity intervals, 5 km time 1036.2 -> 1006.8 s (-3%, P<0.005), submaximal VO2 at 80% VO2max down 6% and caloric expenditure down 7% (P<0.01); cycle taper and control unchanged. The economy claim the researcher makes is accurate. See 'missedEvidence' — this paper's own headline result contradicts the report's myth #3.

citationChecks.citation: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2014;44(10):739-47. PMID 25155475.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. 874 healthy NOVICE runners, GPS-monitored 1 year, 202 injuries, HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96-2.66, P=.07) for distance-related injuries at >30% vs <10% progression over a 2-week period, and 'no statistically significant differences in injury rates were found across the 3 exposure groups' overall. The full injury list quoted by the researcher matches exactly. The researcher's honesty about the non-significance is commendable and matches the source.

citationChecks.citation: Damsted C, Glad S, Nielsen RO, Sorensen H, Malisoux L. Is there evidence for an association between changes in training load and running-related injuries? A systematic review. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2018;13(6):931-42. PMID 30534459.
citationChecks.note: Abstract verbatim. Four eligible articles, three showing an association, 'no difference was found between a 10% and a 24% average increase in weekly volume (HR = 0.8, 95% CI: 0.6; 1.3)', conclusion 'Very limited evidence exists'. All match.

citationChecks.citation: 'No prescriptive taper document was found from World Athletics, UK Athletics, USATF or ACSM as an institutional position stand' — uka.org.uk/coaching cited as checked.
citationChecks.note: This is an unfalsifiable negative and my session's web-search budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could independently re-run the governing-body sweep. My PubMed title searches for taper/tapering reviews returned only sports-science primary literature plus unrelated medical tapering (benzodiazepines, PMID 41558012), which is consistent with the claim. The claim is plausible and honestly framed, but it is asserted rather than evidenced, and the athlete should read it as 'the researcher looked and did not find' rather than 'it has been established that none exists'.

populationMismatches: Aubry 2014 — the -2.6% functional-overreaching penalty that the report uses to VETO his 100 km peak week and to conclude 'arriving overreached converts a five-minute gain into approximately zero' was measured as CYCLING peak-power supercompensation in 33 trained male TRIATHLETES on an 8-week laboratory protocol (1 wk moderate + 3 wk overload + 4 wk taper). Sport, exercise modality, outcome measure and training structure all differ from a 27 y/o recreational marathoner. Worse, the 2.6% comes from 'qualitative statistical analysis' (magnitude-based inference) with no P value, yet the report converts it to a hard '5.8-6.1 min lost' and sets it head-to-head against a Strava-derived marathon finish-time percentage. Two numbers from incommensurable measurement scales.

Shepley 1992 — nine male 1,500 m MIDDLE-DISTANCE specialists (per the abstract), training 80 km/wk with a third of it at 95-100% VO2max, tested by a treadmill run to fatigue at their best 1,500 m velocity. This athlete races 42.195 km at roughly 5:35/km off a 24.4 km/wk six-month average. The report correctly refuses to convert the +22% into marathon minutes, but still uses this n=9 crossover as a co-anchor for 'maintain intensity' and as the source of its glycogen (+15%/+8%) and blood-volume mechanism claims for a marathon.

Wang 2023 — 174 athletes aged 17-32, 'mainly middle-distance, long-distance and ultra distance running, as well as cycling', with time trials ranging from 800 m to 40 km performed on tracks, treadmills AND cycle ergometers. Predominantly male and trained. There is no marathon endpoint anywhere in the pooled sample. Every SMD the report converts into marathon minutes is pooled across this heterogeneity.

Bosquet 2007 — competitive athletes across running, swimming and cycling, with individual study n typically 7-20. The 1.96% the report converts to 4.4-4.6 marathon minutes is explicitly described in the source that quotes it as 'a mean performance improvement of 1.96% in competitive runners, SWIMMERS AND CYCLISTS'. A pooled swimming/cycling/running figure is being applied to a marathon finish time.

Spilsbury 2015 — elite British marathoners, n per event group unstated. Their taper cut running volume to 53% of REGULAR training, but their regular training is plausibly 160-200 km/wk. The report transfers the percentage to a proposed 68 km peak week, which assumes the fractional taper prescription is scale-invariant down to a third of the elite load. Nobody has tested that. Spilsbury's own finding that higher pre-taper volume predicts LARGER taper reductions (R = -0.70) is direct evidence against scale-invariance and the report cites it without drawing the inference.

Houmard 1990 / 1991 / 1994 — well-conditioned runners habituated to 81 +/- 5 km/wk on 6 days/wk, i.e. 3.3x this athlete's six-month average and 42% above his lifetime-best single week. The report uses Houmard 1990 as the reassurance that lets him execute a deep taper without panicking. The reassurance is that runners at 81 km/wk can drop to 24 km/wk with no cost; it says nothing about a runner whose normal week IS 24 km.

Zheng 2022 — the specific subgroup finding used to reassure him ('athletes with higher trained-state VO2max lost significantly more, Q = 4.24, P = 0.03, so a VO2max-53 recreational runner sits at the shallow end') is a LONG-TERM detraining result. The paper states explicitly that training status did not modify the short-term effect. His August gap was 10 days. The reassuring subgroup does not apply to his case.

Coyle 1984 — n=7 highly trained subjects undergoing COMPLETE cessation, still at VO2max 50.8 ml/kg/min after 84 days off (so trained-state ~60+). Used to characterise the physiology of a 10-day partial gap in a VO2max-53 recreational runner who resumed training.

Wang 2025 — the closest population match in the report, but the sample's mean body mass is 64.0 kg overall and 70.4 kg for the 17 males, against this athlete's 85.5 kg. Eccentric loading and impact-related muscle damage scale with body mass, so a 24-48 h recovery window measured in runners ~15 kg lighter is an optimistic transfer. The protocol was also a level treadmill at preferred speed (male mean 1:53:20) rather than a flat-out road half in carbon-plated shoes at 1:46:35 — the report flags the surface issue in its unknowns but not the mass issue. And nothing was measured past 48 h, so 'recovered' is bounded by the measurement window, as the authors themselves note.
Child 2000 — 14 male trained runners, n=7 per group, running ~86 min treadmill half marathons. They are roughly 20 minutes faster over the half than this athlete. Underpowered and faster.

Nielsen 2014 and Damsted 2018 — 874 healthy NOVICE runners on self-structured programmes (Nielsen) and runners aged 18-65 across four studies (Damsted). This athlete has run a 3:55 marathon and has five months of logged training; he is not a novice. Novice-runner injury hazard ratios are the evidence used to constrain his entire volume ramp, and the report acknowledges the mismatch but proceeds on it anyway.

Smyth & Lawlor 2021 is the one genuine population match (158,117 recreational Strava marathoners, ~3.5 activities/week) and the report correctly identifies it as such. Note however that it is the ONLY population-matched source in the entire report, it is observational, and it is the source of the single number the report leans on hardest (2.38%).
effectSizeErrors: THE BIG ONE — the F-OR penalty conversion. 'The F-OR penalty of 2.6% +/- 1.1% = 5.8-6.1 min lost on a 222-236 min marathon... Set against the strict-3-week taper's +5.3-5.6 min, arriving overreached converts a five-minute gain into approximately zero.' The arithmetic (2.6% of 222-236 = 5.77-6.14) is correct, but the operation is not. Aubry's 2.6% is a difference in CYCLING peak-performance supercompensation between two subgroups of triathletes, derived by magnitude-based inference with no P value. The 2.38% is a marathon finish-time-benefit percentile from Strava observational data with a model-predicted counterfactual. Subtracting one from the other to conclude 'the two are the same size' is a rhetorical construction dressed as a calculation. This single move drives the report's headline recommendation to cap the peak week at 68 km.

SMD-ratio-to-minutes conversions. 'Landing in the 21-40% band instead of 41-60% moves you from SMD -0.77 to -0.45, roughly 40% of the taper benefit forgone ~ 1.8-2.0 min'; 'Cutting >60% forgoes ~70% of it ~ 3.2 min'; 'Dropping intensity converts SMD -0.55 to +0.25... forfeits essentially the whole benefit ~ 4.5-5.5 min.' Internally the ratios reproduce (0.45/0.77 = 0.58; 0.21/0.77 = 0.27), but standardised mean differences pooled across 800 m to 40 km time trials on tracks, treadmills and cycle ergometers are not proportional to marathon finish time, and a ratio of two SMDs is not a ratio of two performance effects. The report says 'not directly convertible' in the same field where it converts.

Omitted between-subgroup P values from Wang 2023 Table 2. P inter-group = 0.32 (volume), 0.10 (intensity), 0.42 (frequency). The report presents the volume dose-response as decisive ('the largest and only clearly significant band') and builds the entire km prescription on it, but Wang's own test for a difference BETWEEN volume bands is non-significant at p=0.32. Only duration (p=0.02) supports a genuine between-band difference. Also omitted: the 8-14 day duration subgroup that the report uses to set the taper start date contains n=18 athletes, and the >=22 day subgroup contains n=10.

Ramp arithmetic error, and it contradicts the report's own gate. 'From a 15 km week, weeks of 38 / 52 / 68 km are each roughly a 25-35% step, at or slightly above Nielsen's threshold.' 38/52/68 steps are +37% and +31%, but the first step, 15 -> 38 km, is +153%. The report's own recommended ramp breaches its own cited Nielsen >30%-over-two-weeks threshold by a factor of five at its first step, while the sentence asserts compliance. Contrast this with the report's own condemnation of the ratified plan: '15 km -> 60 km step is a 300% increase' — the recommended alternative is a 153% increase, treated as if it were 25-35%.

Smyth %FTB baseline conflation. The sex-specific 2.38% is a finish-time BENEFIT computed against a model-predicted untapered finish time derived from the runner's fastest 10 km training pace (paper Eqs. 10-12). The abstract's 5:32.4 s / 2.6% is quoted against a 'minimal taper' (relaxed 1-week) baseline. The report treats them as interchangeable. Multiplying 2.38% by his marathon time is arithmetically what Eq. 12 defines, so the number is defensible — but 'a disciplined taper is worth roughly 5 minutes to him' implicitly assumes his counterfactual is essentially no taper. Against a merely sloppy relaxed 2-week taper (male 1.29%), the differential is 1.09%, or about 2.4-2.6 min. The headline is roughly double the realistic decision-relevant figure.

Arithmetic that checks out, for the record. I re-derived every other conversion: Riegel 106.58 x 2^1.06 = 222.2 min (correct); 3:55:54 = 235.9 min (correct); 1.96% of 222-236 = 4.35-4.63 (reported 4.4-4.6); 2.38% = 5.28-5.62 (reported 5.3-5.6); 2.14% = 4.75-5.05 (reported 4.8-5.1); the 0.24% increment = 0.53-0.57 min (reported 0.5-0.6); 3% = 6.66-7.08 and the 0.5-6.0% range = 1.11-14.16 (reported 6.7-7.1 and 1.1-14.2); 3.93% = 8.72-9.27 (reported 8.7-9.3); 100/57.1 = +75% and 100/15 = 6.67x (both correct); the taper block 68 -> 54 -> 40 -> 20 km giving a final-14-day mean of 30 km = -55.9% from peak (reported -56%). The percentage arithmetic in this report is careful. The errors are all in what is being multiplied, not in the multiplication.

Inherited inconsistency, not the researcher's: the athlete profile states the May marathon as 3:55:54 at 5:31/km, but 5:31/km over 42.195 km is 232.9 min, not 235.9 min. The researcher used 235.9 correctly.
missedEvidence: MOST IMPORTANT — Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A. Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;4:1096124. PMID 36704260. Same research group, same Strava corpus, same population as the report's flagship Smyth & Lawlor citation: 15 million activities from 300,000 recreational marathoners, 2014-2017, comparing the SAME runners' disrupted and undisrupted marathons. A complete training cessation of >=7 days costs a 5-8% finish-time penalty; 5% for males specifically; 5.2% when the disruption falls late in training versus 4.4% early. On a 222-236 min marathon that is 11-19 minutes — two to four times the entire taper benefit the report prices. This DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS the report's conclusion that his 10-day August gap has a 'realistic residual cost on 2026-10-24: indistinguishable from zero', and contradicts its listing of 'a ten-day break destroyed my block' as a myth. It also falsifies the report's own stated unknown that 'nobody has run a controlled taper trial with marathon finish time as the endpoint' — this is the marathon-finish-time endpoint, in his exact population. It is observational and confounded (disruptions are usually caused by illness or injury, so part of the 5-8% is the cause not the gap), which is exactly the nuance that should have been surfaced rather than the finding being absent.

Luden N, Hayes E, Galpin A, et al. Myocellular basis for tapering in competitive distance runners. J Appl Physiol. 2010;108(6):1501-9. PMID 20299622. Seven collegiate distance runners, a THREE-WEEK taper, with 8 km cross-country RACE performance as the endpoint: race time improved 3% (P<0.05), MHC IIa fibre diameter +7%, peak force +11% (P=0.06), absolute power +9%, with no change in citrate synthase or cardiovascular function. This is a controlled 3-week taper with a real race outcome in distance runners, and it partly undercuts the report's myth #5 ('Three weeks of taper is proven better than two... the controlled literature says 8-14 days; the 3-week claim rests on one observational Strava data set'). It also supplies the missing myocellular mechanism the report attributes only to Shepley and Mujika. Spilsbury's own manuscript, which the researcher downloaded and quoted from, cites Luden three separate times — so it was one link away.

Mujika I. Intense training: the key to optimal performance before and during the taper. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2010;20 Suppl 2:24-31. PMID 20840559. The single best-titled source for the report's own second-most-important prescription ('cut volume, never pace'), written by the author the report cites four times elsewhere, and it makes the argument explicitly: 'the training load should not be reduced at the expense of intensity during the taper', and high-intensity training before the taper induces maximal adaptations 'in both moderately trained subjects and highly trained athletes' — the latter clause being precisely the population-transfer question the report leaves open.

Vachon A, Berryman N, Mujika I, Paquet JB, Bosquet L. Tapering and Repeated High-Intensity Effort Ability in Young Elite Rugby Union Players: Influence of Pretaper Fatigue Level. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021;16(7):993-1000. PMID 33668014; and Vachon A, et al. Biol Sport. 2022;39(3):735-743. PMID 35959317. These are prospective replications of Aubry's pre-taper-fatigue mechanism by Bosquet's and Mujika's own group. The 2021 study: a 7-day exponential taper with a 55% load reduction, benefit concentrated in the acutely-fatigued group (-5.07% vs -1.45% in normal training, P=.08). The 2022 study: no improvement in either normal-training or functionally-overreached groups, benefit only in acute fatigue, and poor pre-block sleep quality predisposed players to developing F-OR. The sleep finding is directly relevant to an athlete with two nights of sleep data in six months — the report raises exactly that gap in its unknowns and then has no evidence to attach to it. The 2022 paper supplies some.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION the report found and did not resolve. Houmard 1994 (PMID 8007812) is cited in the report — but only for the 6% economy improvement, buried in the unknowns. Its headline result is that a 7-day taper with an EIGHTY-FIVE PERCENT volume reduction improved 5 km time by 3% (P<0.005) in distance runners. The report's myth #3 ('Cut as much volume as possible') uses Child 2000's 85% cut producing nothing, plus Wang's non-significant >=60% band, to argue that cutting harder does not work. Its own cited paper shows an 85% cut working, in runners, with a race-like endpoint, at higher statistical significance than Child's null. The searchesRun list even shows the researcher searched for 'Houmard 1994 reduced training distance runners 5000 m time 10 days taper performance improvement 3%'. The finding was retrieved and then not reconciled.

No search of the post-road-race recovery literature. The report rests a scheduling recommendation on two TREADMILL studies (Wang 2025, Child 2000) and then correctly lists 'the effect of racing a maximal ROAD half marathon... has not been studied' as an unknown — but the searchesRun list contains no attempt to find road-race muscle-damage or recovery work (e.g. the substantial literature on CK, myoglobin, cardiac troponin and neuromuscular recovery after road half and full marathons). The unknown may well survive that search, but it was not run, so the claim that nothing exists is unearned.

No search of the tune-up-race literature. The report's applied section makes a concrete recommendation about a 2026-09-12 half marathon six weeks out and then classes the evidence for tune-up races as absent, without any search term in searchesRun targeting pre-competition or tune-up racing.

domains.title: Sleep, recovery and the modifiable non-training factors

research.domain: Sleep, recovery, and the modifiable non-training factors — quantified for a 27-year-old male recreational marathoner (85.5 kg, VO2max est. 53, HM PB 1:46:35, ~24 km/wk six-month average) attempting a 60/80/100/80/60 km ramp in a six-week block ending at Battersea Park Marathon, 2026-10-24. Working conversion baseline: current fitness projects ~3:45 (225 min) marathon (Riegel from 1:46:35 half: 106.58 min x 2^1.06 = 222 min), so 1% of finishing time = ~2.25 min.

interventions.intervention: Sleep extension for 3 consecutive nights before a hard effort (habitual ~6.8 h -> ~8.4 h actual sleep), as a pre-race protocol for the 12 Sep half and the 24 Oct marathon
interventions.effect: Endurance cycling time-trial performance was better maintained/improved under extended sleep than under habitual or restricted sleep. Sleep achieved: extension 8.6/8.3/8.2 h across three nights, normal 7.1/6.5/6.9 h, restriction 4.7/4.8/4.9 h. Restriction significantly impaired the day-3 time trial (P<0.02). The day-4 extension comparison reported is 58.7 +/- 3.4 vs 56.8 +/- 3.1 min (P<0.02), i.e. a ~3.2% difference. CAUTION: I could not open the paywalled full text, and my extraction of which number belongs to which condition was ambiguous — treat the direction as verified (extension better) but the exact 3.2% as provisional. Proposed mechanism: cumulative sleep time changes the perceived exertion of a given intensity, so higher intensities are tolerated.
interventions.population: 9 trained endurance cyclists/triathletes, counterbalanced crossover. NOT runners, NOT marathon-duration, tiny n, no independent control group.
interventions.citation: Roberts SSH, Teo W-P, Aisbett B, Warmington SA. Extended Sleep Maintains Endurance Performance Better than Normal or Restricted Sleep. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(12):2516-2523. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002071. (Corroborated by the description in Walsh et al. 2021 BJSM consensus, ref 44: 'better endurance performance after three consecutive nights of sleep extension (~8.4 hours sleep each night) compared with habitual sleep (~6.8 hours each night); prompting the authors to recommend endurance athletes sleep >8 hours each night'.)
interventions.duration: 3 nights per condition, testing on days 1-4
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — this is an acute protocol, not an adaptation. It can be applied at both the 12 Sep half and on 21-23 Oct before the marathon. It is one of only two interventions in this whole domain that can produce its full effect inside six weeks.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: reported difference ~3.2% of time-trial time. 3.2% of 225 min = 7.2 min. Discounts applied: (a) cyclists not runners; (b) n=9; (c) crossover with no independent control, so regression-to-the-mean and order effects are not excluded; (d) the benefit is almost certainly proportional to his existing deficit — if he already sleeps 8 h the headroom is near zero. Honest estimate: 0-7 min, best guess 2-4 min IF his habitual sleep is currently under 7 h. He has two nights of data in six months, so nobody — including him — knows which end of that range he is on. That is the single most important fact in this report.

interventions.intervention: Chronic sleep extension across the whole block (targeting >8 h/night for six weeks, i.e. bank sleep continuously rather than only pre-race)
interventions.effect: Mah 2011: total objective nightly sleep increased by 110.9 +/- 79.7 min above baseline (P<0.001); timed sprint 16.2 +/- 0.61 s -> 15.5 +/- 0.54 s (P<0.001, a 4.3% improvement); free-throw accuracy +9%, 3-point accuracy +9.2% (both P<0.001); PVT reaction time and Epworth Sleepiness Scale both improved (P<0.01); POMS vigour up, fatigue down (P<0.001). Schwartz & Simon 2015: one week at >=9 h in bed improved tennis serve accuracy 35.7% -> 41.8% (P<0.05). Cunha 2023 systematic review: 4 sleep-extension studies, extending sleep by 46-113 min for 3-49 nights, and 'all sleep extension studies demonstrated improvements' in cognitive and physical performance.
interventions.population: Mah: 11 male NCAA Division I basketball players, mean age 19.4. Schwartz: 12 college varsity tennis players. Cunha review: 25 studies, ages 13-33, 17 sports. NO study in this literature used distance runners with an endurance endpoint longer than a cycling time trial.
interventions.citation: Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC. The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep. 2011;34(7):943-950. doi:10.5665/sleep.1132. | Schwartz J, Simon RD. Sleep extension improves serving accuracy: A study with college varsity tennis players. Physiology & Behavior. 2015;151:541-544. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2015.08.035. | Cunha LA, Costa JA, Marques EA, Brito J, Lastella M, Figueiredo P. The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2023;9:58. doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00599-z.
interventions.sampleSize: Mah n=11; Schwartz n=12; Cunha review 25 studies, 9-31 participants each
interventions.duration: Mah: 5-7 weeks of extension after a 2-4 week baseline. Schwartz: 1 week. Cunha: 3-49 nights.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — Mah's protocol is 5-7 weeks, almost exactly this block's length, and the improvements were measured within it. It is also the only intervention here that compounds with the training rather than competing with it.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible with confidence. The measured outcomes are a 282-foot sprint, shooting accuracy and a tennis serve — none of which map to marathon pace. The honest statement: no study has ever measured sleep extension against a running endpoint longer than about an hour, so any number I gave you would be invented. What IS convertible: the sprint improved 4.3% and reaction time improved, both CNS-mediated, and the mechanism Roberts 2019 proposes for the endurance effect (lower perceived exertion at a given intensity) is the same one. If forced: 0-7 min, same range as the acute protocol, with the same dependence on his current deficit. Report as 'unquantified in this population' rather than as a number.

interventions.intervention: Avoiding sleep loss on the night before the race (treating the pre-race night as a protected asset, and building a 3-night bank so one bad night does not matter)
interventions.effect: Pooled standardised mean difference of sleep deprivation on endurance performance = -0.52 (95% CI -0.67 to -0.38), a moderate negative effect. Critically for a marathon: longer exercise bouts (>30 min) were significantly MORE affected than shorter ones (P=0.035). Training status, deprivation magnitude, assessment time, exercise mode and endpoint type did NOT moderate the effect. Independently, Gong 2024 found an overall effect of acute sleep deprivation on athletic performance of -0.56, with aerobic endurance specifically at -0.54, and — importantly — partial sleep deprivation at the END of the night (i.e. early waking, exactly what race-morning alarms cause) at -1.17, far worse than whole-night deprivation at -0.23.
interventions.population: Lopes: 31 studies, n=478, healthy humans including both trained and untrained; risk of bias low in only 8% of studies, unclear in 74%, high in 18%. Gong: 27 studies, 75 indicators, athletes.
interventions.citation: Lopes TR, Pereira HM, Bittencourt LRA, Silva BM. How much does sleep deprivation impair endurance performance? A systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Sport Science. 2023;23(7):1279-1292. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2155583. PROSPERO CRD42021229717. | Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S. Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation on Sporting Performance in Athletes: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nature and Science of Sleep. 2024;16:935-948. doi:10.2147/NSS.S467531.
interventions.sampleSize: Lopes n=478 across 31 studies (38 effect sizes); Gong 27 studies, 75 indicators
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — entirely acute, and applies twice (12 Sep half, 24 Oct marathon). Also the reason to bank sleep on the Wed/Thu/Fri before race Saturday rather than relying on Friday night, which pre-race nerves routinely wreck.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Working: SMD -0.52 must be multiplied by the SD of the performance measure to become a percentage. Typical within-subject coefficient of variation for a long endurance time trial is ~2-3%; using 2.5%, 0.52 x 2.5% = 1.3% of finishing time. 1.3% of 225 min = 2.9 min. Using Gong's end-of-night partial-deprivation figure of -1.17: 1.17 x 2.5% = 2.9% = 6.6 min. So roughly 3 min for a merely poor night, up to ~7 min for a genuinely truncated one. The CV assumption is mine and is the weakest link in the chain — the meta-analyses report SMDs, not percentages.

interventions.intervention: Keeping habitual sleep above 8 h during the volume ramp, specifically to reduce injury risk
interventions.effect: Milewski 2014: athletes averaging <8 h/night were 1.7 times more likely to have been injured than those sleeping >=8 h (95% CI 1.0-3.0, P=0.04). Note the lower confidence bound is exactly 1.0 — borderline, not robust. Gao 2019 meta-analysis: adolescents who chronically slept poorly were more likely to be injured, OR 1.58 (95% CI 1.05-2.37, P=0.03); the authors explicitly concluded that current evidence CANNOT determine the effect of acute sleep loss on injury rates.
interventions.population: Milewski: 112 middle/high-school athletes, mean age 15.2 (range 12-18), 54 male 58 female, retrospective injury-record review against an online survey. Gao: 7 studies, all adolescent. THIS IS THE CENTRAL POPULATION PROBLEM IN THE DOMAIN. Both the widely-quoted 1.7x and the pooled 1.58 come from ADOLESCENTS, whose sleep need is 8-10 h and whose injuries are dominated by growth-related pathology. I found no adult replication of comparable quality. Anyone quoting '1.7x injury risk below 7 hours' to a 27-year-old is extrapolating outside the evidence and usually does not say so.
interventions.citation: Milewski MD, Skaggs DL, Bishop GA, Pace JL, Ibrahim DA, Wren TA, Barzdukas A. Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes. Journal of Pediatric Orthopaedics. 2014;34(2):129-133. doi:10.1097/BPO.0000000000000151. | Gao B, Dwivedi S, Milewski MD, Cruz AI Jr. Lack of Sleep and Sports Injuries in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Pediatric Orthopaedics. 2019;39(5):e324-e333.
interventions.duration: Milewski: 21 months of injury records. Gao: varied.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes for the exposure — he can change his sleep tonight. But the evidence is observational: there is NO randomised trial that extended athletes' sleep and measured injury as the endpoint. The causal arrow could point the other way (overreaching athletes sleep worse), and neither study controls training load adequately.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not a mean shift — a tail-risk reduction, which for this athlete matters more. Working: assume a base probability of a block-disrupting injury of ~25% for someone quadrupling weekly volume from a 24.4 km/wk six-month average (this base rate is my estimate, NOT from the literature). Removing a 1.58x multiplier moves 25% to ~17%, an 8 percentage-point absolute reduction.
