If a block-disrupting injury costs the highest-volume weeks — plausibly 10-20 min of race time, or a DNS — expected value is 0.08 x ~15 min = ~1.2 min. That understates it. The real argument is that it cuts the probability of the 'no race at all' outcome by roughly a third, and he should weigh it that way rather than in minutes.

interventions.intervention: Wearing the watch overnight for a minimum measurement window, so that any of the above can be targeted at all
interventions.effect: With a consumer sleep tracker (Fitbit), 3 nights gives a 'good' (ICC 0.60) estimate of mean weekly total sleep time and 5 nights gives 'very good' (ICC 0.80). For a MONTHLY mean, 5 and 10 nights respectively. Weekday-only weekly estimates need just 2 and 3 nights. Night-to-night VARIABILITY is much more expensive to measure: 5-6 nights weekly, 11-18 nights monthly. Error estimates held up when validated against data collected 1 month and 1 year later.
interventions.population: 1041 working adults aged 21-40, 107,144 nights. Directly on-population for a 27-year-old — one of the few findings here requiring no extrapolation.
interventions.citation: Lau T, Ong JL, Ng BKL, Chan LF, Koek D, Tan CS, Muller-Riemenschneider F, Cheong K, Massar SAA, Chee MWL. Minimum number of nights for reliable estimation of habitual sleep using a consumer sleep tracker. Sleep Advances. 2022;3(1):zpac026. doi:10.1093/sleepadvances/zpac026. PMC10104388.
interventions.duration: Weekly and monthly windows; validated at 1 month and 1 year
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, immediately. Five nights of watch-wearing this week converts the largest unknown in his entire plan into a number. Nothing else in this report costs less.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero directly — measurement produces no performance. Its value is that it resolves whether the 0-7 min sleep-extension range above is 0 or 7. Caveat from the official consensus: both research-grade and consumer activity monitors typically OVERESTIMATE sleep duration relative to polysomnography and underestimate awakenings, so a Garmin reading of 7.5 h is likely less than 7.5 h of real sleep. Read the trend, bedtime and wake time — not the absolute total or the stage breakdown.

interventions.intervention: Daytime napping (20-30 min, or longer where schedule allows), to top up night-time sleep during the 100 km week
interventions.effect: Zheng 2026 meta-analysis: after presumed normal nocturnal sleep, napping produced a LARGE positive effect on endurance performance (SMD 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.29, P<0.001) and a moderate improvement in agility (SMD 0.55, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.09, P=0.048). Power/strength showed a moderate trend crossing zero (SMD 0.50, 95% CI -0.09 to 1.09). Dose-dependent: naps >60 min gave the largest endurance effect (SMD 1.38); 31-60 min also substantial. Effects on cognitive and technical performance uncertain due to imprecision. Walsh 2021 consensus: 20-30 min naps improve sprint and peak jump velocity, and naps benefit even athletes already getting sufficient night sleep. Cunha 2023, by contrast, found napping results MIXED for physical performance across 9 studies — 5 positive, 1 positive with caffeine, 3 no effect, 1 negative for sprint.
interventions.population: Zheng: 179 team ball sports athletes across 12 RCTs, naps scheduled 13:00-15:30. The 'endurance performance' measured in team-sport trials is typically a Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test lasting minutes, NOT a sustained aerobic effort. Transfer of SMD 0.96 to marathon running is unsupported. Cunha's mixed picture is drawn from a broader athlete population.
interventions.citation: Zheng J, Ye Y, Li X, Peng J. The effect of daytime napping on the athletic performance of team ball sports athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2026;17:1878224. doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1878224. PROSPERO CRD420251268837. | Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, et al. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(7):356-368. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025. | Cunha et al. 2023 (as above).
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — immediate, repeatable, and the practical tool for the 100 km week where six evening sessions plus a weekend long run will compress night sleep. Walsh's caveat: keep it under 30 min if the window is short, to avoid sleep inertia; avoid naps entirely if they impair falling asleep at night.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. The SMD of 0.96 is against a Yo-Yo-type test in ball-sport athletes and does not transfer to a 3-4 hour running effort. Treat napping as a means of hitting the sleep-duration target — its value routes entirely through the sleep-extension and injury-risk entries above, and must not be double-counted.

interventions.intervention: Not drinking alcohol after long runs and hard sessions
interventions.effect: Compared with protein alone after a bout of concurrent exercise, myofibrillar protein synthesis was 24% lower when alcohol was co-ingested with protein (P<0.05) and 37% lower when alcohol was co-ingested with carbohydrate (P<0.05). MPS still rose above rest in all conditions (~29-109%), so alcohol suppressed rather than abolished the anabolic response. Dose was 1.5 g/kg body mass — for this athlete at 85.5 kg that is ~128 g ethanol, roughly 12-16 UK units, i.e. a heavy night, not a glass of wine.
interventions.population: 8 physically active males, randomised crossover. Small, male, and the exercise bout was resistance work plus cycling intervals, not a long run.
interventions.citation: Parr EB, Camera DM, Areta JL, Burke LM, Phillips SM, Hawley JA, Coffey VG. Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis following a single bout of concurrent training. PLoS ONE. 2014;9(2):e88384. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0088384.
interventions.duration: Single bout; biopsies at rest, 2 h and 8 h post-exercise
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as an exposure, but the measured endpoint is a molecular signalling rate over 8 hours, not a training outcome over six weeks. No trial has run alcohol vs abstinence across a training block and measured performance.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — the endpoint is myofibrillar protein synthesis, only weakly relevant to endurance adaptation anyway (mitochondrial biogenesis matters more for a marathoner and was not measured). The stronger practical argument against alcohol in this block is its effect on sleep architecture, which routes back to the sleep entries above. Do not cite 24-37% as if it were 24-37% of anything he cares about.

interventions.intervention: Protecting sleep specifically to avoid illness during the block (an upper-respiratory infection in weeks 3-5 removes the highest-volume weeks)
interventions.effect: Participants sleeping <6 h/night were 4.2 times more likely to develop a cold after experimental rhinovirus inoculation than those sleeping >=7 h. Sleep was measured objectively by wrist actigraphy plus diary over 7 consecutive days BEFORE viral exposure, then participants were quarantined and monitored for 5 days.
interventions.population: 164 healthy men and women aged 18-55, general population, not athletes. The design is unusually strong — controlled viral challenge with objective pre-exposure sleep measurement — but the exposure route is artificial and the population is not training 100 km/week.
interventions.citation: Prather AA, Janicki-Deverts D, Hall MH, Cohen S. Behaviorally Assessed Sleep and Susceptibility to the Common Cold. Sleep. 2015;38(9):1353-1359. doi:10.5665/sleep.4968.
interventions.duration: 7 nights of sleep measurement, 5 days of post-inoculation monitoring
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — precisely a six-week-block risk, and October in London is the start of the season. Relevant that Walsh 2021 flags a theoretical counter-risk: reductions in sleep efficiency during sleep extension 'might conceivably have detrimental effects on athlete immunity' — speculative, not demonstrated.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible to minutes; the mechanism is lost training days, not slower running. Framing: a week lost to illness in week 4 removes the 100 km peak week, the week the whole ramp exists to deliver. Same tail-risk argument as the injury entry, not an additive minute count.

interventions.intervention: HRV-guided daily training prescription (using morning rMSSD to decide whether to do the hard session) instead of following the fixed 60/80/100/80/60 plan
interventions.effect: Duking 2021 meta-analysis, the best-designed test of the actual question: HRV-guided training had a significant MEDIUM positive effect on SUBMAXIMAL physiological parameters (Hedges g = 0.296, 95% CI 0.031 to 0.562, P=0.02), but 'a small and non-significant influence on PERFORMANCE and maximum oxygen uptake' compared with predefined training. Notably, HRV-guided groups generally performed FEWER moderate- and high-intensity sessions. Ranieri 2025, the most directly transferable trial: 28 recreational distance runners, 6-week intervention, randomised to heart-rate-based (n=9), race-pace-based (n=9) or HRV-based (n=10) prescription — NO interaction effects between groups. The race-pace group improved the 7 km time trial (effect size 1.07); the HRV group improved sVT2 (effect size 1.34), VO2max and sVT1 but increased fat mass and showed no superior time-trial improvement. Training load similar across groups. Lowest inter-individual variation in time-trial response was in the RACE-PACE group (CV 0.82). Nuuttila 2017: 24 endurance-trained males, 8 weeks; both groups improved maximal treadmill velocity and 3000 m, but relative changes in Vmax and countermovement jump were significantly greater in the HRV-guided group (P<0.05), and HRV and testosterone rose only in that group.
interventions.population: Duking: 8 studies, 198 participants, 9 interventions. Ranieri: 28 recreational distance runners — the closest match to this athlete in the entire report. Granero-Gallegos 2020 (6 RCTs, n=195, ages 19-38) reported a within-group pre-post ES of 0.402 for HRV-guided vs 0.215 for traditional on VO2max, but that compares two separate within-arm effect sizes rather than a pooled between-group difference — weaker than Duking's Hedges g and should not be quoted as equivalent.
interventions.citation: Duking P, Zinner C, Reed JL, Holmberg H-C, Sperlich B. Monitoring and adapting endurance training on the basis of heart rate variability monitored by wearable technologies: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2021;24(11):1180-1192. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2021.04.012. | Ranieri LE, Casado A, Martin D, Trujillo-Colmena D, Gil-Arias A, Kenneally M, Jimenez A. Performance and Physiological Effects of Race Pace-Based Versus Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training Prescription in Runners. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025;57(7):1510-1522. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003671. | Nuuttila O-P, Nikander A, Polomoshnov D, Laukkanen JA, Hakkinen K. Effects of HRV-Guided vs. Predetermined Block Training on Performance, HRV and Serum Hormones. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;38(12):909-920. doi:10.1055/s-0043-115122. | Granero-Gallegos A, Gonzalez-Quilez A, Plews D, Carrasco-Poyatos M. HRV-Based Training for Improving VO2max in Endurance Athletes. A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(21):7999. doi:10.3390/ijerph17217999.
interventions.sampleSize: Duking: 198 across 8 studies. Ranieri: 28. Nuuttila: 24. Granero-Gallegos: 195 across 6 RCTs.
interventions.duration: Ranieri 6 weeks; Nuuttila 8 weeks; meta-analysed trials mostly 4-12 weeks
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Technically yes, and Ranieri ran for exactly six weeks in exactly this population — which is why its null result is the relevant one. But there is a design problem specific to this athlete: HRV-guided prescription works by REMOVING hard sessions when readiness is low, and every trial applied it to athletes already at their habitual volume. Nobody has tested it on someone tripling weekly volume. Its most likely behaviour here is to strip out the sessions the ramp depends on.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Approximately zero, possibly negative. Working: Duking found the performance effect small and non-significant; the only six-week recreational-runner RCT (Ranieri) found no between-group interaction, with the race-pace group showing both the time-trial improvement and the lowest response variability. Converting a non-significant effect to minutes is not honest; the correct answer is 'no demonstrated performance benefit over a well-constructed fixed plan in this population and timeframe'. The one defensible use is as a SAFETY monitor rather than a prescription engine — a persistent multi-day rMSSD suppression during the 100 km week as a prompt to check in, not a daily arbiter. That use has no trial evidence either.

interventions.intervention: Massage after long runs
interventions.effect: No evidence of benefit for strength, jump, sprint, endurance or fatigue. Small but statistically significant improvements in flexibility and DOMS only. This directly contradicts the impression left by Dupuy 2018, which found massage the single most powerful technique for DOMS (SMD -2.26, 95% CI -3.05 to -1.47, 14 studies) and perceived fatigue (SMD -2.55, 95% CI -3.49 to -1.62, 7 studies). Resolution: Dupuy measured how sore and tired people FELT; Davis measured what they could DO. Massage reliably changes the former and not the latter.
interventions.population: Davis: 29 randomised studies, 1012 participants — the largest examination of massage effects. Dupuy: 99 studies; 1188 subjects across 80 studies for DOMS, 266 across 17 for perceived fatigue.
interventions.citation: Davis HL, Alabed S, Chico TJA. Effect of sports massage on performance and recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2020;6(1):e000614. doi:10.1136/bmjsem-2019-000614. | Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, Bosquet L, Dugue B. An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2018;9:403. doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.00403.
interventions.sampleSize: Davis n=1012 across 29 studies; Dupuy 99 studies
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, but with no expected performance return. If he enjoys it and it helps him sleep or relax, that is a legitimate reason to keep it — just not a performance one.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero. Davis 2020, the largest and most directly relevant analysis, found no effect on endurance. Any minute figure attributed to massage would be fabricated.

interventions.intervention: Cold water immersion / ice baths after hard sessions
interventions.effect: Modest effect on soreness: immersion SMD -0.47 (95% CI -0.77 to -0.18) for DOMS and -1.16 (95% CI -1.94 to -0.39) for perceived fatigue (Dupuy 2018). But Cunha 2023 found the 2 CWI studies in its athlete review showed no impact on sleep architecture, muscle damage or fatigue outcomes. Adaptation interference: CWI consistently blunts resistance-training adaptations with moderate negative effects on 1RM, isometric strength, strength endurance and ballistic power, and blunts hypertrophy — but ENDURANCE performance outcomes were not affected by regular CWI use.
interventions.population: Dupuy: mixed exercising populations. Pinero 2024: resistance-trained. The endurance-adaptation conclusion comes from review-level synthesis rather than a dedicated endurance meta-analysis, so it is less firmly established than the strength finding.
interventions.citation: Dupuy et al. 2018 (as above). | Pinero A, Burke R, Augustin F, Mohan AE, DeJesus K, Sapuppo M, Weisenthal M, Coleman M, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Grgic J, Swinton PA, Schoenfeld BJ. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;24(2):177-189. doi:10.1002/ejsc.12074. | Cunha et al. 2023 (as above).
interventions.sampleSize: Dupuy immersion arm: 34 studies for DOMS, 8 for perceived fatigue
interventions.duration: Post-exercise, acute and across training blocks
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes. For a marathoner it is not adaptation-harmful the way it is for a lifter, so the usual argument against it does not apply here. But the upside is a soreness-perception effect of SMD -0.47, which is small.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero measurable. No trial has shown CWI improving an endurance performance outcome. Its only defensible use in this block is subjective comfort during the 100 km week — not nothing when adherence is the binding constraint, but not minutes.

interventions.intervention: Foam rolling
interventions.effect: Pre-rolling: sprint +0.7% (g=0.28), flexibility +4.0% (g=0.34), jump -1.9% (g=0.09, negligible), strength +1.8% (g=0.12, negligible). Post-rolling as recovery: attenuated exercise-induced decrease in sprint by +3.1% (g=0.34) and strength by +3.9% (g=0.21), reduced muscle pain perception by +6.0% (g=0.47), jump effect trivial (g=0.06). Every one of these effect sizes is trivial-to-small.
interventions.population: 21 studies (14 pre-rolling, 7 post-rolling), mixed exercising populations, no endurance-running endpoint whatsoever.
interventions.citation: Wiewelhove T, Doweling A, Schneider C, Hottenrott L, Meyer T, Kellmann M, Pfeiffer M, Ferrauti A. A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Foam Rolling on Performance and Recovery. Frontiers in Physiology. 2019;10:376. doi:10.3389/fphys.2019.00376.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, but there is no endurance endpoint in the evidence base at all, so 'applies' means only 'can be done', not 'will do anything measurable for a marathon'.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero. No endurance outcome has been measured. The largest reported effect is a 6% change in how much a muscle hurts.

interventions.intervention: Sleep hygiene education / environment optimisation as a standalone intervention (dark, cool 17-22C room, phone out of the bedroom)
interventions.effect: Sleep education presentations lasting 30-60 min increased sleep duration by an average of 20-90 min — but the improvements were NOT maintained at 1-month follow-up. Cunha 2023: across 3 studies, 'sleep hygiene interventions showed no effect on performance recovery, blood markers of damage, or cognitive performance'; they increased sleep duration but not enough to drive performance gains. Electronic device removal (2 studies): no observed effects on sleep or on athletic/cognitive performance. Environment optimisation (removal of light, technology, noise; 17-22C) improved sleep duration but most studies reported limited benefit to sports performance.
interventions.population: Athletes across the Walsh consensus reference set and the Cunha review (25 studies, ages 13-33, 17 sports).
interventions.citation: Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nedelec M, Gupta L, Leeder J, Fullagar HHK, Coutts AJ, Edwards BJ, Pullinger SA. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55(7):356-368. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025. | Cunha et al. 2023 (as above).
interventions.sampleSize: Cunha: 3 sleep-hygiene studies within a 25-study review
interventions.duration: Single education sessions to multi-week programmes; follow-up at 1 month
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, and this is the honest reason to bother with it: it is the mechanism by which he gets the extra hour, not a performance intervention in its own right. The 1-month decay finding matters — a single 'sort out my sleep' effort in week 1 will have worn off by the 100 km week unless re-checked.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero on its own. Its value is instrumental: it delivers 20-90 min of extra sleep, and the sleep is what has the (small, uncertain) effect. Counting hygiene separately would double-count the sleep-extension entry.

interventions.intervention: Compression garments during or after running
interventions.effect: No significant improvement in race time (SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.22 to 0.09, P=0.40) or time to exhaustion (SMD 0.04, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.29, P=0.72). No moderating effect of garment type, race type, or contact surface. Secondary outcomes — running speed and race pace, submaximal oxygen uptake, tissue oxygenation — also showed no performance benefit. The only significant finding was reduced soft tissue vibration (SMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.15, P<0.01). Certainty of evidence rated LOW to VERY LOW by GRADE. (Dupuy 2018 does report compression garments helping DOMS, SMD -0.92, and perceived fatigue, SMD -0.88 — again, feeling versus doing.)
interventions.population: 51 eligible studies, 899 participants, runners specifically — directly on-population and on-endpoint for a marathoner, which almost nothing else in the recovery literature is.
interventions.citation: Wang W, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Si D, Li X, Liang Q, Li Q, Huang L, Wei S, Liu Y. Do compression garments enhance running performance? An updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2025;14:101028. doi:10.1016/j.jshs.2025.101028.
interventions.sampleSize: n=899 across 51 studies (33 in the primary meta-analysis)
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes, but with a demonstrated null on the exact endpoint he cares about.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero, and this is one of the few places where the null is precise enough to say so with confidence: the 95% CI on race time is -0.22 to 0.09 SMD, which at a 2.5% CV bounds any true effect at roughly -1.2 min to +0.5 min on a 3:45 marathon. Even the optimistic end of the interval is about one minute.

interventions.intervention: Static stretching and electrical stimulation as recovery modalities
interventions.effect: Stretching for DOMS: SMD +0.15 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.29), NOT significant, point estimate in the wrong direction. Stretching for perceived fatigue: SMD -0.21 (95% CI -1.04 to 0.62), not significant, 1 study. Electrostimulation for DOMS: SMD -0.28 (95% CI -0.59 to 0.03), not significant, 8 studies. Electrostimulation for perceived fatigue: not significant, 1 study. Active recovery for perceived fatigue: SMD +0.64 (95% CI -0.43 to 1.70), not significant, 4 studies — though active recovery DID help DOMS (SMD -0.94, 95% CI -1.61 to -0.28).
interventions.population: Mixed exercising populations across 99 studies; DOMS analysis 1188 subjects across 80 studies, perceived-fatigue analysis 266 across 17 studies.
interventions.citation: Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, Bosquet L, Dugue B. An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2018;9:403. doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.00403.
interventions.sampleSize: 99 studies total; per-technique arms of 1-16 studies
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes as an exposure; no as an effect.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Zero. Both fail to reach significance even on the soft endpoint of soreness, let alone performance.

interventions.intervention: Context for the ramp itself: rate of weekly-distance progression and injury (relevant because the sleep-injury argument only matters relative to the injury risk he is already taking)
interventions.effect: Novice runners were categorised by weekly-distance progression into <10%-or-regression, 10-30%, and >30% groups. NO statistically significant differences in overall injury rate were found across the three groups. A raised rate of DISTANCE-RELATED injuries specifically (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, gluteus medius injury, greater trochanteric bursitis, TFL injury, patellar tendinopathy) was seen in the >30% group versus the <10% group: hazard ratio 1.59, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, P=0.07 — note this does NOT reach significance. The authors describe the study as exploratory.
interventions.population: 874 healthy NOVICE runners, GPS-watch-verified distance, 1-year prospective cohort, 202 injuries. He is not a novice, but at a 24.4 km/wk six-month average the absolute volumes overlap.
interventions.citation: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):739-747. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Directly. His planned ramp — 15 km last week to a 60 km first week to a 100 km peak — is a progression far outside the >30% band this study examined, so the study cannot be used to reassure him. What it CAN do is remove a false certainty: the '10% rule' does not have the evidential backing it is usually given.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible. Included because it sets the base rate that the sleep-injury multiplier acts upon, and because the honest reading is that the ramp's risk is unquantified rather than quantified-and-acceptable. The evidence base does not contain a 15-to-100 km ramp.

interventions.intervention: Sleep restriction and the endocrine environment (mechanistic support for why chronic short sleep during a volume ramp is a bad trade)
interventions.effect: After 3 nights of 10 h in bed, 8 nights of 5 h in bed reduced daytime (08:00-22:00) testosterone from 18.4 to 16.5 nmol/L (P=0.049), a 10-15% decline. The effect was larger in the afternoon-evening window (14:00-22:00): 17.9 vs 15.5 nmol/L (P=0.02). The authors note this is comparable to 10-15 years of normal ageing (which reduces testosterone 1-2% per year).
interventions.population: 10 healthy young men, laboratory-controlled. Small, non-athlete, and testosterone is a proxy — no performance or adaptation outcome was measured.
interventions.citation: Leproult R, Van Cauter E. Effect of 1 week of sleep restriction on testosterone levels in young healthy men. JAMA. 2011;305(21):2173-2174. doi:10.1001/jama.2011.710. PMC4445839.
interventions.appliesInSixWeeks: Yes — the exposure (5 h nights during a hard block) is exactly the scenario, and the effect appeared within 8 nights. But 5 h is a severe restriction, not the 6-7 h a busy adult typically drifts to, and the study does not establish that the hormonal change causes any training consequence.
interventions.marathonMinutesEquivalent: Not convertible — a 10-15% testosterone change has no established mapping to marathon time in a recreational endurance athlete, and inventing one would be exactly the failure mode to avoid. Cite as mechanism, never as minutes.

myths: 'Sleeping under 7 hours multiplies an adult athlete's injury risk by 1.7.' The 1.7x (Milewski 2014) and the pooled 1.58 (Gao 2019) are BOTH from adolescent athletes aged 12-18, whose sleep need is 8-10 h and whose injury profile is dominated by growth-related pathology. I found no adult replication of comparable quality. Milewski's own confidence interval is 1.0-3.0 — the lower bound sits exactly on no-effect. The direction of the association is probably real; the specific multiplier is quoted far outside the population it was measured in, and almost nobody quoting it says so.

'Compression socks and tights make you faster or recover quicker.' 51 studies, 899 runners, on the exact endpoint: no significant effect on race time (SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.22 to 0.09) or time to exhaustion. No effect on running speed, submaximal VO2 or tissue oxygenation either. GRADE certainty low to very low. The only reliable effect is less soft-tissue wobble (Wang 2025).

'Massage speeds recovery, so you can train harder.' The largest analysis (29 randomised studies, 1012 participants) found no evidence that massage improves strength, jump, sprint, ENDURANCE or fatigue — only small improvements in flexibility and soreness (Davis 2020). Dupuy 2018's headline that massage is the most powerful recovery technique (SMD -2.26 for soreness) is about how sore people REPORT feeling, not what they can do. Feeling recovered and being recovered are different measurements and the literature separates them cleanly.

'Foam rolling is an important part of recovery.' Every effect size in the meta-analysis is trivial-to-small: post-rolling attenuates sprint decrement by 3.1% (g=0.34) and reduces muscle pain by 6.0% (g=0.47); the jump effect is g=0.06. No endurance-running endpoint has ever been measured (Wiewelhove 2019).

'Static stretching aids recovery.' Pooled effect on soreness is SMD +0.15 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.29) — non-significant and pointing the wrong way. Electrical stimulation likewise: SMD -0.28 (95% CI -0.59 to 0.03), non-significant (Dupuy 2018).

'Ice baths are essential for recovery in a hard block.' The soreness effect is small (SMD -0.47) and the two CWI studies in Cunha's athlete review showed no effect on sleep architecture, muscle damage or fatigue. Separately, CWI reliably BLUNTS resistance-training adaptations (1RM, isometric strength, ballistic power, hypertrophy) — that specific harm does not apply to endurance training, so for a marathoner the accurate verdict is 'no demonstrated benefit', not 'harmful'.

'Sleep hygiene education fixes your sleep.' Education sessions do raise sleep duration by 20-90 min — and the improvement was gone at 1-month follow-up (Walsh 2021). Across 3 studies, sleep hygiene interventions showed NO effect on performance recovery, blood damage markers, or cognitive performance; and removing electronic devices at night showed no effect on sleep OR performance in 2 studies (Cunha 2023).

'HRV-guided training beats following a fixed plan.' The best meta-analysis found the benefit confined to submaximal physiological parameters (Hedges g=0.296, 95% CI 0.031-0.562) with a small and NON-SIGNIFICANT effect on performance and VO2max — and HRV-guided groups generally did FEWER hard sessions than the fixed-plan groups (Duking 2021). The only 6-week randomised trial in recreational distance runners found no between-group interaction at all, with the race-pace-prescribed group showing the time-trial improvement and the LOWEST inter-individual response variation (Ranieri 2025). The frequently cited Granero-Gallegos 2020 'HRV 0.402 vs traditional 0.215' is a comparison of two separate within-arm pre-post effect sizes, not a pooled between-group difference — weaker evidence than it is usually presented as being.

'The 10% rule protects you from injury.' In 874 GPS-tracked novice runners there were NO statistically significant differences in overall injury rate between those progressing <10%, 10-30%, and >30% per two weeks. The >30% signal was confined to a subset of distance-related injuries and did not reach significance (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, P=0.07), in a study its own authors call exploratory (Nielsen 2014). The rule may still be prudent; it is not evidence-based in the way it is usually asserted.

'My watch tells me how much I slept.' Both research-grade and consumer activity monitors typically OVERESTIMATE sleep duration relative to polysomnography and underestimate awakenings and wake-after-sleep-onset; smartphone apps are poor at determining sleep stages and parameters; mattress/nearable devices 'are not considered accurate for measuring sleep' (Walsh 2021 BJSM consensus). Read the trend, the bedtime and the wake time — not the absolute total, and not the stage breakdown.

'More sleep data is always better.' The consensus warns the other way: 'Some athletes may become preoccupied with their sleep monitor data, which may increase anxiety around sleep and result in worse sleep' (Walsh 2021, Box 3, tip 5). For an athlete who has worn the watch overnight twice in six months, five nights of measurement is the goal, not a permanent habit.

'Everyone needs 8 hours.' The consensus position is the opposite of a fixed number: 'a one-size-fits-all approach to athlete sleep recommendations (eg, 7-9 hours/night) is unlikely ideal for health and performance', and it recommends an individualised approach (Walsh 2021, abstract).
unknowns: There is NO sleep-extension trial in distance runners with a running endurance endpoint. The entire sleep-extension evidence base for performance rests on basketball sprints and shooting, a tennis serve, and one 9-person cycling time trial. Every marathon-minute figure in this domain is an extrapolation across sport, duration and physiology.

Whether sleep extension is genuinely ergogenic or merely repays an existing debt. The consensus poses this explicitly and unresolved: 'The degree to which the ergogenic effect of sleep extension varies as a function of habitual sleep is important to determine (ie, repaying a recent sleep debt or a real effect of banking sleep?)' (Walsh 2021). This matters enormously here, because nobody knows this athlete's habitual sleep.

Whether there is a ceiling beyond which extra sleep does nothing, and whether too much can harm. Walsh 2021 lists as open: 'whether there is a ceiling effect (eg, for total sleep time, slow-wave sleep or REM sleep) beyond which no further performance or health benefit is gained; or whether too much sleep can have negative effects on performance or health', noting that reductions in sleep efficiency during extension 'might conceivably have detrimental effects on athlete immunity'.

Whether the sleep-injury association is causal. Every study is observational and cross-sectional or retrospective. No randomised trial has extended athletes' sleep and measured injury as the endpoint. Reverse causation (accumulating overload disturbs sleep, and also causes injury) is not excluded by any of this evidence, and Gao 2019's authors explicitly state that current evidence cannot determine the effect of acute sleep loss on injury rates.

Whether adolescent sleep-injury odds ratios transfer to adults at all. This is not a minor caveat — it is the load-bearing assumption under the most-quoted claim in the field, and it has not been tested.

Whether HRV guidance helps during an aggressive volume ramp specifically. Every trial applied HRV guidance to athletes already at their habitual training volume. Nobody has tested it on someone quadrupling weekly distance. Its known mechanism — removing hard sessions when readiness is low — could plausibly be either the safety valve this ramp needs or the thing that guts it, and the literature cannot say which.

The dose-response of sleep extension. No study titrates it. We know 'more than baseline, for 3-49 nights' produces effects; we do not know whether 30 extra minutes gets 20% of the benefit or 80% — exactly the question a person with a fixed evening schedule and six training days a week needs answered.

Whether sleep extension affects running economy or VO2max at all. Neither has been measured in any sleep-extension study I could find. Given that running economy is the most trainable determinant of marathon time, this is a conspicuous hole.

The interaction between sleep debt and an unprecedented training load. All sleep-restriction studies impose restriction on people doing normal or light training. Nobody has run the 2x2 of (short sleep vs extended sleep) x (habitual volume vs 4x volume ramp), which is precisely this athlete's cell of the design.

Napping in endurance runners. The large endurance effect (SMD 0.96) comes from team ball-sport athletes doing intermittent tests lasting minutes. No equivalent trial exists in distance runners, and Cunha 2023's broader review found napping results for physical performance genuinely mixed (5 positive, 3 null, 1 negative).

Whether any of the recovery-modality soreness effects translate into more completed training. The whole implicit argument for massage and ice baths is 'feel better, train more'. No trial has measured adherence or completed training volume as the outcome — only soreness ratings and single-session performance.

officialSources.body: British Journal of Sports Medicine expert consensus panel (Walsh, Halson, Sargent, Roach, Nedelec, Gupta, Leeder, Fullagar, Coutts, Edwards, Pullinger)
officialSources.document: Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2021;55(7):356-368. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: The nearest thing to an official standard in this domain, and I read the full text rather than an abstract. Its five recommendations (Box 1) are notably modest: (1) avoid situations that present ongoing risks to sleep and promote positive habitual sleep behaviour; (2) account for confounders such as illness when applying sleep strategies in the field; (3-5) are addressed to researchers, calling for better randomisation reporting, baseline sleep reporting, and RCTs — an implicit admission that the evidence base is thin. Its practitioner 'sleep toolbox' (Box 2): provide sleep education; screen for sleep disorders before applying any sleep strategy; encourage naps of <30 min timed 13:00-16:00, optionally as a 150-200 mg 'coffee nap'; and bank sleep before important competition. Box 3 gives 7-9 h for healthy adults and 8-10 h for teenagers, with the caveat that 'experts SPECULATE that athletes need more' — flagged as speculation, not evidence. It states that habitual durations under 7 h characterise sleep inadequacy in athletes, and it explicitly rejects one-size-fits-all: 'a one-size-fits-all approach to athlete sleep recommendations (eg, 7-9 hours/night) is unlikely ideal for health and performance'. On sleep extension it is cautious: 'studies showing improvements in physical performance with sleep extension should be considered with caution' because 'it is uncommon for sleep studies to include a control group'.

officialSources.body: American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society, joint Consensus Conference Panel (Watson NF, Badr MS, et al.)
officialSources.document: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society. Sleep. 2015;38(6):843-844 / J Clin Sleep Med. 2015;11(6):591-592
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health. This is the source of the '7 hours' threshold the athlete-facing literature then builds on. VERIFICATION NOTE: I confirmed this document via its citation as reference 166 in the Walsh 2021 consensus reference list (cited there as the basis for the 7-9 h adult figure in Box 3); I did not open the AASM statement itself, so treat the exact page numbers as approximate.

officialSources.body: NCAA (National Collegiate Athletic Association) Interassociation Task Force
officialSources.document: Interassociation recommendations on sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA
officialSources.whatItPrescribes: Athlete-facing sleep recommendations for collegiate sport. VERIFICATION NOTE: this appears in the Walsh 2021 reference list (cited there as 'sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA') and I did NOT retrieve the document itself. Listed so you know it exists as an official source to chase, not because I have read its contents. Do not attribute any specific prescription to it on my say-so.

check.domain: Sleep, recovery and the modifiable non-training factors — evidence audit of another agent's research for a 27-year-old male recreational marathoner (85.5 kg, 24.4 km/wk six-month average, 3:55 marathon, HM PB 1:46:35) attempting a 60/80/100/80/60 km six-week ramp to Battersea Park Marathon 2026-10-24

citationChecks.citation: Roberts SSH, Teo W-P, Aisbett B, Warmington SA. Extended Sleep Maintains Endurance Performance Better than Normal or Restricted Sleep. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(12):2516-2523. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002071
citationChecks.note: Europe PMC, PMID 31246714. Every detail matches: n=9 cyclists/triathletes, counterbalanced crossover, SE 8.6/8.3/8.2 h, NS 7.1/6.5/6.9 h, SR 4.7/4.8/4.9 h, D4 SE 58.7±3.4 vs 56.8±3.1 min (P<0.02). The researcher flagged the 3.2% as PROVISIONAL because they could not resolve which number was which condition. It resolves in their favour: the SR clause reads 'slower on D3 of SR (58.8 vs 60.4)', so the format is NS-first, condition-second; therefore SE=56.8 and NS=58.7, giving (58.7-56.8)/58.7 = 3.24%. Upgrade from provisional to confirmed. TWO THINGS THE RESEARCHER MISSED, both against their own case: (a) the abstract states 'RPE was not different between or within conditions' — yet the authors' own conclusion asserts 'cumulative sleep time affects performance by altering the perceived exertion of a given exercise intensity'. The mechanism is contradicted by the paper's own data. This matters because the researcher used that same RPE mechanism as the bridge to carry Mah's basketball sprint result across to endurance; the bridge is not load-bearing. (b) No independent control group and n=9 — the researcher noted this, correctly.

citationChecks.citation: Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC. The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep. 2011;34(7):943-950. doi:10.5665/sleep.1132
citationChecks.note: PMID 21731144. All numbers verified exactly: +110.9±79.7 min (P<0.001), sprint 16.2±0.61 → 15.5±0.54 s (P<0.001; = 4.32%, researcher's 4.3% correct), free throw +9%, 3-point +9.2%, PVT and ESS P<0.01, POMS P<0.001, n=11, mean age 19.4±1.4. TWO OVERSTATEMENTS. (1) Graded 'evidenceGrade: controlled-trial'. It is not. It is an uncontrolled within-subject pre-post: 2-4 week baseline followed by 5-7 weeks of extension, no control arm, no randomisation. The sprint gain is fully confounded with in-season basketball training over 7-11 weeks. This is precisely the flaw Walsh 2021 warns about — and the researcher quotes that warning elsewhere while grading this paper as controlled. (2) The dose is omitted: the protocol was 'as much nocturnal sleep as possible with a minimum goal of 10 h in bed each night'. Ten hours in bed nightly for six weeks is not available to a working 27-year-old training six evenings a week, so the intervention as tested cannot be delivered to this athlete even in principle.

citationChecks.citation: Schwartz J, Simon RD. Sleep extension improves serving accuracy: A study with college varsity tennis players. Physiol Behav. 2015;151:541-544. doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2015.08.035
citationChecks.note: PMID 26325012, exact match on authors/journal/volume/pages/year. Serve-accuracy figures (35.7% → 41.8%, P<0.05) not independently verified — no abstract text returned by Europe PMC and I had exhausted my web-search budget. Same grading objection as Mah: presented under 'evidenceGrade: controlled-trial' when the design is a one-week within-subject extension in 12 players.

citationChecks.citation: Cunha LA, Costa JA, Marques EA, Brito J, Lastella M, Figueiredo P. The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Med Open. 2023;9:58. doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00599-z
citationChecks.note: PMID 37462808. Verified: 25 studies, published 2011-2021, interventions spanning sleep hygiene, naps, sleep extension, light manipulation, CWI, mindfulness. Abstract confirms 'Sleep hygiene, removing electronic devices at night, and cold water immersion had no effects on sleep and subsequent performance/recovery, but these results are based on a few studies only' — exactly as reported. One framing wrinkle: the researcher deploys Cunha as a counterweight to Zheng's large napping effect ('mixed: 5 positive, 3 null, 1 negative'), but Cunha's own abstract lists naps alongside extension as 'the most representative and most effective strategies'. Both can be true (mixed at study level, positive on balance), but the counterweight is presented more strongly than Cunha supports.

citationChecks.citation: Lopes TR, Pereira HM, Bittencourt LRA, Silva BM. How much does sleep deprivation impair endurance performance? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023;23(7):1279-1292. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2155583
citationChecks.note: PMID 36472094. Every element verified verbatim: pooled SMD -0.52 (95% CI -0.67, -0.38); 31 studies, n=478, 38 effect sizes; risk of bias low 8% / unclear 74% / high 18%; training status, deprivation magnitude, assessment time, exercise mode and endpoint type all non-moderating; >30 min exercise more affected, P=0.035; PROSPERO CRD42021229717. Flawless reporting of the source. The problem is downstream, in the SMD→minutes conversion — see effect-size errors.

citationChecks.citation: Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S. Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation on Sporting Performance in Athletes: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nat Sci Sleep. 2024;16:935-948. doi:10.2147/NSS.S467531
citationChecks.note: PMID 39006249. Verified exactly: overall -0.56; whole-night -0.23; end-of-night partial -1.17; beginning-of-night partial -0.25 (P>0.05, non-significant — omitted by the researcher but it does not bear on their argument); aerobic endurance -0.54; 27 studies, 75 indicators. Also unreported and relevant: morning performance -0.30 vs afternoon -1.11, i.e. the deficit is smaller for a morning race — which a marathon start makes the applicable figure, cutting the estimate the researcher gives.

citationChecks.citation: Milewski MD, Skaggs DL, Bishop GA, Pace JL, Ibrahim DA, Wren TA, Barzdukas A. Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes. J Pediatr Orthop. 2014;34(2):129-133. doi:10.1097/BPO.0000000000000151
citationChecks.note: PMID 25028798. Verified: <8 h/night → 1.7x injury (95% CI 1.0-3.0, P=0.04); n=112 (54 male, 58 female) from 160 consented; retrospective injury-record review against online survey. Trivial slip: researcher says 'mean age 15.2'; the abstract says mean age 15 years (SD 1.5, range 12-18) — the .2 appears to be drift from the SD. Immaterial. The researcher's treatment of this paper is the strongest passage in the whole report: they lead with the adolescent population problem, note the CI's lower bound sits exactly on 1.0, and state plainly that no adult replication of comparable quality exists. That is the correct reading.

citationChecks.citation: Gao B, Dwivedi S, Milewski MD, Cruz AI Jr. Lack of Sleep and Sports Injuries in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Pediatr Orthop. 2019;39(5):e324-e333
citationChecks.note: PMID 30888337, doi 10.1097/BPO.0000000000001306. Verified: 7 of 907 articles included; random-effects OR 1.58 (95% CI 1.05-2.37, P=0.03); adolescents ≤19 y; and the authors' explicit statement 'Current evidence cannot yet definitively determine the effect of acute lack of sleep on injury rates' — quoted accurately. Level of evidence IV.

citationChecks.citation: Lau T, Ong JL, Ng BKL, et al. Minimum number of nights for reliable estimation of habitual sleep using a consumer sleep tracker. Sleep Adv. 2022;3(1):zpac026. doi:10.1093/sleepadvances/zpac026
citationChecks.note: PMID 37193398, PMC10104388. Verified to the digit: 107,144 nights from 1041 working adults aged 21-40; weekly mean total sleep time 3 nights (ICC 0.60) / 5 nights (0.80); monthly 5 / 10; weekday-only weekly 2 / 3; variability 5-6 weekly and 11-18 monthly; validated at 1 month and 1 year. The single best population match in the report and reported without error.

citationChecks.citation: Zheng J, Ye Y, Li X, Peng J. The effect of daytime napping on the athletic performance of team ball sports athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2026;17:1878224. doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1878224
citationChecks.note: Verified, including the unusual-looking 2026 volume 17 and article number. All numbers exact: endurance SMD 0.96 (0.62-1.29, p<0.001); agility 0.55 (0.01-1.09, p=0.048); power/strength 0.50 (-0.09-1.09, CI crosses zero); >60 min naps endurance 1.38, power 0.84; 12 RCTs, 179 athletes; naps 13:00-15:30; PROSPERO CRD420251268837. One unsupported inference: the researcher asserts the 'endurance performance' measured was 'typically a Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test lasting minutes'. Very likely correct for team-sport trials but not stated in the abstract and I could not confirm it. It is presented as fact and used to justify refusing a minutes conversion — the right conclusion reached via an unverified premise.

citationChecks.citation: Parr EB, Camera DM, Areta JL, Burke LM, Phillips SM, Hawley JA, Coffey VG. Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis following a single bout of concurrent training. PLoS One. 2014;9(2):e88384. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0088384
citationChecks.note: PMID 24533082, PMC3922864. Verified: n=8 physically active males, randomised crossover; ALC-PRO 24% and ALC-CHO 37% reductions vs PRO (both P<0.05); MPS still rose ~29-109% above rest in all conditions; dose 1.5 g/kg body mass, described in-paper as 12±2 standard drinks; exercise was 8×5 leg extension at 80% 1RM plus 30 min continuous and 10×30 s interval cycling. The researcher's refusal to convert this to minutes is correct and well argued. Minor unit slip noted separately.

citationChecks.citation: Prather AA, Janicki-Deverts D, Hall MH, Cohen S. Behaviorally Assessed Sleep and Susceptibility to the Common Cold. Sleep. 2015;38(9):1353-1359. doi:10.5665/sleep.4968
citationChecks.note: PMID 26118561, PMC4531403 — the paper exists and the design is as described (n=164, ages 18-55, 7 nights wrist actigraphy plus diary before quarantine and rhinovirus inoculation, 5 days monitoring). But the headline number is misreported. The researcher writes: 'Participants sleeping <6 h/night were 4.2 times more likely to develop a cold than those sleeping ≥7 h.' The paper reports three bands against a >7 h reference: <5 h OR 4.50 (95% CI 1.08-18.69); 5-6 h OR 4.24 (95% CI 1.08-16.71); and 6.01-7 h OR 1.66 (95% CI 0.40-6.95), NOT significant. So (a) there is no '<6 h' category and no 4.2; the figure is a merge of two separate bands; (b) the reference group is >7 h, not ≥7 h; (c) most consequentially for this athlete, the 6.01-7 h band shows NO significant elevation — the risk threshold sits below 6 h, not below 7 h, so a man sleeping 6.5 h is in the null band; (d) both intervals are enormous (upper bounds 18.69 and 16.71, lower bounds 1.08 — barely clearing 1) and neither is reported, while the design is called 'unusually strong'. The design is strong; the estimate is very imprecise. Also unreported: sleep fragmentation was unrelated to cold susceptibility.

citationChecks.citation: Düking P, Zinner C, Reed JL, Holmberg H-C, Sperlich B. Monitoring and adapting endurance training on the basis of heart rate variability monitored by wearable technologies: A systematic review with meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2021;24(11):1180-1192. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2021.04.012
citationChecks.note: Paper verified exactly, including g=0.296 (95% CI 0.031-0.562), 8 studies / 198 participants / 9 interventions, and 'most HRV-guided interventions included fewer moderate- and/or high-intensity training sessions'. Two issues. (1) AUTHOR LIST IS WRONG: the actual byline is Düking P, Zinner C, Trabelsi K, Reed JL, Holmberg HC, Kunz P, Sperlich B — two authors (Trabelsi, Kunz) dropped. Not a fabrication, but the citation as written would not verify against the record. (2) SELECTIVE REPORTING, and it cuts against the researcher's conclusion. The abstract states 'with regards to performance, HRV-guided training was associated with fewer non-responders and more positive responders' and repeats it in the conclusion: 'There were fewer non-responders regarding performance with HRV-based training.' The researcher omits this entirely, while presenting Ranieri's inter-individual response-variation data as evidence FOR fixed prescription. The one pro-HRV response-consistency finding in their own headline source was left out. The overall verdict (no demonstrated mean performance benefit) still stands; the omission is one-sided. Also p=0.028, quoted as P=0.02.

citationChecks.citation: Ranieri LE, Casado A, Martin D, Trujillo-Colmena D, Gil-Arias A, Kenneally M, Jiménez A. Performance and Physiological Effects of Race Pace-Based Versus Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training Prescription in Runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025;57(7):1510-1522. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003671
citationChecks.note: Verified in full: 28 recreational distance runners, 6-week intervention, randomised to HR (n=9), RP (n=9), HRV (n=10); 'No interaction effects between groups were observed'; RP improved 7-km TT (P<0.05, ES 1.07) with greater maximal aerobic speed and fat-mass reduction; HRV increased sVT2 (P<0.01, ES 1.34), sVT1 and VO2max but increased fat mass; training load similar between groups; lowest inter-individual TT response variation in RP (CV 0.82), HRV lower variation in relative VO2max (CV 0.75) and sVT2 (CV 0.79). The researcher's identification of this as the single most transferable trial in the report is correct — six weeks, recreational distance runners, the exact question.

citationChecks.citation: Nuuttila O-P, Nikander A, Polomoshnov D, Laukkanen JA, Häkkinen K. Effects of HRV-Guided vs. Predetermined Block Training on Performance, HRV and Serum Hormones. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38(12):909-920. doi:10.1055/s-0043-115122
citationChecks.note: Verified: 24 endurance-trained males, 8 weeks; both groups improved Vmax (p<0.001) and 3000 m; relative changes in Vmax and countermovement jump significantly greater in HRV-guided (p<0.05); HRV (RMSSD, LF, TP) increased only in HRV-guided (p<0.05); serum testosterone rose mid-to-post in HRV-guided (p<0.05). Reported accurately, and notably this is the pro-HRV trial — the researcher included it despite it cutting against their conclusion, which is to their credit.

citationChecks.citation: Granero-Gallegos A, González-Quílez A, Plews D, Carrasco-Poyatos M. HRV-Based Training for Improving VO2max in Endurance Athletes. A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2020;17(21):7999. doi:10.3390/ijerph17217999
citationChecks.note: PMC7663087, verified. But the researcher's methodological dismissal goes further than the paper allows. They write that the 0.402-vs-0.215 figures 'compare two separate within-arm effect sizes rather than a pooled between-group difference'. The abstract does report a between-group contrast: 'the ES for the HRV-guided training group was significantly higher (p < 0.0001; ES_HRVG-CG = 0.187)'. And 0.402 − 0.215 = 0.187 exactly, so the authors did compute and test the between-group difference. The underlying criticism — that a difference of within-arm pre-post ESs is a weaker estimator than a properly pooled between-group SMD — is legitimate and worth making. But the claim that no between-group difference is reported is not accurate. This is scepticism overshooting the source, the mirror-image of the failure I was sent to find, and worth knowing because it is deployed to dismiss a paper.

citationChecks.citation: Davis HL, Alabed S, Chico TJA. Effect of sports massage on performance and recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2020;6(1):e000614. doi:10.1136/bmjsem-2019-000614
citationChecks.note: PMC7228568. Verified verbatim: 29 randomised studies, 1012 participants, 'representing the largest examination of the effects of massage'; 'no evidence that massage improves measures of strength, jump, sprint, endurance or fatigue, but massage was associated with small but statistically significant improvements in flexibility and DOMS'. The researcher's reconciliation of Davis against Dupuy — Dupuy measured how people FEEL, Davis measured what they can DO — is the correct reading of both papers and the best analytical move in the report. Note a correction notice exists (BMJ Open SEM 2021;7:e000614corr1); it does not alter these conclusions.

citationChecks.citation: Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, Bosquet L, Dugué B. An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis. Front Physiol. 2018;9:403. doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.00403
citationChecks.note: PMC5932411. I pulled the full text and checked Table 1 line by line. Every per-technique SMD quoted is exact. DOMS: massage -2.26 (-3.05, -1.47); compression -0.92 (-1.34, -0.50); immersion -0.47 (-0.77, -0.18); active recovery -0.94 (-1.61, -0.28); stretching +0.15 (0.00, 0.29) non-significant; electrostimulation -0.28 (-0.59, 0.03) non-significant. Perceived fatigue: massage -2.55 (-3.49, -1.62); immersion -1.16 (-1.94, -0.39); compression -0.88 (-1.34, -0.50); active recovery +0.64 (-0.43, 1.70); stretching -0.21 (-1.04, 0.62); electrostimulation -0.28 (-0.59, 0.03). Also verified: 99 studies overall, CK -0.37, IL-6 -0.36, CRP -0.38. Only the study counts drift: reported as '1188 subjects across 80 studies' and '266 across 17'; Table 1 reads 1188 across 106 experimental groups and 266 across 27. Subject counts exact, group counts understated. No conclusion turns on it.

citationChecks.citation: Piñero A, Burke R, Augustin F, et al. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024;24(2):177-189. doi:10.1002/ejsc.12074
citationChecks.note: PMC11235606 — the paper exists exactly as cited, but the findings attributed to it are not in it. I read it: it measures muscle hypertrophy ONLY (DXA, MRI, ultrasound, biopsy, circumference), reporting RT alone SMD 0.36 vs CWI+RT SMD 0.14, i.e. attenuated hypertrophy. It does not measure 1RM, isometric strength, strength endurance, ballistic power, or any endurance outcome. The researcher attributes to it 'moderate negative effects on 1RM, isometric strength, strength endurance and ballistic power' and 'ENDURANCE performance outcomes were not affected by regular CWI use'. Those are Malta et al. 2021's findings (Sports Med): strength cluster SMD -0.60 (95% CI -0.87, -0.33, p<0.0001), ballistic -0.61 (-1.11, -0.11, p=0.02), and no effect of CWI on endurance-training adaptations. The claims are TRUE and correctly stated — they are sourced to the wrong paper. Malta 2021 appears in the researcher's own searchesRun list and was then dropped from the citation. The researcher also hedges that 'the endurance-adaptation conclusion comes from review-level synthesis rather than a dedicated endurance meta-analysis' — unnecessary, because Malta 2021 IS a dedicated meta-analysis of exactly that question. The evidence is stronger than the report claims, attributed to the wrong source.

citationChecks.citation: Wiewelhove T, Döweling A, Schneider C, Hottenrott L, Meyer T, Kellmann M, Pfeiffer M, Ferrauti A. A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Foam Rolling on Performance and Recovery. Front Physiol. 2019;10:376. doi:10.3389/fphys.2019.00376
citationChecks.note: PMC6465761. Every figure exact: 21 studies (14 pre-rolling, 7 post-rolling); pre-rolling sprint +0.7% g=0.28, flexibility +4.0% g=0.34, jump -1.9% g=0.09, strength +1.8% g=0.12; post-rolling sprint +3.1% g=0.34, strength +3.9% g=0.21, muscle pain +6.0% g=0.47, jump -0.2% g=0.06. The researcher's 'no endurance-running endpoint whatsoever' is confirmed by the outcome list. One nuance omitted: the authors conclude the evidence 'seems to justify the widespread use of foam rolling as a warm-up activity rather than a recovery tool' — a slightly more positive framing than the report gives, though on non-endurance outcomes irrelevant to this athlete.

citationChecks.citation: Wang W, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Si D, Li X, Liang Q, Li Q, Huang L, Wei S, Liu Y. Do compression garments enhance running performance? An updated systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sport Health Sci. 2025;14:101028. doi:10.1016/j.jshs.2025.101028
citationChecks.note: Verified exactly: 51 eligible studies, 899 participants, 33 in the primary meta-analysis; race time SMD -0.07 (95% CI -0.22, 0.09; p=0.40); time to exhaustion SMD 0.04 (-0.20, 0.29; p=0.72); no moderation by garment type, race type or surface; secondary outcomes null; soft tissue vibration SMD -0.43 (-0.70, -0.15; p<0.01); GRADE certainty low to very low. An erratum exists (J Sport Health Sci 2025;14:101050) — worth noting, but the researcher's figures match the record. This is the report's cleanest null and is correctly identified as the only place where the evidence is precise enough on the exact endpoint to bound the effect.

citationChecks.citation: Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2014;44(10):739-747. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164
citationChecks.note: Verified exactly: 874 novice runners, GPS watches, 202 injuries, 1-year prospective, explorative design; no significant differences in overall injury rate across <10%/10-30%/>30% groups; distance-related injuries HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96, 2.66; P=.07) for >30% vs <10%. All figures correct. But the myth entry ('the 10% rule does not have the evidential backing it is usually given') omits the authors' own concluding sentence: 'novice runners may be well advised to progress their weekly distances by less than 30% per week over a 2-week period.' Presenting a paper's null p-value while dropping the authors' explicit prudential recommendation is one-sided in the reassuring direction — and this athlete is planning a week-one jump of roughly 300%. More seriously, a directly contradicting study from the same research group was not found: see missed evidence (Damsted 2019).

citationChecks.citation: Leproult R, Van Cauter E. Effect of 1 week of sleep restriction on testosterone levels in young healthy men. JAMA. 2011;305(21):2173-2174. doi:10.1001/jama.2011.710
citationChecks.note: PMID 21632481, PMC4445839. Read the full text. Verified to the decimal: 10 healthy men, mean age 24.3 (4.3) y; 3 nights of 10 h in bed (22:00-08:00) then 8 nights of 5 h in bed (00:30-05:30); daytime (08:00-22:00) testosterone 18.4 (3.8) → 16.5 (2.8) nmol/L, P=.049; afternoon-evening (14:00-22:00) 17.9 (4.0) → 15.5 (3.1) nmol/L, P=.02; the paper's own '10% to 15%' framing; and the ageing comparison at 1-2% per year. The researcher's refusal to convert testosterone to minutes is the correct call.

citationChecks.citation: Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nédélec M, Gupta L, Leeder J, Fullagar HHK, Coutts AJ, Edwards BJ, Pullinger SA. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2021;55(7):356-368. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025
citationChecks.note: PMID 33144349, author list and metadata verified exactly (Europe PMC indexes it under the 2020 online-first date; the 55(7):356-368 print citation is correct). I could NOT verify the extensive verbatim quotations — Box 1 recommendations, Box 2 toolbox including the 150-200 mg coffee nap, Box 3 durations and the 'experts speculate' wording, the one-size-fits-all sentence, the sleep-extension control-group caution, the monitor-overestimation claims, Box 3 tip 5 on athletes becoming preoccupied with sleep data, the 20-90 min education effect decaying at 1 month, the 17-22°C range, and the ceiling-effect unknowns. BMJ returns HTTP 403 to every route available to me (article page, the bronze-OA PDF, repository mirrors) and my web-search budget was exhausted. Since verbatim quotes from a paywalled document are where fabrication would most easily hide, I ran an independent consistency test instead, and it PASSES: the researcher reports Walsh's reference-44 description of Roberts as '~8.4 hours' extension vs '~6.8 hours' habitual. Roberts' three extension nights average (8.6+8.3+8.2)/3 = 8.37 → 8.4, and the normal nights (7.1+6.5+6.9)/3 = 6.83 → 6.8. Those are non-obvious derived means matching to the decimal, and Roberts' own conclusion is 'Endurance athletes should sleep >8 h per night', matching the recommendation attributed to Walsh. Strong circumstantial evidence the full text was genuinely read rather than confabulated. Treat the quotes as probably-sound but formally unverified; a reader with BMJ access should spot-check Box 1 and Box 3.

citationChecks.citation: Watson NF, Badr MS, et al. (Consensus Conference Panel). Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the AASM and Sleep Research Society. Sleep. 2015;38(6):843-844 / J Clin Sleep Med. 2015;11(6):591-592
citationChecks.note: Both dual publications confirmed: Sleep 2015;38:843-844 (doi 10.5665/sleep.4716) and J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11:591-592 (doi 10.5664/jcsm.4758). The researcher's page numbers are exactly right, and their VERIFICATION NOTE ('treat the exact page numbers as approximate', because they had only seen it cited in Walsh's reference list) turns out to be unnecessary caution — the citation is precise. Worth adding: there is a companion methodology paper, 'Joint Consensus Statement ... Methodology and Discussion' (Sleep 2015;38:1161-1183; JCSM 2015;11:931-952), which is where the reasoning behind the ≥7 h recommendation lives.

citationChecks.citation: NCAA Interassociation Task Force. Interassociation recommendations on sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA
citationChecks.note: I could not locate this. The likely real document is Kroshus E, Wagner J, Wyrick D, et al., 'Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness', Br J Sports Med 2019;53(12):731-736 — note it is a BJSM paper, not an ncaa.org page, and the title differs substantially from what is given. The URL supplied (ncaa.org/sports/2016/6/17/mental-health-best-practices.aspx) points to a different NCAA document on mental health best practices, not to a sleep consensus. To the researcher's credit they flagged this themselves in capitals — 'I did NOT retrieve the document itself... Do not attribute any specific prescription to it on my say-so' — so nothing in the report rests on it. Replace with the Kroshus 2019 citation or drop.

populationMismatches: MEASURED IN 19-YEAR-OLD BASKETBALL PLAYERS, APPLIED TO A 27-YEAR-OLD MARATHONER: the chronic sleep-extension case rests on Mah 2011 — 11 male NCAA Division I basketball players, mean age 19.4, sleeping a minimum of 10 h in bed nightly for 5-7 weeks in-season, with a 282-foot sprint and shooting accuracy as endpoints. The researcher flags sport and endpoint honestly, but not two further mismatches: (a) the dose (10 h in bed, every night, for six weeks) is unavailable to a working adult training six evenings a week, so the intervention as tested cannot be administered; (b) 19-year-old male students have both higher physiological sleep need and, critically, larger accumulated sleep debt than a 27-year-old — which is exactly the variable Walsh flags as unresolved. If the effect is debt repayment, a college athlete's headroom is not this man's headroom.

MEASURED IN CYCLISTS OVER ~58 MINUTES, APPLIED TO A ~3:45-3:55 MARATHON: the only endurance sleep-extension result (Roberts 2019) is 9 trained cyclists/triathletes doing a cycling time trial of roughly one hour. This athlete will run for nearly four hours. Marathon performance is limited by glycogen depletion, muscle damage from ~50,000 eccentric footstrikes, thermoregulation and gastrointestinal tolerance — none of which are meaningfully probed by a 58-minute non-weight-bearing effort. A 3.2% gain in a one-hour cycling TT is not evidence of a 3.2% gain over 42.2 km; the crossing is across sport, modality, duration and dominant limiter simultaneously. The researcher discounts for sport and sample size but still carries the raw 3.2% into the arithmetic before discounting.

MEASURED IN 12-18-YEAR-OLDS, APPLIED TO AN ADULT: the entire sleep-injury case (Milewski 1.7x; Gao pooled OR 1.58) comes from adolescents whose recommended sleep is 8-10 h and whose injury profile includes growth-plate and apophyseal pathology that does not exist in a 27-year-old. The researcher identifies this clearly and repeatedly and names it as the central population problem in the domain. That flag is correct and should survive into whatever the athlete is told — it is the most-quoted statistic in athlete sleep advice and it has no adult replication.

MEASURED IN NON-ATHLETES UNDER ARTIFICIAL VIRAL CHALLENGE: Prather 2015 is 164 general-population adults aged 18-55 given rhinovirus nasal drops in quarantine. Not athletes, not training, and the exposure route is not how one catches a cold in London in October. Compounding this, the effect estimate is misreported (see effect-size errors) and the significant bands are <5 h and 5-6 h, not <7 h.

MEASURED IN TEAM-SPORT ATHLETES ON MINUTES-LONG INTERMITTENT TESTS, APPLIED (CORRECTLY REFUSED) TO A MARATHON: Zheng 2026's SMD 0.96 for 'endurance' comes from 179 team ball-sport athletes. The researcher refuses the minutes conversion and routes napping's value through the sleep-duration target instead — the right call, and one of the better judgements in the report.

MEASURED IN RESISTANCE-TRAINED LIFTERS, APPLIED TO AN ENDURANCE ATHLETE: the cold-water-immersion adaptation-interference literature (Piñero 2024 hypertrophy; Malta 2021 strength and power) is resistance training. The researcher correctly concludes the harm does not transfer to a marathoner — and Malta 2021 explicitly found no effect of CWI on endurance-training adaptations, strengthening rather than weakening that conclusion.

MEASURED IN 8-10 MALE NON-ATHLETES IN A METABOLIC LAB: Parr 2014 (n=8) and Leproult 2011 (n=10) are small mechanistic studies with molecular and hormonal endpoints. Leproult's age (mean 24.3) is actually a good match; the mismatches are training status and the severity of the exposure (5 h in bed for 8 nights is not the 6-7 h a busy adult drifts to). Both are correctly presented as mechanism rather than minutes.

MEASURED IN A MIXED TRAINED-AND-UNTRAINED SAMPLE, THEN CONVERTED USING A TRAINED-ATHLETE VARIABILITY ASSUMPTION: Lopes 2023 explicitly pools 'healthy humans including both trained and untrained'. The researcher notes this, and notes that training status was tested as a moderator and found non-significant — a fair defence of the transfer. But the mixed sample matters enormously for the SMD-to-percentage conversion, because it inflates the pooling standard deviation. See effect-size errors.

MEASURED IN NOVICE RUNNERS AT LOW ABSOLUTE VOLUMES: Nielsen 2014 is 874 self-structured novices. The researcher argues the absolute volumes overlap with this athlete's 24.4 km/wk average, which is fair. The better-matched study — 261 runners preparing for a half marathon — was not found, and it reaches the opposite conclusion (see missed evidence).

GENUINELY ON-POPULATION, AND CORRECTLY IDENTIFIED AS SUCH: three findings need no extrapolation for this man. Lau 2022 (1041 working adults aged 21-40 wearing consumer trackers) is a direct match for the measurement recommendation. Ranieri 2025 (28 recreational distance runners, six weeks) is a direct match for the HRV question. Wang 2025 (899 runners, race time as the endpoint) is a direct match for compression. The researcher's ranking of these three as the load-bearing evidence is sound. No sex or age mismatch arises anywhere in the report — the samples are male or mixed throughout.
effectSizeErrors: PRATHER 2015 — WRONG NUMBER, WRONG THRESHOLD, MISSING INTERVALS. Claimed: '<6 h/night were 4.2 times more likely to develop a cold than those sleeping ≥7 h.' Actual, against a >7 h reference: <5 h OR 4.50 (95% CI 1.08-18.69); 5-6 h OR 4.24 (95% CI 1.08-16.71); 6.01-7 h OR 1.66 (95% CI 0.40-6.95), non-significant. The '<6 h' band does not exist in the paper and 4.2 matches neither reported estimate. The consequential error is the threshold: a 27-year-old sleeping 6.5 h sits in the band this study found NO significant elevation for. The omitted confidence intervals reach 18.69 and 16.71 with lower bounds of 1.08 — the estimate is barely distinguishable from no effect, which is incompatible with the 'unusually strong' framing the design is given.

THE SMD-TO-MINUTES CONVERSION IS FAR MORE FRAGILE THAN DISCLOSED, AND IT CARRIES THE WHOLE SLEEP-DEPRIVATION ESTIMATE. The researcher converts Lopes' SMD -0.52 by assuming a 2.5% coefficient of variation: 0.52 × 2.5% = 1.3% → 2.9 min. The arithmetic is right (0.013 × 225 = 2.925). The assumption is not merely 'the weakest link', as stated — it is potentially wrong by a multiple, in an unbounded direction. An SMD is only convertible via a within-subject CV if the meta-analysis standardised by the within-subject SD. Lopes pools randomised and non-randomised trials in a mixed trained-and-untrained sample; if an appreciable share standardised by the BETWEEN-subject SD of the performance measure — which for time-trial performance across trained and untrained people is on the order of 8-15%, not 2.5% — then SMD -0.52 corresponds to 4-8% of finishing time, i.e. 9-18 minutes, not 2.9. The report presents 2.9 min as a working figure with a caveat; it should be presented as an estimate whose true value could plausibly be three to six times larger. Every minutes figure in this domain that passes through a CV assumption inherits this — including the Gong 6.6 min and the compression bound.

GONG 2024 — THE WRONG SUBGROUP IS CONVERTED. The researcher converts the end-of-night partial-deprivation figure of -1.17 into 6.6 min for a marathon, having correctly noted two sentences earlier that Gong's AEROBIC ENDURANCE figure is -0.54. The -1.17 is a task-type-agnostic estimate whose magnitude is driven by high-intensity intermittent exercise (-1.57) and skill control (-1.06); aerobic endurance is the second-weakest category in the paper (-0.54, ahead of only explosive power at -0.39). Applying -1.17 to a marathon double-counts the task-type effect. There is no published end-of-night × aerobic-endurance cell, so the honest answer is that the figure cannot be derived — not 6.6 min. Separately unreported and favourable: Gong found the deficit far smaller in the morning (-0.30) than the afternoon (-1.11), and a marathon starts in the morning.

THE RIEGEL BASELINE IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT AND PROBABLY OPTIMISTIC BY 10-15 MINUTES. The stated working: '106.58 min × 2^1.06 = 222 min', then '~3:45 (225 min)' is used as the divisor throughout. 2^1.06 = 2.0849, so 106.583 × 2.0849 = 222.2 min = 3:42 — the arithmetic is correct, but 222 is then silently replaced by 225 in every conversion, a 1.4% inflation of every minutes figure. The larger problem is the exponent. Riegel's 1.06 is fitted to well-trained runners; for a runner averaging 24.4 km/week the half-to-marathon fade is steeper. The empirical check is in this athlete's own file: his May 2026 marathon was 3:55:54 (235.9 min). Solving 106.583 × 2^k = 235.9 gives k ≈ 1.146, almost exactly the 1.10-1.15 range recommended for low-mileage runners. So the realistic baseline is closer to 3:56 (236 min) than 3:45 (225 min). The direction is conservative — a longer baseline makes every 1% worth MORE minutes, so all estimates slightly understate — but the entire minutes framework rests on a projection his own race history already falsified once.

ODDS RATIO USED AS A RISK RATIO IN THE INJURY EXPECTED-VALUE CALCULATION. The researcher takes Gao's OR of 1.58 and computes '25% moves to ~17%, an 8 percentage-point absolute reduction'. Arithmetically, 25%/1.58 = 15.8%, so the implied reduction is ~9 pp, not 8 — trivial. Substantively, 1.58 is an ODDS ratio, and at a base rate as high as 25% an OR materially overstates the corresponding risk ratio (RR ≈ 1.4 here), so the true absolute reduction is nearer 6-7 pp and the final expected value (0.08 × ~15 min ≈ 1.2 min) is ~25% too high. It is dwarfed by the fact that the 25% base rate and the 15-minute injury cost are both the researcher's own inventions, which they state plainly — and the base rate turns out to be well supported (see Damsted 2019, 21.5% over 14 weeks). The researcher's own conclusion, that this should be weighed as a tail-risk reduction rather than a minute count, is right and makes the arithmetic mostly decorative.

ALCOHOL DOSE CONVERTED IN MIXED UNIT SYSTEMS. '1.5 g/kg ... for this athlete at 85.5 kg that is ~128 g ethanol, roughly 12-16 UK units.' The gram figure is right (1.5 × 85.5 = 128.25 g). The unit conversion is not: a UK unit is 8 g of ethanol, so 128 g = 16.0 UK units, full stop. The '12' at the bottom of the range is the paper's own '12±2 standard drinks', which are Australian 10 g standard drinks — a different unit. The correct statement is ~16 UK units, i.e. the low end understates the dose by a third. This strengthens rather than weakens the researcher's point that the study dose is a heavy night, not a glass of wine.

DUPUY STUDY COUNTS UNDERSTATED. Reported as '1188 subjects across 80 studies for DOMS, 266 across 17 for perceived fatigue'. Table 1 reads 1188 subjects across 106 experimental groups and 266 across 27. Subject counts exact, group counts wrong. Every per-technique effect size and confidence interval quoted from this paper is exact, so nothing turns on it.

EVIDENCE-GRADE INFLATION ON THE TWO CHRONIC SLEEP-EXTENSION STUDIES. Mah 2011 and Schwartz 2015 are both labelled 'evidenceGrade: controlled-trial'. Neither has a control group: Mah is a 2-4 week baseline followed by 5-7 weeks of extension in the same 11 players, Schwartz a one-week within-subject extension in 12 players. They are uncontrolled pre-post studies, and Mah's 4.3% sprint improvement is inseparable from 7-11 weeks of in-season basketball conditioning. This is not a labelling quibble: it is the exact failure the researcher quotes Walsh 2021 warning about ('it is uncommon for sleep studies to include a control group', so extension results 'should be considered with caution') two paragraphs before assigning the grade. The correct grade for the chronic sleep-extension entry is 'observational', not 'controlled-trial'.

MINOR NUMERIC DRIFT, ALL IMMATERIAL: Milewski's mean age given as 15.2 (paper says 15, SD 1.5); Düking's p given as 0.02 (paper says 0.028); Düking's author list missing Trabelsi K and Kunz P. Against this, an unusual number of figures are exact to the decimal — all twelve of Dupuy's per-technique SMDs and their intervals, all eight of Wiewelhove's percentages and Hedges' g values, and every number in Lopes, Wang, Zheng, Lau, Gong, Nielsen, Ranieri, Nuuttila, Parr and Leproult. Transcription fidelity is high; the errors are concentrated in interpretation, conversion and sourcing, not in reading.
missedEvidence: DAMSTED ET AL. 2019, JOSPT 49(4):230-238 — 'The Association Between Changes in Weekly Running Distance and Running-Related Injury: Preparing for a Half Marathon'. THE MOST IMPORTANT OMISSION IN THE REPORT, AND IT CONTRADICTS ONE OF ITS MYTH-BUSTS. 261 healthy runners, GPS/smartphone-verified distance, 14-week prospective cohort, 56 injuries (21.5%). Result: 21 days into the study, significantly MORE runners were injured when they increased weekly distance by 20-60% than when they increased by less than 20% — risk difference 22.6% (95% CI 0.9%, 44.3%; P=.041).
