Level of evidence 1b. The researcher used Nielsen 2014's null to tell this athlete 'the 10% rule does not have the evidential backing it is usually given'. Damsted, from the same Danish research group, in better-matched runners (half-marathon preparation, not novices), found a significant association at a progression band far BELOW what this athlete plans — he is proposing roughly a 300% week-one increase. The report's reassurance on progression rate should not survive this paper. Silver lining: Damsted's 21.5% injury rate over 14 weeks independently corroborates the researcher's self-invented ~25% base rate, which was the weakest assumption in the injury calculation.

COHEN ET AL. 2009, Arch Intern Med 169(1):62-67 — 'Sleep habits and susceptibility to the common cold'. The predecessor to Prather, same lab, same rhinovirus-challenge design, 153 adults aged 21-55, 14 days of sleep reporting before quarantine. Result: less than 7 hours of sleep → 2.94 times more likely to develop a cold (95% CI 1.18-7.30) versus 8 hours or more; sleep efficiency below 92% → 5.50 times (95% CI 2.08-14.48). This is the paper that actually supports a SEVEN-hour threshold — the threshold the researcher wanted and incorrectly extracted from Prather. It gives a smaller multiplier (2.94, not 4.2) with a tighter interval, and it adds sleep efficiency as a stronger predictor than duration, which is directly actionable and appears nowhere in the report. Finding this would have fixed the Prather error and improved the illness entry.

MALTA ES, DUTRA YM, BROATCH JR, BISHOP DJ, ZAGATTO AM 2021, Sports Medicine — 'The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance'. The researcher searched for this by name and then cited its findings under Piñero 2024. It reports: harmful effect of CWI with resistance training on 1RM, maximum isometric strength and strength endurance (overall SMD -0.60, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.33, p<0.0001) and on ballistic efforts (SMD -0.61, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.11, p=0.02), and NO effect of CWI on endurance-training adaptations. This is a dedicated meta-analysis of exactly the question the researcher hedged about ('comes from review-level synthesis rather than a dedicated endurance meta-analysis'). The CWI conclusion for a marathoner is better supported than the report claims.

BONNAR D, BARTEL K, KAKOSCHKE N, LANG C 2018, Sports Medicine 48:683-703 — 'Sleep Interventions Designed to Improve Athletic Performance and Recovery: A Systematic Review of Current Approaches'. Appears verbatim in the researcher's own searchesRun list and is then cited nowhere. 10 studies, 218 participants aged 18-24, across swimming, soccer, basketball and tennis, covering sleep extension, napping, sleep hygiene and post-exercise recovery, with a formal quality assessment of each included study and an outline of what a deliverable athlete sleep intervention should contain. It is one of the canonical reviews in this exact domain, and it is the one paper that would have told the researcher how good the underlying studies actually are — which is what the evidence-grading problem in this report turns on.

ROBERTS SSH ET AL. 2022, J Strength Cond Res — 'Monitoring Effects of Sleep Extension and Restriction on Endurance Performance Using Heart Rate Indices'. The same group's direct follow-up to the 2019 MSSE paper that anchors the report's acute protocol, sitting at the intersection of two of the report's domains (sleep extension AND heart-rate-derived monitoring). Not cited. Given how thin the sleep-extension-plus-endurance literature is — the researcher correctly says there is essentially one cycling study — omitting the direct follow-up to that one study is a real gap.

CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE HIDING INSIDE A CITED PAPER: Roberts 2019's abstract states 'RPE was not different between or within conditions', yet its conclusion asserts that cumulative sleep time works by 'altering the perceived exertion of a given exercise intensity'. The researcher repeated the authors' mechanism claim and then used it as the bridge to carry Mah's basketball sprint finding across to endurance ('the mechanism Roberts 2019 proposes for the endurance effect is the same one'). The paper's own RPE data do not support that mechanism. Nothing needed to be searched for to catch this — it is in the same abstract as the numbers that were transcribed correctly — and it matters more than a missing citation because it is the load-bearing joint between the report's two sleep-extension entries.

AASM/SRS METHODOLOGY COMPANION: 'Joint Consensus Statement of the AASM and Sleep Research Society on the Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: Methodology and Discussion' (Sleep 2015;38:1161-1183; J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11:931-952). The researcher cites the two-page recommendation but not the twenty-page companion containing the evidence grading and the panel voting behind the ≥7 h figure. For an athlete asking specifically 'what official sources is this drawn from and how do we know it is right', the methodology paper is the document that answers the question; the two-page statement is only the verdict.

CORRECTED CITATION FOR THE NCAA DOCUMENT: the source the researcher flagged as unretrieved is almost certainly Kroshus E, Wagner J, Wyrick D, et al., 'Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness', Br J Sports Med 2019;53(12):731-736. It is a BJSM paper, not the ncaa.org mental-health page that was linked. The researcher was right not to attribute anything to it, but the real document exists, is retrievable, and is an official athlete-facing sleep consensus — the second one in this domain after Walsh.
